children.funFact: The word 'aster' comes from the Greek word for 'star,' referring to the star-like shape of their flower heads with petals radiating outward from the center.

children.name: Silybum
children.description: Silybum is a small genus of large, spiny thistles known for their distinctive white-marbled leaves and purple flower heads. These robust plants are members of the sunflower family and are characterized by their deeply lobed, glossy leaves with prominent white veining that creates a marbled appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Silybum thistles are easily recognized by their large, shiny leaves with distinctive white marbling or veining patterns that other thistle genera lack. They also tend to be larger and more robust than most other thistles.
children.funFact: The white marbling on milk thistle leaves was once believed to be drops of the Virgin Mary's milk, giving rise to both its common name and its long history as a medicinal plant for liver ailments.

children.name: Leontodon
children.description: Hawkbits are a small genus of dandelion-like wildflowers in the aster family, characterized by their bright yellow flower heads and deeply lobed leaves. These perennial herbs produce single flower heads on leafless stems that rise from a basal rosette of leaves. Like their dandelion relatives, they produce fluffy seed heads that disperse on the wind.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true dandelions, hawkbits have hairy or rough-textured leaves and stems, and their flower heads are typically smaller with fewer ray petals. The leaves are also more deeply divided and have a different arrangement of lobes.
children.funFact: The name 'hawkbit' comes from an old belief that hawks would eat these plants to sharpen their eyesight, though this is purely folkloric with no scientific basis.

children.name: Arnoglossum
children.description: Indian Plantains are tall wildflowers in the aster family with distinctive large, broad leaves and clusters of small white or cream-colored flowers. These native perennials typically grow in moist woodlands and along stream banks, reaching heights of 3-9 feet. They get their name from their large, plantain-like leaves, though they're not actually related to true plantains.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Indian Plantains can be identified by their tall stems topped with flat-topped clusters of tubular flowers that lack the typical petal-like ray flowers found in most asters. Their large, triangular to kidney-shaped leaves with prominent veins are also distinctive among members of the aster family.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, Indian Plantains are neither plantains nor were they traditionally used by Native Americans as much as the name suggests - the name likely comes from early European settlers who thought the large leaves resembled those of the unrelated plantain herb.

children.name: Boltonia
children.description: Doll's daisies are tall, graceful wildflowers in the aster family that bloom in late summer and fall. They produce masses of small, white daisy-like flowers with yellow centers that create a delicate, cloud-like appearance when in full bloom. These perennial plants typically grow in wet meadows, marshes, and along stream banks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true asters, doll's daisies have very narrow, linear leaves and their flower heads are arranged in loose, open clusters rather than dense groupings. Their petals are also notably narrower and more delicate-looking than most other daisy-family flowers.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'false aster,' doll's daisies were named after James Bolton, an 18th-century English botanist who was known for his beautiful botanical illustrations rather than field work.

children.name: Chrysopsis
children.description: Golden asters are wildflowers in the sunflower family that produce bright yellow, daisy-like blooms in late summer and fall. These hardy perennials typically grow in sandy or rocky soils and open areas like fields, roadsides, and coastal plains. They get their name from their golden-yellow flower heads that resemble small asters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Golden asters can be distinguished from true asters by their bright yellow flowers (rather than purple, white, or blue) and their earlier blooming period in late summer. Their leaves are also typically more narrow and less toothed than most asters.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, golden asters are more closely related to goldenrods than to true asters, and they're sometimes called 'false asters' because of this relationship.

children.name: Picris
children.description: Oxtongues are wildflowers in the aster family with rough, bristly leaves that feel like sandpaper when touched. These hardy plants produce bright yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and are known for their ability to thrive in disturbed soils and roadsides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other yellow asters, oxtongues have distinctively rough, hairy leaves covered in stiff bristles that give them their sandpaper-like texture. Their flower buds are also surrounded by distinctive outer bracts that are much longer than the inner ones.
children.funFact: The name 'oxtongue' comes from the rough, bristly texture of the leaves, which early botanists thought resembled the coarse surface of an ox's tongue.

children.name: Tithonia
children.description: Mexican Sunflowers are vibrant annual plants in the sunflower family, known for their brilliant orange to red daisy-like flowers that bloom from summer through fall. These tall, fast-growing plants are native to Mexico and Central America but have become popular garden ornamentals worldwide. They produce large, showy flower heads on sturdy stems that can reach 4-6 feet in height.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true sunflowers, Mexican Sunflowers have consistently orange to red petals rather than yellow, and their flower heads are smaller but more numerous. Their leaves are distinctively heart-shaped to rounded with velvety texture, contrasting with the narrower, rougher leaves of most sunflowers.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Mexican Sunflowers,' they're not closely related to common sunflowers and are actually more closely related to Jerusalem artichokes and other dahlia family plants.

children.name: Zinnia
children.description: Zinnias are colorful flowering plants in the daisy family that produce vibrant, multi-layered blooms in shades of red, pink, orange, yellow, and white. These annual flowers are native to Mexico and Central America but have become popular garden plants worldwide. They grow as upright stems with opposite leaves and distinctive flower heads made up of many small flowers packed together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Zinnias can be distinguished from other daisy-family flowers by their thick, sturdy stems, opposite leaves (rather than alternate), and their particularly full, dense flower heads with broad, overlapping petals. Their flowers also tend to have a more geometric, layered appearance compared to the simpler daisy-like blooms of many relatives.
children.funFact: Zinnias were among the first flowers grown in space - NASA astronauts successfully grew them aboard the International Space Station in 2016, making them important pioneers in space agriculture research!

children.name: Polymnia
children.description: Polymnia is a small genus of tall, leafy wildflowers in the sunflower family. These plants are characterized by their large, broad leaves and yellow composite flowers that bloom in late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other members of the sunflower family, Polymnia flowers lack the showy petal-like ray flowers around the edges, having only small disc flowers in the center.
children.funFact: The genus Polymnia is named after the Greek muse of sacred poetry and hymns, perhaps reflecting the plant's stately and dignified appearance in woodland settings.

children.name: Ageratum
children.description: Ageratums are small flowering plants in the aster family known for their clusters of tiny, fluffy flowers that bloom from summer through fall. These compact plants produce dense heads of small tubular flowers that lack the typical petal-like rays found on many of their daisy relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most members of the aster family, ageratum flowers are composed entirely of disc florets with no showy outer petals, giving them their distinctive fuzzy, powder-puff appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'ageratum' comes from Greek words meaning 'does not age,' referring to how the flowers retain their color and form for an unusually long time both on the plant and when cut.

children.name: Chromolaena
children.description: Chromolaena is a genus of flowering plants in the sunflower family that includes shrubs and herbaceous perennials native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. These plants typically produce clusters of small, fluffy white or pale purple flowers that bloom in dense, flat-topped arrangements. Most species in this genus are fast-growing and can spread rapidly in suitable climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chromolaena species are distinguished from other sunflower family members by their distinctive three-veined leaves and their fluffy, thistle-like flower heads that contain only disc flowers (no petal-like ray flowers). The flowers have a characteristic sweet, vanilla-like fragrance that attracts butterflies and other pollinators.
children.funFact: Siam weed (Chromolaena odorata) is considered one of the world's most invasive plants and can grow up to 10 feet tall, earning it the nickname 'jack-in-the-bush' in some regions.

children.name: Euphrosyne
children.description: Marshelders are tall annual plants in the sunflower family that produce small, inconspicuous greenish flowers arranged in clusters. They are wind-pollinated rather than relying on insects, which is unusual for members of the sunflower family. These robust plants can grow quite large and are often found in disturbed soils and agricultural areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most plants in the sunflower family, marshelders have separate male and female flowers on the same plant and rely on wind rather than insects for pollination. Their leaves are broad and often deeply lobed, resembling those of ragweed but much larger.
children.funFact: Despite being in the sunflower family, marshelders were traditionally cultivated by Native Americans as a food crop for their nutritious seeds, long before sunflowers became popular.

children.name: Layia
children.description: Tidytips are annual wildflowers in the sunflower family that produce cheerful daisy-like blooms with distinctive white-tipped yellow petals. These small, delicate flowers typically grow 1-2 feet tall and bloom from spring through early summer in open, sunny areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The white tips on the bright yellow petals create a neat, orderly appearance that gives tidytips their common name. Unlike many other sunflower family members, the white petal tips are consistently present and create a distinctive two-toned effect.
children.funFact: Tidytips got their charming name because their petals look like they were carefully dipped in white paint, as if nature was being extra tidy when coloring these flowers.

children.name: Delairea
children.description: Delairea is a small genus of climbing or trailing plants in the sunflower family that are native to South Africa. These fast-growing vines produce clusters of small, yellow daisy-like flowers and have distinctive heart-shaped or ivy-like leaves. In New England, you'll find Cape-ivy, which has become established in some coastal areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true ivies, Delairea species are actually members of the sunflower family and produce bright yellow composite flowers. Their soft, fleshy stems and aromatic leaves when crushed also help distinguish them from other climbing vines.
children.funFact: Despite being called Cape-ivy, this plant is more closely related to daisies and sunflowers than to true ivy, and its flowers smell like honey when in bloom.

children.name: Heterotheca
children.description: False Goldenasters are a genus of flowering plants in the aster family that produce bright yellow, daisy-like flowers. These hardy plants are typically found in open, disturbed areas like roadsides, fields, and sandy soils. They get their name from their resemblance to true goldenasters, though they belong to a different genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true goldenasters, False Goldenasters have distinctively hairy or fuzzy stems and leaves, giving them a somewhat grayish appearance. Their flower heads also tend to be smaller and more numerous than those of related aster species.
children.funFact: The single New England species, Camphorweed, gets its common name from the strong camphor-like smell it releases when its leaves are crushed or bruised.

children.name: Madia
children.description: Tarweeds are a genus of annual wildflowers in the sunflower family known for their sticky, resinous stems and leaves that can make them feel tacky to the touch. These plants typically have small, yellow daisy-like flowers and are adapted to dry, sunny conditions. Most tarweed species are native to western North America, making their presence in New England quite unusual.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tarweeds are easily recognized by their distinctively sticky, glandular hairs that cover the stems and leaves, giving them their common name. Unlike many other members of the sunflower family, their flower heads are often clustered in tight, compact groups.
children.funFact: The sticky resin produced by tarweeds was traditionally used by Native American tribes as a waterproofing agent for baskets and as an adhesive.

children.name: Melampodium
children.description: Melampodium is a genus of small flowering plants in the sunflower family, known for their cheerful daisy-like blooms with white petals and yellow centers. These hardy plants are typically low-growing and compact, forming neat mounds or mats of flowers and foliage. They're native to the Americas and are valued for their ability to bloom continuously in sunny, dry conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Melampodium flowers have distinctively small, simple daisy heads with relatively few white ray petals (usually 8-13) surrounding bright yellow centers. The leaves are small, opposite, and often have a somewhat fuzzy texture, helping distinguish them from other small daisies.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'blackfoot daisy,' Melampodium leucanthum gets its common name not from having black roots, but from the dark-colored dried flower heads that remain after the white petals fall off.

children.name: Stokesia
children.description: Stokesia is a small genus containing just one species, Stokes' aster, a beautiful wildflower native to the southeastern United States. These plants are members of the aster family and produce large, showy blue or purple flower heads that bloom in late summer and fall. They are low-growing perennial herbs with distinctive spiny-edged leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stokes' aster stands out from other asters with its uniquely large flower heads that can reach 3-4 inches across and its characteristic deeply divided, fringed petals that give the blooms a almost cornflower-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being native to the Southeast, Stokes' aster is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant throughout New England because of its stunning late-season blooms and ability to attract butterflies.

children.name: Centratherum
children.description: Centratherum is a small genus of flowering plants in the aster family that are native to tropical regions of the Americas. These plants are characterized by their small, button-like flower heads that are typically purple or pink in color. They are herbaceous plants that can grow as annuals or short-lived perennials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Centratherum species have distinctive small, compact flower heads with tubular disc flowers but no ray petals, giving them their characteristic 'button' appearance. The flowers are arranged in dense, rounded clusters that distinguish them from many other aster family members.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Brazilian bachelor's button,' Centratherum punctatum has become naturalized in many warm regions around the world and is sometimes considered a weedy species that can quickly colonize disturbed areas.

children.name: Dahlia
children.description: Dahlias are vibrant flowering plants originally from Mexico that belong to the sunflower family. They produce large, showy blooms with multiple layers of colorful petals arranged in complex patterns. These plants grow from underground tubers and are popular in gardens for their spectacular late-summer displays.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dahlias are distinguished from other flowers in their family by their elaborate, multi-layered flower heads with densely packed petals that can form pompom, cactus, or dinner-plate shapes. Unlike many relatives, they grow from thick, fleshy tubers rather than simple roots.
children.funFact: Dahlia tubers were originally cultivated by the Aztecs as a food source, and the flowers weren't bred for ornamental purposes until they reached Europe in the 1700s.

children.name: Sinacalia
children.description: Sinacalia is a small genus of perennial wildflowers in the aster family that are native to Asia. These plants produce clusters of bright yellow, daisy-like flowers and have distinctive heart-shaped or triangular leaves. They typically grow in mountainous regions and prefer cool, moist conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sinacalia species are distinguished from other ragworts by their unique leaf shapes and their specific Asian origin. Their flowers lack the ray petals that many related asters have, appearing as dense clusters of small yellow disc flowers.
children.funFact: Despite being native to the mountains of China and Tibet, Chinese Ragwort has successfully established itself in New England's cooler climates, making it one of the few Asian ragworts to naturalize in North America.

children.name: Telekia
children.description: Telekia is a small genus of tall, robust perennial wildflowers in the sunflower family. These impressive plants are known for their large, heart-shaped leaves and bright yellow daisy-like flowers that bloom in summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Telekia can be distinguished from other sunflower family members by their unusually large, deeply heart-shaped basal leaves and their tall stature, often reaching 4-6 feet in height.
children.funFact: Despite being native to southeastern Europe and western Asia, Yellow Oxeye has naturalized in some parts of New England where it was originally planted in gardens for its striking appearance.

children.name: Syneilesis
children.description: Syneilesis is a small genus of perennial wildflowers in the aster family, known for their distinctive umbrella-like leaves that unfurl in spring. These woodland plants produce clusters of small white or pinkish flowers and are native to eastern Asia, with one species naturalized in parts of North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature is their large, deeply divided leaves that emerge folded like an umbrella and gradually open flat, creating a unique parasol appearance in the forest understory.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Syneilesis' comes from Greek words meaning 'rolled together,' referring to how the young leaves are tightly furled when they first emerge from the ground each spring.

children.description: The Asteraceae family, commonly known as the sunflower or daisy family, is one of the largest plant families in the world. What looks like a single flower is actually a collection of many tiny flowers packed together into a flower head, surrounded by petal-like rays. This diverse family includes everything from towering sunflowers and cheerful daisies to dandelions in your lawn and goldenrod in autumn fields.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have their flowers arranged in dense heads called capitula, which are surrounded by green bracts (modified leaves) that form what looks like a single flower. Many species also produce seeds with fluffy white attachments (like dandelion seeds) that help them spread on the wind.
children.funFact: With over 331 species in New England alone, Asteraceae is so successful that it makes up about 10% of all flowering plant species on Earth - you've probably seen dozens of different family members just on a single nature walk!

children.name: Campanulaceae
Campanula
children.description: Bellflowers are a charming group of flowering plants known for their distinctive bell-shaped or tubular flowers that come in shades of blue, purple, pink, or white. These plants range from low-growing creepers to tall upright perennials, and they're popular in both wild landscapes and cultivated gardens. Most bellflowers bloom during summer months and are excellent for attracting bees and other pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bellflowers are easily recognized by their characteristic bell-shaped flowers with five pointed petals that often curve backward. Unlike many similar flowers, bellflower buds typically hang downward before opening, and the flowers have a distinctive milky sap when stems are broken.
children.funFact: The Common Harebell is so hardy it can grow in rocky crevices and has earned the nickname 'bluebell of Scotland,' where it's considered the national flower and appears in folklore as a fairy's thimble.

children.name: Lobelia
children.description: Lobelias are a diverse group of flowering plants known for their distinctive tubular flowers that split open on one side, creating an irregular, two-lipped appearance. These plants range from tiny aquatic species to tall garden favorites, but all share this unique flower structure that makes them easily recognizable once you know what to look for.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The split, tubular flowers with their characteristic two-lipped shape set lobelias apart from other flowering plants, along with their milky sap that appears when stems or leaves are broken.
children.funFact: The brilliant red cardinal flower was so prized by European collectors that it became one of the first North American wildflowers to be cultivated in European gardens in the 1600s.

children.name: Triodanis
children.description: Venus' Looking-Glasses are delicate annual wildflowers in the bellflower family with small, violet-blue flowers that bloom along their stems. These plants get their charming name from their round, flat seed pods that were thought to resemble hand mirrors or looking glasses used by the Roman goddess Venus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bellflowers, Venus' Looking-Glasses have flowers that grow directly from the leaf joints along the stem rather than in clusters, and their distinctive round, flat seed capsules set them apart from their relatives.
children.funFact: The flowers of Venus' Looking-Glass are unusual because the lower flowers on the stem often never open at all - they self-pollinate while still in bud form, ensuring the plant can reproduce even without insect visitors.

children.name: Jasione
children.description: Sheep's Bits (Jasione) is a small genus of flowering plants in the bellflower family that produces distinctive globe-shaped clusters of tiny blue flowers. These plants are annual or perennial herbs with narrow leaves and flower heads that look somewhat like scabious or small thistles, despite being unrelated to either.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bellflower family members with typical bell-shaped flowers, Jasione species have their small flowers densely packed into rounded, pincushion-like heads surrounded by leafy bracts.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'Sheep's-bit,' this plant is not actually related to scabious (which also goes by that name) - it's a case of convergent evolution where unrelated plants developed similar-looking flower heads.

children.name: Platycodon
children.description: Platycodon is a small genus containing just one species - the balloon flower. These perennial plants are native to East Asia and are popular in gardens for their distinctive inflated flower buds that pop open into star-shaped blue, purple, pink, or white flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature is the balloon-like flower buds that inflate before opening, giving the plant its common name. The flowers have five pointed petals that open into a bell or star shape, and the leaves are typically oval with serrated edges.
children.funFact: The flower buds can be gently squeezed to make them 'pop' open with a small sound, which makes them especially popular with children in gardens.

children.name: Palustricodon
children.description: Palustricodon is a small genus of delicate wildflowers that thrive in wetland environments. These plants are characterized by their tiny, bell-shaped flowers and preference for marshy, boggy areas where few other flowering plants can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bellflowers, Palustricodon species have extremely small, inconspicuous flowers and grow in wet, marshy habitats rather than typical garden or woodland settings.
children.funFact: The genus name Palustricodon literally means 'marsh bell,' perfectly describing both the plant's wetland habitat and its tiny bell-shaped flowers that are often smaller than a pinky nail.

children.name: Campanulastrum
children.description: Tall bellflowers are a small genus of wildflowers known for their distinctive bell-shaped blue flowers that bloom in summer. These native North American plants are closely related to other bellflowers but form their own unique group. They typically grow quite tall, often reaching 3-6 feet in height, and prefer rich, moist woodland soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other bellflowers, tall bellflowers have flowers that are more tubular and less flared at the opening, and they produce distinctive flat, round seed pods. Their flowers also tend to be a deeper blue color and are arranged more loosely along the stem compared to their relatives.
children.funFact: The tall bellflower was once considered part of the larger Campanula genus but was reclassified into its own genus because of its unique flower structure and the way its seeds are dispersed through pores in the side of the seed capsule rather than at the top.

children.name: Hippobroma
children.description: Hippobroma is a small genus of flowering plants in the bellflower family known for their distinctive star-shaped white flowers and toxic properties. These plants are characterized by their long, tubular flowers that bloom at night and emit a sweet fragrance to attract nocturnal pollinators like moths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bellflowers, Hippobroma species have extremely long, narrow flower tubes that can extend several inches, and all parts of the plant contain highly toxic alkaloids that make them poisonous to humans and animals.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'Star of Bethlehem,' Hippobroma longiflora is actually native to the West Indies and is so toxic that it was historically used as a fish poison by indigenous peoples.

children.description: The bellflower family includes plants known for their distinctive bell-shaped or tubular flowers that come in shades of blue, purple, pink, or white. These flowering plants typically have simple leaves and produce flowers with five petals that are often fused together into a tube or bell shape. Many species in this family are popular garden plants and wildflowers found throughout New England's fields, woodlands, and wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be identified by their characteristic bell-shaped or tubular flowers with five fused petals and five stamens. The flowers often have a milky sap, and the ovary is positioned below the petals (inferior ovary).
children.funFact: Cardinal flower (Lobelia cardinalis), with its brilliant red blooms, is specifically adapted to attract hummingbirds and is one of the few native New England flowers that relies primarily on hummingbird pollination.

children.name: Menyanthaceae
Nymphoides
children.description: Nymphoides are small aquatic plants commonly known as floatinghearts that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These delicate water plants have heart-shaped or round floating leaves and produce small, bright yellow flowers that bloom at the water's surface. They are members of the gentian family and create beautiful displays across New England's quiet waterways.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true water lilies, floatinghearts have much smaller flowers (usually under an inch across) with fringed or toothed petals that give them a delicate, lacy appearance. Their leaves are also typically smaller and more heart-shaped than the large, round pads of water lilies.
children.funFact: The flowers of floatinghearts often have beautifully fringed petals that look like they've been cut with decorative scissors, earning water fringe its common name and making these tiny blooms surprisingly intricate when viewed up close.

children.name: Menyanthes
children.description: Menyanthes is a genus containing only one species - the bogbean, a unique aquatic plant that grows in wetlands and shallow water. Despite its name, bogbean is not actually a bean but gets its name from its three-leaflet leaves that resemble those of bean plants. This hardy perennial produces beautiful white or pinkish flowers with fringed petals that emerge above the water surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Menyanthes stands out from other wetland plants with its distinctive three-part compound leaves and star-shaped flowers with deeply fringed, feathery petals. Unlike true beans, it's actually related to gentians and grows as a creeping aquatic plant.
children.funFact: The bogbean's flowers have intricate fringed petals that look almost crystalline or frost-covered, earning it folk names like 'water shamrock' and 'marsh trefoil' in different regions.

children.description: The bogbean family is a small group of aquatic and wetland plants that thrive in shallow water, bogs, and marshy areas. These plants are known for their distinctive flowers that often have fringed or feathery petals, and their ability to grow both floating on water surfaces and rooted in wet soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plant families, bogbean family members have flowers with deeply fringed or bearded petals that give them a unique, almost fuzzy appearance. Their leaves can be either heart-shaped and floating (like water lilies) or three-parted and emerging above water.
children.funFact: The bogbean (Menyanthes trifoliata) gets its name from its three-leaflet leaves that somewhat resemble bean plants, and it was historically used as a bitter flavoring agent in beer before hops became popular.

children.description: This diverse order includes some of New England's most recognizable flowers, from the cheerful sunflowers and daisies we see in fields to the delicate bellflowers that grace our gardens. Most members of this group are herbaceous plants that produce their flowers in specialized arrangements, with many species being excellent sources of nectar for pollinators like bees and butterflies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What unites these seemingly different plants is their flower structure and the way they develop from the flower bud. Many have flowers arranged in dense clusters that appear as single blooms, like in daisies where tiny individual flowers are packed together in a composite head.
children.funFact: The sunflower family alone contains over 250 species in New England, making it one of the largest plant families in our region and including everything from towering sunflowers to tiny roadside weeds!

children.name: Lamiales
Lamiaceae
Lamium
children.description: Deadnettles and archangels are a group of square-stemmed plants in the mint family that produce distinctive hooded flowers arranged in whorls around the stem. Despite their common name, they're not actually nettles and don't sting - they just have similar-looking leaves. These hardy plants often bloom early in spring and can be found in gardens, waste areas, and woodland edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true nettles, deadnettles have square stems, hooded two-lipped flowers, and leaves that don't sting when touched. Their flowers are typically arranged in dense clusters at leaf joints, creating a layered appearance up the stem.
children.funFact: Red deadnettle and henbit are among the first wildflowers to bloom in spring, often pushing through snow to provide crucial early nectar for bees and other pollinators when few other food sources are available.

children.name: Scutellaria
children.description: Skullcaps are small flowering plants in the mint family known for their distinctive helmet-shaped flowers that bloom along upright stems. These perennial herbs typically grow in moist areas like wetlands, stream banks, and shaded woodlands throughout New England. All skullcap species share the characteristic two-lipped flowers that look like tiny caps or helmets, giving the group its common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Skullcaps are easily recognized by their unique flowers which have a prominent ridge or 'crest' on the upper lip that resembles a Roman soldier's helmet. Unlike other mint family members, their flowers are typically arranged in one-sided clusters or pairs along the stem rather than in dense whorls.
children.funFact: Many skullcap species have been used in traditional herbal medicine for centuries, with some Native American tribes using them as natural remedies for anxiety and nervous tension.

children.name: Mentha
children.description: Mints are aromatic herbs in the genus Mentha, famous for their refreshing scent and cooling sensation when touched or tasted. These perennial plants typically have square stems, opposite leaves with serrated edges, and small flowers arranged in dense clusters or spikes. All mint species contain menthol and other essential oils that give them their characteristic fragrance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mints can be distinguished from other members of the mint family by their intense, cooling aroma and the tingling sensation they produce on the tongue. Their leaves are typically more strongly scented than related plants, and they often grow in moist habitats near water sources.
children.funFact: Mint plants are notorious for hybridizing with each other in the wild, making species identification challenging even for botanists - many of our common mints like spearmint and peppermint are actually natural hybrids!

children.name: Pycnanthemum
children.description: Mountain mints are aromatic native wildflowers in the mint family that produce clusters of small white or pale purple flowers from summer into fall. Despite their name, they're found in various habitats from meadows to woodland edges, not just mountains. All species have strongly scented foliage that releases a fresh, minty fragrance when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mountain mints are distinguished from other mints by their dense, rounded flower clusters and their preference for drier, sunnier habitats rather than the moist conditions most mints favor.
children.funFact: Mountain mints are pollinator magnets that can attract over 40 different species of bees, wasps, and butterflies to a single plant, making them some of the most valuable native plants for supporting local insect communities.

children.name: Lycopus
children.description: Water horehounds are a group of mint family plants that love wet places like stream banks, pond edges, and marshy areas. These perennial herbs have square stems (typical of mints) and small white or pale flowers arranged in dense clusters around the stem at leaf joints.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mints, water horehounds have very small, inconspicuous flowers and lack the strong minty fragrance. Their leaves are typically narrow and toothed, and they spread by underground runners to form colonies.
children.funFact: Despite being in the mint family, water horehounds were traditionally used as a substitute for hops in brewing beer, giving them the nickname 'water hops' in some regions.

children.name: Salvia
children.description: Sages are aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their distinctive square stems and fragrant leaves. These plants produce tubular flowers arranged in spikes or clusters, and many species have been valued for centuries for culinary, medicinal, and ornamental purposes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sages can be identified by their two-lipped flowers with a unique lever mechanism where the upper stamens bend down to dust pollen on visiting bees. Their leaves are often textured or fuzzy and release strong scents when crushed.
children.funFact: The seeds of some sage species, like chia, can absorb up to 12 times their weight in water, creating a gel-like coating that was prized by ancient civilizations as a portable energy source.

children.name: Monarda
children.description: Beebalms and bergamots are aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their distinctive tubular flowers arranged in dense, showy clusters. These native North American plants have square stems and opposite leaves that release a pleasant, minty fragrance when crushed. They're beloved by pollinators, especially bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the mint family, Monarda species have their flowers arranged in distinctive dense, rounded or tiered heads at the top of stems. Their flowers have a unique two-lipped shape with prominent stamens that extend beyond the petals.
children.funFact: Scarlet beebalm was used by Native Americans to make a tea called 'Oswego tea' after the Boston Tea Party, when colonists boycotted traditional tea imports from Britain.

children.name: Stachys
children.description: Hedgenettles are square-stemmed plants in the mint family that produce spikes of small, tubular flowers arranged in whorls around the stem. These hardy perennials are found in a variety of habitats from wetlands to prairies, and despite their name, they're not related to true nettles and don't sting. Most species have toothed leaves and can spread by underground runners to form colonies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mint family members, hedgenettles have flowers arranged in dense, interrupted spikes rather than in continuous clusters. Their flowers typically have a distinctive hooded upper lip and their leaves are often more coarsely toothed than related plants.
children.funFact: The name 'woundwort' comes from the traditional use of some Stachys species to treat cuts and wounds - the leaves were crushed and applied as a natural bandage due to their supposed healing properties.

children.name: Clinopodium
children.description: Calamints are aromatic herbs in the mint family that produce small, tubular flowers arranged in clusters along square stems. These plants are known for their pleasant, minty fragrance when crushed and their ability to attract bees and butterflies. All three New England species are perennial herbs that typically grow in dry, sunny locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calamints can be distinguished from other mints by their small, white to pale purple flowers that are arranged in loose, branching clusters rather than dense whorls around the stem. Their leaves are typically smaller and more oval-shaped than many other mint family members.
children.funFact: The name 'calamint' comes from the Greek words 'kalos' meaning beautiful and 'minthe' meaning mint, reflecting both their attractive appearance and their membership in the mint family.

children.name: Agastache
children.description: Hyssops are aromatic perennial herbs in the mint family that produce tall spikes of small, tubular flowers. These plants are known for their strong, pleasant fragrance and their ability to attract bees, butterflies, and other pollinators. They typically grow 2-4 feet tall with opposite leaves and dense flower clusters at the tops of their stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mints, hyssops have a distinctly upright growth habit with prominent terminal flower spikes rather than flowers scattered along the stems. Their leaves are also typically longer and more lance-shaped than the rounded leaves of most mint relatives.
children.funFact: Anise hyssop flowers and leaves have a delicious licorice-like flavor and are often used to make herbal tea or as a seasoning in cooking.

children.name: Ajuga
children.description: Bugles are low-growing perennial plants in the mint family that are easily recognized by their distinctive flower spikes and creeping growth habit. These hardy wildflowers produce dense clusters of small, tubular flowers that rise above rosettes of oval leaves, often forming colorful carpets in woodlands and gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mint family members, bugles have strongly one-sided flower spikes where all the blooms face the same direction, and their leaves lack the strong aromatic scent typical of most mints.
children.funFact: Carpet bugle spreads so effectively through underground runners that it can quickly form dense mats, earning it the nickname 'living carpet' and making it a popular groundcover plant.

children.name: Leonurus
children.description: Motherworts are hardy perennial herbs in the mint family that are easily recognized by their deeply lobed, palm-shaped leaves and clusters of small pink or white flowers arranged in whorls around square stems. These plants typically grow 2-4 feet tall and have a somewhat weedy appearance, often found in disturbed soils, gardens, and along roadsides. Like other mints, motherworts have the characteristic square stems and opposite leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Motherworts can be distinguished from other mints by their distinctively cut, palmate leaves that look almost hand-like, and their dense clusters of small tubular flowers that form tight rings around the stem at each leaf node.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting maternal care, motherworts got their name from their traditional use as a medicinal herb for "nervous conditions of mothers," and the species name "cardiaca" refers to historical beliefs about their heart-strengthening properties.

children.name: Trichostema
children.description: Bluecurls are small annual wildflowers in the mint family that bloom in late summer and fall. These delicate plants produce tiny blue or purple flowers with distinctively long, curved stamens that stick out prominently from each bloom. They typically grow in sandy or disturbed soils and dry, open areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The extremely long, arching stamens that curl outward from the flowers make bluecurls instantly recognizable among mint family plants. Unlike most mints, they are annual plants rather than perennials and lack the strong aromatic scent typical of the family.
children.funFact: The genus name Trichostema literally means 'hair stamens' in Greek, referring to the thread-like stamens that can be twice as long as the flower itself.

children.name: Thymus
children.description: Thymes are small, aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their tiny, fragrant leaves and dense clusters of small flowers. These low-growing perennial plants form mat-like carpets and release a distinctive, pleasant scent when their leaves are crushed. They thrive in sunny, well-drained locations and are beloved by both gardeners and pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thymes can be distinguished from other mint family members by their extremely small, narrow leaves (usually less than half an inch long) and their creeping, ground-hugging growth habit. Their flowers are arranged in dense, rounded clusters rather than the spike-like arrangements seen in many other mints.
children.funFact: Thyme has been used for over 4,000 years - ancient Egyptians used it in mummification, while medieval knights carried thyme sprigs as symbols of courage and bravery.

children.name: Galeopsis
children.description: Hempnettles are annual herbs in the mint family that produce small, two-lipped flowers arranged in dense clusters around their square stems. Despite their common name, they're not related to true nettles or hemp, but get their name from their somewhat nettle-like appearance and tough, fibrous stems. These European natives have become established in disturbed soils throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hempnettles can be identified by their swollen nodes (joints) on square stems and their distinctive two-lipped flowers with a prominent lower lip that serves as a landing platform for pollinators. The upper lip forms a hood over the reproductive parts, creating a tunnel-like entrance.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Galeopsis' comes from Greek words meaning 'weasel-like,' referring to the shape of the flower that resembles a weasel's face with its pointed snout and beady eyes.

children.name: Hedeoma
children.description: Hedeoma is a genus of small, aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their strong, minty fragrance. These low-growing plants produce tiny flowers and have been traditionally used for their essential oils and medicinal properties.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hedeoma species are distinguished from other mints by their very small size, typically growing only a few inches tall, and their particularly potent, camphor-like scent that's much stronger than most other mint relatives.
children.funFact: American pennyroyal was once so commonly used as a natural insect repellent that colonial settlers would scatter it on floors and stuff it in mattresses to keep fleas and other pests away.

children.name: Clerodendrum
children.description: Glorybowers are flowering shrubs and small trees known for their showy, fragrant blooms and colorful berries. These plants typically produce clusters of tubular flowers with long, protruding stamens, followed by bright blue or purple berries that are often surrounded by colorful, star-shaped calyxes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Glorybowers are distinguished from other flowering shrubs by their distinctive berry presentation, where the fruit sits within persistent, often brightly colored sepals that remain after flowering. Their flowers also have characteristically long, protruding stamens that extend well beyond the petals.
children.funFact: Many glorybower species are known for their strong, sometimes unpleasant smell when the leaves are crushed, earning some species the nickname 'stinkweed,' despite their beautiful flowers.

children.name: Vitex
children.description: Chastetrees are aromatic shrubs or small trees in the mint family, known for their distinctive palm-shaped leaves with multiple leaflets radiating from a central point. They produce clusters of small, tubular flowers that are typically blue, purple, or white, followed by small berry-like fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chastetrees are easily recognized by their palmately compound leaves (like fingers on a hand) and their spicy, pepper-like fragrance when crushed. Unlike most other members of the mint family, they grow as woody shrubs or trees rather than herbaceous plants.
children.funFact: The Lilac chaste tree gets its name from ancient Greek traditions where monks used its seeds as a spice substitute for pepper, believing it would help suppress romantic desires and maintain their vows of chastity.

children.name: Blephilia
children.description: Wood mints are aromatic wildflowers in the mint family that grow in woodlands and forest edges. These perennial herbs have square stems typical of mints and produce clusters of small, tubular flowers that bloom in summer. They get their name from their minty fragrance and preference for partially shaded woodland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wood mints can be distinguished from other mints by their distinctive flowers that have long, protruding stamens and are arranged in dense, rounded clusters. Unlike many other mints, they prefer woodland settings rather than wet meadows or stream banks.
children.funFact: The genus name Blephilia comes from the Greek word for 'eyelash,' referring to the fringed or hairy appearance of the flower bracts that surround each bloom cluster.

children.name: Glechoma
children.description: Ground-ivies are low-growing, creeping plants in the mint family that spread along the ground by runners. They have small, rounded leaves with scalloped edges and produce tiny purple or blue flowers in spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true ivies, ground-ivies are actually mints with square stems and opposite leaves that give off a strong minty aroma when crushed.
children.funFact: Ground-ivy was historically called "gill-over-the-ground" and was used by early settlers to brew beer before hops became widely available.

children.name: Prunella
children.description: Selfheals are low-growing perennial herbs in the mint family known for their distinctive purple flower spikes and square stems. These hardy plants spread by underground runners and are commonly found in lawns, fields, and disturbed areas throughout New England. They bloom from late spring through fall, producing dense clusters of small purple flowers arranged in compact, cylindrical heads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Selfheals can be identified by their unique flower arrangement - purple blooms packed tightly into dense, oval-shaped spikes at the top of square stems. Unlike many other mints, their flowers are distinctly hooded and the flower heads have a characteristic blunt, club-like appearance.
children.funFact: Common selfheal gets its name from its long history as a medicinal plant - it was traditionally used to treat wounds and was considered so valuable that an old saying claimed 'no one wants a surgeon who keeps Prunella in his garden.'

children.name: Teucrium
children.description: Woodsages are a genus of mint family plants known for their distinctive square stems and aromatic leaves. These perennial herbs typically produce small, tubular flowers arranged in spikes or clusters, and they're found in various habitats from woodlands to wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many mint family members, woodsages have flowers with a very reduced or absent upper lip, giving them an unusual one-lipped appearance. Their flowers are typically white, pink, or purple and have prominent stamens that extend well beyond the petals.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'woodsages,' these plants aren't true sages at all - they got their common name because their leaves were historically used as a sage substitute for flavoring and folk medicine.

children.name: Physostegia
children.description: Physostegia, commonly known as dragonheads or obedient plants, is a small genus of perennial wildflowers in the mint family. These plants are characterized by their square stems, opposite leaves, and distinctive tubular flowers that bloom in dense, four-sided spikes. They get their 'obedient' nickname because individual flowers can be bent to a new position and will stay there temporarily.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mint family members, Physostegia flowers are arranged in neat, four-ranked spikes rather than whorls around the stem. The flowers are also notably larger and more tubular than typical mint flowers, with a distinctive hooded upper lip.
children.funFact: The obedient plant earned its charming common name because when you gently push a flower to one side of the spike, it will actually stay in that new position for several minutes before slowly returning to its original spot.

children.name: Collinsonia
children.description: Horsebalms are aromatic perennial herbs in the mint family known for their distinctive lemon-citrus scent when crushed. These woodland plants produce tall spikes of small, irregular flowers and have opposite, toothed leaves that grow quite large.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mint family members, horsebalms have strongly asymmetrical flowers with only two functional stamens, and their flowers are arranged in loose, branching clusters rather than dense whorls.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'horse balm,' this plant was traditionally used by people as a folk remedy for cuts, bruises, and sore muscles, earning it the nickname 'heal-all' or 'stone root.'

children.name: Nepeta
children.description: Catmints are aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their square stems and opposite leaves that release a distinctive fragrance when crushed. These perennial plants produce small, tubular flowers arranged in spikes or clusters, typically in shades of white, blue, or purple. Most species are beloved by cats due to chemical compounds in their leaves that trigger euphoric responses in felines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Catmints can be distinguished from other mints by their specific scent profile and the unique reaction they cause in cats. Unlike many other mint family members, Nepeta species contain nepetalactone, the compound responsible for cats' famous attraction to these plants.
children.funFact: The active compound in catnip, nepetalactone, not only drives cats wild but also serves as an effective natural mosquito repellent - in fact, it's about 10 times more effective than DEET at repelling mosquitoes!

children.name: Origanum
children.description: Marjorams are a genus of aromatic herbs in the mint family, known for their small, fragrant leaves and clusters of tiny flowers. These perennial plants are prized for their essential oils, which give them their distinctive scent and flavor. Most species are native to the Mediterranean region and have been cultivated for thousands of years as culinary and medicinal herbs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Marjorams can be distinguished from other mint family members by their small, oval leaves that are often grayish-green and covered in tiny hairs, plus their characteristic spicy-sweet fragrance. Their flowers are typically arranged in dense, rounded clusters at the tips of branches.
children.funFact: The word 'oregano' comes from the Greek words 'oros' (mountain) and 'ganos' (joy), literally meaning 'joy of the mountain' - ancient Greeks believed the herb growing on hillsides was a sign of happiness bestowed by the goddess Aphrodite.

children.name: Melissa
children.description: Melissa is a small genus of aromatic herbs in the mint family, known for their lemony-scented leaves and clusters of small white or pale flowers. These perennial plants are beloved by bees and other pollinators, which is reflected in their name - 'Melissa' comes from the Greek word for honeybee. They spread by underground runners and can form dense patches in gardens and naturalized areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Melissa plants are distinguished from other mints by their strong lemon scent when the leaves are crushed, and their typically white or very pale yellow flowers arranged in loose clusters along the stems.
children.funFact: Lemon balm has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and was once believed to promote longevity - some medieval herbalists claimed it could help people live to be 100 years old!

children.name: Perilla
children.description: Perilla is a small genus of aromatic annual herbs in the mint family, known for their strongly scented, serrated leaves and spikes of small white or purple flowers. These plants are native to Asia and are characterized by their square stems and opposite leaves, which release a distinctive fragrance when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Perilla can be distinguished from other mint family members by its large, deeply serrated leaves with a unique spicy-minty aroma and its tendency to self-seed readily in disturbed soils.
children.funFact: The beefsteak plant gets its common name from its reddish-purple leaf varieties that were thought to resemble raw beef, and it's widely used in Asian cuisine as both a culinary herb and natural food coloring.

children.name: Elsholtzia
children.description: Elsholtzia is a genus of aromatic annual herbs in the mint family that are native to Asia. These plants produce small, densely packed flowers arranged in distinctive spike-like clusters and have toothed leaves that release a strong, spicy fragrance when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mints, Elsholtzia species have flowers arranged in dense, cylindrical spikes rather than whorled clusters, and their stamens extend well beyond the flower petals.
children.funFact: The genus is named after Johann Sigismund Elsholtz, a 17th-century German botanist and physician who served as court doctor to the Elector of Brandenburg.

children.name: Callicarpa
children.description: Beautyberries are shrubs in the mint family known for their spectacular clusters of small, brightly colored berries that appear in late summer and fall. These deciduous plants have simple leaves arranged opposite each other on the stem and produce tiny flowers in dense clusters where the leaves meet the stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature is their vibrant purple, magenta, or white berries that form in tight clusters around the stem, creating an almost jewel-like appearance that's unlike most other native shrubs.
children.funFact: The berries are so perfectly round and brilliantly colored that they almost look artificial, which is why they're prized by gardeners and florists for fall decorations.

children.name: Tripora
children.description: Tripora is a genus of small, colonial marine animals called bryozoans that build intricate, lace-like structures on the seafloor. These tiny filter-feeders live in interconnected chambers within their calcium carbonate skeletons, working together as a colony to capture plankton and organic particles from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tripora colonies are distinguished by their delicate, branching growth pattern that creates openwork structures resembling fine lacework or coral. Their distinctive three-dimensional branching sets them apart from the flat, encrusting growth forms of many other bryozoan genera.
children.funFact: Despite being made up of hundreds of tiny individual animals, a Tripora colony functions as a single coordinated organism, with specialized individuals performing different roles like feeding, reproduction, and defense.

children.name: Lavandula
children.description: Lavenders are aromatic flowering plants in the mint family, known for their distinctive fragrant purple flower spikes and narrow, silvery-green leaves. These Mediterranean herbs have been prized for centuries for their essential oils and are commonly grown in gardens worldwide. Most lavender species prefer sunny, well-drained locations and are drought-tolerant once established.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lavenders can be distinguished from other mint family plants by their characteristic dense spikes of small tubular flowers, typically in shades of purple or blue, and their highly aromatic, needle-like leaves that are often covered in fine hairs giving them a silvery appearance.
children.funFact: Lavender's name comes from the Latin word 'lavare,' meaning 'to wash,' because the Romans used it to scent their bathwater and laundry.

children.name: Satureja
children.description: Savories are aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their small, narrow leaves and tiny white or pale purple flowers. These plants are highly valued for their strong, peppery fragrance and have been used for centuries as culinary herbs and natural remedies. They typically grow as low, bushy annual or perennial plants in sunny, well-drained locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Savories can be distinguished from other mint family members by their distinctive sharp, spicy scent that's more peppery than minty, and their very small, linear leaves that are much narrower than typical mint leaves.
children.funFact: Summer Savory was so prized by ancient Romans that they dedicated it to the satyrs and considered it an aphrodisiac, which is how the genus got its name 'Satureja.'

children.name: Ballota
children.description: Ballota is a genus of aromatic perennial herbs in the mint family, known for their square stems and opposite leaves typical of mints. These plants produce small, tubular flowers arranged in dense clusters around the stem at leaf joints, and they often have a strong, somewhat unpleasant odor when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mints, Ballota species have a distinctly fetid smell rather than a pleasant minty fragrance, and their flowers are typically arranged in tight, rounded clusters that encircle the stem.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'black horehound,' Ballota nigra is not closely related to true horehound and gets its name from its similarly bitter taste and historical use in folk medicine.

children.name: Ocimum
children.description: Basils are aromatic herbs in the mint family known for their fragrant, often spicy-scented leaves. These plants produce small white or purple flowers arranged in spikes and are characterized by their distinctive essential oils that give them their powerful aroma.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Basils can be distinguished from other mint family plants by their particularly strong, clove-like or spicy fragrance and their smooth-edged leaves that are often glossy and tender.
children.funFact: Sweet basil contains over 60 different aromatic compounds, which is why different varieties can smell like cinnamon, lemon, or even licorice!

children.name: Moluccella
children.description: Moluccella is a small genus of annual herbs in the mint family, best known for the popular garden plant Bells-of-Ireland. These plants are characterized by their distinctive inflated, bell-shaped green calyces (the outer part of the flower) that surround small white flowers. Despite their common name, they are actually native to the Mediterranean region and western Asia, not Ireland.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Moluccella is their large, papery, bell-shaped green calyces that are much more prominent and showy than the actual small white flowers inside them. This gives the flowering spikes their characteristic appearance that looks like strings of green bells.
children.funFact: The green 'bells' that make Bells-of-Ireland so popular in flower arrangements are not actually the flowers themselves, but rather enlarged sepals that protect the tiny white flowers hidden inside.

children.name: Leonotis
children.description: Lion's ears (Leonotis) is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family known for their distinctive tubular flowers that are arranged in dense, spherical clusters around the stem. These plants are characterized by their square stems, opposite leaves, and vibrant orange or reddish flowers that bloom in whorls, creating a striking architectural appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mint family members, lion's ears have uniquely long, curved tubular flowers that cluster in dense balls around the stem, and their flowers are typically bright orange rather than the purple, white, or pink colors common in related genera.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Leonotis' literally means 'lion's ear' in Greek, referring to the fuzzy, ear-shaped appearance of the flower buds before they open.

children.name: Dracocephalum
children.description: Dragonheads are a small genus of mint family plants known for their distinctive flowers that resemble the open mouth of a dragon. These annual or perennial herbs produce tubular, two-lipped flowers arranged in dense clusters along square stems, typical of the mint family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mint family members, dragonhead flowers have a particularly prominent upper lip that arches over the lower lip like a hood, creating their characteristic dragon-mouth appearance. The flowers are also notably large compared to most other mints.
children.funFact: Despite their fierce-sounding name, dragonheads are actually gentle plants that are often used in traditional medicine and are beloved by bees and other pollinators.

children.name: Betonica
children.description: Betonies are perennial herbs in the mint family known for their distinctive flower spikes and traditional medicinal uses. These plants typically grow in meadows, grasslands, and woodland edges, producing dense clusters of tubular flowers arranged in whorls around a central stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Betonies can be identified by their characteristic dense, cylindrical flower spikes that sit atop square stems, along with their wrinkled, oval leaves that have prominent veining and toothed edges.
children.funFact: The common hedge-nettle was once considered so medicinally valuable that there was an old Italian saying 'Sell your coat and buy betony,' reflecting its reputation as a cure-all herb in medieval times.

children.description: The Mint Family is a large and aromatic group of plants that includes many familiar herbs and wildflowers. Most members of this family have square stems, opposite leaves, and distinctive two-lipped flowers that are often arranged in whorls or spikes. These plants are known for their strong scents and oils, which range from refreshing mint to pungent sage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The combination of square stems, opposite leaves, and two-lipped flowers makes mint family plants easy to identify. Many also have a distinctive aromatic quality when their leaves are crushed.
children.funFact: Many mint family plants contain natural compounds that repel insects while attracting beneficial pollinators like bees and butterflies, making them excellent choices for both herb gardens and pollinator habitats.

children.name: Plantaginaceae
Veronica
children.description: Speedwells are a diverse group of small flowering plants in the snapdragon family, found in habitats ranging from dry fields to wetlands throughout New England. These hardy plants are easily recognized by their distinctive four-petaled flowers, typically blue, white, or pink, which bloom from spring through fall. Most speedwells are low-growing herbs that form mats or creeping patches, though some species grow more upright.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Speedwells have characteristic flowers with four unequal petals (the bottom petal is smallest) and only two stamens, unlike most flowers which have more. Their seed capsules are distinctively heart-shaped or notched at the top, helping to distinguish them from other small wildflowers.
children.funFact: The name 'speedwell' comes from the old belief that these plants would bring good fortune and speed travelers safely on their journeys, leading to them being tucked into clothing or bags before departing on trips.

children.name: Plantago
children.description: Plantains are small herbaceous plants with distinctive ribbed leaves arranged in a basal rosette close to the ground. They produce tiny flowers on tall, slender spikes that rise above the foliage, and are found in a wide variety of habitats from lawns and roadsides to coastal areas and prairies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plantains are easily recognized by their parallel-veined leaves with prominent ribs running from base to tip, and their characteristic flower spikes that look like tiny bottlebrushes. Unlike most flowering plants, their leaves have parallel veins similar to grasses, but they're not related to grasses at all.
children.funFact: Greater plantain was called 'white man's footprint' by Native Americans because it seemed to appear wherever European colonists had walked, as the seeds were often carried on shoes and wagon wheels.

children.name: Linaria
children.description: Toadflaxes are delicate wildflowers known for their distinctive snapdragon-like blooms that feature a prominent spur extending backward from the flower. These hardy plants typically have narrow, linear leaves and produce clusters of small, colorful flowers that can be yellow, purple, pink, or white. Most species are quite adaptable and can thrive in poor soils and disturbed areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Toadflaxes are easily recognized by their spurred flowers that resemble tiny snapdragons, along with their characteristically narrow, grass-like leaves. The flowers have a distinctive two-lipped shape with a closed mouth that opens when squeezed, just like their larger snapdragon relatives.
children.funFact: Common toadflax is sometimes called 'butter-and-eggs' because its bright yellow flowers with orange centers resemble the colors of those breakfast foods, and the flowers were once used as a yellow dye for cloth.

children.name: Digitalis
children.description: Foxgloves are tall, elegant flowering plants known for their distinctive tubular flowers that hang like bells from towering spikes. These beautiful perennials and biennials produce colorful blooms in shades of purple, yellow, white, and rusty orange that attract bees, hummingbirds, and other pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Foxgloves are easily recognized by their characteristic bell-shaped or thimble-like flowers that grow in dense, one-sided clusters along tall stems, often reaching 3-6 feet in height. The flowers have a distinctive spotted or speckled interior that serves as a landing pad and nectar guide for visiting insects.
children.funFact: Despite their beauty, all foxglove species contain powerful cardiac compounds called digitalis glycosides, which have been used in heart medicine for centuries but make the entire plant highly toxic to humans and animals if ingested.

children.name: Penstemon
children.description: Beardtongues are a genus of wildflowers known for their distinctive tubular flowers that are perfectly shaped for attracting bees and other pollinators. These perennial plants produce tall spikes of colorful blooms, typically in shades of white, pink, purple, or blue, and are beloved by both gardeners and wildlife enthusiasts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets beardtongues apart is the unique sterile stamen (called a staminode) that extends from the flower's throat like a fuzzy tongue or beard, giving the genus its common name. Their tubular flowers are typically two-lipped and arranged in terminal clusters.
children.funFact: The 'beard' in beardtongue refers to the hairy, sterile stamen that acts like a landing platform for bees, helping guide them to the flower's nectar while ensuring they pick up pollen along the way.

children.name: Callitriche
children.description: Water Starworts are small aquatic plants that form distinctive star-shaped rosettes of leaves floating on the water's surface or growing submerged. These delicate plants are commonly found in ponds, streams, and wetlands throughout New England, where they play an important role in aquatic ecosystems by providing oxygen and habitat for small creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, Water Starworts have opposite leaves that form characteristic star patterns when viewed from above, and their tiny flowers lack petals entirely. Their leaves can look quite different depending on whether they're growing underwater (often narrow and ribbon-like) or floating on the surface (broader and more oval).
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they're related to starfish, Water Starworts are actually flowering plants in the plantain family, and one species can even grow on dry land when water levels drop!

children.name: Chelone
children.description: Turtleheads are native wildflowers that get their name from their distinctive snapdragon-like flowers that resemble a turtle's head with its mouth slightly open. These perennial herbs typically grow 2-4 feet tall in wet areas like stream banks, swamps, and moist meadows. All three New England species bloom in late summer to early fall with tubular flowers arranged in dense clusters at the top of their stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other snapdragon-family plants, turtlehead flowers have a very inflated, rounded upper lip that creates the characteristic turtle-head shape. Their flowers are also notably large and chunky compared to most other members of the plantain family.
children.funFact: Turtlehead flowers are specially adapted to be pollinated by bumblebees, which are strong enough to force open the tightly closed flower lips - smaller bees simply can't get inside to reach the nectar!

children.name: Gratiola
children.description: Hedge-hyssops are small, delicate flowering plants that grow in wet areas like pond edges, marshes, and muddy shores. These low-growing herbs produce tiny white or yellow tubular flowers and have opposite leaves arranged in pairs along their stems. They're members of the plantain family and thrive in the moist, sandy or muddy soils of wetland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hedge-hyssops can be identified by their distinctive four-petaled flowers that are deeply notched, giving them a fringed appearance, and their preference for growing directly in wet soil or shallow water. Unlike many wetland plants, they have very small, inconspicuous flowers that are easy to overlook.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, hedge-hyssops are considered toxic plants that were historically used in folk medicine, earning them the nickname 'herb of grace' in some regions.

children.name: Cymbalaria
children.description: Cancerworts are small, creeping plants with distinctive ivy-shaped leaves and tiny snapdragon-like flowers. These hardy perennials are masters of finding footholds in the tiniest cracks and crevices of walls, rocks, and pavement. They spread by trailing stems that root at the nodes, forming delicate carpets in urban and wild rocky places.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the plantain family, cancerworts have distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves and long trailing stems. Their small purple or white flowers have a distinctive spur and lower lip, giving them a miniature snapdragon appearance.
children.funFact: Ivy-leaved toadflax has a fascinating behavior called negative phototropism - after flowering, the stems actually grow away from light to push seeds deep into dark wall crevices where they're more likely to germinate successfully.

children.name: Collinsia
children.description: Blue-eyed Marys are small annual wildflowers in the snapdragon family known for their distinctive two-lipped flowers that often display beautiful blue and white color combinations. These delicate plants typically bloom in spring and early summer, producing clusters of small, tubular flowers along their stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other snapdragon family members, Blue-eyed Marys have flowers with a very distinctive two-toned appearance, typically with blue upper petals and white lower petals that create their characteristic 'blue-eyed' look.
children.funFact: The genus Collinsia is named after Philadelphia botanist Zaccheus Collins, and these flowers are sometimes called 'innocence' due to their pure, delicate appearance.

children.name: Veronicastrum
children.description: Culver's roots are tall perennial wildflowers in the plantain family known for their distinctive spikes of small white or pale blue flowers. These plants typically grow in moist meadows and prairies, producing whorled leaves arranged in circles around their sturdy stems. They bloom in mid to late summer, creating impressive vertical displays that can reach 3-7 feet tall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most members of the plantain family, Culver's roots have their small flowers densely packed into tall, narrow spikes rather than spread out in clusters. Their leaves are arranged in distinctive whorls of 3-7 leaves per circle around the stem.
children.funFact: The genus was named after Dr. Culver, an 18th-century physician who used the plant's roots as medicine, but it was later discovered to belong to the same group as speedwells (Veronica) and was renamed Veronicastrum, meaning 'false Veronica.'

children.name: Chaenorhinum
children.description: Dwarf snapdragons are a small genus of delicate annual plants in the snapdragon family. These tiny wildflowers produce small, two-lipped flowers that resemble miniature versions of garden snapdragons. They typically grow in disturbed soils and rocky areas where other plants struggle to establish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger snapdragon relatives, dwarf snapdragons have much smaller flowers (usually less than half an inch long) and a more sprawling, low-growing habit. Their flowers also tend to be more open and less tubular than true snapdragons.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, dwarf snapdragons are surprisingly tough colonizers that often appear on railroad tracks, gravel paths, and even in sidewalk cracks where few other flowering plants can survive.

children.name: Antirrhinum
children.description: Snapdragons are flowering plants known for their distinctive tubular flowers that can be squeezed at the sides to make them 'snap' open and closed like a dragon's mouth. These popular garden plants produce colorful spikes of flowers that bloom from bottom to top throughout the growing season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flowers in the figwort family, snapdragons have a unique hinged flower structure that requires strong pollinators like bumblebees to push inside and access the nectar.
children.funFact: The snapdragon's flower mechanism acts as a natural 'quality control' system - only large, strong bees can force the flower open, ensuring effective pollination while keeping out smaller, less efficient pollinators.

children.name: Hippuris
children.description: Mare's-tails are aquatic plants that live partially or completely submerged in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They have distinctive whorls of narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles around their stems, creating a bottle-brush appearance. These perennial plants can grow both underwater and emerge above the water's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mare's-tails are easily recognized by their unique leaf arrangement - multiple narrow leaves radiating out from each joint on the stem like spokes on a wheel. Unlike many aquatic plants, their leaves are always simple and never divided or feathery.
children.funFact: Mare's-tail is one of the most widely distributed flowering plants in the world, found on every continent except Antarctica and Australia.

children.name: Kickxia
children.description: Cancerworts are a small genus of low-growing annual plants in the snapdragon family. These delicate wildflowers produce tiny, spurred flowers that resemble miniature snapdragons and typically grow as trailing or prostrate plants along the ground.
