children.funFact: The segmented seed pods of sweetvetches inspired their scientific name Hedysarum, which comes from the Greek words meaning 'sweet broom,' and the pods were historically used as a survival food by indigenous peoples and early explorers.

children.name: Styphnolobium
children.description: Styphnolobium is a small genus of deciduous trees in the legume family, commonly known as pagoda trees or scholar trees. These elegant trees are prized for their graceful branching pattern, compound leaves with small oval leaflets, and clusters of creamy white flowers that bloom in late summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other legumes, Styphnolobium trees don't form root nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Their flowers also bloom much later in the season compared to most other members of the legume family.
children.funFact: The Japanese pagoda tree was considered sacred in ancient China and was traditionally planted near temples and scholars' homes, earning it the nickname 'scholar tree' because it was believed to bring wisdom and good fortune to students.

children.name: Laburnum
children.description: Laburnums are small deciduous trees in the pea family known for their spectacular drooping clusters of bright yellow flowers that bloom in late spring. These ornamental trees have compound leaves with three leaflets and produce seed pods similar to other legumes. They are popular landscape trees originally from Europe that have been widely planted in gardens and parks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Laburnums are easily recognized by their long, pendulous chains of golden-yellow pea-like flowers that hang gracefully from the branches, earning them the common name 'golden chain tree.' Their three-part leaves and dangling flower clusters make them unmistakable when in bloom.
children.funFact: Despite their beautiful appearance, all parts of laburnum trees are highly poisonous, containing toxic alkaloids that can be dangerous to humans and animals if ingested.

children.name: Pueraria
children.description: Kudzus are fast-growing climbing vines in the legume family known for their vigorous growth and ability to quickly cover large areas. These perennial plants produce distinctive three-leaflet compound leaves and can climb trees, buildings, and other structures using twining stems that can reach impressive lengths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kudzus are distinguished from other climbing legumes by their extremely rapid growth rate, large heart-shaped leaflets arranged in groups of three, and their ability to form dense, smothering mats over vegetation and structures.
children.funFact: Kudzu can grow up to a foot per day during peak growing season, earning it the nickname 'the vine that ate the South' for its ability to completely engulf trees, buildings, and entire landscapes.

children.name: Lablab
children.description: Lablab is a small genus of climbing legume plants in the bean family, with only one widely recognized species. These vigorous vines produce distinctive flat, purple-tinged pods and showy purple or white flowers that attract pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lablab is distinguished from other bean genera by its broad, heart-shaped leaflets and distinctive flat, curved seed pods that are often purple or reddish in color.
children.funFact: Despite being called hyacinth bean, Lablab purpureus is actually more closely related to black-eyed peas than to true beans, and has been cultivated for over 4,000 years as both food and ornamental plant.

children.name: Maackia
children.description: Maackias are small to medium-sized deciduous trees in the pea family, known for their attractive compound leaves and fragrant white flower clusters. These Asian natives are popular ornamental trees that bloom in mid to late summer, producing upright spikes of small, densely packed flowers. They're hardy trees that can tolerate various soil conditions and are valued for their late-season blooms when few other trees are flowering.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other members of the pea family, Maackias produce their flowers in dense, upright racemes rather than hanging clusters, and they bloom much later in the summer than most flowering trees. Their bark is also distinctive, often peeling in thin strips to reveal a shiny bronze or copper-colored underlayer.
children.funFact: Maackia trees are named after Richard Maack, a 19th-century Russian naturalist who explored Siberia and collected the first specimens of these trees along the Amur River.

children.name: Caragana
children.description: Peashrubs are hardy, nitrogen-fixing shrubs in the legume family that produce small yellow flowers and distinctive seed pods. These tough plants are well-adapted to cold climates and poor soils, making them popular for windbreaks and erosion control in harsh environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peashrubs can be identified by their compound leaves with small oval leaflets, bright yellow pea-like flowers, and inflated seed pods that split open when ripe. Unlike many other legumes, they typically grow as multi-stemmed shrubs rather than vines or herbaceous plants.
children.funFact: The Siberian peashrub is so cold-hardy it can survive temperatures down to -40°F and was widely planted across the northern United States and Canada as 'living fences' during the Great Depression.

children.name: Entada
children.description: Callingcard vines are tropical and subtropical climbing plants in the legume family, known for producing some of the world's largest seed pods. These woody vines use their strong stems to climb high into forest canopies, where they produce distinctive flat, segmented pods that can grow several feet long.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They are distinguished from other legumes by their massive, flat seed pods that break apart into individual segments, each containing a single large, hard seed that can float across oceans.
children.funFact: The seeds of sea heart vines can drift across entire oceans and still germinate after washing up on distant shores, earning them the nickname 'sea beans' among beachcombers.

children.name: Oxytropis
children.description: Locoweed (Oxytropis) is a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, known for their distinctive pea-like flowers and compound leaves. These hardy perennial herbs are adapted to harsh environments and can be found in arctic, alpine, and prairie regions across the Northern Hemisphere. Many species in this genus contain toxic compounds that can be harmful to livestock, which is how they earned their common name 'locoweed.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Locoweed can be distinguished from related legumes by their keel-shaped flower petals that come to a sharp, pointed tip or beak. Unlike many other legumes, most Oxytropis species are stemless or nearly stemless, with leaves and flower stalks arising directly from the ground.
children.funFact: The name 'locoweed' comes from the Spanish word 'loco' meaning crazy, because livestock that eat these plants can develop neurological symptoms and erratic behavior due to the toxic alkaloids they contain.

children.name: Arachis
children.description: Arachis is a genus of legumes that includes the familiar peanut, despite its name being quite misleading since peanuts aren't actually nuts at all. These plants are members of the bean and pea family, producing their seeds underground in a fascinating process where the flowers push their developing pods into the soil. Only one species from this tropical South American genus is commonly found in New England as a cultivated crop.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other legumes, Arachis species develop their pods underground through a unique process called geocarpy, where fertilized flowers elongate and push the developing seeds into the soil to mature. The plants also have distinctive compound leaves with four leaflets arranged in pairs.
children.funFact: Peanut flowers are self-pollinating and after fertilization, they grow a special structure called a 'peg' that literally drills the developing pod several inches underground where it matures in complete darkness.

children.name: Dalea
children.description: Prairie clovers are a genus of wildflowers in the legume family that are specially adapted to dry, open grasslands and prairies. These plants produce distinctive dense, cylindrical flower clusters that bloom from the bottom up, creating a unique flowering pattern. Despite their common name, they're not true clovers but are closely related to them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Prairie clovers can be identified by their compact, cone-shaped flower spikes and their small compound leaves with narrow leaflets. Unlike true clovers which have rounded flower heads, prairie clover flowers are arranged in tight cylindrical spikes that gradually bloom upward.
children.funFact: Prairie clovers have deep taproots that can extend 15 feet underground, helping them survive droughts and making them excellent plants for preventing soil erosion on the Great Plains.

children.name: Anthyllis
children.description: Kidney-vetches are small perennial plants in the legume family that produce distinctive clusters of yellow, orange, or red flowers. These hardy plants are adapted to poor soils and coastal conditions, making them excellent for stabilizing sandy or rocky ground. Like other legumes, they form partnerships with soil bacteria to fix nitrogen from the air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kidney-vetches can be identified by their dense, rounded flower heads and their silky-hairy leaves that are often divided into leaflets. The inflated, papery seed pods that develop after flowering are also characteristic of this genus.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, kidney-vetches are incredibly tough plants that can thrive in salt spray and poor soils where most other flowers would struggle to survive.

children.name: Indigofera
children.description: Indigos are a genus of flowering plants in the legume family, known for their compound leaves and small, pea-like flowers that typically bloom in pink, purple, or white clusters. These plants are nitrogen-fixing legumes, meaning they have a beneficial relationship with soil bacteria that helps enrich the soil. Most species are found in tropical and subtropical regions, with only one species naturally occurring in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Indigos can be identified by their pinnately compound leaves (with multiple small leaflets arranged along a central stem) and their distinctive spike-like clusters of small flowers. Unlike many other legumes, indigo plants often have a more delicate, fine-textured appearance with smaller leaflets.
children.funFact: True Indigo was historically one of the world's most valuable crops, as it was the primary source of blue dye for textiles before synthetic indigo was invented in the late 1800s.

children.name: Mimosa
children.description: Sensitive Plants are a genus of flowering plants known for their remarkable ability to respond to touch and other stimuli. These plants have compound leaves that fold up quickly when disturbed, and their flowers are typically small, fluffy, and ball-shaped. Most species in this genus are native to tropical and subtropical regions around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Mimosa apart from other plants is their rapid leaf movement in response to physical contact, vibration, or changes in light. This dramatic folding behavior, called thigmonasty, happens within seconds of being touched.
children.funFact: The Sensitive Plant can close its leaves in less than a second when touched, earning it the nickname 'shy plant' - this defense mechanism may help protect it from herbivores and reduce water loss during harsh conditions.

children.name: Ornithopus
children.description: Bird's-foots and Serradellas are a small genus of delicate annual plants in the legume family. These low-growing herbs produce tiny yellow or white pea-like flowers and distinctive segmented seed pods that resemble a bird's foot, which gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic bird's foot-shaped seed pods with their curved, claw-like segments make this genus easily recognizable among other small legumes. Unlike many of their pea family relatives, these plants remain quite small and prostrate rather than climbing or growing upright.
children.funFact: The scientific name Ornithopus literally means 'bird's foot' in Greek, directly referencing the resemblance of their curved seed pods to the toes and claws of a small bird.

children.description: Legumes are a diverse family of flowering plants that includes everything from tiny clovers to towering locust trees. What unites this group is their distinctive seed pods that split open along two seams, and their remarkable ability to partner with soil bacteria to convert nitrogen from the air into nutrients plants can use.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most legumes produce characteristic pea-like flowers with five petals arranged in a distinctive pattern, and their fruits are typically dry pods that split open when ripe. Many also have compound leaves divided into multiple leaflets.
children.funFact: Legumes are nature's fertilizer factories - the root nodules of most species house bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen into plant food, which is why farmers often rotate crops with legumes to naturally enrich their soil.

children.name: Polygalaceae
Senega
children.description: American Milkworts are small wildflowers in the genus Senega that produce distinctive irregular flowers with a unique structure. These native plants typically have simple leaves and create small, often colorful blooms that can be white, pink, purple, or yellow. They're found in various habitats from fields and meadows to woodlands throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets American Milkworts apart is their characteristic flower shape - each bloom has two petal-like sepals called 'wings' and a fringed lower petal that forms a distinctive tube or keel. Unlike many other small wildflowers, their flowers are arranged in dense clusters or spikes at the tips of stems.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'milkwort,' these plants don't actually produce milky sap - they got this name from an old folk belief that they could increase milk production in nursing mothers and livestock.

children.name: Polygaloides
children.description: False milkworts are small, delicate wildflowers that belong to the milkwort family but were recently separated into their own genus. These low-growing plants produce distinctive flowers with fringed petals and prefer shady woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true milkworts, false milkworts have prominently fringed flower petals and typically grow much closer to the ground in a more prostrate manner.
children.funFact: The fringed polygala is sometimes called 'flowering wintergreen' because its evergreen leaves remain visible under the snow all winter long, even though it's not related to true wintergreens.

children.description: Milkworts are a family of small flowering plants that get their name from the old belief that they could increase milk production in nursing mothers and livestock. These plants typically have small, irregular flowers that often appear in dense clusters or spikes, and they can be found in various habitats from woodlands to meadows throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Milkworts have uniquely shaped flowers with two large, petal-like sepals called 'wings' that give the flowers their distinctive appearance. Unlike true peas and beans which they sometimes resemble, milkworts have flowers with a different internal structure and are not legumes.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, milkworts don't actually increase milk production - this was just an old folk belief based on the 'doctrine of signatures,' where people thought plants that looked milky or had white sap could help with milk production.

children.description: The Fabales order brings together two main plant families that might seem different at first glance but share important evolutionary traits. This group includes the familiar legume family with beans, peas, and clovers, as well as the smaller milkwort family with their distinctive asymmetrical flowers. Despite their differences in appearance, these plants share similar root chemistry and often form partnerships with soil bacteria.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have compound leaves and specialized root nodules that house nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Many also produce similar types of chemical compounds in their tissues that help defend against insects and diseases.
children.funFact: Legumes in this order are nature's fertilizer factories - the bacteria in their root nodules can convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms that plants can use, actually enriching the soil around them!

children.name: Ericales
Ericaceae
Rhododendron
children.description: Rhododendrons and azaleas are a diverse group of woody shrubs known for their spectacular spring flower displays. These plants produce clusters of showy, funnel-shaped or bell-shaped flowers that come in vibrant colors ranging from white and pink to deep red, purple, and yellow. They typically have leathery, evergreen or deciduous leaves and prefer acidic soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their distinctive flower structure with 5-10 stamens that extend beyond the petals, and their fruit which is a dry capsule that splits open to release numerous small seeds. Unlike many other flowering shrubs, their leaves often have a waxy coating and may have fuzzy undersides.
children.funFact: Many rhododendrons and azaleas contain toxic compounds called grayanotoxins in their leaves and flowers - ancient Greek soldiers were reportedly poisoned by honey made from rhododendron nectar, leading to the term 'mad honey'!

children.name: Vaccinium
children.description: The genus Vaccinium includes some of New England's most beloved wild berries, from the blueberries and cranberries you might find in your local grocery store to their wild cousins growing in bogs, forests, and mountainsides. These shrubs are members of the heath family and typically produce small, bell-shaped flowers that develop into distinctive berries with a crown-like indentation at the bottom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Vaccinium species are distinguished by their berries having a distinctive crown or calyx at the bottom (opposite the stem end) and their preference for acidic soils. Unlike many other berry-producing plants, most Vaccinium species are low-growing shrubs adapted to nutrient-poor environments.
children.funFact: Many Vaccinium species require mycorrhizal fungi partnerships with their roots to thrive, which is why wild blueberries and cranberries are often found in specific soil conditions that support these beneficial fungal relationships.

children.name: Pyrola
children.description: Wintergreens are small, woodland wildflowers that stay green year-round with their distinctive rosettes of basal leaves. These delicate plants produce nodding, waxy flowers that hang like little lanterns from slender stalks, typically blooming in summer in the deep shade of coniferous and mixed forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other evergreen forest plants, wintergreens have their flowers arranged along a single central stem (raceme) with each flower hanging downward on its own little stalk. Their thick, often glossy leaves remain green through winter and grow directly from the base of the plant rather than along stems.
children.funFact: Despite their name, true wintergreens (Pyrola) don't actually smell like wintergreen - that distinctive minty scent comes from a completely different plant family!

children.name: Kalmia
children.description: Mountain-laurels are beautiful evergreen shrubs known for their distinctive cup-shaped flowers and leathery leaves. These hardy plants are well-adapted to acidic soils and can thrive in various habitats from wetlands to rocky mountain slopes. All members of this genus produce clusters of pink or white flowers with a unique spring-loaded mechanism that helps with pollination.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mountain-laurels can be identified by their thick, oval-shaped evergreen leaves and their characteristic flowers with ten stamens that bend backward, creating a distinctive bowl or cup shape. Unlike other members of the heath family, their flower buds are held in terminal clusters and have a waxy, almost plastic-like appearance.
children.funFact: Mountain-laurel flowers have a clever catapult mechanism - when a bee lands on the flower, it triggers the stamens to spring forward and dust the insect with pollen, ensuring efficient pollination.

children.name: Gaylussacia
children.description: Huckleberries are small shrubs in the heath family that produce edible berries beloved by both wildlife and people. These native plants typically grow in acidic soils and can be found in various habitats from sandy coastal areas to mountain slopes. All huckleberries have simple, alternate leaves and small bell-shaped flowers that develop into dark berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the blueberries, true huckleberries have exactly 10 large, hard seeds inside each berry rather than many tiny soft seeds. The berries also tend to be darker and have a slightly different flavor profile.
children.funFact: The seeds of huckleberries are so hard that they can crack your teeth if you bite down on them, which is why many people prefer to swallow the berries whole or strain out the seeds when cooking with them.

children.name: Monotropa
children.description: Indian pipes are unusual flowering plants that have completely given up photosynthesis and instead get their nutrients by tapping into underground fungal networks. These ghostly white or pale plants emerge from the forest floor looking more like fungi than typical flowers, with waxy, translucent stems and scale-like leaves. They're parasitic on mycorrhizal fungi that connect to tree roots, making them indirect parasites of forest trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other flowering plants, Indian pipes contain no chlorophyll and appear completely white, pale yellow, or pinkish rather than green. They have a distinctive waxy, translucent appearance and their flower heads nod downward before turning upright as seeds develop.
children.funFact: Indian pipes turn completely black when touched or picked, earning them folk names like 'corpse plant' - this blackening happens because they contain no protective pigments like chlorophyll.

children.name: Chimaphila
children.description: Wintergreens are small, evergreen woodland plants that stay green year-round and produce delicate white or pink flowers in summer. These low-growing plants have thick, waxy leaves and prefer to live in acidic soil under pine and oak forests. They're part of the heath family and have a distinctive minty fragrance when their leaves are crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the heath family, wintergreens have distinctive umbrella-like clusters of nodding flowers and leaves arranged in whorls around the stem. Their thick, leathery leaves often have prominent white veining that helps distinguish them from other forest floor plants.
children.funFact: Native Americans and early settlers used these plants to make a natural wintergreen-flavored tea, and the leaves contain the same compound (methyl salicylate) found in aspirin, making them a traditional remedy for headaches and muscle pain.

children.name: Gaultheria
children.description: Wintergreens are small, woody shrubs that stay green year-round and produce distinctive aromatic oils. These low-growing plants bear small, waxy leaves and produce tiny bell-shaped white or pinkish flowers followed by colorful berries. Both species native to New England are found creeping along the forest floor in acidic, woodland soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wintergreens can be identified by their evergreen leaves that release a strong minty fragrance when crushed, and their characteristic small, urn-shaped flowers. Their berries are also distinctive - bright red in teaberry and white in creeping snowberry.
children.funFact: The leaves and berries of Eastern Teaberry contain natural wintergreen oil (methyl salicylate), the same compound originally used to flavor wintergreen gum and medicine before synthetic versions were developed.

children.name: Lyonia
children.description: Lyonias are small to medium-sized shrubs in the heath family that thrive in acidic, sandy soils throughout New England's woodlands and wetlands. These deciduous shrubs produce clusters of small, bell-shaped white or pinkish flowers in late spring to early summer, followed by dry seed capsules. They're important native plants that provide food for wildlife and help stabilize soil in challenging growing conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heath family shrubs, lyonias have distinctively papery, persistent seed capsules that remain on the plant long after flowering. Their leaves are also typically more oval and less leathery than related evergreen heaths like rhododendrons.
children.funFact: Staggerbush gets its common name because it was once believed to cause livestock to stagger when eaten, though this toxic effect is actually quite rare and the plant is generally avoided by grazing animals.

children.name: Empetrum
children.description: Crowberries are low-growing, evergreen shrubs that thrive in harsh, acidic environments like mountain peaks, bogs, and coastal areas. These tough little plants produce small, dark berries that persist through winter and can survive extreme cold and poor soils where many other plants cannot grow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most berry-producing shrubs, crowberries have tiny, needle-like leaves that are rolled under at the edges, giving them a heath-like appearance. Their small flowers lack petals and are easily overlooked, but their dark berries are distinctive and long-lasting.
children.funFact: Crowberries are so hardy they can photosynthesize even when covered in snow, making them one of the few plants that can continue growing during mild winter days in New England's mountains.

children.name: Leucothoe
children.description: Doghobble plants are low-growing, evergreen shrubs in the heath family that thrive in acidic, shady woodland environments. These graceful plants produce clusters of small, white, bell-shaped flowers that hang delicately from their branches in spring, followed by small dry capsules containing seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Doghobble can be identified by their leathery, alternate leaves and distinctive drooping clusters of urn-shaped flowers that dangle beneath the branches. Their arching, somewhat zigzag branching pattern and preference for moist, shaded areas help separate them from other heath family shrubs.
children.funFact: The name 'doghobble' comes from the plant's dense, arching branches that can tangle around the legs of dogs and other animals trying to walk through them.

children.name: Pieris
children.description: Pieris is a genus of evergreen shrubs in the heath family, commonly known as andromedas. These beautiful ornamental plants are prized for their clusters of small, bell-shaped flowers that bloom in spring and their glossy, leathery leaves that remain green year-round.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pieris can be distinguished from other heath family shrubs by their distinctive urn-shaped or bell-shaped flowers that hang in drooping clusters, and their thick, waxy leaves with smooth edges.
children.funFact: All parts of Pieris plants contain toxic compounds called grayanotoxins, which can be harmful to humans and animals if ingested - ancient Greeks actually knew about this toxicity and called the plants 'andromedotoxin' after the mythological princess Andromeda.

children.name: Epigaea
children.description: Trailing arbutuses are low-growing, woody shrubs that creep along the forest floor rather than growing upright. These evergreen plants are members of the heath family and are specially adapted to life in acidic, sandy soils under pine and oak trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heath family members, trailing arbutuses have a distinctly prostrate growth habit with trailing stems that root at the nodes. Their leathery, oval leaves and fragrant, pink or white bell-shaped flowers that appear in early spring also set them apart.
children.funFact: Trailing arbutus was so beloved by the Pilgrims as the first flower to bloom after their harsh first winter that it became known as the 'Mayflower' and is now the state flower of Massachusetts.

children.name: Chamaedaphne
children.description: Leatherleaves are small evergreen shrubs in the heath family that thrive in acidic, wet environments like bogs and swamps. They're characterized by their tough, leathery leaves that help them survive in nutrient-poor conditions and harsh weather.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heath family members, leatherleaves have distinctive small white bell-shaped flowers arranged along one side of arching branches, and their leaves have a unique scaly underside.
children.funFact: Leatherleaf is one of the most widespread shrubs in the world, found across the northern hemisphere from New England to Alaska and even into Siberia.

children.name: Arctostaphylos
children.description: Arctostaphylos is a genus of low-growing evergreen shrubs in the heath family, commonly known as bearberries and manzanitas. These hardy plants are adapted to harsh conditions and produce small, urn-shaped flowers followed by bright red berries that persist through winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heath family members, Arctostaphylos species have distinctive smooth, reddish bark that often peels in thin layers, and their leaves are typically thick, leathery, and arranged alternately rather than in whorls.
children.funFact: The name 'bearberry' comes from the fact that bears love to eat the tart red fruits, while 'manzanita' means 'little apple' in Spanish, referring to the small apple-like berries.

children.name: Andromeda
children.description: Andromeda is a small genus of low-growing evergreen shrubs in the heath family that thrive in acidic, boggy environments. These hardy plants are adapted to cold climates and nutrient-poor soils, making them well-suited to New England's wetland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Andromeda can be distinguished from other heath family shrubs by their narrow, leathery leaves with rolled edges and their distinctive pink, bell-shaped flowers that hang in small clusters.
children.funFact: Wild Rosemary gets its name from its narrow leaves that resemble those of culinary rosemary, but it's actually toxic to humans and livestock if consumed.

children.name: Corema
children.description: Corema is a small genus of low-growing evergreen shrubs that thrive in sandy, acidic soils. These hardy plants are specially adapted to harsh coastal environments and poor growing conditions where few other woody plants can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, Corema species have separate male and female plants, with tiny flowers that lack petals and are wind-pollinated rather than insect-pollinated.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Corema' comes from the Greek word 'korema' meaning 'broom,' referring to the plant's dense, broom-like branching pattern.

children.name: Eubotrys
children.description: Eubotrys is a small genus of flowering shrubs in the heath family that are commonly known as fetterbushes. These woody plants are characterized by their clusters of small, bell-shaped white or pink flowers and their preference for acidic, wet soils. They are closely related to other heath family members like blueberries and azaleas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eubotrys can be distinguished from other heath family shrubs by their distinctive racemes (elongated flower clusters) of drooping, urn-shaped flowers and their alternate, simple leaves that often have a leathery texture.
children.funFact: The common name 'fetterbush' comes from the belief that these shrubs could 'fetter' or entangle grazing livestock, as the dense growth and somewhat toxic leaves made them hazardous to animals.

children.name: Orthilia
children.description: Orthilia is a small genus of evergreen wildflowers that contains just one species worldwide - the one-sided wintergreen. These low-growing woodland plants are members of the heath family and produce distinctive spikes of small, bell-shaped white or greenish flowers that all face the same direction along one side of the stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wintergreens, Orthilia flowers are arranged in a distinctive one-sided raceme where all the blooms point in the same direction rather than being evenly distributed around the stem.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'one-sided wintergreen,' this plant was reclassified from the Pyrola genus into its own unique genus Orthilia, making it the sole member of this exclusive botanical group.

children.name: Moneses
children.description: Moneses is a genus containing just one species worldwide - the delicate One-flowered Wintergreen. This small evergreen plant is part of the heath family and thrives in cool, acidic soils of northern forests. Like other wintergreens, it stays green year-round and has thick, waxy leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wintergreens that produce clusters of flowers, Moneses is unique in having just a single, nodding white flower per stem. The flower faces downward on a distinctive curved stalk.
children.funFact: Despite being called a wintergreen, One-flowered Wintergreen doesn't actually produce the minty wintergreen scent - that fragrance comes from a different group of plants entirely.

children.name: Calluna
children.description: Calluna is a genus containing just one species - the common heather, a low-growing evergreen shrub that creates colorful carpets across landscapes. These hardy plants produce tiny, bell-shaped flowers that range from white to deep purple and bloom in dense clusters along their branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heather family members, Calluna has distinctive scale-like leaves that overlap each other closely along the stems, and its flowers have both petals and sepals that are nearly the same size and color.
children.funFact: Common heather has been used for centuries to make brooms, bedding, and even beer - honey made from heather nectar was considered so valuable that it was once used as currency in parts of Europe.

children.name: Phyllodoce
children.description: Mountain-heathers are small, low-growing shrubs that thrive in harsh, cold environments like mountaintops and arctic regions. These hardy plants produce delicate, bell-shaped flowers that seem almost too beautiful for their rugged habitat. They're specially adapted to survive freezing temperatures and strong winds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heath family members, mountain-heathers have very small, needle-like leaves that are densely packed along their stems. Their flowers are distinctively urn-shaped or bell-shaped and typically hang downward in small clusters.
children.funFact: Mountain-heathers can live for over 100 years, slowly forming dense mats that help prevent soil erosion on steep mountain slopes.

children.name: Harrimanella
children.description: Moss bell-heathers are tiny evergreen shrubs that form dense, mat-like cushions close to the ground. These miniature plants belong to the heath family and are specially adapted to survive in harsh, cold mountain environments where few other plants can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other heath family members, moss bell-heathers have extremely small, needle-like leaves that overlap like scales and create a moss-like appearance. Their bell-shaped flowers are solitary and much smaller than those of typical heathers.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'moss' bell-heather, this plant is actually a flowering shrub that can live for decades while staying only a few inches tall, making it one of the most compact woody plants in New England.

children.name: Arctous
children.description: Alpine bearberries are low-growing, woody shrubs that thrive in harsh mountain and arctic environments. These hardy plants are part of the heath family and are specially adapted to survive extreme cold, strong winds, and nutrient-poor soils at high elevations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their evergreen bearberry relatives, alpine bearberries are deciduous, losing their leaves each fall and displaying beautiful red and orange autumn colors before winter.
children.funFact: Alpine bearberry leaves contain natural compounds that were traditionally used by indigenous peoples as a smoking mixture and herbal medicine.

children.name: Oxydendrum
children.description: Oxydendrum is a genus containing just one species - the sourwood tree, a beautiful deciduous tree native to eastern North America. These trees are members of the heath family and are known for their distinctive sour-tasting leaves and elegant drooping clusters of small, white, bell-shaped flowers that bloom in summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sourwood is easily distinguished from other trees by its glossy, oval leaves that turn brilliant red in fall and its long, curved sprays of tiny white flowers that hang like cascading chains from the branches.
children.funFact: The sourwood gets its name from the sour, acidic taste of its leaves, which were historically chewed by Native Americans and early settlers as a remedy for thirst and to soothe mouth sores.

children.name: Pterospora
children.description: Pinedrops are unusual parasitic plants that lack chlorophyll and cannot make their own food through photosynthesis. Instead, they obtain nutrients by forming partnerships with fungi that are connected to the roots of trees, making them indirect parasites of forest trees. These ghostly plants appear as tall, reddish-brown stalks emerging from the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plants, pinedrops are completely non-green and produce distinctive tall spikes covered with small, urn-shaped flowers that hang downward like tiny bells. They emerge directly from decaying forest litter without any visible leaves.
children.funFact: Pinedrops can remain dormant underground for years or even decades before sending up their spectacular flowering stalks, which can grow up to 4 feet tall in a single season.

children.name: Enkianthus
children.description: Enkianthuses are small to medium-sized deciduous shrubs in the heath family that are prized for their delicate, bell-shaped flowers and stunning fall foliage. These Asian natives produce clusters of small, drooping flowers that hang like tiny lanterns from their branches in late spring. The leaves turn brilliant shades of orange, red, and yellow in autumn, making them popular ornamental plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other heath family members, enkianthuses have distinctly bell-shaped or urn-shaped flowers that hang downward in clusters, rather than upright or outward-facing blooms. Their leaves are also typically arranged in whorls or clusters at branch tips, giving them a layered appearance.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Enkianthus' comes from Greek words meaning 'pregnant flower,' referring to the swollen, bell-like shape of their blooms.

children.description: The heath family is a diverse group of woody plants that includes many of New England's most beloved shrubs and small trees. From the blueberries we pick in summer to the vibrant rhododendrons in our gardens, these plants are united by their small, often bell-shaped flowers and their ability to thrive in acidic soils that many other plants can't tolerate.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Heath family plants have a unique relationship with soil fungi that helps them extract nutrients from poor, acidic conditions. Their flowers typically have parts in multiples of four or five, and many produce berries or dry capsules as fruits.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, like Indian pipes, have lost their ability to photosynthesize and instead live as parasites on fungi, appearing ghostly white in the forest understory.

children.name: Primulaceae
Lysimachia
children.description: Loosestrifes are a diverse group of flowering plants that can be found in many different habitats, from wetlands and pond edges to woodlands and even your garden. Despite their varied appearances, they all share the characteristic of having flowers with typically 5-7 petals that are often yellow, white, or occasionally red. Many species spread by creeping stems or runners, making them excellent ground covers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets loosestrifes apart from other flowering plants is their unique combination of simple leaves (often arranged in whorls around the stem) and their distinctive flower structure with petals that are separate from each other rather than fused together.
children.funFact: The name 'loosestrife' comes from an old belief that these plants could calm aggressive animals - farmers would place the flowers around the necks of oxen to make them more peaceful while working!

children.name: Primula
children.description: Primroses are a genus of charming perennial flowers known for their distinctive five-petaled blooms that often appear in clusters. These low-growing plants typically produce colorful flowers in shades of yellow, pink, purple, or white, emerging from rosettes of wrinkled or textured leaves. Many species bloom early in spring, bringing bright color to gardens and natural areas when few other flowers are present.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Primroses are distinguished by their characteristic five-petaled flowers with a flat or slightly cupped face, often featuring a contrasting center or 'eye.' Unlike many similar spring flowers, primrose petals are typically notched or heart-shaped at the tips, and the flowers arise directly from the base of the plant on individual stalks.
children.funFact: Many primrose species exhibit heterostyly, meaning individual plants produce flowers with either long or short reproductive parts, which prevents self-pollination and ensures genetic diversity by requiring cross-pollination between different plants.

children.name: Hottonia
children.description: Hottonia is a small genus of aquatic flowering plants in the primrose family that are specially adapted for life in quiet waters. These delicate plants grow submerged or floating in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams, producing feathery underwater leaves and showy flower spikes that emerge above the water surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most primrose family members that grow on land, Hottonia species are truly aquatic with finely divided, feather-like submerged leaves and hollow stems filled with air spaces that help them float.
children.funFact: The common name 'featherfoil' comes from their distinctive underwater leaves that look like delicate green feathers swaying in the current.

children.name: Samolus
children.description: Samolus is a small genus of flowering plants in the primrose family that includes delicate herbaceous plants adapted to wet, salty environments. These plants typically grow in coastal areas and salt marshes, producing small white or pink flowers arranged in loose clusters. They are characterized by their ability to thrive in challenging conditions where salt spray and tidal flooding would kill most other flowering plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Samolus plants are distinguished from other primrose family members by their tolerance for salt water and their preference for coastal wetland habitats. Their small, simple leaves and tiny five-petaled flowers help separate them from the showier primroses found in gardens.
children.funFact: Despite being in the primrose family, Samolus species have evolved to live in some of the harshest plant environments on Earth - the edges of salt marshes where few other flowering plants can survive the constant salt exposure.

children.name: Cyclamen
children.description: Cyclamen is a genus of low-growing perennial plants known for their distinctive swept-back flowers that appear to be flying backwards. These plants grow from underground tubers and produce heart-shaped or rounded leaves that often have attractive silver or white patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cyclamen flowers have a unique upside-down appearance with reflexed petals that curve sharply backward, unlike most other flowers that face upward or outward.
children.funFact: The seed pods of cyclamen plants coil up like springs when ripe, helping to catapult their seeds away from the parent plant.

children.description: The primrose family includes a diverse group of flowering plants that typically produce colorful, five-petaled flowers arranged in clusters or whorls. Most members of this family are herbaceous perennials that grow in moist soils, from woodland edges to wetland margins. These plants are found worldwide and include both terrestrial species like primroses and aquatic species like water violet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Primrose family plants are characterized by their distinctive flower structure with five petals that are often fused at the base, and stamens that are positioned directly opposite the petals rather than alternating with them. Many species also have leaves arranged in a basal rosette pattern.
children.funFact: Despite their name, loosestrifes in the primrose family are completely unrelated to the invasive purple loosestrife - they just happened to receive similar common names due to their superficial resemblance!

children.name: Polemoniaceae
Phlox
children.description: Phloxes are a beloved group of flowering plants known for their showy, fragrant blooms that come in shades of pink, purple, blue, and white. These plants typically have five-petaled flowers arranged in clusters and opposite leaves, making them easy to recognize in gardens and wild spaces. They range from low, creeping groundcovers to tall, upright garden favorites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phloxes can be distinguished from other flowering plants by their distinctive five-petaled flowers with a long, narrow tube at the base and their opposite leaf arrangement. The flowers often have a sweet fragrance and form dense, showy clusters that attract butterflies and hummingbirds.
children.funFact: The name 'phlox' comes from the Greek word for 'flame,' referring to the brilliant colors of their flowers that can light up a garden or woodland floor.

children.name: Polemonium
children.description: Jacob's ladders are delicate woodland wildflowers named for their distinctive compound leaves that resemble the rungs of a ladder. These perennial herbs produce clusters of bell-shaped flowers in shades of blue, purple, or occasionally white, and are members of the phlox family. They typically bloom in spring and early summer, favoring moist, shaded areas in forests and wetlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jacob's ladders can be identified by their unique pinnately compound leaves with multiple pairs of small leaflets arranged like ladder rungs, combined with their bell-shaped flowers that have prominent stamens extending beyond the petals.
children.funFact: The genus name Polemonium comes from a Greek word meaning 'war,' because ancient Greek philosopher Pliny claimed that two kings once went to war over which one first discovered the medicinal properties of these plants.

children.name: Gilia
children.description: Gilias are delicate annual wildflowers in the phlox family, known for their small, colorful blooms that cluster together in attractive displays. These hardy plants typically grow in open, sunny areas and produce flowers with five petals that come in shades of blue, purple, pink, or white, often with contrasting centers or markings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gilias can be distinguished from other phlox family members by their typically smaller, more delicate flowers and their preference for drier, more open habitats rather than woodland settings.
children.funFact: Bird's-eye gilia gets its common name from the distinctive dark spots at the center of each pale blue flower that resemble tiny eyes looking up at you.

children.name: Cobaea
children.description: Cobaea is a small genus of climbing vines native to tropical Mexico and Central America, known for their distinctive bell-shaped flowers that sit within saucer-like green sepals. These vigorous climbers use tendrils to scramble up supports and can grow quite large in a single season. Only one species, the cup-and-saucer vine, is found in New England as a cultivated garden plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature is the unique flower structure with large, bell-shaped blooms that emerge from prominent, flat, green sepals that remain after flowering, creating the characteristic 'cup-and-saucer' appearance. The compound leaves end in branched tendrils that help the vine climb.
children.funFact: The flowers of cup-and-saucer vine start out greenish-white and gradually change to deep purple over several days, creating a striking two-toned display on the same plant.

children.description: The phlox family is a group of flowering plants that includes some of our most beloved garden flowers and wildflowers. These plants typically have five-petaled flowers that are often brightly colored and arranged in clusters, making them popular with both gardeners and pollinators like butterflies and hummingbirds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the phlox family can be identified by their tubular flowers with five petals that spread out flat, and their leaves are usually arranged in opposite pairs or spirals along the stem. The flowers often have a sweet fragrance and come in vibrant colors ranging from white and pink to purple and red.
children.funFact: Garden phlox flowers are specially shaped to attract long-tongued butterflies and moths - their narrow tubes perfectly match the length of a butterfly's proboscis!

children.name: Balsaminaceae
Impatiens
children.description: Balsams are annual flowering plants known for their distinctive seed pods that explode when touched, earning them the nickname 'touch-me-nots.' These plants typically have succulent stems, serrated leaves, and colorful sac-shaped flowers with curved spurs that hang like tiny slippers or jewels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowers, balsam blooms have an irregular shape with a distinctive curved spur at the back, and their seed pods burst open with surprising force when ripe, shooting seeds several feet away.
children.funFact: The explosive seed pods of balsams can launch their seeds up to 6 feet away at speeds of up to 10 feet per second - one of nature's most dramatic seed dispersal mechanisms!

children.description: The balsam family consists of tender, succulent-stemmed plants known for their distinctive irregular flowers and explosive seed pods. These annual herbs thrive in moist, shaded areas and are easily recognized by their swollen stem joints and somewhat translucent appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have uniquely shaped flowers with a prominent curved spur and seed pods that literally explode when touched, forcefully ejecting seeds several feet away.
children.funFact: Touch-me-not plants earned their name because their ripe seed pods burst open at the slightest touch, shooting seeds up to 4 feet away as a clever seed dispersal strategy.

children.name: Diapensiaceae
Diapensia
children.description: Diapensia is a genus of small, cushion-forming evergreen shrubs that grow in extremely harsh arctic and alpine environments. These tough little plants form dense, low mats or cushions that help them survive bitter cold, strong winds, and short growing seasons in some of the world's most challenging habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Diapensia plants are recognized by their small, leathery evergreen leaves arranged in tight rosettes and their solitary white flowers that sit on short stems above the cushion-like foliage.
children.funFact: Diapensia can live for over 100 years and grows so slowly that a cushion just a few inches across may be decades old, making it one of the longest-lived plants in alpine regions.

children.name: Galax
children.description: Galax is a genus containing just one species, a distinctive evergreen perennial plant with round, leathery leaves and tall spikes of tiny white flowers. This single species is found in the mountainous regions of eastern North America, including parts of New England. The plant forms low-growing colonies through underground stems called rhizomes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Galax is easily recognized by its glossy, heart-shaped to round leaves that turn bronze or reddish in fall and winter, and its dense, narrow clusters of small white flowers on tall stalks that rise well above the foliage.
children.funFact: Galax leaves were once commercially harvested and shipped to florists worldwide because they stay fresh and attractive for weeks after being cut, making them prized for floral arrangements and wreaths.

children.name: Shortia
children.description: Shortia is a small genus of low-growing perennial wildflowers found in shaded woodland areas. These plants are known for their evergreen, rounded leaves and delicate white or pink bell-shaped flowers that bloom in early spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Shortia can be distinguished from other woodland wildflowers by its distinctive glossy, heart-shaped leaves that turn bronze or reddish in fall, and its solitary nodding flowers with fringed petals.
children.funFact: Oconee bells was one of the most famous 'lost plants' in botanical history - first collected in 1788 but then not seen again for nearly 100 years until it was rediscovered in 1877 in a remote gorge in South Carolina.

children.description: The diapensia family is a small group of low-growing, evergreen plants that thrive in harsh, cold environments. These hardy perennials are known for their beautiful white or pink flowers and thick, leathery leaves that help them survive in challenging conditions like mountaintops and northern climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many flowering plants, diapensia family members have flowers with exactly 5 stamens that are positioned opposite the petals rather than alternating with them. Their leaves are typically arranged in rosettes or clusters at the base of the plant.
children.funFact: Diapensia plants are so tough they can survive being buried under snow for months, and some species grow in cushion-like mats that create their own microclimate to stay warmer than the surrounding air.

children.name: Actinidiaceae
Actinidia
children.description: Actinidia is a genus of woody climbing vines known for producing kiwi fruits. These deciduous plants are characterized by their heart-shaped leaves, fragrant white or cream-colored flowers, and small to medium-sized edible fruits that are typically fuzzy or smooth-skinned.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fruiting vines, Actinidia species are dioecious, meaning individual plants are either male or female, requiring both sexes for fruit production. Their fruits contain numerous small black seeds arranged in a distinctive star pattern around a white or pale center.
children.funFact: The familiar grocery store kiwi fruit comes from this genus, but New England's hardy species can survive much colder temperatures and produce smaller, smooth-skinned fruits that can be eaten whole like grapes.

children.description: The Actinidiaceae family includes woody vines and shrubs best known for producing kiwifruit, the fuzzy brown fruit with green flesh found in grocery stores. These plants typically have large, heart-shaped leaves and produce small, fragrant flowers that develop into berry-like fruits. Most members are climbing vines that use twining stems to reach sunlight in forest canopies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other climbing plants, Actinidiaceae vines twine around supports rather than using tendrils or rootlets to climb. Their flowers are typically white or cream-colored with many stamens, and the fruits contain numerous small seeds embedded in soft, juicy flesh.
children.funFact: The fuzzy kiwifruit sold in stores was originally called 'Chinese gooseberry' and wasn't commercially grown outside of China until the 20th century, when it was renamed 'kiwifruit' after New Zealand's national bird by marketers trying to make it more appealing to international buyers.

children.name: Styracaceae
Halesia
children.description: Silverbells are small to medium-sized deciduous trees known for their distinctive bell-shaped white flowers that hang in clusters from the branches in spring. These native North American trees belong to the storax family and are prized as ornamental plants for their graceful flowering display and attractive fall foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Silverbells are easily recognized by their drooping, bell-shaped white flowers and their unique four-winged fruits that persist into winter, giving them a papery, lantern-like appearance.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Halesia' honors Stephen Hales, an 18th-century English botanist who was one of the first scientists to study how plants transport water and nutrients.

children.name: Styrax
children.description: Snowbells are small to medium-sized deciduous trees and shrubs known for their delicate, drooping white flowers that hang like tiny bells from the branches. These plants typically bloom in late spring to early summer, creating a stunning display of fragrant, bell-shaped blossoms. They prefer partially shaded woodland environments with well-drained, slightly acidic soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snowbells are easily recognized by their distinctive pendant white flowers that hang downward from the branches, unlike many other flowering trees whose blooms point upward or outward. The flowers have a characteristic bell or cup shape with prominent yellow stamens visible inside.
children.funFact: The Japanese snowbell's scientific name 'japonicus' reflects its Asian origin, but this beautiful ornamental tree has become so popular in New England gardens that it's now considered naturalized in some areas.

children.description: The snowbell family is a group of woody plants known for their beautiful, drooping white flowers that bloom in spring. These trees and shrubs produce distinctive bell-shaped or star-shaped flowers that hang downward from the branches, often covering the entire plant in a spectacular floral display.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their pendulous white flowers that hang like little bells or snowflakes from the branches. The flowers typically have 4-5 petals that are often fused at the base, creating their characteristic bell or funnel shape.
children.funFact: The common names 'snowbell' and 'silverbell' come from the flowers' resemblance to tiny white bells hanging from the branches, creating a magical snow-like effect when in full bloom.

children.name: Sarraceniaceae
Sarracenia
children.description: North American pitcher plants are carnivorous plants that catch and digest insects in their distinctive pitcher-shaped leaves. These bog-dwelling plants have evolved hollow, water-filled leaves that act as deadly traps for unsuspecting prey. They supplement their nutrition by breaking down trapped insects, allowing them to thrive in nutrient-poor wetland soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other carnivorous plants that use sticky surfaces or snap traps, Sarracenia species use passive pitfall traps with slippery walls and downward-pointing hairs that prevent insects from escaping once they fall in.
children.funFact: The purple pitcher plant can survive being frozen solid in winter ice and is so hardy that it's the only carnivorous plant that grows as far north as Canada's subarctic regions.

children.description: New World pitcher plants are carnivorous plants that have evolved specialized leaves shaped like deep pitchers or tubes to trap and digest insects. These remarkable plants grow in nutrient-poor, acidic wetlands where they supplement their diet by capturing prey that falls into their water-filled traps. The trapped insects are broken down by enzymes and bacteria, providing the plants with essential nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other carnivorous plants that use sticky traps or snap traps, pitcher plants use passive pitfall traps filled with digestive fluid. Their pitcher-shaped leaves have slippery rims and downward-pointing hairs that prevent insects from climbing back out once they fall in.
children.funFact: The purple pitcher plant is so effective at its carnivorous lifestyle that a single plant can capture hundreds of insects in a season, and some pitcher plants have been found containing small frogs, salamanders, and even baby mice!

children.name: Clethraceae
Clethra
children.description: Clethra is a genus of flowering shrubs known for their distinctive sweet-scented flower spikes that bloom in summer. These deciduous shrubs are well-adapted to wet, acidic soils and are often found in swamps, marshes, and along stream banks. They produce small white or pink flowers arranged in dense, elongated clusters that attract numerous pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Clethra can be distinguished from other wetland shrubs by its distinctive bottle-brush-like flower clusters and its strongly fragrant blooms that appear in mid to late summer. The flowers have a unique spicy-sweet scent that sets them apart from other native shrubs.
children.funFact: Sweet Pepperbush gets its common name from its small, round seed capsules that were once dried and used as a pepper substitute by early colonists.

children.description: The clethra family is a small group of flowering shrubs and small trees known for their fragrant, white flower clusters that bloom in summer. These plants are commonly called sweet pepperbush or summersweet and are popular in gardens for their pleasant scent and ability to attract pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive spikes or racemes of small, five-petaled white flowers and alternate, serrated leaves. Their flowers have prominent stamens and produce a strong, sweet fragrance that sets them apart from other summer-blooming shrubs.
children.funFact: Sweet pepperbush earned its common name because its seed capsules were once ground up and used as a substitute for black pepper.

children.name: Symplocaceae
Symplocos
children.description: Symplocos is a genus of small trees and shrubs known for their clusters of small, fragrant white or yellow flowers and colorful berries. These plants are found in temperate and tropical regions around the world, with most species occurring in Asia and only one species naturally found in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Symplocos plants are distinguished by their simple, alternate leaves and their distinctive berries that often turn bright blue or purple when ripe, giving them their common name of sapphire-berry.
children.funFact: The bright blue berries of sapphire-berry contain natural dyes that have been used traditionally for coloring fabrics and other materials.

children.description: The symplocos family is a small group of flowering plants that includes shrubs and small trees. These plants are characterized by their simple, alternate leaves and small, fragrant white or yellow flowers that often grow in clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive flowers with many stamens (often 15-100) that are partially fused to the petals, and their fruits are typically small drupes with a single seed.
children.funFact: Many species in this family are known as 'sweetleaf' because their leaves have a sweet taste and were historically used as a natural sweetener and to flavor tobacco.

children.name: Ebenaceae
Diospyros
children.description: Persimmons are deciduous trees and shrubs known for their sweet, orange fruits that ripen in fall. They have simple, alternate leaves that turn beautiful yellow to orange colors in autumn, and small, inconspicuous flowers that bloom in late spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Persimmons are unique among New England trees for their distinctive orange, tomato-like fruits that hang from branches after the leaves fall. The bark has a characteristic blocky, checkered pattern that becomes more pronounced with age.
children.funFact: American persimmon fruits are extremely astringent and mouth-puckering when unripe, but become sweet and delicious after the first frost breaks down the tannins.

children.description: The persimmon family is a group of trees and shrubs known for their distinctive fruits and beautiful wood. Most members of this family are tropical, but one hardy species has made its way north to New England. These plants typically have simple, oval leaves and produce fleshy, often sweet fruits that ripen in fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Persimmon family members are easily recognized by their large, orange fruits that hang like ornaments on bare branches in late fall and winter. The fruits have a unique, sweet-astringent taste and contain large, flat seeds.
children.funFact: Ebony wood, prized for making piano keys and fine furniture, comes from tropical members of the persimmon family - the same family as the persimmon trees that grow wild in New England forests!

children.description: The Ericales is a diverse order of flowering plants that includes many beloved New England species like blueberries, rhododendrons, primroses, and pitcher plants. Despite their varied appearances, these plants share similar flower structures and often prefer acidic soils. This group ranges from tiny woodland wildflowers to shrubs that define our region's landscapes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most members have flowers with parts arranged in fives (5 petals, 5 sepals) and often produce capsule fruits or berries. Many species in this order have adapted to nutrient-poor, acidic environments that other plants struggle to colonize.
children.funFact: This order contains both some of New England's most important food plants (like blueberries and cranberries) and our region's only carnivorous plants (pitcher plants that trap and digest insects).

children.name: Ranunculales
Ranunculaceae
Ranunculus
children.description: Buttercups are a diverse group of flowering plants known for their cheerful yellow blooms that seem to glow with a waxy, almost metallic sheen. These plants can be found in a wide variety of habitats throughout New England, from dry meadows and woodlands to wetlands and even floating in ponds and streams. Most species are herbaceous perennials that bloom in spring and early summer, though some are annuals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Buttercups are easily recognized by their glossy, cup-shaped flowers with typically five bright yellow petals that have a distinctive waxy or buttery appearance. Their leaves are often deeply divided or lobed, and many species have a characteristic three-part leaf structure.
children.funFact: The shiny, reflective quality of buttercup petals comes from a unique layer of cells that acts like tiny mirrors, which may help attract pollinators by creating an especially bright visual signal.

children.name: Thalictrum
children.description: Meadow-rues are delicate wildflowers in the buttercup family that produce distinctive clusters of small, fluffy flowers without petals. Instead of showy petals, their flowers feature prominent stamens and sepals that create a soft, feathery appearance. These perennial plants typically grow in moist woodlands and meadows throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowers, meadow-rues lack petals entirely and rely on their colorful sepals and fluffy stamens for their ornamental appeal. Their compound leaves are also distinctive, resembling those of columbines but typically more finely divided.
children.funFact: Many meadow-rue species are either male or female plants (dioecious), meaning you need both types growing nearby for the plants to produce seeds - the male plants produce the showy, pollen-laden flowers while females have smaller, less conspicuous blooms.

children.name: Anemonoides
children.description: Anemonoides is a genus of delicate woodland wildflowers commonly known as windflowers or wood anemones. These perennial herbs emerge from underground rhizomes in early spring, producing distinctive flowers with petal-like sepals (usually white, yellow, or blue) that lack true petals. They're among the first flowers to bloom in deciduous forests, often carpeting the woodland floor before the tree canopy fully leafs out.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true anemones (Anemone genus), Anemonoides species have flowers that sit directly on stems without stalks and typically have a whorl of three deeply divided leaves below each flower. Their fruits are also distinctly different, lacking the long, feathery tails found on many Anemone seeds.
children.funFact: The name 'windflower' comes from the Greek belief that these delicate flowers would only open when the wind blew, though they actually respond more to temperature and light than to air movement.

children.name: Aquilegia
children.description: Columbines are distinctive wildflowers known for their unique spurred petals that extend backward from the bloom, creating an elegant, almost bird-like appearance. These perennial herbs typically grow in woodland areas and mountain meadows, producing delicate flowers with five petals and five sepals in various color combinations including red, blue, purple, white, and yellow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The long, hollow spurs extending from the back of each flower are the columbine's signature feature, setting them apart from all other wildflowers. Their compound leaves are also distinctive, being divided into three-lobed leaflets that give them a delicate, lacy appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'columbine' comes from the Latin word 'columba' meaning dove, because the inverted flower was thought to resemble a cluster of five doves drinking together.

children.name: Actaea
children.description: Baneberries and cohoshes are woodland wildflowers in the buttercup family that produce distinctive clusters of small white flowers in spring and early summer. These perennial plants are found in rich, moist forest soils throughout New England and are known for their deeply divided, compound leaves and conspicuous berry-like fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their tall spikes or rounded clusters of small white flowers with numerous stamens, followed by colorful berries (white, red, or dark purple-black depending on species). The flowers lack petals, with the showy white parts actually being sepals that fall off early.
children.funFact: White baneberry gets the nickname 'doll's eyes' because its waxy white berries with black spots look remarkably like old-fashioned porcelain doll eyes, though all parts of the plant are highly toxic if eaten.

children.name: Clematis
children.description: Clematis is a genus of woody vines and climbing plants known for their distinctive flowers and feathery seed heads. These plants are members of the buttercup family and are popular both as wild native species and cultivated ornamentals. They typically climb by wrapping their leaf stems around supports like fences, trees, or trellises.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Clematis can be identified by their opposite compound leaves and flowers that lack true petals - what appear to be petals are actually colorful sepals. Their fluffy, plume-like seed heads that persist into fall and winter are also highly distinctive.
children.funFact: The name 'clematis' comes from the Greek word 'klema' meaning vine branch, and some species are called 'old man's beard' because of their wispy, white seed heads that look like flowing whiskers.

children.name: Anemone
children.description: Anemones and thimbleweeds are delicate wildflowers in the buttercup family that bloom in spring and early summer. These perennial plants have deeply divided, palmate leaves and produce simple flowers with petal-like sepals surrounding a central cluster of stamens. After flowering, they develop distinctive fluffy seed heads that give thimbleweeds their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true petals, anemone flowers have colorful sepals that look like petals, while the actual petals are either very small or absent entirely. Their characteristic thimble-shaped, cotton-like seed heads make them easy to identify even after the flowers have faded.
children.funFact: The name 'anemone' comes from the Greek word for wind, as these plants often grow in windy locations and their feathery seeds are dispersed by the breeze.

children.name: Hepatica
children.description: Hepaticas are small woodland wildflowers known for their distinctive three-lobed leaves and delicate early spring blooms. These low-growing perennials emerge from the forest floor while snow may still be present, producing charming flowers in shades of white, pink, or blue before most other wildflowers appear.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hepaticas are easily recognized by their three-lobed, leathery leaves that persist through winter and their solitary flowers that bloom directly from the ground on fuzzy stems before new leaves emerge.
children.funFact: The name 'hepatica' comes from the liver-shaped appearance of their leaves, and early herbalists believed they could treat liver ailments following the medieval 'doctrine of signatures' that suggested plants resembling body parts could heal those organs.

children.name: Eranthis
children.description: Winter aconites are small, cheerful wildflowers that belong to the buttercup family and are among the very first flowers to bloom each spring. These hardy perennials push through snow and frozen ground to display bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers surrounded by a collar of deeply divided green leaves. They grow from small tubers and typically reach only 3-6 inches tall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Winter aconites are easily recognized by their distinctive bright yellow flowers that sit atop a ruff of finely divided, finger-like green bracts that look almost like a collar. Unlike other early spring flowers, they bloom directly from the ground with no visible stem, and their flowers have 5-8 glossy yellow petals.
children.funFact: Winter aconites can bloom even when temperatures are below freezing, and their flowers can actually generate a small amount of heat to help melt surrounding snow and attract early pollinators like bees.

children.name: Aconitum
children.description: Monkshoods are distinctive perennial wildflowers known for their tall spikes of helmet-shaped blue or purple flowers. These plants belong to the buttercup family and grow from tuberous roots in moist, shaded woodland areas. All parts of monkshood plants contain powerful alkaloids that make them highly toxic to humans and animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The unique hood-like upper petal (called a helmet or galea) that covers the flower's reproductive parts makes monkshoods instantly recognizable among New England wildflowers. Their deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves also help distinguish them from other members of the buttercup family.
children.funFact: Monkshood is one of the most poisonous plants in North America - historically, it was used to poison arrows and spear tips, earning it the nickname 'wolfsbane' because it was used to kill wolves.

children.name: Helleborus
children.description: Hellebores are distinctive perennial wildflowers known for their early blooming season and unusual flower structure. These hardy plants produce nodding, cup-shaped flowers that actually consist of colorful sepals rather than true petals, and they often bloom while snow is still on the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowers, hellebores have showy sepals that look like petals, while their true petals are modified into small, tubular nectaries. Their thick, leathery leaves are deeply divided and often evergreen, persisting through winter.
children.funFact: Hellebores are sometimes called "Christmas rose" or "Lenten rose" because they bloom during the winter and early spring months when few other flowers are in bloom.

children.name: Trollius
children.description: Globeflowers are buttercup family plants that produce distinctive spherical yellow flowers that never fully open, giving them their globe-like appearance. These perennial wildflowers typically grow in wet meadows, marshes, and along stream banks where the soil stays consistently moist. They bloom in late spring to early summer and are adapted to cool, northern climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other buttercups, globeflower petals curve inward to form a nearly closed ball shape rather than opening flat. The flowers also lack the glossy, waxy surface typical of most buttercup flowers.
children.funFact: The Eastern Globeflower is one of New England's rarest wildflowers, found only in a handful of locations and considered endangered in several states due to habitat loss.

children.name: Coptis
children.description: Goldthreads are small woodland wildflowers known for their bright golden-yellow underground stems, called rhizomes, which give them their name. These low-growing perennial herbs belong to the buttercup family and thrive in cool, moist forests and boggy areas. They produce delicate white flowers in spring and have distinctive evergreen leaves that persist through winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Goldthreads are easily recognized by their golden-yellow underground stems that can be seen when the plant is carefully uprooted. Their small white flowers have 5-7 narrow petals and are held singly on thin stalks above the leaves.
children.funFact: The bright golden rhizomes of goldthread were traditionally used by Native Americans and early settlers as a natural remedy for mouth sores and sore throats, earning it the folk name 'canker-root.'

children.name: Caltha
children.description: Caltha is a genus of perennial wildflowers commonly known as marsh marigolds, despite not being true marigolds. These wetland plants are members of the buttercup family and thrive in wet soils, producing bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers in early spring. They have glossy, heart-shaped or kidney-shaped leaves and grow in marshy areas, wet meadows, and along stream banks.
