children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true buttercups, marsh marigolds have flowers without petals - their showy yellow parts are actually sepals. Their leaves are also distinctively thick, glossy, and deeply heart-shaped rather than the divided leaves typical of most buttercup family members.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'marsh marigold,' these plants are not related to garden marigolds at all - the name comes from the Old English 'merso-meargealla' meaning 'horse-blob,' referring to their marsh habitat and rounded flower buds.

children.name: Ficaria
children.description: Fig buttercups are small, low-growing wildflowers that belong to the buttercup family. They are characterized by their bright yellow, glossy petals and heart-shaped or kidney-shaped leaves that emerge early in spring. These plants spread by small bulbils (tiny bulb-like structures) and often form dense carpets on the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other buttercups, fig buttercups have distinctive heart-shaped leaves and produce small underground bulbils instead of relying primarily on seeds for reproduction. Their flowers typically have 8-12 narrow, glossy yellow petals rather than the usual 5 petals found in most buttercups.
children.funFact: Lesser celandine was once believed to cure scurvy due to its high vitamin C content, and sailors would gather it in early spring before long voyages.

children.name: Anemonastrum
children.description: Anemonastrum is a genus of perennial wildflowers that were recently separated from the larger anemone genus based on genetic studies. These plants produce delicate white flowers with five petals and grow from underground rhizomes that allow them to spread and form colonies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true anemones, Anemonastrum species have flowers with actual petals rather than petal-like sepals, and they typically form spreading colonies through their creeping underground stems.
children.funFact: The Canada anemone can form large patches covering several acres through its aggressive underground rhizome system, sometimes earning it the nickname 'meadow anemone' for its ability to blanket open areas with white flowers in late spring.

children.name: Xanthorhiza
children.description: Yellowroots are a small genus of low-growing shrubs in the buttercup family, with only one species found worldwide. These woodland plants are known for their bright yellow roots and inner bark, which give them their common name. They produce small clusters of brownish-purple flowers in early spring before their leaves fully emerge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the buttercup family, yellowroots are woody shrubs rather than herbs, and their flowers lack petals, having only colorful sepals instead.
children.funFact: Shrub yellowroot's bright yellow roots were historically used by Native Americans and early settlers as a natural dye and for medicinal purposes.

children.name: Hydrastis
children.description: Goldenseals are small woodland perennial herbs known for their distinctive bright yellow rhizomes (underground stems) that have been valued for medicinal purposes. These plants produce simple white flowers in spring followed by raspberry-like clusters of red berries, and have characteristic palmate leaves with deep lobes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Goldenseals are distinguished by their single white flower that lacks petals (having only sepals), their bright golden-yellow rhizomes, and their deeply divided palmate leaves that typically come in pairs on each stem.
children.funFact: The genus name Hydrastis comes from Greek words meaning 'water' and 'to accomplish,' referring to the plant's traditional use in treating various ailments, though it has become increasingly rare in the wild due to over-harvesting.

children.name: Nigella
children.description: Love-in-a-mist is a small genus of delicate annual flowers in the buttercup family, known for their intricate, lacy foliage that creates a misty appearance around the blooms. These plants produce distinctive flowers with colorful petals surrounded by thread-like, feathery bracts that give them their romantic common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the buttercup family, Nigella flowers are nestled within a distinctive collar of finely divided, thread-like leaves that create a veil-like effect around each bloom.
children.funFact: The seeds of some Nigella species, particularly black cumin (Nigella sativa), have been used as a spice for over 2,000 years and were even found in King Tutankhamun's tomb.

children.name: Halerpestes
children.description: Halerpestes is a small genus of aquatic buttercups that have adapted to life in wet, alkaline environments. These low-growing perennial plants produce small yellow flowers and have the ability to spread along muddy shores and shallow water edges through creeping stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical buttercups, Halerpestes species have kidney-shaped or rounded leaves and grow as creeping plants along wet alkaline soils rather than standing upright in meadows.
children.funFact: The name Halerpestes comes from Greek words meaning 'salt' and 'creeper,' referring to their ability to thrive in salty or alkaline conditions where most other buttercups cannot survive.

children.name: Delphinium
children.description: Larkspurs are showy flowering plants known for their tall spikes of colorful, distinctively shaped flowers. These plants produce flowers with a characteristic backward-pointing spur that gives the genus its common name, and they typically bloom in vibrant blues, purples, pinks, or whites.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Larkspur flowers have a unique structure with a prominent spur extending backward from the upper petal, unlike other members of the buttercup family. The flowers are also arranged in dense, upright clusters called racemes.
children.funFact: The name 'larkspur' comes from the flower's resemblance to the long, straight claw (or spur) found on the hind toe of larks and other ground-dwelling birds.

children.name: Pulsatilla
children.description: Pasqueflowers are early spring wildflowers in the buttercup family that bloom before their leaves fully develop. These low-growing perennials produce cup-shaped flowers with silky, feathery seed heads that follow the blooms. They're adapted to cold climates and often push through snow to flower in late winter or early spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other buttercup family members, pasqueflowers are covered in fine, silky hairs that give them a fuzzy appearance and help protect them from cold. Their distinctive feathery, plume-like seed heads are much more prominent than those of related plants.
children.funFact: The name 'pasqueflower' comes from the French word 'pasque' meaning Easter, because these hardy flowers often bloom around Easter time, sometimes even pushing up through snow.

children.name: Enemion
children.description: False rue anemones are delicate spring wildflowers in the buttercup family that bloom in rich, moist woodlands. These small herbaceous plants produce clusters of white flowers with 5 petals and distinctive three-parted leaves that emerge directly from the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true rue anemones, false rue anemones have flowers with actual petals (rather than petal-like sepals) and their leaves are alternate rather than whorled around the stem.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they're imposters, false rue anemones were actually named first - the "true" rue anemone got its name later!

children.name: Eriocapitella
children.description: Fall-blooming anemones are a group of perennial wildflowers that produce their showy blooms in late summer and autumn, unlike most wildflowers that bloom in spring or early summer. These plants have distinctive palmate leaves and produce delicate, five-petaled flowers on tall, branching stems that can reach several feet in height.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike spring-blooming anemones, these species bloom from August through October and have woolly, cotton-like seed heads that give the genus its name (Eriocapitella means 'woolly little head').
children.funFact: These plants were originally classified as true anemones (Anemone genus) but were recently moved to their own genus based on genetic studies, making them botanical newcomers despite being garden favorites for over a century.

children.description: The buttercup family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes many familiar wildflowers and garden favorites. Members of this family typically have flowers with multiple petals (often 5) and numerous stamens, though some species have highly modified flower shapes like the spurred columbines or hooded monkshoods. These plants range from delicate woodland flowers like hepaticas to showy garden plants like larkspurs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most buttercup family members have flowers with parts arranged in spirals rather than distinct whorls, and they typically lack a fused corolla tube. Many species also have deeply divided or compound leaves and produce small, dry fruits called achenes.
children.funFact: Many members of the buttercup family contain toxic compounds called alkaloids, which is why livestock typically avoid grazing on buttercups and why names like 'baneberry' and 'monkshood' hint at their poisonous nature.

children.name: Papaveraceae
Corydalis
children.description: Corydalises are delicate wildflowers in the fumitory family known for their distinctive spurred flowers that often resemble tiny birds or abstract sculptures. These low-growing plants typically bloom in spring and early summer, producing clusters of tubular flowers with a characteristic backward-pointing spur that contains nectar.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the fumitory family, corydalises have flowers with only one spur (rather than two) and their leaves are often deeply divided or fern-like in appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'corydalis' comes from the Greek word for 'crested lark' because the flower's spur resembles the elongated hind claw of this small songbird.

children.name: Papaver
children.description: Poppies are annual or perennial flowering plants known for their papery, colorful petals and distinctive seed pods. All members of this genus produce flowers with four delicate petals that often appear crinkled, like tissue paper, and contain a milky sap. These plants typically have deeply lobed leaves and produce round or elongated capsules filled with tiny seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Poppies can be distinguished from other flowers by their characteristic papery petals that fall off easily when touched, and their unique seed pods that release seeds through small pores at the top like a salt shaker.
children.funFact: The iconic red poppies that grew on World War I battlefields in Europe belong to this genus (Papaver rhoeas), and their ability to quickly colonize disturbed soil made them a powerful symbol of remembrance.

children.name: Dicentra
children.description: Bleedinghearts are delicate woodland wildflowers known for their distinctive heart-shaped or uniquely formed flowers that dangle from arching stems. These perennial herbs emerge in early spring from underground bulbs or rhizomes, blooming before the forest canopy fully leafs out. All members of this genus have deeply divided, fern-like leaves and produce flowers with four petals arranged in characteristic drooping clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets bleedinghearts apart from other wildflowers is their unmistakable flower shape - either resembling tiny pantaloons hanging on a clothesline (like Dutchman's breeches) or classic heart shapes with droplets. Unlike most spring wildflowers, their petals form pouches or spurs that give each species its own distinctive silhouette.
children.funFact: Dutchman's breeches got their whimsical name because the white flowers with yellow tips look exactly like tiny pairs of pants hanging upside down to dry!

children.name: Chelidonium
children.description: Celandines are members of the poppy family known for their bright yellow, four-petaled flowers and distinctive orange or yellow sap that flows when stems or leaves are broken. These herbaceous plants typically bloom in spring and early summer, producing small pods filled with seeds that have special attachments to attract ants for dispersal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other poppies, celandines have consistently yellow flowers (never other colors) and produce a notably bright orange-yellow latex sap when damaged. Their leaves are also more deeply lobed and divided compared to most other poppy family members.
children.funFact: The orange sap of greater celandine was traditionally used as a natural remedy for warts and other skin conditions, earning it the folk name 'wart wort' - though modern science doesn't recommend this use!

children.name: Glaucium
children.description: Glaucium is a genus of distinctive poppies known as horned poppies, named for their unusually long, curved seed pods that can grow 6-12 inches long and resemble horns or sickles. These hardy plants produce large, papery flowers in bright colors like yellow and red, and are well-adapted to sandy, coastal environments. Both New England species are typically found near shorelines and in disturbed soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Horned poppies are easily distinguished from other poppies by their dramatically long, narrow, curved seed pods that split open to release seeds. They also have deeply lobed, blue-green leaves that are often covered with a waxy coating.
children.funFact: The curved seed pods of horned poppies can be over a foot long and were historically used as natural containers or scoops by coastal communities.

children.name: Pseudofumaria
children.description: Rock-fumitories are delicate wildflowers that belong to the poppy family and are known for their distinctive spurred flowers and finely divided, feathery leaves. These plants typically grow in rocky crevices, stone walls, and disturbed soils, often in shaded or partially shaded locations. Both New England species produce small, tubular flowers with a characteristic spur at the back.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rock-fumitories can be distinguished from other fumitory relatives by their preference for rocky habitats and their more robust, perennial growth habit. Unlike annual fumitories, these plants form persistent clumps that return year after year.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, rock-fumitories are incredibly resilient and can grow directly out of tiny cracks in stone walls and cliff faces, earning them the nickname 'wall plants' in some regions.

children.name: Fumaria
children.description: Fumitories are delicate annual plants with finely divided, feathery leaves that give them a soft, lacy appearance. These small wildflowers produce clusters of tiny, tubular pink or white flowers that have an unusual spurred shape. They are often found growing as weeds in disturbed soils, gardens, and waste areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fumitories can be identified by their unique flowers that have one petal extended into a distinctive spur at the back, and their extremely fine, thread-like leaf segments that look almost smoke-like in texture.
children.funFact: The name 'fumitory' comes from the Latin 'fumus terrae' meaning 'smoke of the earth,' because the plant's fine, grayish foliage was thought to resemble smoke rising from the ground.

children.name: Sanguinaria
children.description: Bloodroots are small spring wildflowers in the poppy family known for their distinctive white flowers and deeply lobed leaves. They get their name from the bright red-orange sap that flows from their underground stems when cut or broken. These woodland plants emerge early in spring before the forest canopy leafs out, taking advantage of the abundant sunlight.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bloodroots are easily recognized by their single white flower with 8-12 petals that emerges wrapped in a distinctive kidney-shaped leaf. The red-orange sap that gives them their name is unique among New England spring wildflowers.
children.funFact: Native Americans and early settlers used bloodroot's red sap as a natural dye and paint, and it was also used medicinally, though the plant contains toxic compounds that make it dangerous to ingest.

children.name: Capnoides
children.description: Capnoides is a small genus of delicate wildflowers in the fumitory family, characterized by their distinctive spurred flowers and finely divided, fern-like leaves. These plants are closely related to bleeding hearts and share similar intricate flower structures with pouched or spurred petals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Capnoides flowers have a distinctive spur at the base and are typically pink to purple in color, while their leaves are more finely dissected than those of their bleeding heart relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'Capnoides' comes from the Greek word meaning 'smoke-like,' referring to the plant's delicate, wispy appearance when growing among rocks.

children.name: Lamprocapnos
children.description: Lamprocapnos is a small genus of perennial flowering plants native to Asia, best known for the beloved garden plant called bleeding-heart. These plants produce distinctive heart-shaped flowers that dangle from arching stems, creating a romantic and delicate appearance in shade gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bleeding-heart relatives, Lamprocapnos species have flowers with two prominent outer petals that form the classic heart shape, while the inner petals are much smaller and often white-tipped.
children.funFact: The scientific name Lamprocapnos means 'bright smoke,' referring to the plant's relationship to the fumitory family, whose members were once thought to grow from vapors in the earth.

children.name: Eschscholzia
children.description: Desert poppies are a genus of colorful annual flowers known for their silky, cup-shaped blooms and finely divided, blue-green foliage. These hardy plants are adapted to dry conditions and produce vibrant orange, yellow, or cream-colored flowers that close at night and on cloudy days. They belong to the poppy family and are native to western North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true poppies, desert poppies have four petals instead of multiple petals, and their seed pods are long and slender rather than round. Their leaves are also more finely dissected and have a distinctive blue-gray color.
children.funFact: The California poppy was so abundant across California's landscapes that Spanish sailors could see the orange glow of hillsides covered in blooms from miles out at sea, calling the land 'the land of fire.'

children.name: Adlumia
children.description: Adlumia is a genus containing just one species of delicate climbing vine found in eastern North America. These plants are members of the fumitory family and are known for their graceful, twining habit and fern-like foliage. They produce clusters of small, heart-shaped flowers that dangle from the vine.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the fumitory family, Adlumia is a climbing vine that uses its leaf stalks to wrap around supports. Its flowers are distinctively heart-shaped and pink or white, hanging in drooping clusters.
children.funFact: Climbing fumitory is a biennial plant that spends its first year as a small rosette, then dramatically transforms in its second year into a climbing vine that can reach 12 feet tall.

children.name: Macleaya
children.description: Plume-poppies are tall, striking perennial plants in the poppy family that produce distinctive feathery flower clusters. Despite their name, they don't actually produce showy poppy-like flowers, but instead create impressive plumes of small, white or cream-colored blooms that lack petals entirely.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical poppies with their colorful, papery petals, plume-poppies have tiny flowers without petals that are arranged in large, airy, plume-like clusters. They also have distinctive large, lobed leaves with silvery undersides and can grow quite tall, reaching 6-8 feet in height.
children.funFact: Plume Poppy was traditionally used in Chinese medicine and contains alkaloids that make it naturally deer-resistant, though it can spread aggressively in garden settings through underground rhizomes.

children.name: Hylomecon
children.description: Hylomecon is a small genus of woodland poppies that includes just one species found in New England - the Forest Poppy. These are delicate perennial wildflowers that belong to the poppy family and are specially adapted to life in shaded forest environments. They produce bright yellow, four-petaled flowers in spring and have deeply lobed leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their more familiar poppy relatives that prefer sunny meadows and disturbed soils, Hylomecon species are true shade lovers that thrive in moist, rich woodland soils. Their flowers are consistently bright yellow with four petals, distinguishing them from other forest poppies that may have different colors or petal numbers.
children.funFact: The name Hylomecon literally means 'forest poppy' in Greek, perfectly describing these plants' preferred woodland habitat - a rare trait among poppies, most of which are sun-loving plants.

children.description: The Poppy Family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes the familiar garden poppies, delicate bleeding hearts, and several wildflowers found throughout New England. Most members of this family produce distinctive flowers with four petals (though some have six) and often contain colorful latex or sap when their stems or leaves are broken. These plants range from showy garden favorites to small woodland wildflowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Poppy family members typically have flowers with petals in multiples of two (usually 4 or 6) and often produce colored sap or latex when cut. Many species have distinctive seed pods that split open to release numerous small seeds.
children.funFact: Many plants in the poppy family contain alkaloids - the opium poppy produces morphine, while celandine produces a bright orange-yellow sap that was once used as a natural dye and folk remedy for warts.

children.name: Berberidaceae
Berberis
children.description: Barberries are shrubs known for their thorny stems and clusters of small, often yellow flowers that develop into colorful berries. Most species have spiny leaves or sharp thorns along their branches, making them popular choices for defensive hedging. These hardy plants can thrive in various conditions from full sun to partial shade.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barberries are easily recognized by their sharp thorns or spines and their distinctive flower structure with six petals arranged in two whorls. Their berries are typically elongated rather than round, and many species have leaves that turn brilliant colors in fall.
children.funFact: The inner bark and roots of barberries contain berberine, a bright yellow compound that has been used as a natural dye for centuries and was historically valued for its medicinal properties.

children.name: Caulophyllum
children.description: Blue cohoshes are distinctive woodland wildflowers that belong to the barberry family. These perennial herbs are characterized by their large, compound leaves that are divided into three main sections, and their small clusters of yellowish-green or purplish flowers that bloom in spring. They produce bright blue berry-like seeds that give the genus its common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blue cohoshes can be distinguished from other woodland plants by their unique three-part compound leaves with oval leaflets and their characteristic bright blue seeds that develop after flowering. The seeds are exposed rather than enclosed in a pod or capsule like many other plants.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'berries,' the bright blue structures are actually naked seeds with a fleshy outer coating, and they're toxic to humans but provide food for various woodland birds.

children.name: Epimedium
children.description: Barrenworts are delicate woodland perennials known for their distinctive spurred flowers and heart-shaped leaflets. These shade-loving plants produce small, intricate flowers with four petals that often have curved spurs extending backward, giving them an almost fairy-like appearance. They typically bloom in spring before their leaves fully emerge, creating a charming display in woodland gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barrenworts can be identified by their unique four-petaled flowers with prominent backward-pointing spurs and their compound leaves made up of heart-shaped leaflets. The flowers hang delicately from thin stems and come in colors ranging from white and yellow to pink and purple.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting barren or poor growing conditions, barrenworts are actually prized garden plants that can slowly spread to form attractive groundcover in shady areas where many other flowers struggle to grow.

children.name: Podophyllum
children.description: Mayapples are distinctive woodland plants known for their large, umbrella-like leaves and single white flower. These perennial herbs grow from underground rhizomes and are among the first plants to emerge in spring forests, creating carpets of green before the tree canopy fully leafs out.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mayapples are easily recognized by their deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves that look like green umbrellas, and their single nodding white flower that blooms beneath the leaves. Unlike most woodland wildflowers, they form large colonies through their spreading underground root system.
children.funFact: The mayapple's fruit is edible when fully ripe and yellow, but all other parts of the plant are toxic - Native Americans traditionally used the roots medicinally but knew to handle them with great care.

children.name: Jeffersonia
children.description: Jeffersonia is a small genus of woodland wildflowers known for their distinctive twin-lobed leaves that look like they've been split down the middle. These delicate spring ephemerals bloom early in the year before the forest canopy fills in, producing small white flowers that quickly give way to unusual seed pods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The deeply divided, butterfly-shaped leaves that appear to be split into two identical halves make Jeffersonia instantly recognizable. Their seed pods open with a hinged lid, like a tiny treasure chest.
children.funFact: Twinleaf was named after Thomas Jefferson, not only because he was president when it was first described scientifically, but also because he was an avid botanist who collected and studied native plants.

children.name: Nandina
children.description: Nandina is a small genus containing just a few species of evergreen shrubs native to eastern Asia. These plants are characterized by their compound leaves that change color seasonally and their clusters of small white flowers followed by bright red berries. Despite being called 'bamboo,' they are not related to true bamboos but belong to the barberry family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nandina can be distinguished from other shrubs by its delicate, finely divided compound leaves that turn brilliant shades of red and orange in fall and winter, combined with upright clusters of bright red berries that persist through winter.
children.funFact: The name 'heavenly bamboo' comes from the plant's bamboo-like appearance and its traditional use in Asian gardens as a symbol of good fortune, though it's actually more closely related to barberries than bamboos.

children.name: Diphylleia
children.description: Diphylleia is a small genus of woodland wildflowers known for their distinctive large, umbrella-like leaves and clusters of white flowers. These perennial herbs grow in shaded, moist forest environments and are characterized by their unique leaf structure and berry-like fruits that turn blue when ripe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have large, deeply lobed leaves that are typically arranged in pairs (hence 'Diphylleia' meaning 'two leaves'), and their white petals fall off easily after blooming, leaving behind the developing blue berries.
children.funFact: The leaves of Diphylleia become nearly transparent when wet, earning some species the nickname 'skeleton flower' - though our New England species is better known as umbrella-leaf for its broad, sheltering foliage.

children.description: The barberry family is a diverse group of plants that includes shrubs like barberries with their thorny stems and bright berries, as well as woodland wildflowers like mayapples with their umbrella-like leaves. Most members of this family have flowers with parts arranged in multiples of two or three, and many produce colorful fruits that are important food sources for wildlife. These plants can be found in various habitats from sunny garden borders to shady forest floors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barberry family members typically have flowers with twice as many stamens as petals, and their stamens often move when touched by insects. Many species also have compound leaves or leaves that are deeply divided, giving them a distinctive appearance.
children.funFact: The stamens of barberry flowers are like tiny spring-loaded catapults - when a bee touches them while seeking nectar, they quickly snap inward to dust the bee with pollen!

children.name: Menispermaceae
Menispermum
children.description: Moonseeds are climbing woody vines known for their distinctive crescent-shaped seeds that resemble a crescent moon. These plants produce small, inconspicuous flowers and dark blue to black berries that contain the characteristic curved seeds. They are part of a larger family of tropical and subtropical plants, though our New England species is well-adapted to temperate climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moonseeds can be identified by their unique crescent or moon-shaped seeds, which separate them from other climbing vines. The seeds have a distinctive curved ridge that creates their characteristic lunar appearance.
children.funFact: The moonseed's berries look very similar to wild grapes but are actually toxic to humans - the telltale difference is that grapes have round seeds while moonseeds have their signature crescent-shaped seeds.

children.description: The moonseed family is a small group of climbing vines known for their distinctive crescent-shaped seeds that resemble a half moon. These woody vines typically have heart-shaped or lobed leaves and produce small clusters of inconspicuous flowers that develop into grape-like berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Moonseed vines can be distinguished from similar climbing plants like wild grapes by their characteristic crescent-shaped seeds and the fact that their leaf stems attach to the blade away from the edge rather than at the base.
children.funFact: Despite looking similar to wild grapes, moonseed berries are highly toxic to humans - the crescent-shaped seed inside each berry is a key identifying feature that can help prevent dangerous confusion with edible grapes.

children.name: Lardizabalaceae
Akebia
children.description: Akebias are woody climbing vines in the chocolate vine family that produce distinctive compound leaves and fragrant flowers. These deciduous plants are native to East Asia but have been introduced to other regions as ornamental vines. They're known for their vigorous growth and ability to quickly cover fences, trellises, and other structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Akebias can be identified by their distinctive palmate compound leaves (typically with 3-5 leaflets) and their unique purple-brown flowers that lack petals. Unlike many other climbing vines, they produce edible sausage-shaped fruits that split open when ripe to reveal seeds surrounded by translucent pulp.
children.funFact: The name 'chocolate vine' comes from the sweet, chocolate-like fragrance of their spring flowers, though the scent is most noticeable in the evening hours.

children.description: The Lardizabalaceae family consists of woody climbing vines with distinctive compound leaves and separate male and female flowers on the same plant. These plants are known for their twining growth habit and ability to scramble up trees and structures. Most species in this family are native to East Asia, with only a few found in other regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their palmately compound leaves (like fingers on a hand) and their dioecious or monoecious flowering pattern where male and female flowers are separate. The flowers lack petals but have colorful sepals, and the fruits are distinctive sausage-shaped pods.
children.funFact: The name 'Lardizabalaceae' comes from the Spanish naturalist Miguel de Lardizábal, and some species in this family produce edible fruits that are considered delicacies in parts of Asia, despite being relatively unknown in North America.

children.description: This diverse order includes some of New England's most recognizable wildflowers and garden plants, from cheerful yellow buttercups in meadows to vibrant poppies and colorful columbines. Despite their varied appearances, these plants share ancient evolutionary relationships and similar flower structures, with many petals and reproductive parts arranged in spirals or circles. The group spans from tiny woodland herbs to climbing vines and shrubs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have flowers with numerous stamens and often multiple separate pistils, giving them a more primitive flower structure compared to most modern flowering plants. Many also produce unique alkaloid compounds that can be toxic to animals.
children.funFact: This order includes some of the most poisonous plants in New England, including bittersweet nightshade and bloodroot, but also gives us beautiful garden favorites like peonies and clematis vines.

children.name: Brassicales
Brassicaceae
Cardamine
children.description: Bittercresses and toothworts are a diverse group of small flowering plants in the mustard family, known for their delicate four-petaled white or pink flowers and distinctive seed pods that split open explosively when ripe. These plants range from tiny weeds that pop up in garden paths to woodland wildflowers that carpet the forest floor in early spring. Many have a peppery taste and have been used as wild edibles throughout history.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mustard family plants, many Cardamine species have explosive seed pods that can shoot seeds several feet away when touched, earning some the nickname 'pop weeds.' The group also includes both annual weeds and perennial woodland plants with underground tubers or rhizomes.
children.funFact: Hairy bittercress can complete its entire life cycle from seed to flowering plant in just 5-6 weeks, making it one of the fastest-growing wildflowers in New England!

children.name: Lepidium
children.description: Pepperweeds are a group of small flowering plants in the mustard family known for their tiny white flowers and peppery-tasting leaves. These hardy plants typically grow as weeds in disturbed soils like roadsides, fields, and garden beds, and produce small, flattened seed pods that help distinguish them from other mustard family members.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pepperweeds can be identified by their characteristic small, oval to round seed pods that are flattened and notched at the tip, unlike the longer, cylindrical pods of many other mustard family plants.
children.funFact: The leaves of pepperweeds have a sharp, peppery taste that early settlers used as a spice and salad green, earning them the common name 'peppergrass.'

children.name: Barbarea
children.description: Wintercresses are hardy mustard family plants that thrive in cool weather and can often be found growing throughout winter months. These yellow-flowered herbs typically grow in moist areas like stream banks, ditches, and wet meadows, forming rosettes of deeply lobed leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mustard family plants, wintercresses have distinctively shaped leaves with a large terminal lobe and smaller side lobes, giving them an almost lyrate appearance. They also bloom earlier in the season than most related plants, often starting in late winter or early spring.
children.funFact: Several wintercress species are edible and were traditionally used as early spring greens, earning them the nickname 'poor man's watercress' for their peppery, vitamin-rich leaves that could sustain people through the lean winter months.

children.name: Brassica
children.description: The Brassica genus includes some of our most familiar vegetables and wild plants, all sharing the characteristic four-petaled flowers arranged in a cross pattern. These plants are part of the mustard family and produce seed pods that split open when ripe to release small, round seeds. Many species have a spicy or peppery taste due to natural compounds called glucosinolates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brassica plants are distinguished by their four-petaled flowers that form a distinctive cross shape, giving the mustard family its alternate name 'Cruciferae' meaning 'cross-bearing.' Their fruits are elongated pods called siliques that contain seeds in two rows.
children.funFact: Many vegetables we think of as completely different - like cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts - are actually all varieties of the same species, Brassica oleracea, selectively bred over thousands of years for different plant parts!

children.name: Draba
children.description: Drabas are small, delicate wildflowers in the mustard family that typically grow close to the ground in rosettes or low mats. These hardy little plants produce tiny white or yellow four-petaled flowers and are often among the first to bloom in spring, even in harsh conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Drabas can be distinguished from other mustard family members by their extremely small size, often less than 6 inches tall, and their characteristic heart-shaped or oval seed pods that are flattened and typically less than half an inch long.
children.funFact: Common Whitlowgrass got its name because people once believed it could cure whitlows - painful infections around fingernails and toenails.

children.name: Erysimum
children.description: Wallflowers are slender annual or biennial plants in the mustard family that produce clusters of small, four-petaled flowers typically in shades of yellow or orange. These hardy plants often grow in disturbed soils, roadsides, and waste areas, and are known for their ability to thrive in poor growing conditions. All wallflower species have narrow, elongated seed pods that split open when mature to release their seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wallflowers can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive long, narrow seed pods (called siliques) and their preference for growing in linear clusters along stems. Their flowers also tend to be more intensely colored than many of their mustard relatives.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they're shy bloomers, wallflowers are actually quite bold - some species can produce flowers almost year-round in mild climates, earning them the nickname 'winter bloomers.'

children.name: Borodinia
children.description: Rockcresses are small to medium-sized flowering plants in the mustard family that typically grow in rocky or sandy habitats. These hardy perennials produce clusters of small, four-petaled white or pale yellow flowers and have narrow, elongated seed pods that help distinguish them from other mustard family members.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Borodinia rockcresses can be identified by their distinctive curved or sickle-shaped seed pods and their preference for growing in rocky, well-drained soils. Their leaves are often hairy or fuzzy, and the plants tend to form low rosettes at the base.
children.funFact: The sicklepod rockcress gets its common name from its dramatically curved seed pods that resemble tiny sickles or crescent moons.

children.name: Rorippa
children.description: Yellowcresses are small wetland plants in the mustard family that produce tiny yellow flowers arranged in clusters. These hardy plants are specially adapted to grow in moist soils, wet meadows, and even areas that flood periodically. All three New England species share the characteristic four-petaled yellow blooms and preference for wet habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mustard family plants, yellowcresses have very small, inconspicuous yellow petals that are often shorter than their sepals. Their wetland habitat preference also sets them apart from most other members of the mustard family.
children.funFact: The Amphibious Yellowcress can actually grow both on land and partially submerged in water, producing different leaf shapes depending on whether it's growing above or below the waterline.

children.name: Sisymbrium
children.description: Hedgemustards are a group of weedy plants in the mustard family that typically grow in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, and garden edges. These annual herbs produce small yellow flowers arranged in clusters and develop distinctive narrow, pod-like fruits called siliques that contain their seeds. Most species are non-native plants that have adapted well to life in human-modified environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hedgemustards can be identified by their combination of small four-petaled yellow flowers, deeply divided or lobed leaves, and especially their long, narrow seed pods that are much thinner than those of most other mustard family plants.
children.funFact: The Tall Tumblemustard lives up to its name by breaking off at the base when mature and tumbling across the landscape like a tumbleweed, scattering thousands of seeds as it rolls.

children.name: Arabidopsis
children.description: Arabidopsis is a small genus of delicate annual herbs in the mustard family, known for their tiny white four-petaled flowers and small, often deeply-lobed leaves. These unassuming plants are typically found in disturbed soils, fields, and rocky areas throughout temperate regions. Despite their modest appearance, they play an outsized role in scientific research.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other mustards by their combination of very small white flowers, deeply divided or lobed leaves, and slender, upright seed pods called siliques that are much longer than they are wide.
children.funFact: Mouse-ear cress (Arabidopsis thaliana) was the first plant to have its entire genome sequenced and is considered the 'lab rat' of the plant world, helping scientists understand how all plants grow and develop.

children.name: Nasturtium
children.description: Watercresses are aquatic or semi-aquatic plants in the mustard family that grow in shallow water, streams, and wet areas. These perennial herbs have small white flowers arranged in clusters and produce edible leaves with a distinctive peppery taste that has made them popular in salads and cooking for centuries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the mustard family, watercresses are specially adapted for aquatic life with hollow stems that help them float and roots that can grow from stem nodes when in contact with water or mud.
children.funFact: Watercress is considered one of the most nutrient-dense foods on Earth, containing more vitamin C per serving than oranges and more iron than spinach!

children.name: Boechera
children.description: Rockcresses are small wildflowers in the mustard family that typically grow in rocky or disturbed soils. These hardy plants produce clusters of small, four-petaled white or pale flowers and have narrow, elongated seed pods that split open when mature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rockcresses can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive narrow, upright seed pods and their preference for growing in rocky habitats rather than rich soils.
children.funFact: Many rockcress species can reproduce without pollination through a process called apomixis, essentially cloning themselves to create genetically identical offspring.

children.name: Mutarda
children.description: Mutarda is a genus of wild mustard plants that are common weeds throughout New England. These annual herbs produce clusters of small, four-petaled yellow flowers and have deeply lobed or toothed leaves that often have a spicy, mustard-like smell when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mutarda can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive seed pods (siliques) that have a prominent beak at the tip and their characteristic leaf shapes that vary from deeply lobed to irregularly toothed.
children.funFact: Black mustard seeds from Mutarda nigra have been used for thousands of years to make the condiment we know as mustard, and the plants can grow over 6 feet tall under ideal conditions.

children.name: Diplotaxis
children.description: Wall-rockets are small mustard family plants that specialize in growing in disturbed, rocky areas like walls, sidewalk cracks, and waste places. These hardy plants produce small yellow four-petaled flowers and deeply divided leaves, thriving in poor soils where many other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wall-rockets can be separated from other mustard plants by their deeply lobed leaves and their preference for growing directly from cracks in walls and pavement. Their seed pods are also notably long and narrow compared to many related species.
children.funFact: Despite their weedy appearance, wall-rockets are actually edible and have been used as salad greens in Europe for centuries, with a peppery flavor similar to arugula.

children.name: Iberis
children.description: Candytufts are small flowering plants in the mustard family that produce distinctive clusters of tiny white or pink flowers. These hardy plants typically bloom in spring and early summer, creating dense carpets of flowers that are beloved by gardeners and pollinators alike. Most species are low-growing and spread horizontally, making them excellent ground covers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Candytufts can be identified by their unique flower clusters that are flat-topped or slightly rounded, with the outer flowers having larger petals than the inner ones, creating an umbrella-like appearance. Unlike many other mustard family members, their flowers are notably asymmetrical.
children.funFact: The name 'candytuft' comes from Candia, the former name for Crete, where many species in this genus naturally occur, though the flowers' resemblance to small white candies certainly fits the name!

children.name: Alliaria
children.description: Garlic mustards are herbaceous plants in the mustard family that get their name from the distinctive garlic-like odor their leaves release when crushed. These biennial plants form a basal rosette of heart-shaped leaves in their first year, then produce tall flowering stalks with small white four-petaled flowers in their second year.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mustard family plants, garlic mustards have the unique characteristic of smelling strongly of garlic when their leaves are bruised or crushed, making them easily identifiable even without flowers.
children.funFact: Garlic mustard was brought to North America by European settlers in the 1860s for use as a culinary herb, but it has since become one of the most aggressive invasive plants in eastern forests, capable of dominating the forest floor and reducing native plant diversity.

children.name: Hesperis
children.description: Hesperis is a small genus of flowering plants in the mustard family, known for their fragrant, four-petaled flowers that bloom in spring and early summer. These plants are herbaceous perennials or biennials that produce clusters of purple, pink, or white flowers followed by long, narrow seed pods typical of the mustard family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hesperis plants are distinguished from other mustard family members by their sweet evening fragrance and their relatively large, showy flowers arranged in loose clusters. The flowers have a distinctive cross-shaped arrangement of four petals and release their strongest scent at dusk.
children.funFact: Dame's rocket, the sole New England representative of this genus, was brought to North America by European settlers who valued it as both an ornamental garden flower and a source of evening fragrance, earning it the nickname 'evening rocket.'

children.name: Cakile
children.description: Searockets are succulent plants in the mustard family that have specially adapted to life on sandy beaches and coastal shores. These hardy plants can tolerate salt spray, shifting sands, and harsh coastal conditions that would kill most other flowering plants. They produce small, four-petaled flowers typical of mustard family plants and distinctive seed pods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mustard family plants, searockets have thick, fleshy leaves that store water and help them survive in sandy, salt-rich environments. Their seed pods are uniquely segmented and cork-like, designed to float in seawater for dispersal.
children.funFact: Searocket seeds can survive floating in ocean water for months, allowing them to colonize distant beaches and islands by riding ocean currents like tiny botanical rafts.

children.name: Turritis
children.description: Tower mustards are tall, slender wildflowers in the mustard family that get their name from their distinctive towering growth habit. These plants produce narrow spikes of small white or pale yellow flowers that can reach several feet in height, creating an impressive vertical display in their woodland and meadow habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tower mustards are easily recognized by their exceptionally tall, narrow flower spikes and their characteristic basal rosette of leaves at ground level. Unlike many other mustards, they have a distinctly columnar appearance with flowers arranged closely along the stem.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'tower' mustards for their impressive height, these plants are actually quite rare in New England, with only one species found in the region.

children.name: Lunaria
children.description: Honesties are distinctive flowering plants in the mustard family known for their unique seed pods that develop transparent, papery partitions after the seeds are released. These annual or biennial herbs produce clusters of purple or white four-petaled flowers in spring, followed by large, flat, oval seed pods. The plants are popular in gardens both for their attractive blooms and their ornamental dried seed pods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Honesties are easily recognized by their large, flat, circular to oval seed pods that become translucent and silvery when mature, resembling coins or medallions. Unlike most other mustard family plants, their seed pods are broad and disc-like rather than long and narrow.
children.funFact: The common name "honesty" comes from the transparent seed pods that allow you to see right through them, symbolizing truthfulness and openness.

children.name: Berteroa
children.description: Berteroa is a small genus of flowering plants in the mustard family, with delicate white flowers that have deeply notched petals. These annual or biennial herbs are covered in star-shaped hairs that give them a grayish, hoary appearance. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species that was introduced from Europe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Berteroa can be distinguished from other white-flowered mustards by its deeply divided petals that appear almost like four separate petals, and its distinctive grayish coloration from dense star-shaped hairs covering the entire plant.
children.funFact: The star-shaped hairs covering hoary alyssum are so dense that they create a felt-like texture, helping the plant retain moisture and reflect excess sunlight in harsh conditions.

children.name: Thlaspi
children.description: Penny cresses are small annual herbs in the mustard family that get their name from their distinctive flat, round seed pods that resemble old pennies. These weedy plants typically have small white flowers arranged in clusters and produce characteristic heart-shaped or circular flattened fruits. They're often found in disturbed soils like farm fields, roadsides, and waste areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The flat, coin-shaped seed pods with a distinct notch at the tip are the most reliable way to identify penny cresses from other mustard family plants. Unlike many other mustards, their fruits are notably flattened and disc-like rather than long and narrow.
children.funFact: Field penny-cress seeds can remain viable in the soil for decades, and a single plant can produce up to 15,000 seeds, making it both a persistent agricultural weed and a survivor in harsh conditions.

children.name: Capsella
children.description: Shepherd's-purses are small annual plants in the mustard family with distinctive heart-shaped seed pods that give them their common name. These hardy weeds produce tiny white flowers in clusters and can be found growing in disturbed soils, gardens, and roadsides throughout the year.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The triangular, heart-shaped seed pods that resemble an old-fashioned shepherd's leather pouch are the key identifying feature that sets this genus apart from other mustard family plants.
children.funFact: Shepherd's-purse has been used as a medicinal herb for thousands of years to help stop bleeding, and its seeds can remain viable in soil for up to 35 years!

children.name: Raphanus
children.description: Radishes are a genus of flowering plants in the mustard family known for their edible roots and distinctive four-petaled flowers. These annual or biennial herbs produce fleshy taproots that can range from small and round to long and cylindrical, depending on the species and variety. Both wild and cultivated radishes share similar flower structures and seed pods, though they differ significantly in root development.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Radishes can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their inflated, spongy seed pods that don't split open when mature, and their typically swollen, fleshy taproots. Their flowers are usually white, pink, or purple with visible veining on the petals.
children.funFact: Wild radish seeds can remain viable in the soil for over 20 years, allowing them to persist through multiple crop rotations and emerge when conditions are favorable.

children.name: Teesdalia
children.description: Shepherdscress is a small genus of delicate annual plants in the mustard family. These tiny wildflowers are characterized by their basal rosette of leaves and small white flowers that bloom on nearly leafless stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many mustard family plants, Shepherdscress has distinctly unequal petals - the outer petals are noticeably larger than the inner ones, giving the flowers an asymmetrical appearance.
children.funFact: Despite its common name suggesting a connection to shepherds, this plant is actually named after Robert Teesdale, an 18th-century English botanist who studied Yorkshire flora.

children.name: Lobularia
children.description: Lobularia is a small genus of low-growing annual plants in the mustard family, best known for the popular garden flower sweet alyssum. These compact plants produce masses of tiny, four-petaled flowers that form dense, fragrant clusters. They are native to the Mediterranean region but have become widely cultivated and occasionally naturalized in temperate areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweet alyssum can be distinguished from other small mustard family flowers by its distinctive honey-like fragrance and its tiny flowers that are densely packed into rounded, dome-shaped clusters. The individual flowers are much smaller than most other members of the mustard family.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'alyssum,' sweet alyssum was moved from the genus Alyssum to Lobularia based on genetic studies, though gardeners and seed packets often still use the old name!

children.name: Armoracia
children.description: Armoracia is a small genus of perennial plants in the mustard family, best known for containing horseradish. These plants are characterized by their large, coarse leaves and thick, fleshy roots that contain pungent compounds called glucosinolates, which give them their distinctive sharp, fiery taste.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mustard family plants, Armoracia species have exceptionally thick, deeply penetrating taproots that can extend several feet into the ground. Their roots contain much higher concentrations of volatile oils and sharp-tasting compounds than typical mustard relatives.
children.funFact: Horseradish roots contain enzymes that only create their fiery bite when the root tissue is damaged - intact roots are relatively mild, but grating or cutting them triggers a chemical reaction that produces the sinus-clearing heat we associate with horseradish sauce.

children.name: Eruca
children.description: Eruca is a small genus of annual plants in the mustard family, best known for the species we commonly call arugula or rocket salad. These Mediterranean natives are fast-growing herbs with deeply lobed, somewhat spicy-tasting leaves that have been cultivated as salad greens for thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eruca species are distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive deeply-cut, pinnatifid leaves and four-petaled white or pale yellow flowers with dark veins. The leaves have a characteristic peppery, nutty flavor that becomes more pronounced as the plant matures.
children.funFact: The name 'rocket' comes from the French 'roquette,' which derives from the Latin 'eruca' - the Romans considered arugula an aphrodisiac and dedicated it to Priapus, the god of fertility!

children.name: Mummenhoffia
children.description: Mummenhoffia is a small genus of flowering plants in the mustard family (Brassicaceae) that includes just a few species of small annual herbs. These plants are characterized by their tiny white flowers arranged in clusters and their distinctive seed pods that split open to release small seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mummenhoffia is distinguished from other mustard family plants by its very small, rounded seed pods (silicles) and its tendency to grow in disturbed soils and waste places.
children.funFact: The genus was named after botanist Ihsan A. Al-Shehbaz's mentor, and despite being in the mustard family, the garlic penny-cress gets its name from its subtle garlic-like smell when crushed.

children.name: Erucastrum
children.description: Dog Mustards are a small genus of annual plants in the mustard family that produce clusters of small, four-petaled yellow flowers. These Mediterranean natives have deeply lobed leaves and develop long, narrow seed pods called siliques that split open when mature to release their seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dog Mustards can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their combination of deeply divided, hairy leaves and their relatively large yellow flowers that are arranged in loose clusters at the top of branching stems.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Dog Mustards,' these plants are actually edible and their young leaves can be used in salads, though they have a somewhat bitter, peppery taste similar to arugula.

children.name: Arabis
children.description: Rock-cresses are a genus of small flowering plants in the mustard family that typically grow in rocky, mountainous areas or disturbed soils. These hardy plants produce clusters of small, four-petaled white or pink flowers and have narrow, elongated seed pods that split open to release tiny seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rock-cresses can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their characteristically long, slender seed pods that stand upright and their preference for growing in rocky or sandy habitats where few other plants thrive.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, rock-cresses are incredibly tough survivors that can grow in harsh conditions like cliff faces and gravelly roadside ditches where most other plants cannot establish themselves.

children.name: Malcolmia
children.description: Malcolmia is a small genus of delicate annual flowering plants in the mustard family. These plants are characterized by their small, four-petaled flowers that bloom in clusters and their simple, narrow leaves that grow along slender stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Malcolmia species can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive seed pods that are long, narrow, and slightly flattened, along with their particularly small flower size compared to most other members of the family.
children.funFact: Despite being called Virginia Stock, Malcolmia maritima is actually native to the Mediterranean region and was likely introduced to coastal areas of New England, where it thrives in sandy soils near the ocean.

children.name: Crambe
children.description: Sea-kales are robust perennial plants in the mustard family that grow in coastal environments. They produce thick, fleshy leaves and clusters of small white flowers that develop into round, corky seed pods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mustard family plants, sea-kales have unusually thick, cabbage-like leaves and distinctive cork-covered fruits that help them survive harsh seaside conditions.
children.funFact: Sea kale leaves were historically blanched under pots or sand and eaten as a delicacy in Europe, similar to how asparagus is prepared today.

children.name: Coincya
children.description: Coincya is a small genus of flowering plants in the mustard family (Brassicaceae) that are closely related to cabbage and other cruciferous vegetables. These plants are typically found in coastal areas and are known for their four-petaled yellow flowers and ability to thrive in harsh, salty environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coincya species can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive seed pods that are beaked at the tip and their preference for maritime habitats with sandy or rocky soils.
children.funFact: The Isle of Man Cabbage is one of Britain's rarest native plants and was thought to be extinct until a small population was rediscovered in 1998 on the west coast of the Isle of Man.

children.name: Noccaea
children.description: Noccaea is a small genus of annual herbs in the mustard family, commonly known as penny-cresses. These plants are characterized by their small white flowers arranged in clusters and their distinctive flat, round seed pods that resemble tiny coins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Noccaea can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their uniquely shaped silicles (seed pods) that are broadly winged and notched at the tip, giving them a distinctive penny-like appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'penny-cress' comes from the seed pods that look remarkably similar to small coins, and these seeds were historically sometimes used as a substitute for coins in children's games.

children.name: Aurinia
children.description: Aurinia is a small genus of low-growing perennial plants in the mustard family, known for their clusters of tiny four-petaled flowers and ability to thrive in rocky, well-drained conditions. These hardy plants form dense mats or cushions of small, often fuzzy leaves that help them survive in challenging mountain and alpine environments. They are popular in rock gardens and as ground cover in sunny, dry locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aurinia can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their distinctive bright yellow flower clusters that bloom in dense, rounded heads above silvery-gray or green foliage. The flowers have four petals arranged in a cross pattern, and the leaves are typically small, narrow, and often covered with fine hairs.
children.funFact: Gold-dust (Aurinia saxatilis) gets its common name from its spectacular spring display of brilliant yellow flowers that can completely cover the plant, creating the appearance of golden dust sprinkled across rocky hillsides.

children.name: Conringia
children.description: Conringia is a small genus of annual plants in the mustard family, characterized by their distinctive clasping leaves that wrap around the stem. These plants produce small, pale yellow flowers in clusters and develop long, narrow seed pods typical of mustard family members.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The key feature that sets Conringia apart from other mustard family plants is its smooth, waxy leaves that clasp tightly around the stem with ear-like lobes at the base, giving it the common name 'hare's-ear mustard.'
children.funFact: Despite its common name suggesting it's native to New England, hare's-ear mustard is actually an introduced species from Europe and Asia that has become naturalized in disturbed soils across North America.

children.name: Isatis
children.description: Woads are annual or biennial plants in the mustard family known for their bright yellow flowers and distinctive flat, winged seed pods. These hardy herbs typically grow 2-4 feet tall with smooth, blue-green leaves that clasp around the stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Woads are easily recognized by their unique flat, oval seed pods that hang like tiny shields from the branching stems, quite different from the cylindrical pods of most mustard family plants.
children.funFact: Woad leaves contain a blue dye that was historically used to create the famous 'woad blue' color worn by ancient Celtic warriors and later became an important trade commodity in medieval Europe.

children.name: Subularia
children.description: Subularia is a small genus of aquatic plants in the mustard family (Brassicaceae) that are specially adapted to life underwater or in very wet conditions. These tiny plants produce small white flowers and have narrow, awl-shaped leaves that give them their common name of awlwort.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most members of the mustard family which are terrestrial, Subularia species are aquatic or semi-aquatic plants that can grow completely submerged in water. Their narrow, pointed leaves and ability to flower underwater distinguish them from other mustard family plants.
children.funFact: Awlwort is one of the few members of the mustard family that can complete its entire life cycle underwater, including producing flowers and seeds while completely submerged.

children.name: Matthiola
children.description: Stock (Matthiola) is a genus of fragrant flowering plants in the mustard family, known for their distinctive four-petaled flowers and sweet evening scent. These plants are typically herbaceous annuals or short-lived perennials that produce clusters of colorful blooms along upright stems. Most species are native to the Mediterranean region and southwestern Asia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stock can be distinguished from other mustard family plants by their densely clustered, four-petaled flowers that release an intense, sweet fragrance, especially in the evening. The flowers are typically much showier and more fragrant than most other members of the mustard family.
children.funFact: Evening Stock releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract night-flying moths for pollination, making it a perfect addition to moon gardens designed for evening enjoyment.

children.name: Tomostima
children.description: Tomostima is a small genus of delicate annual wildflowers in the mustard family. These tiny plants are characterized by their low-growing, spreading habit and small white flowers that bloom in early spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mustard family plants, Tomostima species have a distinctly creeping or mat-forming growth pattern with very small leaves and flowers that appear almost flat against the ground.
children.funFact: Carolina draba was once thought to be native only to the southeastern United States, but populations have been discovered as far north as New England, showing how plant distributions can surprise botanists.

children.description: The mustard family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes familiar vegetables like cabbage, broccoli, and radishes, as well as many wild species found throughout New England's fields, roadsides, and woodlands. These plants are united by their distinctive four-petaled flowers arranged in a cross shape and their often peppery or spicy taste. Members range from tiny weeds to garden crops, but all share similar flower and fruit structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mustard family plants can be identified by their four-petaled flowers arranged in a cross pattern and their seed pods that split open along two seams when mature. Many also have a characteristic sharp, peppery taste due to sulfur-containing compounds called glucosinates.
children.funFact: The tiny plant Arabidopsis thaliana, a member of this family, was the first plant to have its entire genome sequenced and is now one of the most studied organisms in plant biology research worldwide.

children.name: Cleomaceae
Cleome
children.description: Spider flowers are distinctive annual plants known for their unusual flower clusters that bloom throughout the summer. The flowers have long, thin stamens that extend far beyond the petals, creating a spidery appearance that gives these plants their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spider flowers are easily recognized by their extremely long, protruding stamens and pistils that extend well beyond the flower petals, creating a distinctive spidery look unlike most other flowering plants.
children.funFact: Spider flowers are self-cleaning plants that drop their spent flowers on their own, so gardeners never need to deadhead them to keep them blooming continuously.

children.name: Polanisia
children.description: Clammyweeds are annual wildflowers in the caper family known for their sticky, glandular stems and leaves that feel clammy to the touch. These plants produce small white or pinkish flowers with long, protruding stamens that give them a delicate, wispy appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives in the cleome genus, clammyweeds have shorter seed pods and typically smaller flowers with fewer stamens.
children.funFact: The sticky, clammy texture that gives these plants their name helps them trap small insects, which may provide additional nutrients even though they're not true carnivorous plants.

children.description: The Spider Flower Family consists of annual herbs with distinctive flowers that have long, thin stamens extending well beyond the petals, giving them a spider-like appearance. These plants typically have palm-shaped compound leaves and produce small pods containing seeds. Most members of this family prefer disturbed soils and open, sunny areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The extremely long, protruding stamens that extend far beyond the flower petals are the most distinctive feature, creating the characteristic 'spidery' look that gives the family its common name.
children.funFact: Spider flowers are popular in butterfly gardens because their long stamens make perfect landing platforms for butterflies and other pollinators to perch on while feeding on nectar.

children.name: Limnanthaceae
Limnanthes
children.description: Meadowfoams are small annual wildflowers that thrive in wet meadows, vernal pools, and other seasonally moist areas. These delicate plants produce bowl-shaped flowers with five white or yellow petals that often have distinctive veining patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Meadowfoams can be identified by their deeply lobed leaves and their preference for growing in areas that flood in winter and spring but dry out in summer. Their flowers have a unique structure with stamens that bend inward toward the center.
children.funFact: Despite being called meadowfoams, these plants are actually native to western North America and Douglas' meadowfoam in New England is likely an introduced garden escapee that has naturalized in suitable wet habitats.

children.name: Floerkea
children.description: False mermaids are small, delicate annual wildflowers that belong to a unique plant family found only in North America. These tiny plants produce inconspicuous flowers and grow in moist, shaded areas like floodplains and rich woodlands. Despite their whimsical name, they are terrestrial plants with no connection to aquatic environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: False mermaids are distinguished by their deeply divided, feathery leaves that give them an almost fern-like appearance, and their extremely small white flowers that are easily overlooked. They are the sole genus in their own plant family, Limnanthaceae, making them quite unique among North American wildflowers.
children.funFact: The genus Floerkea is so distinctive that it represents an entire plant family by itself in New England, making the false mermaid one of the region's most taxonomically isolated wildflowers.

children.description: The meadowfoam family is a small group of delicate annual wildflowers that thrive in moist, often marshy habitats. These low-growing plants produce small, cup-shaped flowers with 3-5 petals and have deeply divided, feathery leaves that give them a distinctive appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have flowers with the same number of petals as sepals (usually 3-5), and their fruits split into separate nutlets. The leaves are alternate and deeply dissected into narrow segments, creating a lacy, fern-like texture.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'meadowfoam,' these plants don't actually produce foam - the name comes from their tendency to grow in dense patches that can make wet meadows appear white and frothy from a distance when in bloom.

children.name: Tropaeolaceae
Tropaeolum
children.description: Nasturtiums are colorful flowering plants known for their round, shield-like leaves and bright, spurred flowers that come in shades of yellow, orange, and red. These climbing or trailing plants are popular in gardens and have a distinctive peppery taste that makes both their flowers and leaves edible. They belong to their own unique plant family and are native to South and Central America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nasturtiums can be easily identified by their circular, flat leaves with veins radiating from the center like wheel spokes, and their distinctive flowers with long spurs extending backward from the bloom.
children.funFact: Nasturtium flowers and leaves have a spicy, peppery flavor similar to watercress and are completely edible, making them popular additions to salads and as garnishes for their bright colors and peppery kick.

children.description: The nasturtium family is a small group of flowering plants known for their distinctive round, shield-like leaves and bright, spurred flowers. These plants typically have a peppery taste and climbing or trailing growth habits, making them popular in both gardens and as edible additions to salads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their unique flowers with five petals and a prominent backward-pointing spur, along with their circular leaves that are often attached to the stem at the center rather than the edge.
children.funFact: Nasturtium flowers and leaves are completely edible and have a peppery, watercress-like flavor that makes them a colorful and spicy addition to salads and garnishes.

children.name: Caricaceae
Carica
children.description: Carica is a small genus of tropical trees best known for the common papaya, which produces large, sweet orange fruits. These fast-growing trees have hollow stems, large lobed leaves clustered at the top, and most are either male or female plants that need both to produce fruit.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Carica trees are distinguished by their unbranched trunks with soft, hollow stems and their distinctive large, deeply-lobed leaves that grow in a crown at the top of the tree.
children.funFact: Papaya trees can grow from seed to fruit-bearing in just one year, making them one of the fastest fruit trees to mature!

children.description: The papaya family consists of tropical and subtropical plants known for their soft, fast-growing woody stems and large, deeply lobed leaves. Most members produce latex (milky sap) and have separate male and female flowers, often on different plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other flowering plant families, papaya family members have very soft, spongy wood that's almost succulent-like, and their leaves are typically arranged in spiral clusters at the tops of unbranched stems.
children.funFact: The papaya tree can grow from seed to fruit-bearing maturity in just 6-12 months, making it one of the fastest-growing fruit trees in the world.

children.description: The Brassicales is a diverse order of flowering plants that includes many familiar garden vegetables and wildflowers. Most members of this group produce compounds called glucosinolates, which give plants like mustard, cabbage, and radishes their distinctive sharp, peppery flavors. These plants range from tiny weeds to large trees, but they're united by their unique chemistry and flower structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Brassicales apart is their production of glucosinolates - sulfur-containing compounds that create spicy, bitter, or pungent flavors as a defense against herbivores. Many also share a characteristic flower pattern with four petals arranged in a cross shape, especially in the mustard family.
children.funFact: This order includes an amazing variety of foods we eat daily - from broccoli, kale, and Brussels sprouts (all the same species!) to horseradish, watercress, and even tropical papayas!

children.name: Apiales
Apiaceae
Sanicula
children.description: Sanicles are woodland herbs in the carrot family that produce small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in tight, rounded clusters. These perennial plants typically grow in shaded forest environments and have deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves. All sanicles develop distinctive bur-like fruits covered with hooked bristles that easily attach to clothing and animal fur.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other members of the carrot family, sanicles have flowers arranged in dense, ball-like clusters rather than flat-topped umbels. Their fruits are also uniquely covered with hooked bristles, setting them apart from the smooth or ribbed fruits of related plants.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'snakeroot' for some species, sanicles were historically considered a cure-all herb, with their Latin name derived from 'sanare,' meaning 'to heal.'

children.name: Anthriscus
