children.description: Chervils are delicate annual or biennial herbs in the carrot family, characterized by their finely divided, lacy leaves and small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters. These plants typically grow in disturbed soils, woodland edges, and gardens, with most species preferring partial shade to full sun. All members of this genus produce small, elongated fruits with distinctive ridges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chervils can be distinguished from other carrot family plants by their smooth, often shiny stems and their fruits which are typically longer than they are wide, often with a distinctive beak-like projection.
children.funFact: Garden Chervil has been cultivated for over 2,000 years as a culinary herb, prized by French chefs for its delicate anise-like flavor that's said to enhance the taste of other herbs.

children.name: Heracleum
children.description: Hogweeds are large, impressive plants in the carrot family with huge umbrella-shaped flower clusters and deeply divided leaves that can grow several feet wide. These robust perennials are known for their towering height, with some species reaching 8-15 feet tall, making them among the most imposing wildflowers you'll encounter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hogweeds stand out from other carrot family members by their enormous size and massive, coarsely-toothed leaflets that are much broader than those of similar plants like wild parsnip or Queen Anne's lace.
children.funFact: Giant Hogweed's sap contains chemicals that can cause severe burns and blistering when exposed to sunlight, earning it the nickname 'the plant that burns' and making it one of the most dangerous plants in New England.

children.name: Angelica
children.description: Angelicas are tall, impressive wildflowers in the carrot family that can tower over other plants in wet meadows, marshes, and woodland edges. These robust perennials produce large, umbrella-shaped clusters of small white or greenish flowers atop thick, often hollow stems that can reach 6 feet or more in height. Their large, compound leaves are divided into many leaflets, giving them a bold, architectural appearance in the landscape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Angelicas stand out from other carrot family members by their exceptional size and preference for moist habitats, often growing much taller than related plants. Their thick, sometimes purple-tinged stems and massive flower clusters make them among the most imposing wildflowers in New England.
children.funFact: Many angelica species have been used medicinally and as food by indigenous peoples and early settlers, with the stems sometimes candied as a sweet treat, though proper identification is crucial since some related plants in the carrot family can be toxic.

children.name: Osmorhiza
children.description: Sweet cicely is a genus of woodland wildflowers in the carrot family, known for their delicate white flower clusters and sweet-scented, anise-like fragrance. These perennial herbs typically grow in shaded forest areas and have compound leaves that are divided into leaflets. All three New England species produce small white flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters called umbels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweet cicely plants can be distinguished from other carrot family members by their distinctly sweet, licorice-like scent when crushed and their preference for shaded woodland habitats rather than open areas. Their seeds are also notably long and narrow with bristly surfaces.
children.funFact: Indigenous peoples and early settlers used sweet cicely roots and leaves as a natural sweetener and flavoring agent, often chewing the roots for their pleasant anise taste or brewing them into teas.

children.name: Eryngium
children.description: Eryngos are spiky, thistle-like plants in the carrot family that produce distinctive globe-shaped flower heads surrounded by sharp, pointed bracts. Despite their prickly appearance, they're actually more closely related to parsley and Queen Anne's lace than to true thistles. These hardy perennials often have deeply divided, leathery leaves and produce clusters of tiny flowers packed into dense, rounded heads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the carrot family that have flat-topped umbrella-like flower clusters, eryngos have compact, globe-shaped flower heads surrounded by spiny, collar-like bracts. Their overall appearance is much more thistle-like and spiky compared to their softer carrot family relatives.
children.funFact: Rattlesnake master got its name because Native Americans and early settlers believed its tough, fibrous roots could cure snakebites, though it has no actual medicinal properties for treating venom.

children.name: Zizia
children.description: Alexanders are native wildflowers in the carrot family that produce clusters of small, bright yellow flowers arranged in umbrella-like formations called umbels. These perennial plants typically grow 1-3 feet tall and bloom in late spring to early summer, creating cheerful golden displays in meadows, prairies, and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plants in the carrot family that have white flowers, Alexanders are notable for their distinctive bright yellow blooms. They can be distinguished from similar yellow-flowered relatives by their specific leaf shapes and growth patterns.
children.funFact: Golden Alexanders are named after Alexander the Great, though the connection to the ancient conqueror remains a botanical mystery!

children.name: Cicuta
children.description: Water hemlocks are highly toxic wetland plants in the carrot family that grow in marshy areas, along pond edges, and in wet meadows throughout New England. These tall perennial herbs produce clusters of small white flowers in umbrella-like arrangements and have deeply divided, serrated leaves. Despite their innocent appearance, all parts of these plants contain deadly toxins that make them among the most poisonous plants in North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Water hemlocks can be distinguished from other members of the carrot family by their distinctive chambered roots with cross-partitions and their preference for wet habitats. The bulblet-bearing species is unique in producing small bulblets along its leaf stems that can grow into new plants.
children.funFact: Water hemlock is so toxic that just a small piece of root the size of a walnut can be fatal to an adult human, earning it the grim reputation as North America's most deadly plant.

children.name: Cryptotaenia
children.description: Honeworts are a small genus of woodland herbs in the carrot family, known for their distinctive three-parted leaves and delicate white flower clusters. These shade-loving plants typically grow in moist, rich soils of deciduous forests and woodland edges. They produce small umbrella-like clusters of tiny white flowers followed by ribbed seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Honeworts can be distinguished from other carrot family plants by their characteristic three-lobed leaflets that are often asymmetrically divided, giving them an irregular, almost maple-like appearance.
children.funFact: Japanese honewort is commonly cultivated as a leafy vegetable called 'mitsuba' in East Asian cuisine, where its celery-like flavor makes it a popular garnish and seasoning herb.

children.name: Torilis
children.description: Hedge parslies are small annual plants in the carrot family that produce tiny white or pinkish flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters. These weedy plants are covered in bristly hairs and have finely divided, feathery leaves that resemble those of their carrot family relatives. Both New England species are actually introduced from Europe and Asia, where they commonly grow along roadsides and in disturbed soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets hedge parslies apart from other carrot family plants is their distinctively bristly, rough-textured fruits that are covered in hooked spines. These spiny fruits readily stick to clothing and animal fur, making them excellent hitchhikers.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they're related to parsley, hedge parslies are not closely related to culinary parsley and should never be eaten, as many plants in the carrot family can be toxic.

children.name: Oenanthe
children.description: Water-dropworts are semi-aquatic plants in the carrot family that thrive in wetlands, marshes, and along stream edges. These perennial herbs produce clusters of small white flowers in umbrella-shaped arrangements and have hollow stems that help them survive in waterlogged soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other plants in the carrot family, water-dropworts have specialized hollow, chambered stems that allow them to grow partially submerged in water. Their leaves are often deeply divided and may look different above and below water.
children.funFact: Many water-dropworts contain potent toxins that historically made them some of the most dangerous plants in Europe, earning them the nickname 'dead man's fingers' - though our New England species are generally less toxic.

children.name: Daucus
children.description: Daucus is a genus of flowering plants in the carrot family, best known for containing the wild carrot that gave rise to our cultivated garden carrots. These plants are characterized by their distinctive umbrella-shaped flower clusters called umbels, which are typically white and often have a single dark purple flower in the center. They are biennial herbs that form a taproot in their first year and flower in their second.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Daucus species are distinguished from other carrot family members by their unique flower heads that curl inward as they age, forming a bird's nest-like shape. The leaves are finely divided and feathery, and the plants often have bristly stems.
children.funFact: Wild carrot flowers start white but curl up into a distinctive 'bird's nest' shape as they go to seed, which is why Daucus carota is commonly called Queen Anne's lace or bird's nest plant.

children.name: Aegopodium
children.description: Aegopodium is a small genus of perennial herbs in the carrot family, with compound leaves divided into three leaflets and clusters of small white flowers. These plants spread by underground rhizomes and are known for their ability to form dense colonies in shaded areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their distinctive three-part compound leaves and their aggressive spreading habit through underground stems, unlike most other plants in the carrot family.
children.funFact: The common name 'goutweed' comes from medieval times when the plant was believed to cure gout, though it's now better known as a persistent garden escapee that can be nearly impossible to eradicate once established.

children.name: Pastinaca
children.description: Parsnips are robust biennial herbs in the carrot family that produce large, umbrella-shaped clusters of small yellow flowers. These plants grow tall hollow stems and have deeply divided, compound leaves that can cause skin irritation in some people. They're known for their thick, edible taproot that sweetens after exposure to cold temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Parsnips are distinguished from other carrot family members by their bright yellow flower clusters and their characteristic leaf shape with broad, toothed leaflets. Unlike many relatives, all parts of the plant contain compounds that can cause burns when skin is exposed to sunlight.
children.funFact: Wild parsnip is actually the same species as the garden parsnip we eat - the cultivated variety was developed from wild populations and can still cross-breed with its wild cousins.

children.name: Sium
children.description: Water parsnips are aquatic or semi-aquatic flowering plants in the carrot family that grow in wetlands, marshes, and along stream edges. These perennial herbs have distinctive compound leaves with toothed leaflets and produce small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels, typical of their plant family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Water parsnips can be distinguished from other members of the carrot family by their aquatic habitat and their pinnately compound leaves with sharply toothed, lance-shaped leaflets that are often partially submerged.
children.funFact: Despite their name and family relationship to carrots and parsnips, water parsnips should never be eaten as they can be confused with deadly poisonous water hemlocks that grow in similar habitats.

children.name: Ligusticum
children.description: Lovages are aromatic herbs in the carrot family with compound leaves and clusters of small white or greenish flowers. These perennial plants are known for their strong, celery-like fragrance and have been used traditionally for both culinary and medicinal purposes. They typically grow in coastal or mountainous areas and can reach several feet in height.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lovages can be distinguished from other carrot family plants by their particularly strong, distinctive aroma that smells like a cross between celery and parsley. Their leaves are usually more deeply divided and glossy compared to many similar-looking relatives.
children.funFact: Scots Lovage was historically so important to coastal communities that it was known as 'sea parsley' and sailors would eat it to prevent scurvy during long voyages due to its high vitamin C content.

children.name: Foeniculum
children.description: Foeniculum is a small genus of aromatic herbs in the carrot family, best known for the common fennel plant. These plants are characterized by their feathery, thread-like leaves and distinctive anise-like fragrance. They produce clusters of small yellow flowers in umbrella-shaped arrangements typical of their family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Foeniculum stands out from other carrot family members by its extremely fine, hair-like leaf segments and strong licorice scent. The combination of these delicate, almost wispy foliage and powerful aromatic oils makes it easily recognizable.
children.funFact: Fennel has been cultivated for over 4,000 years and was so valued by ancient Romans that they called it 'foeniculum' meaning 'little hay' - though Roman soldiers chewed the seeds to suppress appetite during long marches.

children.name: Conium
children.description: Conium is a small genus of highly toxic plants in the carrot family, with only one species found in New England. These are tall, branching herbs with finely divided, fern-like leaves and small white flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters called umbels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Conium is distinguished from other carrot family plants by its smooth, hollow stems marked with distinctive purple or reddish spots, and its extremely poisonous nature affecting the nervous system.
children.funFact: Poison hemlock from this genus was famously used to execute the ancient Greek philosopher Socrates in 399 BCE, making it one of history's most notorious plants.

children.name: Myrrhis
children.description: Myrrhis is a genus containing just one species worldwide - the sweet cicely, a tall perennial herb in the carrot family. These plants are known for their feathery, fern-like leaves and clusters of small white flowers that bloom in umbrella-shaped arrangements typical of their family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweet cicely stands out from other carrot family members by its distinctly sweet, anise-like fragrance and large, elongated seeds that turn dark brown when ripe. The entire plant has a pleasant licorice scent when crushed, unlike many of its relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sweet cicely,' this plant is actually not native to New England - it's a European herb that has naturalized in some areas and was historically used as a natural sweetener and flavoring agent before sugar became widely available.

children.name: Coriandrum
children.description: Coriandrum is a small genus of aromatic herbs in the carrot family, with only one or two species worldwide. These annual plants are known for their distinctive fragrant leaves and seeds, which have been used as culinary herbs and spices for thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Coriandrum species are easily recognized by their strong, distinctive scent and their deeply divided, lacy leaves that become more finely cut toward the top of the plant. The small white or pinkish flowers are arranged in umbrella-like clusters typical of the carrot family.
children.funFact: The leaves and seeds of coriander have completely different flavors - the fresh leaves (cilantro) taste bright and citrusy to some people but soapy to others due to genetic differences in smell receptors, while the seeds have a warm, nutty flavor.

children.name: Carum
children.description: Carum is a small genus of aromatic herbs in the carrot family, best known for producing caraway seeds. These plants are characterized by their feathery, finely divided leaves and small white or pink flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Carum species can be distinguished from other carrot family members by their distinctive aromatic compounds that give caraway its characteristic spicy, slightly sweet scent and flavor.
children.funFact: The caraway seeds we use in cooking are actually fruits - each 'seed' contains two small seeds inside and has been prized as a culinary spice for over 5,000 years.

children.name: Pimpinella
children.description: Burnet-saxifrages are delicate flowering plants in the carrot family, characterized by their finely divided, feathery leaves and small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels. These perennial herbs typically grow in meadows, grasslands, and rocky areas, producing aromatic foliage when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other carrot family members, burnet-saxifrages have particularly fine, thread-like leaf segments and relatively small, compact flower umbels. Their leaves are more finely dissected than most related genera, giving them an almost fern-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their common name containing 'saxifrage,' burnet-saxifrages are not actually related to true saxifrages at all - they belong to the carrot family and got their misleading name because they were once believed to have similar medicinal properties for breaking up kidney stones.

children.name: Lilaeopsis
children.description: Grassworts are small aquatic plants that look remarkably like grass, with thin, hollow, tube-like leaves that emerge directly from creeping underground stems. These plants grow in shallow water or muddy areas along coastlines, where they form dense mats that can look like underwater lawns. Despite their grass-like appearance, they're actually members of the carrot family and produce tiny white flowers on short stalks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, grassworts have hollow, cylindrical leaves that are actually modified leaf stalks, and they produce small umbrella-shaped flower clusters typical of the carrot family. Their leaves also have internal cross-walls that can be seen when held up to light.
children.funFact: Grassworts can survive being completely submerged at high tide and then exposed to air at low tide, making them true amphibious plants that have mastered life in the ever-changing tidal zone.

children.name: Ptilimnium
children.description: Mock bishopweeds are delicate annual herbs in the carrot family with finely divided, thread-like leaves that give them a feathery appearance. They produce small white flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters called umbels, typical of their plant family. These plants prefer wet habitats like marshes, pond edges, and other areas with standing or slow-moving water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mock bishopweeds can be distinguished from other carrot family members by their extremely fine, hair-like leaf segments and their preference for aquatic or semi-aquatic habitats. Their delicate, almost grass-like foliage sets them apart from the broader-leafed members of their family.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting a connection to bishopweed, mock bishopweeds are actually more closely related to water hemlock and other aquatic members of the carrot family.

children.name: Aethusa
children.description: Aethusa is a small genus of plants in the carrot family that contains just one species found in New England: fool's parsley. This annual herb produces small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters and has finely divided, feathery leaves that give it a delicate appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fool's parsley can be distinguished from other carrot family members by its distinctive long, drooping bracts beneath each flower cluster and its smooth, hairless stems with a bluish-green tint.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'fool's parsley,' this plant is actually toxic and got its name because inexperienced foragers might mistake it for edible parsley, though it has a very unpleasant smell when crushed.

children.name: Astrantia
children.description: Masterwort is a small genus of flowering plants in the carrot family, known for their distinctive umbrella-like flower clusters called umbels. These perennial herbs are native to mountainous regions of Europe and western Asia, and are prized for their ornate, papery bracts that surround their tiny flowers like decorative collars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other members of the carrot family, masterwort flowers are surrounded by prominent, pointed bracts that form a star-like pattern around each flower cluster, giving them an almost architectural appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'masterwort' comes from medieval beliefs that these plants were a 'master' remedy against many ailments, and they were once considered so valuable that they were used as currency in some parts of Europe.

children.name: Peucedanum
children.description: Hogg's Fennels are tall, aromatic plants in the carrot family that produce umbrella-shaped clusters of small white flowers. These perennial herbs have finely divided, feathery leaves and hollow stems that can grow quite tall in wet meadows and marshes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other carrot family plants, Hogg's Fennels have distinctively broad, flat-topped flower clusters and prefer wetland habitats rather than dry soils.
children.funFact: The name 'Hogg's Fennel' comes from the plant's historical use as livestock fodder, though despite its fennel-like appearance, it's not closely related to true fennel.

children.name: Anethum
children.description: Anethum is a small genus of aromatic herbs in the carrot family, best known for the culinary herb dill. These plants are characterized by their feathery, thread-like leaves and umbrella-shaped clusters of small yellow flowers. They are annual herbs that produce the distinctive seeds and leaves used in cooking and pickling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anethum can be distinguished from other carrot family members by its extremely fine, hair-like leaf segments that give it a delicate, almost wispy appearance. The combination of its unique aroma and these ultra-fine leaves makes it unmistakable among related plants.
children.funFact: The name 'dill' comes from the Old Norse word 'dilla,' meaning 'to soothe,' referring to the plant's traditional use in calming fussy babies and aiding digestion.

children.name: Petroselinum
children.description: Petroselinum is a small genus of aromatic herbs in the carrot family, best known for the common garden parsley that flavors our meals. These plants are characterized by their deeply divided, bright green leaves and small white or yellowish flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Petroselinum can be distinguished from other carrot family members by its distinctive flat or curly, triangular leaves that are typically three times divided, and its characteristic fresh, clean scent.
children.funFact: Ancient Greeks associated parsley with death and the underworld, crowning victors of funeral games with parsley wreaths, while Romans later adopted it as a symbol of festivity and joy at banquets.

children.name: Taenidia
children.description: Taenidia is a small genus of native wildflowers in the carrot family, with only one species found in New England. These perennial herbs produce small yellow flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters called umbels, which is characteristic of their plant family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Taenidia can be distinguished from other carrot family members by its bright yellow flowers and smooth-edged leaves that lack the typical divided or toothed appearance of most umbel-bearing plants.
children.funFact: Yellow pimpernel is sometimes called 'yellow pimpernel' despite not being related to true pimpernels, and its seeds were historically used by Native Americans as a seasoning similar to caraway.

children.name: Conioselinum
children.description: Hemlock-parsleys are delicate wildflowers in the carrot family that grow in wetlands and along stream banks. They produce small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels, which is typical of plants in this family. These perennial herbs have finely divided, feathery leaves that give them an elegant, lacy appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hemlock-parsleys can be distinguished from other carrot family plants by their preference for wet habitats and their particularly fine, thread-like leaf segments. Unlike many of their relatives that prefer dry soils, these plants thrive in marshy areas and wet meadows.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting a connection to hemlock trees, hemlock-parsleys are actually named for their resemblance to the poisonous herb hemlock, though they belong to a completely different plant family than the coniferous hemlock trees.

children.name: Levisticum
children.description: Levisticum is a small genus containing just one species - lovage, a tall perennial herb in the carrot family. This aromatic plant produces large, divided leaves and clusters of small yellowish flowers, and has been cultivated for centuries as both a culinary herb and medicinal plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lovage is distinguished from other carrot family plants by its intense celery-like aroma, its impressive height (up to 6 feet tall), and its large, glossy, deeply divided leaves that are much bigger than those of most related herbs.
children.funFact: Lovage was so valued by ancient Romans that they called it 'ligusticum' after Liguria, a region where it grew abundantly, and it was considered essential for both cooking and medicine.

children.name: Bupleurum
children.description: Thorow-wax is a genus of annual herbs in the carrot family that are characterized by their distinctive leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem. These plants produce small yellow flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters typical of their family. Most species are native to Europe and Asia, with only one species found in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Thorow-wax is how the stem appears to grow directly through the middle of the oval leaves, creating a unique 'perfoliate' appearance that's uncommon among plants.
children.funFact: The name 'thorow-wax' is an old English term meaning 'through wax,' referring to how the waxy leaves appear to be pierced by the stem growing through them.

children.name: Chaerophyllum
children.description: Chaerophyllum is a genus of delicate annual herbs in the carrot family, characterized by their finely divided, fern-like leaves and small white flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters. These plants are often found in shaded woodlands and disturbed areas, where they grow as low, spreading herbs that complete their life cycle in a single growing season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other members of the carrot family, Chaerophyllum species have distinctively hairy or fuzzy stems and leaves. Their fruits are also notably elongated and narrow compared to the broader, flatter fruits of related genera like wild carrot.
children.funFact: The name Chaerophyllum comes from Greek words meaning 'to rejoice' and 'leaf,' possibly referring to the plant's pleasant, parsley-like fragrance when the leaves are crushed.

children.name: Selinum
children.description: Selinum is a small genus of delicate flowering plants in the carrot family, characterized by their finely divided, feathery leaves and clusters of small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like formations. These perennial herbs typically grow in wetlands and meadows, where their graceful foliage creates an almost fern-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Selinum can be distinguished from other carrot family plants by its particularly fine, thread-like leaf segments and its preference for wet habitats, unlike many of its relatives that prefer drier conditions.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'milk-parsley,' Cambridge Milk-parsley is extremely rare in New England and was once thought to be extinct in the region before small populations were rediscovered in Massachusetts wetlands.

children.name: Berula
children.description: Berula is a small genus of aquatic plants in the carrot family that grow in shallow water and wet areas. These perennial herbs have distinctive finely divided, feathery leaves and produce small white flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters typical of their plant family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Berula can be distinguished from other water parsnips by its very finely cut, almost lace-like leaflets and its preference for growing directly in water rather than just in wet soil.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'water parsnip,' Berula is actually quite toxic and should never be eaten, unlike the true parsnip which is a popular root vegetable.

children.name: Conopodium
children.description: Conopodium is a small genus of perennial wildflowers in the carrot family, known for their delicate white flower clusters and edible underground tubers. These plants typically grow in woodlands and grasslands, producing finely divided, feathery leaves and small umbrella-shaped flower heads characteristic of their family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other carrot family plants, Conopodium species have distinctive tuberous roots that are round and nut-like. Their leaves are also more finely divided than most relatives, giving them an almost fern-like appearance.
children.funFact: The common name 'pignut' comes from the edible tubers that wild pigs would dig up and eat, and these same tubers were historically consumed by humans as a crunchy, nutty snack.

children.name: Smyrnium
children.description: Alexanders are robust herbs in the carrot family that produce clusters of small yellowish-green flowers and have distinctively divided, glossy leaves. These Mediterranean natives were historically cultivated as vegetables and herbs, with their stems, leaves, and roots all being edible. They typically grow in coastal areas and disturbed soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other carrot family plants, Alexanders have very shiny, dark green leaves that are divided into three broad leaflets, and their flowers are yellowish-green rather than white.
children.funFact: Alexanders were so popular as a pot herb in medieval times that they were called "black lovage" and were widely cultivated before celery became the preferred vegetable - you can still eat the young stems like celery today!

children.name: Thaspium
children.description: Meadow-parsnips are native wildflowers in the carrot family that bloom in late spring and early summer. They produce small yellow flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters called umbels, and grow in woodland edges, meadows, and along stream banks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other members of the carrot family, meadow-parsnips have distinctive yellow flowers rather than white ones, and their stems often have small hairs at the joints between leaf segments.
children.funFact: The name 'meadow-parsnip' comes from their leaves, which resemble those of the edible parsnip, though these wild plants are not closely related to the garden vegetable.

children.description: The carrot family includes herbs with distinctive umbrella-shaped flower clusters called umbels, where many small flowers radiate out from a central point like the spokes of an umbrella. These plants typically have hollow stems and finely divided, often feathery leaves. The family includes many familiar garden vegetables and herbs like carrots, parsley, and dill, as well as numerous wildflowers found throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The umbrella-shaped flower clusters (umbels) are the most distinctive feature, often arranged in compound umbels where smaller umbels cluster together to form larger ones. Many species also have characteristic ridged or ribbed fruits that split into two parts when mature.
children.funFact: This family contains both some of our most beloved kitchen herbs and vegetables alongside some of the most deadly poisonous plants in North America, including water hemlock and poison hemlock - making proper identification crucial for foragers!

children.name: Araliaceae
Aralia
children.description: Spikenards are a diverse group of plants in the ginseng family that range from low-growing herbaceous perennials to tall, spiny trees. They're known for their distinctive compound leaves that are often divided into multiple leaflets, and their clusters of small white or greenish flowers that develop into dark berries. Despite their varied appearances, all spikenards share similar flower and fruit structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spikenards can be distinguished from other ginseng family members by their often thorny or bristly stems and their typically larger, more dramatically divided leaves. Their flowers are arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels, but unlike true umbel plants, they often have multiple tiers of these flower clusters.
children.funFact: Despite their common names suggesting otherwise, wild sarsaparilla and bristly sarsaparilla are not related to true sarsaparilla - they just have aromatic roots that were used as substitutes for the real thing in root beer and folk medicine.

children.name: Hydrocotyle
children.description: Water pennyworts are small aquatic and semi-aquatic plants that get their name from their distinctive round, coin-shaped leaves that often float on or emerge from water surfaces. These low-growing perennials thrive in wet habitats like marshes, pond edges, and shallow water, where they form creeping mats along muddy shores or float freely in calm waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wetland plants, water pennyworts have perfectly round, shield-like leaves with the stem attached to the center of the leaf (called peltate leaves), giving them their characteristic penny appearance. Their tiny, inconspicuous white or greenish flowers are clustered in small umbrella-like arrangements.
children.funFact: Some water pennywort species can live both underwater and on land - their leaves will grow differently depending on whether they're submerged or floating, making them incredibly adaptable to changing water levels.

children.name: Hedera
children.description: Ivies are evergreen climbing vines known for their distinctive lobed leaves and ability to cling to surfaces using tiny rootlets. These hardy plants can climb walls, trees, and other structures, forming dense mats of foliage that persist year-round. All ivy species produce small clusters of greenish flowers followed by dark berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other climbing vines, ivies attach themselves using specialized aerial rootlets rather than twining stems or tendrils. Their leaves are characteristically palmate (hand-shaped) with 3-5 lobes, though mature plants may develop unlobed oval leaves on flowering branches.
children.funFact: Ivy leaves actually change shape as the plant matures - juvenile leaves are lobed and found on climbing stems, while adult leaves are oval and appear only on horizontal flowering branches at the top of the vine.

children.name: Panax
children.description: Ginsengs are distinctive woodland plants known for their palmately compound leaves arranged in a whorl around the stem and their clusters of small white flowers that develop into bright red berries. These perennial herbs grow from thick, fleshy roots and are found in rich, shaded forest soils. Both New England species have a characteristic umbrella-like appearance with their leaves radiating from a central point.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ginsengs are easily recognized by their unique leaf arrangement - typically 3-5 leaflets per compound leaf, with all leaves emerging from the same point on the stem like spokes of a wheel. The combination of this distinctive foliage pattern and bright red berry clusters makes them unmistakable among forest floor plants.
children.funFact: American ginseng root has been so highly valued for medicinal purposes that it was one of America's first major exports to China in the 1700s, leading to severe over-harvesting that still affects wild populations today.

children.name: Kalopanax
children.description: Kalopanax is a small genus of deciduous trees native to East Asia, with only one species found in cultivation in New England. These trees are members of the ginseng family and are known for their large, deeply lobed leaves that can reach impressive sizes. They produce small white flowers in large, showy clusters followed by small black berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kalopanax stands out from other trees with its enormous palmate leaves that can be over a foot wide, combined with thorny bark on younger branches. The distinctive leaf shape and spiny stems make it easily recognizable among other deciduous trees.
children.funFact: Despite being called Castor-Aralia, this tree is actually more closely related to ginseng than to true aralias, and its massive leaves are among the largest of any hardy tree that can survive New England winters.

children.name: Eleutherococcus
children.description: Eleutherococcus is a genus of deciduous shrubs in the ginseng family, known for their distinctive compound leaves that are divided into several leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand. These hardy shrubs are native to Asia but have been introduced to North America, where they can thrive in various growing conditions from full sun to partial shade.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other ginseng family plants by their palmately compound leaves (leaflets radiating from a central point) and their ability to produce thorny or prickly stems, though not all species are spiny.
children.funFact: Some species in this genus, particularly Eleutherococcus senticosus, are valued in traditional medicine as 'Siberian ginseng,' though they're not actually true ginseng plants but rather distant relatives in the same botanical family.

children.description: The ivy family is a diverse group of plants that includes familiar species like English ivy, American ginseng, and wild sarsaparilla. Most members of this family are characterized by their distinctive flower clusters arranged in umbrella-like formations called umbels, and they often produce small berries as fruits. These plants range from creeping groundcovers to climbing vines to shrubs and trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the ivy family typically have compound leaves (divided into multiple leaflets) and small flowers arranged in rounded, umbrella-shaped clusters. Unlike their close relatives in the carrot family, ivy family plants usually have woody stems and produce berry-like fruits rather than dry seeds.
children.funFact: American ginseng, a member of this family, was so valuable in colonial times that it became known as 'green gold' and was one of America's first major export crops to China.

children.description: The Apiales are an order of flowering plants that includes familiar species like carrots, parsley, poison hemlock, and English ivy. Most members of this group are herbs, shrubs, or vines that produce their small flowers in distinctive umbrella-like clusters called umbels. These plants are found in diverse habitats from wetlands to forests to gardens throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most recognizable feature of this group is their characteristic flower arrangement in umbels - flat-topped or rounded clusters that radiate out like the spokes of an umbrella. Many species also have hollow stems and deeply divided, often feathery leaves.
children.funFact: This order includes both some of our most useful culinary plants (carrots, celery, parsley, dill) and some of the most deadly poisonous plants in North America, like poison hemlock - which ancient Greeks used to execute prisoners, including the philosopher Socrates.

children.name: Saxifragales
Crassulaceae
Sedum
children.description: Stonecrops are a diverse group of succulent plants known for their thick, fleshy leaves that store water, making them incredibly drought-tolerant. These hardy perennials typically grow in rocky, sandy, or poor soils where other plants struggle to survive. Most species produce clusters of small, star-shaped flowers in colors ranging from white and yellow to pink and red.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stonecrops can be distinguished from other succulents by their distinctive star-shaped flowers with typically five petals and their leaves arranged in various patterns along thick stems. Unlike cacti, they lack spines and have soft, plump leaves rather than modified spine-bearing structures.
children.funFact: Some stonecrops like Biting Stonecrop get their name from their peppery taste and were historically used as food and medicine, while others can change color dramatically with the seasons, turning from green to brilliant reds and purples in fall.

children.name: Hylotelephium
children.description: Live-forever plants are succulent perennials known for their thick, fleshy leaves that store water, allowing them to survive in dry conditions. These hardy plants produce clusters of small, star-shaped flowers in late summer and fall, typically in shades of pink, red, or white. As their name suggests, they're incredibly long-lived and can persist in gardens for decades with minimal care.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other stonecrops, Live-forever species are typically larger and more robust, with thicker stems and broader leaves. They also bloom later in the season than most of their relatives, providing important late-season nectar for pollinators.
children.funFact: These plants earned their common name 'Live-forever' because broken pieces can survive for weeks without soil or water, eventually growing roots and forming new plants - making them nearly indestructible!

children.name: Phedimus
children.description: Phedimus is a genus of succulent plants commonly known as stonecrops, characterized by their thick, fleshy leaves that store water and their ability to thrive in rocky, dry conditions. These hardy perennials produce clusters of small, star-shaped flowers and are popular in rock gardens and green roofs due to their drought tolerance. All species in this genus share the distinctive succulent leaf structure and low-growing, mat-forming growth habit.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phedimus stonecrops are distinguished from other succulent genera by their specific leaf arrangement and flower structure, with leaves typically arranged in opposite pairs or whorls of three. They also have a unique ability to change leaf color seasonally, often developing reddish or purplish tints in cooler weather.
children.funFact: Many Phedimus species can survive being completely dried out for weeks and will spring back to life when watered, earning them the nickname 'resurrection plants' among gardeners.

children.name: Petrosedum
children.description: Petrosedum is a genus of small, succulent plants commonly known as stonecrops that thrive in rocky, dry environments. These hardy perennials have thick, fleshy leaves that store water, allowing them to survive in challenging conditions where other plants struggle. They produce clusters of small, star-shaped flowers that are typically yellow, white, or pink.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Petrosedum species are distinguished from other stonecrops by their particularly robust, needle-like or cylindrical leaves and their preference for growing directly on rocks or in very thin soil. They tend to form dense, carpet-like mats that can spread across rocky surfaces.
children.funFact: These tough little plants can actually grow directly on bare rock surfaces, slowly breaking down the stone over time and helping to create soil for other plants to eventually colonize.

children.name: Rhodiola
children.description: Roseroots are succulent perennial plants in the stonecrop family that grow from thick, fleshy underground stems called rhizomes. These hardy plants are adapted to harsh, rocky environments and produce clusters of small, star-shaped flowers that can be yellow, red, or pink. They store water and nutrients in their thick leaves and stems, helping them survive in challenging conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Roseroots are distinguished from other stonecrops by their rose-scented roots and rhizomes, which give the group its common name. They also tend to have more densely clustered flower arrangements compared to their relatives.
children.funFact: Roseroot has been used as a traditional medicine for over 3,000 years and was so valued by Vikings that they would trade it like precious metal to boost their strength and endurance.

children.name: Crassula
children.description: Stonecrops are succulent plants known for their thick, fleshy leaves that store water, helping them survive in dry conditions. They belong to a large genus found worldwide, with species ranging from tiny aquatic plants to larger garden varieties. These hardy plants are adapted to challenging environments where water may be scarce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stonecrops can be identified by their distinctive succulent leaves that feel thick and watery when squeezed, and their small star-shaped flowers that typically have the same number of petals as stamens.
children.funFact: Despite being known as drought-tolerant succulents, New England's only native stonecrop species is actually aquatic, growing submerged in ponds and slow-moving streams!

children.name: Sempervivum
children.description: Houseleeks are succulent plants that form tight rosettes of thick, fleshy leaves designed to store water. These hardy perennials are masters of survival, able to thrive in rocky, dry conditions where many other plants would struggle. They reproduce by sending out runners that create new plantlets around the parent plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other succulents, houseleeks form very compact, symmetrical rosettes and produce distinctive star-shaped flowers on tall stalks. Their leaves often have fine hairs along the edges and can change color based on sunlight exposure and temperature.
children.funFact: The name 'houseleek' comes from the ancient practice of growing these plants on rooftops, where people believed they would protect homes from lightning strikes and fires.

children.description: The stonecrop family includes succulent plants with thick, fleshy leaves that store water, making them perfectly adapted to dry conditions. These hardy perennials are known for their ability to thrive in poor soils and rocky places where other plants struggle to survive. Most produce clusters of small, star-shaped flowers in various colors from white and yellow to pink and red.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other flowering plants, stonecrops have distinctively thick, water-storing leaves and stems that give them a plump, rubbery appearance. Their flowers typically have the same number of petals as sepals, often in multiples of four or five.
children.funFact: Some stonecrops can survive being completely dried out for months and will spring back to life when water returns, earning them common names like 'live-forever' and making them nearly indestructible garden plants.

children.name: Saxifragaceae
Saxifraga
children.description: Saxifrages are small, hardy perennial plants that specialize in growing in rocky, mountainous environments where few other plants can survive. These tough little wildflowers typically form low cushions or mats and produce delicate five-petaled flowers in white, yellow, or purple. They're masters of extreme habitats, thriving in alpine zones, cliff faces, and rocky crevices throughout New England's mountains.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Saxifrages are distinguished by their ability to grow directly from rock cracks and their characteristic five-petaled flowers with ten stamens. Unlike many alpine plants, they often have succulent or leathery leaves that help them conserve water in harsh, exposed conditions.
children.funFact: The name 'saxifrage' literally means 'rock-breaker' in Latin, referring to their remarkable ability to grow in tiny cracks in solid rock, where their roots can actually help split the stone over time.

children.name: Tiarella
children.description: Foamflowers are delicate woodland wildflowers known for their distinctive fluffy white flower spikes that resemble seafoam. These low-growing perennial herbs thrive in the cool, moist soils of deciduous forests and have heart-shaped or lobed leaves that form attractive ground-covering mats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Foamflowers can be distinguished from similar woodland plants by their unique feathery white flower clusters and their tendency to spread via underground runners or stolons, creating colonies of connected plants.
children.funFact: The name 'foamflower' comes from the plant's tiny white flowers that have thread-like stamens extending far beyond the petals, creating a frothy, bubble-like appearance when viewed up close.

children.name: Micranthes
children.description: Early saxifrages are small perennial wildflowers that bloom in spring, often appearing before many other plants have emerged. They typically have clusters of tiny white flowers held above rosettes of leaves, and they're well-adapted to growing in rocky or wet areas where other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other saxifrages, Micranthes species have very small flowers (hence 'micro-anthes' meaning small flowers) arranged in branching clusters, and their leaves form distinct basal rosettes rather than growing up the stem.
children.funFact: These hardy little plants can bloom as early as March in New England, sometimes pushing up through the last patches of snow to herald the arrival of spring.

children.name: Mitella
children.description: Miterworts are delicate woodland wildflowers that bloom in late spring, producing distinctive white flower spikes that rise above their heart-shaped leaves. These small perennial herbs are members of the saxifrage family and thrive in the cool, moist conditions of New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They get their common name from their tiny flowers, which have fringed petals that resemble ornate bishop's caps or miters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Miterworts are easily recognized by their unique flowers with deeply fringed or feathery white petals that look like tiny snowflakes along the flowering spike. Unlike many other spring wildflowers, their petals are intricately divided rather than simple and smooth-edged.
children.funFact: The genus name Mitella comes from the Latin word for 'little cap,' referring to the shape of the seed capsule that develops after flowering and was once thought to resemble a bishop's ceremonial headdress.

children.name: Heuchera
children.description: Alumroots are a genus of perennial wildflowers known for their distinctive round, lobed leaves that form attractive ground-hugging rosettes. These woodland plants produce delicate spikes of tiny bell-shaped flowers that rise above the foliage on slender stems. They're popular both as native wildflowers and cultivated garden plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Alumroots can be identified by their characteristic rounded, heart-shaped leaves with scalloped edges and their airy flower spikes bearing numerous small, bell-like blooms. Unlike many other woodland flowers, their leaves remain attractive throughout the growing season, often developing beautiful colors in fall.
children.funFact: The name 'alumroot' comes from the astringent properties of the plant's roots, which Native Americans traditionally used for medicinal purposes, particularly for treating wounds and sore throats.

children.name: Rodgersia
children.description: Rodgersias are striking perennial plants known for their large, dramatic leaves that resemble those of horse chestnuts or may apples. These Asian natives produce tall spikes of small, creamy-white or pinkish flowers in summer, creating an impressive architectural presence in shaded garden areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plants in the saxifrage family, rodgersias have distinctively large, compound leaves that are palmately divided (like fingers on a hand) and can reach over a foot across. Their substantial size and bold foliage texture set them apart from most other shade perennials.
children.funFact: Despite their exotic appearance, rodgersias are surprisingly hardy and can tolerate New England winters, with their leaves turning beautiful bronze or reddish colors in fall before dying back.

children.name: Chrysosplenium
children.description: Golden-saxifrages are small, delicate wildflowers that thrive in wet, shady places like stream banks and seeps. These low-growing plants produce tiny yellow-green flowers in early spring and have succulent, rounded leaves that often take on golden or reddish hues.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other saxifrages, golden-saxifrages lack petals entirely and instead rely on colorful sepals and bracts to attract pollinators. Their preference for constantly moist soil also sets them apart from most other members of the saxifrage family.
children.funFact: Golden-saxifrages are among the earliest wildflowers to bloom in New England, often flowering while snow still lingers in their boggy habitats.

children.name: Astilbe
children.description: False goat's beards are perennial flowering plants known for their feathery, plume-like flower clusters that rise above deeply divided, fern-like leaves. These shade-loving plants typically grow in moist, woodland environments and produce delicate sprays of tiny flowers in summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true goat's beard (Aruncus), false goat's beards have more finely divided leaves and denser, more compact flower plumes. Their flowers are also typically smaller and more numerous within each cluster.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'false' goat's beards, Astilbe plants are popular garden specimens that were originally native to Asia and are prized for their ability to add elegant texture to shady garden spots.

children.name: Bergenia
children.description: Elephant-ears (Bergenia) are hardy perennial plants known for their large, thick, rounded leaves that resemble elephant ears. These low-growing plants form attractive clumps and produce clusters of small, colorful flowers on sturdy stems above the foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bergenia can be distinguished from other broad-leaved plants by their exceptionally thick, leathery leaves that often turn bronze or reddish in cold weather, combined with their distinctive flower clusters held on red-tinged stems.
children.funFact: The leaves of elephant-ears are so thick and waxy that they've been traditionally used as natural bandages in some cultures, earning them the nickname 'pig squeak' because they make a squeaking sound when rubbed together.

children.description: The saxifrage family is a diverse group of herbaceous plants that are especially well-adapted to rocky, mountainous environments and cool, moist conditions. Most members produce delicate flowers with five petals arranged in clusters or spikes, and many form attractive rosettes of leaves at their base. These hardy plants are often among the first to bloom in spring and can thrive in challenging habitats where other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Saxifrage family members typically have flowers with twice as many stamens as petals (usually 10 stamens to 5 petals) and distinctive seed capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. Their leaves often have toothed or lobed margins and may be succulent or hairy.
children.funFact: The name 'saxifrage' literally means 'stone-breaker' in Latin, referring to these plants' remarkable ability to grow in rock crevices and their historical reputation for being able to dissolve kidney stones.

children.name: Grossulariaceae
Ribes
children.description: Ribes includes all the currants and gooseberries, small to medium shrubs that produce clusters of small, often edible berries. These plants are easily recognized by their distinctive palmately-lobed leaves (shaped like a hand with fingers) and their tendency to grow in cool, moist environments throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Currants typically have smooth stems and hang their berries in drooping clusters, while gooseberries usually have thorny or bristly stems and produce berries singly or in small groups.
children.funFact: Many Ribes species were once banned in parts of New England because they can host white pine blister rust, a disease that threatened the timber industry, though most restrictions have now been lifted.

children.description: The Gooseberry Family consists of shrubs that produce small, round berries in clusters or individually along their branches. These plants are known for their distinctive lobed leaves and their edible fruits, which can be smooth like currants or spiny like gooseberries. They're commonly found in cooler climates and woodland edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have characteristic palmately-lobed leaves (shaped like an open hand) and small, bell-shaped flowers that hang in drooping clusters. The fruits are true berries that remain attached to the plant until fully ripe, unlike many other berry-producing shrubs.
children.funFact: Gooseberries and currants were once banned in many U.S. states because they can harbor white pine blister rust, a disease that threatened the timber industry - though many of these bans have since been lifted!

children.name: Haloragaceae
Myriophyllum
children.description: Milfoils are aquatic plants that live submerged in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They're easily recognized by their feathery, finely-divided underwater leaves that look like tiny green bottle brushes arranged in whorls around the stem. Most species produce small flowers that stick up above the water surface on spike-like stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, milfoils have extremely fine, thread-like leaf segments that create a distinctive feathery appearance underwater. Their leaves are typically arranged in whorls of 3-6 around the stem, giving them a very symmetrical, organized look.
children.funFact: The name 'milfoil' comes from Latin meaning 'thousand leaves,' referring to their incredibly finely divided foliage that can have hundreds of tiny segments per leaf.

children.name: Proserpinaca
children.description: Mermaidweeds are small aquatic plants that live in shallow water and wetlands throughout New England. They're unique because they can grow both underwater and on land, changing their leaf shape depending on whether they're submerged or above water. These adaptable plants belong to the loosestrife family and play important roles in wetland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mermaidweeds are easily recognized by their dramatically different leaf forms - underwater leaves are feathery and finely divided like a mermaid's hair, while leaves above water are simple and toothed. This shape-shifting ability helps them photosynthesize efficiently in both aquatic and terrestrial conditions.
children.funFact: The name 'mermaidweed' comes from their underwater leaves, which look like flowing hair and sway gracefully in the current, resembling the mythical sea creatures they're named after.

children.description: The water milfoil family is a group of aquatic and semi-aquatic plants that have adapted to life in or near water. Most members of this family are submerged or floating plants with finely divided, feathery leaves that help them capture nutrients and oxygen from the water around them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants are easily recognized by their distinctive leaf patterns - either finely dissected feathery leaves (in milfoils) or deeply lobed leaves that may be both above and below water (in mermaidweeds). Their small, inconspicuous flowers are typically arranged in spikes that emerge above the water surface.
children.funFact: Eurasian watermilfoil can grow up to 10 feet long and is so efficient at photosynthesis underwater that a single plant fragment as small as 1/4 inch can grow into a whole new plant colony.

children.name: Hamamelidaceae
Hamamelis
children.description: Witch-hazels are distinctive shrubs or small trees known for their unique spidery flowers that bloom in fall or early spring when most other plants are dormant. These hardy plants produce fragrant yellow, orange, or red flowers with four narrow, ribbon-like petals that can withstand freezing temperatures. They're also famous for their explosive seed dispersal mechanism and their use in traditional medicine and cosmetics.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Witch-hazels are easily recognized by their unusual flowers with long, thin, twisted petals that look like colorful ribbons or spider legs. Unlike most flowering plants, they bloom during the coldest months of the year, making them stand out dramatically in the winter landscape.
children.funFact: Witch-hazel seeds can be launched up to 30 feet away from the parent plant when their woody capsules explosively split open, earning them the nickname 'snapping hazel.'

children.description: The witch-hazel family consists of woody plants known for their distinctive flowers that bloom at unusual times of year. Members of this family are characterized by their small, often fragrant flowers with narrow, ribbon-like petals and their ability to explosively disperse seeds from woody capsules.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, witch-hazels bloom in late fall or winter when their leaves have fallen, making their spidery yellow flowers highly visible against bare branches. Their seed capsules also have a unique mechanism that violently ejects seeds up to 30 feet away.
children.funFact: Native Americans and early settlers used witch-hazel bark and leaves to make astringent remedies, and witch-hazel extract is still commonly found in modern skincare products today.

children.name: Paeoniaceae
Paeonia
children.description: Peonies are a genus of flowering plants known for their large, showy blooms and deeply divided leaves. These perennial herbs produce spectacular flowers in late spring to early summer, with many petals arranged in layers around a center of bright yellow stamens. Most peonies are long-lived plants that can thrive for decades once established.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peonies are easily recognized by their distinctive large flowers (often 3-5 inches across) with numerous overlapping petals and their characteristic deeply lobed, compound leaves. Unlike many other flowering plants, peonies have a unique fruit type called a follicle that splits open to reveal large, colorful seeds.
children.funFact: Peony flowers are so heavy with petals that they often need the help of ants to fully open - the ants eat sweet nectar from the flower buds, and their movement helps the tight buds unfurl into full blooms.

children.description: The peony family consists of herbaceous perennial plants known for their spectacular, large, showy flowers that bloom in late spring to early summer. These plants have deeply divided, compound leaves and produce flowers with multiple petals that can be white, pink, red, or yellow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Peonies are distinguished by their massive, often fragrant flowers that can reach 4-6 inches across, along with their distinctive seed pods that split open to reveal large, dark seeds.
children.funFact: Peony flowers are so heavy when fully bloomed that they often need support stakes, and some varieties can live for over 100 years, becoming more beautiful with age.

children.name: Penthoraceae
Penthorum
children.description: Penthorum is a small genus of succulent-like plants that are actually members of the saxifrage family rather than true stonecrops. These perennial herbs have thick, fleshy leaves and produce small clusters of star-shaped flowers. They typically grow in wet areas like ditches, pond edges, and marshy ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true stonecrops (Sedum), Penthorum plants have flowers with 5 petals that are often absent or very small, and their seed capsules split into 5 distinct sections. Their leaves are also more elongated and less obviously succulent than typical stonecrops.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'ditch stonecrop,' Penthorum sedoides is not actually related to true stonecrops but gets its common name from its superficial resemblance and preference for growing in roadside ditches.

children.description: The Penthorum family is a small family of succulent plants that includes only one genus found in New England. These plants are characterized by their thick, fleshy leaves and small, star-shaped flowers arranged in curved clusters. They typically grow in wet areas like marshes, pond edges, and other moist habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive five-parted flowers with no petals, only sepals, and their fruits split open in a star pattern. Their succulent leaves and unique flower structure help distinguish them from other wetland plants.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'ditch stonecrop,' Virginia stonecrop (the only New England member) isn't actually related to true stonecrops and was once thought to be closely related to roses before DNA studies revealed its unique evolutionary position.

children.name: Altingiaceae
Liquidambar
children.description: Sweetgums are deciduous trees known for their distinctive star-shaped leaves and spiky, round seed balls that hang from branches. These trees are prized for their brilliant fall colors, displaying vibrant yellows, oranges, reds, and purples all on the same tree. They produce a fragrant resin that has been used historically for various purposes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweetgums are easily recognized by their unique palmate leaves with 5-7 pointed lobes that look like stars, and their characteristic spiky seed balls that persist through winter. Unlike maples which have similar leaf shapes, sweetgum leaves are arranged alternately on branches rather than opposite each other.
children.funFact: The spiky seed balls are actually composed of dozens of tiny capsules, each containing 1-2 seeds, and Native Americans traditionally used the tree's aromatic resin as chewing gum and for medicinal purposes.

children.description: The sweetgum family consists of deciduous trees known for their distinctive star-shaped leaves and spiky, round seed balls. These trees are popular in landscaping and are easily recognized by their deeply lobed leaves that turn brilliant colors in fall. Most sweetgums are native to warmer climates, but one species has adapted to temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweetgums are distinguished from other trees by their perfectly symmetrical star-shaped leaves with 5-7 pointed lobes and their unique spiky spherical fruits that hang like ornaments from the branches.
children.funFact: The resin from sweetgum trees was historically chewed like gum by Native Americans and early settlers, giving the tree its common name.

children.name: Cercidiphyllaceae
Cercidiphyllum
children.description: Cercidiphyllum is a small genus of deciduous trees known for their distinctive heart-shaped leaves and unique branching patterns. These ancient trees are considered living fossils, representing one of the most primitive flowering tree lineages still alive today.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most trees, Cercidiphyllum species have simple, opposite leaves that are perfectly heart-shaped with rounded teeth along the edges. Their flowers are tiny and lack petals, appearing before the leaves in early spring.
children.funFact: The fallen autumn leaves of katsura trees smell remarkably like cotton candy or caramel due to the sugar compound maltol they release as they decompose.

children.description: The katsura family is a small group of deciduous trees known for their distinctive heart-shaped leaves and unique seasonal displays. These trees are famous for their spectacular fall color and the sweet, cotton candy-like fragrance their leaves release when they drop in autumn.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Katsura trees have opposite, simple leaves with rounded teeth and produce small flowers that lack petals, appearing before the leaves emerge in spring.
children.funFact: The fallen leaves of katsura trees smell remarkably like cotton candy, cinnamon, or brown sugar due to a compound called maltol that's released as the leaves decompose.

children.name: Iteaceae
Itea
children.description: Sweetspires are deciduous shrubs known for their distinctive clusters of small, fragrant white flowers that bloom in late spring to early summer. These native plants produce long, narrow flower spikes called racemes that arch gracefully and attract butterflies and other pollinators. They typically grow in moist, shaded areas and are valued both for their showy blooms and their brilliant fall foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweetspires can be identified by their unique cylindrical flower clusters that hang like bottle brushes, each containing dozens of tiny five-petaled flowers. Their simple, alternate leaves have finely serrated edges and turn spectacular shades of orange, red, and purple in autumn.
children.funFact: Virginia sweetspire can spread by underground runners to form colonies, making it an excellent choice for naturalizing wet areas and controlling erosion along stream banks.

children.description: The sweetspire family is a small group of flowering shrubs known for their distinctive bottle-brush-like clusters of small, fragrant white flowers. These plants typically have simple, alternate leaves with finely toothed edges and produce their showy flower spikes in late spring to early summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweetspires are easily recognized by their dense, cylindrical flower clusters that resemble bottle brushes, with each tiny flower having five narrow petals and long, protruding stamens that give the clusters their fuzzy appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'sweetspire' for their sweet-scented flowers, these shrubs are actually more closely related to currants and gooseberries than to true spirea plants.

children.description: Saxifrages, stonecrops, and allies form a diverse order of flowering plants that includes everything from tiny succulent stonecrops growing on rocks to large witch-hazel shrubs in the forest understory. Most members of this group have simple leaves and small flowers with parts arranged in fives, though they vary dramatically in size, habitat, and appearance. What unites these seemingly different plants is their shared evolutionary history and similar flower structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flowering plant orders, Saxifragales often have flowers with multiple separate carpels (seed-bearing parts) rather than fused ones. Many species in this group are also adapted to harsh conditions like rocky crevices or seasonal flooding.
children.funFact: This order includes both some of the tiniest rock garden plants (like saxifrages that form cushions smaller than your palm) and massive trees like sweetgums that can tower over 100 feet tall.

children.name: Gentianales
Rubiaceae
Galium
children.description: Bedstraws are a diverse group of small herbaceous plants known for their distinctive whorled leaves that radiate outward from square stems like the spokes of a wheel. These plants produce tiny four-petaled flowers, usually white or yellow, and often have a sprawling or climbing growth habit that helps them weave through other vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The combination of square stems, leaves arranged in whorls (typically 4-8 per node), and small four-petaled flowers makes bedstraws easily recognizable from other plant families.
children.funFact: Many bedstraw species have tiny hooked hairs on their stems and leaves that act like velcro, allowing them to scramble up and cling to other plants - catchweed bedstraw is so clingy it's also called 'cleavers' because it cleaves to everything it touches!

children.name: Houstonia
children.description: Flowering bluets are a group of small, delicate wildflowers that produce tiny four-petaled blooms, typically in shades of blue, purple, or white. These low-growing plants are members of the coffee family and are known for their simple, opposite leaves and their ability to form colorful carpets in fields, lawns, and woodland edges. All bluets share a similar flower structure with four petals that often have a pale center or 'eye.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bluets can be distinguished from other small wildflowers by their consistently four-petaled flowers and their opposite leaf arrangement. Unlike many other members of the coffee family, bluets are small herbaceous plants rather than shrubs or trees.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, bluets are surprisingly hardy and can bloom from early spring through fall, with some species producing flowers almost year-round in mild climates.

children.name: Mitchella
children.description: Mitchella is a small genus of low-growing, evergreen plants in the coffee family. These creeping woodland plants are characterized by their small, round leaves arranged in pairs and their ability to form dense mats along the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the coffee family, Mitchella species have a distinctive trailing growth habit and produce pairs of white flowers that fuse together to create a single red berry with two "eyes" or dimples.
children.funFact: Each bright red partridgeberry is actually formed from two separate flowers that grow together, which is why every berry has two small dimples on top where the flower parts once were.

children.name: Cephalanthus
children.description: Buttonbushes are a small genus of shrubs in the coffee family known for their distinctive spherical flower clusters that look like white pincushions. These wetland-loving plants produce dense, round balls of tiny tubular flowers that bloom in summer, followed by clusters of small nutlets that persist into winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The perfectly round, globe-shaped flower heads are unique among New England shrubs, making buttonbushes instantly recognizable when in bloom. Unlike most coffee family members, they thrive in wet soils and swampy conditions.
children.funFact: Each buttonbush flower ball contains dozens of individual flowers, and the plant got its name because the spherical seed heads that follow the flowers look remarkably like the cloth-covered buttons used on old-fashioned clothing.

children.name: Hexasepalum
children.description: Hexasepalum is a small genus of low-growing annual plants in the madder family (Rubiaceae). These plants are characterized by their tiny white or pinkish flowers and small, narrow leaves that grow in pairs along square stems. They typically grow as weedy plants in disturbed soils and open areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hexasepalum can be identified by its six sepals (the green parts beneath the petals), which is unusual since most plants in the madder family have four sepals. The flowers are extremely small and the fruits split into two parts when mature.
children.funFact: Despite being in the same plant family as coffee and gardenias, rough buttonweed is considered one of the most inconspicuous flowering plants in New England due to its tiny 1-2mm flowers that are easily overlooked.

children.name: Sherardia
children.description: Sherardia is a small genus containing just one species worldwide - the tiny field madder. This delicate annual herb belongs to the coffee family and produces clusters of small pink or purple flowers surrounded by spiky bracts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Field madder can be distinguished from other small bedstraws and coffee family plants by its distinctive star-shaped arrangement of spiky bracts that surround each flower cluster, giving it a unique bristly appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being in the coffee family, field madder is so small that it's often overlooked - the entire plant typically grows only 2-4 inches tall and the flowers are barely 1/8 inch across.

children.name: Diodia
children.description: Diodia is a genus of small flowering plants in the coffee family, commonly known as buttonweeds. These low-growing herbs typically have small, white, four-petaled flowers and narrow leaves arranged in pairs along their stems. They are often found in sandy or disturbed soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Buttonweeds are distinguished by their tiny white flowers that emerge directly from where the leaves meet the stem, and their characteristic linear leaves with prominent stipules (small leaf-like structures) between them.
children.funFact: Despite being in the same family as coffee plants, buttonweeds are considered weedy plants that often grow in lawns and along roadsides, where their small size allows them to survive regular mowing.

children.name: Cruciata
children.description: Crossworts are small herbaceous plants in the bedstraw family that get their name from their distinctive cross-shaped arrangement of leaves. These low-growing plants typically have four leaves arranged in whorls around each stem node, creating a symmetrical cross pattern when viewed from above. They produce small, delicate flowers and are often found in grassy or woodland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bedstraws which usually have 6-8 narrow leaves per whorl, crossworts have exactly 4 broader, oval-shaped leaves arranged in perfect crosses around the stem. Their flowers are also typically yellow rather than the white flowers common in many other bedstraw relatives.
