children.funFact: The Piedmont Bedstraw found in New England is actually native to Europe and was likely introduced accidentally, making it one of the few members of this primarily Old World genus to establish itself in North America.

children.name: Oldenlandia
children.description: Oldenlandia is a genus of small herbaceous plants in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that are found primarily in tropical and subtropical regions around the world. These delicate plants typically produce tiny four-petaled flowers and have opposite leaves with small stipules between them, which is characteristic of the coffee family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oldenlandia species can be distinguished from other coffee family members by their very small, usually white or pale flowers and their often weedy, low-growing habit. They typically have much smaller flowers than most other Rubiaceae genera found in New England.
children.funFact: Despite being in the same family as coffee plants, Oldenlandia species are tiny weeds that can grow in sidewalk cracks and disturbed soils, showing how diverse the coffee family really is!

children.description: The madder family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes everything from tiny woodland wildflowers to shrubs. Most members of this family have simple leaves arranged in pairs or whorls around the stem, and their small flowers typically have four or five petals fused into a tube. You'll find these plants in various New England habitats, from forest floors to wetland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the madder family can be identified by their characteristic leaf arrangement (opposite or whorled) and their small, tubular flowers that often cluster together. Many species also have distinctive fruits that split into two parts when ripe.
children.funFact: This family includes the coffee plant (Coffea) and was historically important for producing red and yellow dyes from madder root, which were used to color everything from military uniforms to Persian carpets.

children.name: Apocynaceae
Asclepias
children.description: Milkweeds are perennial wildflowers known for their distinctive white, milky sap that oozes when stems or leaves are broken. They produce clusters of small, intricate flowers with a unique crown-like structure and develop large seed pods that split open to release seeds with silky white hairs that help them float on the wind.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wildflowers, milkweeds have a toxic milky latex sap and flowers with a distinctive corona (crown) structure above the petals. Their seeds are equipped with long, silky hairs called coma that make them easily recognizable when dispersing.
children.funFact: Monarch butterfly caterpillars can only survive by eating milkweed plants, and the toxic compounds they absorb make both the caterpillars and adult butterflies poisonous to predators.

children.name: Vinca
children.description: Periwinkles are low-growing, evergreen plants with glossy, oval leaves and distinctive five-petaled flowers that bloom in shades of blue, purple, or white. These hardy groundcover plants spread by trailing stems that root at the nodes, creating dense mats of vegetation. They belong to the dogbane family and produce a milky sap when their stems or leaves are broken.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Periwinkles can be distinguished from other groundcover plants by their pinwheel-shaped flowers with five flat, overlapping petals and their thick, leathery leaves that remain green year-round. The milky white sap that emerges when the plant is damaged is also a key identifying characteristic.
children.funFact: Despite their innocent appearance, periwinkles contain alkaloids that have been used in cancer research and treatment, with compounds from tropical relatives leading to important chemotherapy drugs.

children.name: Apocynum
children.description: Dogbanes are perennial wildflowers known for their milky white sap and tough, fibrous stems. These plants produce small, bell-shaped flowers that are typically white or pink, followed by long, narrow seed pods that split open to release seeds with silky white hairs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dogbanes can be identified by their milky sap that appears when stems or leaves are broken, and their distinctive seed pods that come in pairs and contain seeds with fluffy, cotton-like attachments for wind dispersal.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'hemp dogbane,' this plant is not related to hemp at all - the name comes from its strong, rope-like fibers that Indigenous peoples traditionally used to make cordage, nets, and textiles.

children.name: Vincetoxicum
children.description: Dog-strangling vines are climbing or twining perennial plants in the milkweed family that produce pods filled with seeds topped with silky white hairs. These invasive vines from Europe and Asia wrap around other plants and can eventually smother or 'strangle' them by blocking sunlight and competing for resources. Both New England species are considered serious threats to native ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike native milkweeds, dog-strangling vines have small, inconspicuous flowers that are typically dark purple or maroon rather than showy pink or orange. They also have a more aggressive twining growth habit that allows them to climb high into trees and shrubs.
children.funFact: Despite being in the milkweed family, dog-strangling vines are toxic to monarch butterfly caterpillars - female monarchs sometimes mistake them for native milkweeds and lay eggs on them, but the caterpillars cannot survive on these plants.

children.name: Amsonia
children.description: Bluestars are a small genus of native wildflowers known for their clusters of pale blue, star-shaped flowers that bloom in late spring. These perennial plants belong to the dogbane family and are prized by gardeners for their delicate beauty and excellent fall foliage that turns bright yellow or orange.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bluestars can be identified by their distinctive five-petaled, pale blue flowers arranged in terminal clusters, and their narrow, alternate leaves that create a fine-textured appearance. Unlike many other members of the dogbane family, bluestars have a more delicate, herbaceous growth habit rather than being woody or vine-like.
children.funFact: Despite producing milky sap like other dogbane family members, bluestars are much less toxic and are considered safe garden plants, making them popular choices for pollinator gardens and native plant landscapes.

children.name: Catharanthus
children.description: Periwinkle (Catharanthus) is a small genus of flowering plants in the dogbane family, originally native to Madagascar and other parts of the Indian Ocean region. These plants are characterized by their simple, opposite leaves and five-petaled flowers that are typically pink, purple, or white. They are popular ornamental plants that have been widely cultivated around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true periwinkles (Vinca), Catharanthus flowers have a flat face rather than a tube-like appearance, and their seed pods are upright rather than spreading. The leaves are also typically more oval-shaped and glossy compared to their Vinca relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'periwinkle,' Madagascar Periwinkle contains powerful alkaloids that have been used to develop important cancer-fighting medications, including treatments for childhood leukemia and Hodgkin's disease.

children.name: Gomphocarpus
children.description: Gomphocarpus is a small genus of milkweed plants that are native to Africa but have spread to many other regions around the world. These plants are closely related to the common milkweeds in the genus Asclepias and share many of their characteristics, including milky sap and seed pods that split open to release fluffy seeds. Like other milkweeds, they serve as important host plants for monarch butterfly caterpillars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gomphocarpus species are distinguished from other milkweeds by their inflated, balloon-like seed pods that are often used in dried flower arrangements. The pods are typically larger and more dramatically swollen than those of most Asclepias species.
children.funFact: The balloonplant's inflated seed pods make a satisfying 'pop' sound when squeezed, which is why it's sometimes called 'swan plant' or 'balloon milkweed' and is popular with children and florists alike.

children.description: The Dogbane Family is a diverse group of plants that share one distinctive trait: they produce a milky, often toxic sap when their stems or leaves are broken. This family includes everything from the beloved monarch butterfly host plants (milkweeds) to common garden flowers like periwinkles. Most members of this family have simple, usually opposite leaves and five-petaled flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The milky latex sap is the most reliable identifying feature of this family, along with their typically opposite leaves and flowers with five petals that often have a distinctive shape. Many species also have pods that split open to release seeds with silky white hairs.
children.funFact: Many plants in this family have evolved incredibly complex flower structures - milkweeds have some of the most intricate pollination mechanisms in the plant kingdom, with pollen packed into special structures that attach to insects' legs like tiny saddlebags!

children.name: Gentianaceae
Gentiana
children.description: Gentians are a group of wildflowers known for their distinctive deep blue to purple tubular flowers that often remain partially or completely closed, giving them a bottle-like appearance. These perennial herbs typically bloom in late summer and fall, growing in wet meadows, bogs, and other moist habitats throughout New England. All gentians in this region share the characteristic of having opposite leaves and flowers with four or five petals fused into a tube.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most wildflowers that open wide to attract pollinators, many gentians keep their petals tightly closed or only partially open, creating a unique bottle or urn shape. Their intense blue-purple coloration is also much deeper and richer than most other New England wildflowers.
children.funFact: Bottle gentians have such tightly closed flowers that only strong bumblebees can force their way inside to reach the nectar, making them completely dependent on these powerful pollinators for reproduction.

children.name: Sabatia
children.description: Rose gentians are delicate wildflowers known for their star-shaped pink or white blooms that brighten wetlands and coastal areas throughout New England. These annual plants typically have slender stems and narrow leaves, producing showy flowers with five petals that often have a distinctive notched or fringed appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their true gentian relatives, rose gentians have flat, star-shaped flowers that open wide rather than the tubular or bell-shaped blooms typical of other gentians. Their petals are also characteristically notched at the tips, giving the flowers a delicate, fringed look.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, rose gentians aren't actually roses at all - they belong to the gentian family and get their name from their rosy-pink flower color and their bitter taste, which is characteristic of true gentians.

children.name: Bartonia
children.description: Screwstems are delicate, thread-like plants that belong to the gentian family. These unusual wildflowers have extremely thin, wiry stems and tiny scale-like leaves that are barely noticeable. They are parasitic or semi-parasitic plants that often depend on other plants or fungi for some of their nutrition.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Screwstems can be identified by their incredibly thin, almost hair-like stems and their tiny, inconspicuous flowers that are typically yellowish or white. Unlike most plants, their leaves are reduced to mere scales, giving them a very sparse, skeletal appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, screwstems are tough survivors that can grow in poor, sandy soils where many other plants cannot thrive, often appearing in pine barrens and other challenging habitats.

children.name: Centaurium
children.description: Centauries are small annual wildflowers in the gentian family known for their delicate pink or white flowers that bloom in late summer. These petite plants typically grow in open, disturbed areas like roadsides, fields, and sandy soils. Both New England species are actually non-native plants that have naturalized from Europe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Centauries can be identified by their tiny 4-5 petaled flowers that are typically pink with white centers, and their opposite leaves arranged along slender, branching stems. Unlike many other small wildflowers, their flowers have a distinctive star-like shape when fully open.
children.funFact: Common centaury has been used medicinally for over 2,000 years and was named after the centaur Chiron from Greek mythology, who was said to have used the plant to heal wounds.

children.name: Gentianopsis
children.description: Fringed gentians are a small group of annual wildflowers known for their stunning blue to purple flowers with distinctive fringed petals that look like delicate lace. These plants typically bloom in late summer to fall and prefer wet meadows, marshes, and other moist habitats. They are part of the gentian family but form their own distinct genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other gentians, fringed gentians have petals with beautifully fringed or finely cut edges that give them their common name. Their flowers are also typically larger and more showy than most other gentian species.
children.funFact: Fringed gentian flowers only open on sunny days and close up tight during cloudy weather and at night, making them sometimes called 'fair weather flowers.'

children.name: Halenia
children.description: Spurred gentians are delicate annual wildflowers in the gentian family that produce small, four-petaled flowers with distinctive hollow spurs extending from the back of each bloom. These spurs are unique among North American gentians and give the plants their common name. They typically grow in moist, shaded areas and bloom in late summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The hollow spurs projecting from behind each flower are the key identifying feature that separates spurred gentians from all other gentians in North America. These spurs contain nectar and are thought to attract specific pollinators.
children.funFact: Despite being in the gentian family known for bitter compounds used in herbal medicine, spurred gentians are much smaller and more inconspicuous than their showy relatives like fringed gentians.

children.name: Gentianella
children.description: Dwarf gentians are small, delicate wildflowers that belong to the gentian family. These annual plants produce tiny, tubular flowers that are typically pink, purple, or white, and they prefer moist, cool habitats like wetlands and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger gentian relatives, dwarf gentians are much smaller in stature and have flowers with fringed petals that give them a delicate, almost lacy appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, dwarf gentians are incredibly hardy and can bloom well into fall, sometimes even after the first frost when most other wildflowers have finished for the season.

children.name: Lomatogonium
children.description: Lomatogonium is a small genus of delicate annual wildflowers in the gentian family. These plants are characterized by their small, four-petaled flowers that typically bloom in late summer and early fall in wet, marshy areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most gentians which have five petals, Lomatogonium flowers consistently have four petals arranged in a cross-like pattern. The petals also have distinctive fringed or divided tips that help separate them from other small wetland flowers.
children.funFact: Marsh Felwort is so rare in New England that it's only been confirmed in a handful of locations, making it one of the region's most elusive wildflowers for botanists to find.

children.description: The gentian family consists of herbaceous plants known for their distinctive tubular or funnel-shaped flowers that come in vibrant colors like deep blue, purple, pink, and white. These plants typically have opposite leaves (growing in pairs across from each other on the stem) and flowers with parts arranged in fours or fives. Most members prefer moist habitats like wetlands, meadows, and boggy areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gentian family members can be identified by their flowers having united petals forming a tube, and stamens that are attached directly to the inside of the flower tube rather than at its base. The bitter taste of many species in this family is also characteristic and has made them valuable in traditional medicine.
children.funFact: Many gentians have flowers that only open in bright sunlight and close on cloudy days or at night, earning some species the nickname 'fair weather flowers.'

children.description: The Gentianales are a diverse group of flowering plants that includes some of our most beloved wildflowers like bedstraws and bluets, as well as common weeds like cleavers. Most members of this order have simple leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, and their flowers typically have four or five petals that are often fused together into a tube. These plants can be found in many different habitats across New England, from woodland floors to wetlands to roadsides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are united by having flowers with fused petals and stamens that are attached to the petal tube. Many also have distinctive stipules (small leaf-like structures) where the leaves meet the stem, which is especially noticeable in the madder family.
children.funFact: This order includes coffee (a member of the madder family) and many important medicinal plants - digitalis from dogbane relatives has been used to treat heart conditions, while quinine from cinchona trees in the madder family was historically crucial for treating malaria.

children.name: Fagales
Fagaceae
Quercus
children.description: Oaks are majestic deciduous trees known for their distinctive lobed leaves and acorns - the nuts that develop from their flowers. All oak species share the characteristic of producing these acorns, which serve as crucial food sources for wildlife including squirrels, deer, and many bird species. These long-lived trees are keystone species in forest ecosystems, supporting more types of caterpillars and other insects than almost any other tree genus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oaks are easily identified by their acorns, which no other tree produces, and their typically lobed leaves (though some species have smooth-edged leaves). The acorns sit in distinctive caps called cupules, and oak flowers appear as drooping catkins in spring.
children.funFact: A single mature oak tree can support over 500 species of caterpillars, making them incredibly valuable for birds that need thousands of caterpillars to raise their young each breeding season.

children.name: Castanea
children.description: Chestnuts are deciduous trees and shrubs known for their distinctive spiny burs that contain edible nuts. All members of this genus produce serrated, lance-shaped leaves and creamy white flower clusters called catkins in late spring or early summer. They belong to the beech family and are valued both for their timber and their sweet, nutritious nuts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chestnuts are easily recognized by their spiny, round burs that split open to reveal glossy brown nuts inside. Unlike other nut trees, chestnut leaves have prominent parallel veins that end in sharp teeth along the leaf edges.
children.funFact: The American chestnut was once called the 'redwood of the East' because these giants could reach 100 feet tall and live for centuries, but a devastating fungal blight in the early 1900s wiped out nearly 4 billion trees, making it one of the greatest ecological disasters in North American history.

children.name: Fagus
children.description: Beeches are majestic deciduous trees known for their smooth, gray bark and distinctive oval leaves with prominent parallel veins. They produce small, triangular nuts enclosed in spiny husks and are among the most recognizable trees in New England's forests. These slow-growing giants can live for centuries and create dense canopies that provide important wildlife habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beeches are easily identified by their uniquely smooth, elephant-like gray bark that remains unbroken even on mature trees, unlike other forest trees that develop rough, furrowed bark with age. Their leaves also have a distinctive pattern of straight, parallel veins running from the midrib to the leaf edge.
children.funFact: Beech trees are famous for retaining their bronze-colored leaves throughout winter, creating a rustling canopy that won't drop until new leaves push them off in spring.

children.description: The beech family includes some of New England's most iconic and economically important trees, including all our native oaks, chestnuts, and beeches. These are typically large, long-lived deciduous trees that produce nuts as their fruits, often enclosed in protective husks or cups. Most species in this family are important sources of food for wildlife and have played significant roles in human history.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the beech family are distinguished by their hard-shelled nuts (like acorns and chestnuts) that are partially or completely enclosed in a protective covering called a cupule. Their leaves are typically simple with prominent veining, and they often have distinctive bark patterns.
children.funFact: Oak trees can live for over 1,000 years and a single mature oak can support over 500 species of insects, making them among the most ecologically valuable trees in North American forests.

children.name: Betulaceae
Betula
children.description: Birches are deciduous trees and shrubs known for their distinctive bark that often peels in thin, papery layers. These hardy plants are well-adapted to cooler climates and are among the first trees to colonize disturbed areas after fires or logging. All birches produce small, cone-like fruits called catkins and have serrated leaves that turn bright yellow in fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Birches can be distinguished from other trees by their characteristic peeling bark, small triangular or oval leaves with double-serrated edges, and their distinctive hanging male catkins that release pollen in early spring.
children.funFact: Paper birch bark was traditionally used by Native Americans to make canoes, baskets, and wigwam coverings because it's naturally waterproof and doesn't rot even when the tree's inner wood has decayed.

children.name: Corylus
children.description: Hazels are deciduous shrubs and small trees known for producing edible nuts that have been valued by humans for thousands of years. These plants are characterized by their heart-shaped, serrated leaves and their unique flowering system where male catkins dangle prominently in early spring before the leaves emerge, while tiny red female flowers appear on the same plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hazels can be distinguished from other nut-producing trees by their distinctive papery or leafy bracts that partially or completely enclose each nut, and their early spring blooming catkins that appear before most other trees leaf out.
children.funFact: Hazel branches have been traditionally used for "water witching" or dowsing - the practice of using forked sticks to locate underground water sources, though this method has no scientific basis.

children.name: Alnus
children.description: Alders are deciduous trees and shrubs in the birch family that thrive in wet soils along streams, ponds, and wetlands. They're nitrogen-fixing plants, meaning they can take nitrogen from the air and add it to the soil through special root nodules, making them important for improving soil fertility. Most alders have dark, serrated leaves and produce small cone-like fruits that persist through winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the birch family, alders have woody, cone-like catkins that remain on the tree after releasing seeds, and they possess nitrogen-fixing root nodules that create small bumps on their roots. Their bark is typically darker and smoother than birches, and they're almost always found in consistently moist or wet soils.
children.funFact: Alder wood doesn't rot when submerged in water, making it historically valuable for building docks, pilings, and even the foundations of Venice, Italy!

children.name: Carpinus
children.description: Hornbeams are small to medium-sized deciduous trees in the birch family, known for their distinctive smooth, gray bark that often has a muscle-like appearance with sinuous ridges. These hardy trees produce small, winged nuts and have serrated leaves that turn beautiful yellow to orange colors in fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hornbeams can be distinguished from other trees by their unique fluted or muscular-looking bark and their papery, three-lobed bracts that surround the small nuts in drooping clusters.
children.funFact: The American hornbeam is sometimes called 'musclewood' because its smooth bark develops distinctive muscle-like ridges and sinews, making it look like a flexed arm!

children.name: Ostrya
children.description: Hop-hornbeams are small to medium-sized deciduous trees in the birch family known for their distinctive papery, hop-like seed clusters that dangle from branches in summer and fall. These hardy trees have elm-like leaves with prominent veins and produce small, inconspicuous flowers in spring. They're often called ironwood because of their exceptionally hard, dense wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hop-hornbeams can be distinguished from other trees by their unique inflated, papery seed pouches that look remarkably similar to hops used in brewing beer. Their bark is also distinctive, being gray and shreddy, peeling off in thin, narrow strips.
children.funFact: The wood of hop-hornbeams is so incredibly hard and durable that Native Americans and early settlers used it to make tool handles, mallets, and even fence posts that could last for decades without rotting.

children.description: The birch family includes deciduous trees and shrubs that are wind-pollinated and produce distinctive catkins (hanging flower clusters). These hardy plants are well-adapted to cooler climates and poor soils, making them common throughout New England's forests and landscapes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have simple, serrated leaves and produce both male and female flowers on the same plant in separate catkins. Their fruits are small nuts or nutlets, often with papery wings for wind dispersal.
children.funFact: Birch bark was traditionally used by Native Americans to make canoes, baskets, and even paper because of its waterproof and flexible properties.

children.name: Juglandaceae
Carya
children.description: Hickories are a group of deciduous trees known for their compound leaves, hard wood, and distinctive nuts. These tall forest trees produce edible nuts enclosed in thick, four-sectioned husks that split open when ripe. All hickories have alternate, pinnately compound leaves with 5-17 leaflets arranged along a central stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hickories can be distinguished from other nut trees by their compound leaves and their nuts' characteristic four-part husks that split completely open. Unlike walnuts, hickory nuts have smooth shells rather than deeply grooved ones.
children.funFact: Hickory wood is prized for tool handles and smoking meats because it's incredibly strong and burns hot with a sweet, smoky flavor - early settlers relied on hickory for everything from axe handles to flavoring their bacon!

children.name: Juglans
children.description: Walnuts are large, deciduous trees known for their compound leaves and distinctive nuts enclosed in thick, rounded husks. These majestic trees produce aromatic foliage and valuable timber, while their nuts have been an important food source for both wildlife and humans for thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nut trees, walnuts have large compound leaves with multiple leaflets arranged along a central stem, and their nuts are enclosed in a thick, fleshy husk that doesn't split open naturally like other tree nuts.
children.funFact: Black walnut trees produce a natural herbicide called juglone in their roots, leaves, and bark that prevents many other plants from growing nearby, earning them the nickname 'allelopathic trees.'

children.description: The walnut family includes trees known for their compound leaves and hard-shelled nuts that are prized by both wildlife and humans. These deciduous trees are characterized by their aromatic wood and leaves, and they produce nuts enclosed in thick husks that split open when ripe. Most members of this family are large, long-lived trees that play important ecological roles in New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nut-producing trees, walnut family members have pinnately compound leaves (multiple leaflets arranged along a central stem) and their nuts are enclosed in thick, fleshy or fibrous husks. The trees also contain aromatic oils that give them their distinctive smell when crushed.
children.funFact: Black walnut trees produce a natural herbicide called juglone in their roots, leaves, and husks that prevents many other plants from growing nearby - a phenomenon called allelopathy.

children.name: Myricaceae
Morella
children.description: Bayberries are aromatic shrubs that thrive in coastal and wetland areas throughout New England. These hardy plants are known for their waxy, berry-like fruits and their ability to fix nitrogen in the soil through specialized root bacteria, helping them grow in sandy, nutrient-poor conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other shrubs, bayberries produce small, waxy fruits covered in a thick coating of natural wax that persists through winter. Their leaves are typically leathery and aromatic when crushed, often with a spicy or resinous scent.
children.funFact: The waxy coating on bayberry fruits was traditionally harvested by early colonists to make candles that burned with a pleasant, sweet fragrance and produced less smoke than regular tallow candles.

children.name: Comptonia
children.description: Sweet-ferns are low-growing shrubs that aren't actually ferns at all, despite their name and fern-like leaves. They belong to the bayberry family and are known for their distinctive fragrant, deeply-lobed leaves that release a sweet, spicy scent when crushed. These hardy plants thrive in poor, sandy soils where many other plants struggle to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true ferns, sweet-ferns produce flowers and seeds rather than spores, and their leaves grow alternately along woody stems. The deeply cut, elongated leaves with their distinctive lobes make them easily recognizable among New England's native shrubs.
children.funFact: Sweet-fern leaves were traditionally used by Native Americans and early settlers as a natural insect repellent and were also brewed into tea for treating stomach ailments.

children.name: Myrica
children.description: Bog myrtles are aromatic shrubs that thrive in wetland environments like bogs, marshes, and pond edges. These hardy plants are specially adapted to grow in acidic, nutrient-poor soils where many other plants struggle to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bog myrtles have distinctive waxy, fragrant leaves that release a sweet, resinous scent when crushed, and they produce small catkin-like flowers followed by waxy berries.
children.funFact: Bog myrtle leaves contain natural compounds that repel insects, so they were traditionally used as a natural bug spray and even stuffed into bedding to keep pests away.

children.description: The wax trees and shrubs are a small family of woody plants known for producing waxy, berry-like fruits and often growing in challenging environments like wetlands and sandy soils. These hardy plants typically have simple, alternate leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers that bloom before the leaves emerge in spring. Most species in this family can fix nitrogen in their roots, helping them thrive in nutrient-poor soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their waxy, often grayish-white berries that persist through winter and their ability to grow in poor, acidic soils where other woody plants struggle. The waxy coating on their fruits is particularly thick and notable compared to other berry-producing shrubs.
children.funFact: Early American colonists harvested the waxy berries of bayberry shrubs to make candles that burned cleaner and smelled better than animal fat candles, and bayberry candles are still made today as a traditional craft.

children.description: The Fagales are an order of trees and shrubs that includes some of New England's most iconic and economically important woody plants. These plants are united by their simple leaves and their reproductive structures - they produce small, often inconspicuous flowers that are typically wind-pollinated, and many develop distinctive nuts or catkins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many flowering plants, Fagales members rarely have showy, colorful flowers since they rely on wind rather than insects for pollination. Most species in this group are also monoecious, meaning individual plants produce both male and female flowers.
children.funFact: This order includes trees that produce some of the world's most recognized nuts - from the acorns of oaks that feed countless wildlife species, to the walnuts and hickory nuts that have been important food sources for both wildlife and humans for thousands of years.

children.name: Dipsacales
Caprifoliaceae
Lonicera
children.description: Honeysuckles are a diverse group of flowering shrubs and woody vines known for their sweetly fragrant, tubular flowers that often come in pairs. Most species produce small, colorful berries and have opposite leaves arranged along their stems. While some are beloved native plants that attract hummingbirds and butterflies, others are aggressive non-native species that can overwhelm local ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Honeysuckles are distinguished by their paired, tubular flowers that are often two-lipped, and their characteristic opposite leaf arrangement. Many species also produce distinctive paired berries that may be fused together at their base.
children.funFact: The sweet nectar in honeysuckle flowers can actually be tasted by gently pulling the stamen through the flower tube - a childhood favorite that gives these plants their common name!

children.name: Valeriana
children.description: Valerian is a genus of perennial herbs known for their fragrant flowers and distinctive root systems. These plants typically grow in moist soils and produce clusters of small, tubular flowers that range from white to pink. Both New England species are herbaceous plants that die back to their roots each winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Valerians are distinguished from other plants by their opposite leaves and their characteristic strong, musky scent, especially from their roots. Their small flowers are arranged in dense, branching clusters called cymes.
children.funFact: Valerian root has been used as a natural sleep aid and anxiety remedy for over 2,000 years, and its strong scent is also irresistibly attractive to cats, similar to catnip.

children.name: Dipsacus
children.description: Teasels are tall, spiny plants with distinctive egg-shaped flower heads covered in sharp, curved bracts that give them a prickly appearance. These robust wildflowers produce dense clusters of small tubular flowers that bloom in rings around their characteristic cone-like heads. Both species found in New England are non-native plants that have naturalized in fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Teasels are easily recognized by their tall stems (often 3-6 feet high) topped with large, spiny oval flower heads that remain standing through winter. The sharp, hooked bracts surrounding each flower head are much more prominent and rigid than those found on similar-looking plants like burdock or thistle.
children.funFact: Wild teasel flower heads were historically used by textile workers to raise the nap on woolen cloth - the hooked bracts were perfect natural tools for combing and preparing fabric, giving the plant its common name.

children.name: Symphoricarpos
children.description: Snowberries are small deciduous shrubs in the honeysuckle family known for their distinctive clusters of white or pinkish berries that persist well into winter. These hardy native shrubs typically grow 2-6 feet tall and produce small, bell-shaped flowers in summer followed by their characteristic waxy berries. They're commonly found in woodland edges, thickets, and disturbed areas throughout much of North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snowberries can be distinguished from other honeysuckle family shrubs by their distinctive berries - either bright white and spongy (snowberry) or coral-red and clustered (coralberry). Their simple, opposite leaves and small tubular flowers also help separate them from similar shrubs.
children.funFact: The white berries of Common Snowberry contain a soap-like compound called saponin, which Native Americans traditionally used as a natural detergent for washing clothes and hair.

children.name: Triosteum
children.description: Horse Gentians are unusual woodland wildflowers that produce distinctive orange-red berries and have opposite leaves that often appear to be pierced by the stem. These perennial herbs typically grow 2-4 feet tall in shaded forest areas and bloom with small, inconspicuous reddish or yellowish flowers in early summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true gentians, Horse Gentians have opposite leaves that are often perfoliate (appearing pierced by the stem) and produce colorful berries rather than capsules. Their flowers are small and clustered in leaf axils rather than showy and terminal.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, Horse Gentians aren't actually related to true gentians at all - they belong to the honeysuckle family and were likely named for their bitter taste, which was thought to be good medicine for horses.

children.name: Diervilla
children.description: Bush honeysuckles are low-growing, deciduous shrubs native to North America that produce small, yellow, tubular flowers in summer. These hardy plants typically grow 1-4 feet tall and spread by underground stems, forming colonies in woodland areas. They belong to the honeysuckle family but have a distinctly shrubby, bushy growth habit rather than climbing like many of their relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true honeysuckles which are often vining plants, bush honeysuckles are compact shrubs with a clumping growth pattern. Their flowers are consistently yellow and much smaller than those of ornamental honeysuckles, and they produce dry capsules rather than berries.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, bush honeysuckles are actually more closely related to weigelas than to the familiar climbing honeysuckles, and they're one of the few honeysuckle family members that are truly native to northeastern North America.

children.name: Linnaea
children.description: Twinflowers are delicate, creeping evergreen plants that form low mats on the forest floor. They produce pairs of small, bell-shaped pink or white flowers that hang gracefully from slender stalks, giving them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the honeysuckle family, twinflowers have a distinctive trailing, woody stem that creeps along the ground and consistently produce their flowers in pairs on Y-shaped stalks.
children.funFact: This genus was named Linnaea in honor of Carl Linnaeus, the father of modern taxonomy, who considered the humble twinflower his personal emblem and favorite plant.

children.name: Kolkwitzia
children.description: Kolkwitzia is a genus containing just one species - the Beauty Bush, a deciduous flowering shrub native to China but commonly planted in New England gardens. These shrubs are known for their graceful arching branches and abundant spring blooms that attract pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beauty Bush is distinguished from other honeysuckle family shrubs by its small, tubular pink flowers with yellow throats that bloom in dense clusters, and its distinctive bristly, hairy fruits.
children.funFact: Despite being called Beauty Bush, Kolkwitzia amabilis is actually the only species in its entire genus, making it a botanical 'singleton' in the plant kingdom.

children.name: Knautia
children.description: Knautia is a genus of flowering plants in the honeysuckle family that produces distinctive pincushion-like flower heads. These plants are herbaceous perennials with opposite leaves and flowers arranged in dense, rounded clusters that attract butterflies and other pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Knautia flowers have an irregular, pincushion appearance with outer flowers being larger and more showy than inner ones, and their fruits are crowned with bristly sepals that help with seed dispersal.
children.funFact: The name Knautia honors German botanist Christoph Knaut, and despite being called 'scabious,' these plants were once believed to cure scabies and other skin ailments in traditional medicine.

children.name: Scabiosa
children.description: Pincushion flowers are distinctive wildflowers named for their rounded, cushion-like flower heads that bristle with numerous small florets. These perennial herbs produce delicate, often pale-colored blooms that sit atop slender stems and attract various pollinators including butterflies and bees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other wildflowers, pincushion flowers have a unique pincushion-like appearance with their densely packed florets creating a rounded, textured bloom. The outer florets are typically larger than the inner ones, giving the flower head an distinctive layered look.
children.funFact: The genus name Scabiosa comes from the Latin word 'scabies' because these plants were historically used as herbal remedies to treat skin conditions and wounds.

children.name: Heptacodium
children.description: Heptacodium is a small genus of flowering shrubs in the honeysuckle family, with only one species found anywhere in the world. These deciduous shrubs are native to China but have become popular ornamental plants in New England gardens. They're known for their clusters of small, fragrant white flowers that bloom in late summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the honeysuckle family, Heptacodium has flowers arranged in groups of seven (hence the name), and its flower clusters are followed by colorful, persistent sepals that remain showy long after the petals fall.
children.funFact: The Seven Sons Tree was thought to be extinct until it was rediscovered in eastern China in 1980, making it a true 'living fossil' that you can now find growing in New England landscapes.

children.name: Centranthus
children.description: Centranthus is a small genus of flowering plants in the valerian family, known for producing clusters of small, fragrant flowers. These plants are perennial herbs that typically grow from thick, fleshy roots and have opposite leaves arranged along sturdy stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true valerians (Valeriana), Centranthus flowers have a distinctive long spur at the base and only one stamen instead of three. The flowers are also typically more brightly colored, often appearing in shades of red, pink, or white.
children.funFact: Red Valerian was originally native to the Mediterranean region but has become so well-established in many parts of the world that it's often mistaken for a native wildflower, earning it the nickname 'garden refugee.'

children.name: Succisa
children.description: Succisa is a small genus of perennial wildflowers in the honeysuckle family, known for their distinctive rounded flower heads made up of tiny tubular blooms. These plants typically grow in grasslands and meadows, forming clumps with basal leaves and tall flowering stems that bloom in late summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Succisa differs from other scabious plants by having flower heads with all florets the same size, rather than having larger outer florets around smaller inner ones. The leaves are also typically undivided, unlike many related genera.
children.funFact: The common name 'Devil's-bit' comes from the plant's short, abruptly ending rootstock that looks as if it has been bitten off - according to folklore, the devil bit it off in a fit of rage because the plant was too useful to humans.

children.name: Sixalix
children.description: Sixalix is a small genus of flowering plants in the honeysuckle family that includes plants commonly known as scabious. These are herbaceous plants that produce clusters of small, tubular flowers arranged in dense, rounded flower heads. They are native to the Mediterranean region but have been introduced to other parts of the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sixalix can be distinguished from other scabious genera by its specific flower structure and the arrangement of its seeds, which have distinctive bristles or awns that help with wind dispersal.
children.funFact: The name 'scabious' comes from the Latin word 'scabies' because these plants were traditionally used in folk medicine to treat skin conditions and wounds.

children.name: Weigela
children.description: Weigela bushes are deciduous flowering shrubs in the honeysuckle family that produce abundant tubular flowers in late spring to early summer. These hardy shrubs are native to East Asia but have become popular ornamental plants in gardens and landscaping throughout temperate regions. They typically grow 4-10 feet tall with arching branches and opposite leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Weigela flowers are distinctively funnel-shaped and often change color as they age, typically starting lighter and deepening to pink or red. Unlike many other honeysuckle family members, Weigela flowers grow directly from the branches rather than in terminal clusters.
children.funFact: Weigela flowers are designed to attract hummingbirds - their tubular shape and bright colors are perfectly suited for the birds' long beaks and excellent color vision.

children.description: The honeysuckle family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes fragrant climbing vines, sturdy shrubs, and delicate woodland herbs. Most members produce tubular or clustered flowers that are often sweetly scented and attractive to pollinators like hummingbirds, butterflies, and bees. Many species in this family produce colorful berries that provide food for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have opposite leaves and flowers with fused petals forming tubes or flat-topped clusters. The flowers often have an irregular shape with protruding stamens, and the fruits are usually berries or small dry capsules.
children.funFact: The twinflower (Linnaea) in this family was named after the famous botanist Carl Linnaeus, who developed our modern system of naming plants and animals - it was his personal favorite flower!

children.name: Viburnaceae
Viburnum
children.description: Viburnums are a diverse group of shrubs and small trees known for their showy clusters of small white or pink flowers that bloom in spring or early summer. These woody plants typically produce colorful berries that range from red to blue-black, providing important food for birds and wildlife throughout the seasons.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Viburnums can be identified by their opposite leaves and flat-topped or rounded flower clusters called cymes. Their berries contain a single flat seed, unlike many other berry-producing shrubs that have multiple seeds.
children.funFact: Many viburnum berries are edible when fully ripe and were traditionally used by Native Americans to make jellies and preserves, though some species taste better than others - northern wild raisin berries are particularly sweet when ripe!

children.name: Sambucus
children.description: Elders are shrubs or small trees known for their clusters of small, creamy-white flowers that bloom in late spring or early summer, followed by berries in late summer. These hardy plants are commonly found along woodland edges, roadsides, and disturbed areas throughout New England. Both species produce berries that are important food sources for birds and wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elders can be distinguished from other shrubs by their opposite, compound leaves with 5-11 leaflets and their distinctive flat-topped or pyramid-shaped flower clusters. The two New England species are easily separated by their berry color - red-berried elder produces bright red berries while American black elderberry produces dark purple-black berries.
children.funFact: American black elderberries have been used for centuries to make jams, syrups, and traditional remedies, but the raw berries and other parts of the plant can cause stomach upset if not properly prepared.

children.description: The elder family consists of shrubs and small trees that produce clusters of small, often fragrant flowers followed by colorful berries. These woody plants are commonly found in forests, wetlands, and woodland edges throughout New England, where they provide important food sources for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their opposite leaves and distinctive flat-topped or rounded flower clusters that develop into berry-like fruits. The flowers typically have 5 petals and are arranged in showy, conspicuous clusters.
children.funFact: Elderberries have been used for centuries to make jams, wines, and traditional medicines, while the hollow stems of elder plants were historically used to make flutes and other musical instruments.

children.description: The Dipsacales are an order of flowering plants that includes many familiar shrubs and small trees found throughout New England's forests and gardens. Most members of this group produce their flowers in clusters and have opposite leaves, meaning the leaves grow in pairs across from each other on the stem. These plants often develop colorful berries that are important food sources for birds and other wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Dipsacales apart from other plant orders is their distinctive flower arrangement in dense clusters or heads, and their consistent pattern of opposite leaf arrangement. Many also have a unique ovary structure with multiple chambers that develop into their characteristic berries.
children.funFact: Many Dipsacales have evolved clever strategies to attract both pollinators and seed dispersers - elderflowers produce fragrant, creamy white flower clusters that attract insects, then develop into dark purple berries that birds love to eat and spread throughout the forest.

children.name: Solanales
Solanaceae
Solanum
children.description: The nightshades are a diverse group of flowering plants that includes many familiar species from both wild and cultivated varieties. Members of this genus typically produce small, star-shaped flowers with five petals and distinctive fruits that are often berries. You'll find everything from weedy species growing in disturbed soils to some of our most important food crops in this remarkable plant group.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nightshades are characterized by their five-petaled flowers with prominent yellow stamens that form a cone shape in the center. Their fruits are typically berries or berry-like structures, and many species contain alkaloid compounds that can be toxic.
children.funFact: This genus contains some of the world's most important food crops including potatoes, tomatoes, and eggplants, yet many wild nightshades are poisonous - earning the family its ominous common name.

children.name: Physalis
children.description: Groundcherries are a group of plants in the nightshade family that produce small, round fruits enclosed in papery, lantern-like husks called calyces. These annual or perennial herbs are found throughout New England, growing in fields, gardens, and disturbed soils. The fruits are often edible and can range from sweet to tart in flavor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The inflated, papery husk that completely surrounds each fruit is the most distinctive feature of groundcherries, making them easily recognizable from other nightshade family members like tomatoes or peppers.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, groundcherries aren't actually cherries at all - they're more closely related to tomatoes and are sometimes called 'husk tomatoes' for their papery fruit coverings.

children.name: Datura
children.description: Devil's Trumpets are a genus of striking flowering plants known for their large, trumpet-shaped blooms that open in the evening. These robust annual herbs produce distinctive spiny seed pods and contain powerful alkaloids that make all parts of the plant highly toxic. They're members of the nightshade family and are found growing in disturbed soils, gardens, and waste areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Devil's Trumpets can be identified by their large, funnel-shaped flowers (often 3-8 inches long) and their characteristic spiny, egg-shaped seed capsules that split open when mature. Unlike many nightshade relatives with small flowers, Datura species produce some of the largest and most showy blooms in the family.
children.funFact: The flowers of Devil's Trumpets are pollinated primarily by hawk moths, opening at dusk and releasing an intense, sweet fragrance to attract these night-flying visitors.

children.name: Nicotiana
children.description: Tobaccos are flowering plants in the nightshade family known for their large, soft leaves and tubular flowers that often release sweet fragrances in the evening. These plants contain nicotine, a natural compound they produce to protect themselves from insects and other herbivores. Most species are native to the Americas and have been cultivated by humans for thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tobacco plants are distinguished from other nightshade family members by their sticky, hairy leaves that contain high concentrations of nicotine and their distinctive trumpet-shaped flowers that are often white, pink, or greenish-yellow.
children.funFact: Many tobacco species, including jasmine tobacco, open their flowers and release their strongest fragrance at night to attract sphinx moths and other nocturnal pollinators with their sweet scent.

children.name: Alkekengi
children.description: Japanese-lanterns are distinctive plants in the nightshade family known for their papery, balloon-like seed pods that resemble colorful lanterns. These perennial herbs produce small white flowers in summer, but it's their inflated orange-red calyxes (the outer part of the flower) that surround the fruit and give them their common name. The bright, decorative seed pods make them popular in dried flower arrangements and fall decorations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nightshade family members, Japanese-lanterns are easily recognized by their inflated, papery orange calyxes that completely enclose the small cherry-like fruit inside. The lantern-shaped pods are much larger and more colorful than the actual fruit they contain.
children.funFact: The papery 'lanterns' are actually modified sepals that inflate after flowering to protect the developing fruit, and they can persist on the plant well into winter, creating natural decorations in the garden.

children.name: Nicandra
children.description: Nicandra is a small genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, containing just one species that has spread around the world. These plants are annual herbs that produce distinctive papery, inflated seed pods that completely enclose their small berries. They're originally from South America but have become naturalized in many temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nicandra can be identified by its unique pale blue to white bell-shaped flowers and its most distinctive feature - large, papery, balloon-like calyxes that inflate around the fruit after flowering. Unlike many nightshade relatives, the inflated seed pods are much larger than the actual fruit inside.
children.funFact: Apple-of-Peru gets its common name not because it's related to apples or native to Peru, but because early botanists thought its inflated seed pods resembled small apples, and it was first scientifically described from specimens collected in Peru.

children.name: Lycium
children.description: Boxthorns are a genus of thorny shrubs in the nightshade family that produce small, often brightly colored berries. These hardy plants are known for their ability to thrive in poor soils and harsh conditions, making them common in arid regions around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boxthorns can be identified by their thorny branches, small tubular flowers, and distinctive bright red or orange berries that often persist through winter.
children.funFact: The matrimony vine, our local boxthorn species, produces goji berries - the same 'superfruit' that has become popular in health food stores worldwide.

children.name: Hyoscyamus
children.description: Henbanes are a small group of toxic plants in the nightshade family, known for their distinctive funnel-shaped flowers and deeply lobed leaves. These annual or biennial herbs produce seeds in characteristic urn-shaped capsules and have a long history of use in traditional medicine, though they contain dangerous alkaloids that make them poisonous to humans and animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Henbanes can be distinguished from other nightshade family members by their sticky, hairy stems and leaves, and their pale yellow flowers with distinctive dark purple veins and centers.
children.funFact: Black henbane was historically used as an ingredient in 'witches' brews' and flying ointments due to its hallucinogenic properties, and Shakespeare referenced it as the poison used to kill Hamlet's father.

children.name: Petunia
children.description: Petunias are a genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family, known for their trumpet-shaped, colorful blooms. These plants are native to South America but have become popular garden flowers worldwide due to their showy petals and long blooming season. Most petunias are low-growing plants that spread along the ground or trail from containers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Petunias have distinctive funnel-shaped flowers with five fused petals that flare out at the opening, creating their characteristic trumpet appearance. Unlike many other nightshade family members, petunias are primarily grown for ornamental purposes rather than food or medicine.
children.funFact: While most people know petunias as colorful garden flowers, wild petunias like the violetflower petunia actually have much smaller, more modest blooms and are quite different from the large, ruffled varieties commonly sold at garden centers.

children.name: Salpiglossis
children.description: Painted-tongues are ornamental flowering plants in the nightshade family, originally from South America but commonly grown in gardens throughout New England. These annual plants produce trumpet-shaped flowers with distinctively veined petals that create intricate, painterly patterns in rich colors like purple, yellow, and red.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other nightshade family members, painted-tongues have uniquely patterned flowers with dark veining that resembles brushstrokes or marble patterns across the petals. Their funnel-shaped blooms are also much more ornate and decorative than the typically simple flowers of related plants.
children.funFact: The name 'painted-tongue' comes from the flower's resemblance to an artist's paintbrush dipped in multiple colors, with the intricate vein patterns looking like delicate brushwork across each petal.

children.description: The nightshade family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes many familiar species, from edible tomatoes and potatoes to ornamental petunias. These plants typically produce five-petaled flowers that are often star-shaped or tubular, followed by fruits that can be berries, capsules, or other seed-containing structures. Members of this family are found worldwide and range from small herbs to shrubs and even some trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nightshade family plants are characterized by their five-petaled flowers with five stamens that alternate with the petals, and their leaves are typically arranged alternately on the stem. The flowers often have a distinctive wheel or trumpet shape, and many species produce alkaloid compounds.
children.funFact: This family includes both some of our most beloved food crops (tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, eggplants) and some of the most toxic plants in North America, with many species containing powerful alkaloids that can be deadly if consumed.

children.name: Convolvulaceae
Ipomoea
children.description: Morning-glories are a diverse group of flowering vines and plants known for their trumpet-shaped blooms that often open in the early morning hours. Most species are climbing or trailing vines with heart-shaped leaves, though the group also includes the familiar sweet potato. Their showy flowers come in various colors including purple, blue, white, and red.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Morning-glories can be identified by their distinctive funnel or trumpet-shaped flowers and their twining, climbing growth habit. Unlike many other vines, they typically have smooth-edged, heart-shaped leaves and flowers that open and close at specific times of day.
children.funFact: The sweet potato is actually a morning-glory! While most people think of morning-glories as ornamental flowering vines, this genus includes one of the world's most important food crops.

children.name: Cuscuta
children.description: Dodders are unusual parasitic plants that look like orange or yellow stringy vines wrapped around other plants. Unlike typical plants, they have no leaves and don't produce their own food through photosynthesis. Instead, they steal nutrients and water directly from their host plants by penetrating them with specialized structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dodders are easily recognized by their thin, thread-like orange or yellow stems that spiral around host plants, completely lacking green leaves or roots in the soil. Their parasitic lifestyle makes them unique among flowering plants in New England.
children.funFact: Dodder seedlings can actually "smell" their preferred host plants and will grow toward them, sometimes even changing direction mid-growth to find a better target!

children.name: Calystegia
children.description: False bindweeds are climbing or trailing vines in the morning glory family known for their large, showy trumpet-shaped flowers that are typically white or pink. These hardy perennials spread by underground rhizomes and can quickly cover fences, shrubs, and other plants with their heart-shaped or arrowhead-shaped leaves. They're often considered aggressive garden weeds due to their vigorous growth habits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true bindweeds (Convolvulus), false bindweeds have large bracts that partially or completely hide the flower sepals, giving their blooms a cleaner, more prominent appearance. Their flowers are also typically larger and more showy than those of their true bindweed cousins.
children.funFact: The flowers of false bindweeds open in the morning and typically close by afternoon, earning them a place in the morning glory family and making them perfect for early-rising pollinators like bees.

children.name: Convolvulus
children.description: Bindweeds are climbing or trailing plants in the morning glory family known for their distinctive funnel-shaped flowers and heart-shaped leaves. These hardy perennials produce showy white, pink, or blue trumpet-like blooms that open in the morning and often close by afternoon. They spread through extensive underground root systems and twining stems that wrap around other plants for support.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bindweeds can be distinguished from other morning glories by their smaller flowers (typically 1-2 inches across) and their persistent, often problematic spreading habit through deep rhizomes.
children.funFact: Field bindweed's root system can extend up to 20 feet deep and 10 feet wide, making it one of the most persistent weeds in agriculture - a single plant can produce up to 500 seeds!

children.description: The bindweed family consists of plants known for their distinctive trumpet or funnel-shaped flowers and often twining, vine-like growth habits. Most members of this family are climbing or trailing plants that wrap around other vegetation for support, though some grow as upright herbs or even parasitic vines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants are easily recognized by their characteristic funnel-shaped flowers that often appear pleated in bud, and their heart-shaped or arrow-shaped leaves. Unlike many other climbing plant families, bindweeds typically have flowers that open and close at specific times of day.
children.funFact: Morning glories got their name because their flowers typically open in the early morning and close by afternoon, while some evening-blooming species in this family do exactly the opposite!

children.description: The Solanales are a diverse group of flowering plants that includes some of our most familiar garden vegetables and ornamental flowers. This order brings together plants that might seem quite different at first glance - from tomatoes and petunias to morning glories and sweet potatoes - but they share important underlying characteristics in their flower structure and genetics.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have flowers with five petals that are fused together into a tube or funnel shape, and they often produce berries or capsules as fruits. Many species in this group also contain unique chemical compounds called alkaloids.
children.funFact: This order includes both some of the world's most important food crops (tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, sweet potatoes) and some of the most toxic plants known to humans - many nightshades contain powerful alkaloids that can be deadly if consumed.

children.name: Myrtales
Onagraceae
Oenothera
children.description: Evening primroses, sundrops, and beeblossoms are a diverse group of flowering plants known for their showy, four-petaled flowers that often open in the evening or early morning. Many species have bright yellow or pink blooms and produce distinctive seed pods that split open when ripe. These hardy plants can be found in a variety of habitats from roadsides to meadows throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their four-petaled flowers arranged in a cross pattern and their characteristic long, tube-like flower buds. Most species also have a distinctive X-shaped stigma (the female part of the flower) and produce elongated seed capsules.
children.funFact: Many evening primroses are "night bloomers" that open their fragrant flowers at dusk to attract night-flying moths for pollination, then close them again by the next morning.

children.name: Epilobium
children.description: Willowherbs are a group of flowering plants in the evening primrose family that typically grow in wet or disturbed areas like marshes, streambanks, and forest clearings. These plants produce small, four-petaled flowers that are usually pink, purple, or white, and their seeds have fluffy white hairs that help them disperse on the wind. Most willowherbs are perennial herbs that spread both by seeds and underground stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Willowherbs can be distinguished from other members of the evening primrose family by their four-petaled flowers arranged in terminal clusters and their distinctive narrow seed pods that split open to release fluffy-tailed seeds. Their leaves are typically lance-shaped and arranged alternately or opposite on the stem.
children.funFact: The fluffy seed dispersal mechanism of willowherbs is so effective that some species, like Great Willowherb, were among the first plants to colonize bomb sites in London after World War II, earning them the nickname 'bombweed.'

children.name: Ludwigia
children.description: Primrose-willows are a group of wetland plants that love to have their feet wet, growing in marshes, pond edges, and other watery places throughout New England. These plants are members of the evening primrose family and typically produce small, four-petaled flowers that can be yellow or sometimes inconspicuous. Despite their name, they're not related to primroses or willows, but got their common name from their flower shape and preference for moist soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many wetland plants, primrose-willows have distinctive four-petaled flowers and produce unique seed capsules that can be box-like or spherical depending on the species. Their leaves are typically simple and alternate, and they can grow both as floating aquatic plants or upright marsh plants.
children.funFact: The Seedbox gets its name from its distinctive square, box-shaped seed capsules that split open at the top like a lid, releasing tiny seeds that can float to new wetland homes.

children.name: Circaea
children.description: Enchanter's nightshades are delicate woodland wildflowers that produce tiny white flowers with deeply notched petals, giving them a distinctive heart-shaped appearance. These shade-loving plants grow in moist forest understories and have opposite leaves with smooth or slightly toothed edges. Despite their mysterious name, they're actually members of the evening primrose family and are completely harmless.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the evening primrose family, enchanter's nightshades have only two petals per flower (instead of four) and produce small, pear-shaped fruits covered in hooked bristles that stick to clothing and animal fur.
children.funFact: The name 'enchanter's nightshade' comes from medieval folklore when these plants were associated with the sorceress Circe from Greek mythology, though they have no actual connection to deadly nightshade or magic.

children.name: Chamaenerion
children.description: Fireweeds are tall, showy wildflowers in the evening primrose family known for their distinctive spikes of bright pink-purple flowers. These hardy perennials are pioneer species that quickly colonize disturbed areas like burned forests, cleared land, and roadsides. They spread both by wind-dispersed seeds and underground rhizomes, forming colorful colonies in open habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fireweeds stand out from other pink wildflowers with their tall flower spikes that bloom from bottom to top, narrow willow-like leaves arranged alternately on the stem, and distinctive four-petaled flowers with deeply notched petals.
children.funFact: Fireweed gets its name from its remarkable ability to be among the first plants to sprout after forest fires, creating spectacular purple displays across burned landscapes and helping to restore the ecosystem.

children.name: Clarkia
children.description: Clarkias are annual wildflowers in the evening primrose family known for their showy, four-petaled flowers that bloom in summer. These colorful plants typically have slender stems and narrow leaves, with flowers that range from pink and purple to white.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Clarkias can be identified by their distinctive four-petaled flowers with clawed petals (narrow at the base, wider at the tip) and eight stamens. Unlike many related plants, their flower buds nod downward before opening.
children.funFact: Clarkias were named after Captain William Clark of the famous Lewis and Clark expedition, who collected specimens of these beautiful wildflowers during their journey across the American West.

children.description: The evening primrose family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes many colorful wildflowers and garden favorites. Most members of this family have four-petaled flowers and produce distinctive seed pods, with many species blooming in the evening or at night to attract moth pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants typically have flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern and often produce long, narrow seed capsules that split open to release many small seeds. Many species also have a unique floral tube structure where the petals and stamens appear to arise from the top of the ovary.
children.funFact: Evening primroses earned their name because many species open their fragrant flowers at dusk and close them by morning, creating a nightly floral display that attracts night-flying moths with their sweet perfume.

children.name: Lythraceae
Lythrum
children.description: Lythrum loosestrifes are herbaceous plants that typically grow in wet areas like marshes, pond edges, and stream banks. These plants are known for their showy spikes of small, colorful flowers that bloom from summer into fall, and their simple, often narrow leaves arranged oppositely on the stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Loosestrifes can be identified by their distinctive flowers with 4-6 petals that have a wrinkled, papery texture, and their preference for consistently moist soils. Unlike many wetland plants, they produce tall, dense flower spikes that stand well above the foliage.
children.funFact: Purple loosestrife exhibits a fascinating reproductive strategy called tristyly, where individual plants have flowers with stamens and pistils at three different heights, requiring cross-pollination between different flower types to produce viable seeds.

children.name: Decodon
children.description: Swamp loosestrifes are wetland shrubs that thrive in the shallow waters and muddy shores of marshes, swamps, and pond edges. These hardy plants are specially adapted to life in waterlogged soils, where they form dense colonies along the water's edge.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other loosestrifes, swamp loosestrifes are woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants, and they have distinctive arching stems that can root where they touch the water or mud.
children.funFact: Swamp loosestrife stems can grow in graceful arcs that bend down and root at their tips, allowing the plant to 'walk' across shallow water and colonize new areas.

children.name: Trapa
children.description: Water chestnuts are aquatic plants that float on the surface of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving rivers. They produce distinctive four-horned nuts that sink to the bottom and can remain viable for years before sprouting into new plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants are easily recognized by their diamond-shaped floating leaves arranged in rosettes and their unique spiny, four-horned fruits that look like ancient caltrops (spiked weapons).
children.funFact: The hard, spiny fruits were historically used as natural weapons called 'caltrops' to stop cavalry and foot soldiers, which is why water caltrop is sometimes called 'water caltrop' after these medieval defensive devices.

children.name: Rotala
children.description: Toothcups are small aquatic or semi-aquatic flowering plants that grow in shallow water or muddy areas. They are members of the loosestrife family and produce tiny, inconspicuous flowers along their stems. These plants are well-adapted to wet environments and can grow both submerged and on exposed mudflats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Toothcups are distinguished by their tiny, tooth-like sepals that give the group its common name, and their small four-petaled flowers that are often pink or white. Unlike many aquatic plants, they have opposite leaves arranged in pairs along square stems.
children.funFact: Despite being native to North America, toothcups are so small and inconspicuous that they're easily overlooked - the entire plant often grows less than 8 inches tall and the flowers are barely visible to the naked eye.

children.name: Ammannia
children.description: Redstems are small aquatic or semi-aquatic flowering plants that typically grow in shallow water, wet soils, or muddy areas. They are characterized by their reddish stems and small, colorful flowers that bloom in summer and fall. These plants are adapted to fluctuating water levels and can survive both flooded and dry conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Redstems can be identified by their distinctive reddish or purplish stems and their ability to grow both submerged in water and on exposed mudflats. Their small flowers are clustered in the leaf axils rather than arranged in showy displays like many other wetland plants.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, redstems are incredibly resilient and can quickly colonize newly exposed mudflats when water levels drop, sometimes creating colorful carpets of tiny flowers across former pond bottoms.

children.description: The Lythrum family consists of plants that are typically found in wet places like marshes, pond edges, and streambanks. Most members of this family produce colorful flowers with four to six petals and have a distinctive cup-shaped base that holds the flower parts together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants can be identified by their opposite or whorled leaves and flowers that have their petals and stamens attached to a tubular or cup-shaped structure called a hypanthium, rather than directly to the base of the flower.
children.funFact: Purple loosestrife, one of the most recognizable members of this family, was brought to New England in the 1800s as a garden ornamental but has since become one of our most aggressive wetland invaders, capable of producing over 2 million seeds per plant each year.

children.name: Melastomataceae
Rhexia
children.description: Meadowbeauties are delicate wildflowers that brighten wet meadows, bogs, and sandy shores throughout New England. These low-growing perennials produce showy four-petaled flowers in shades of pink to purple, typically blooming from summer into early fall. They thrive in acidic, moist soils and are often found in the same habitats as cranberries and other bog plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Meadowbeauties can be identified by their distinctive four-petaled flowers with prominent yellow stamens that curve dramatically like tiny bananas. Their leaves are opposite, oval-shaped, and marked with three to five prominent parallel veins.
