children.funFact: The curved, bright yellow stamens of meadowbeauties buzz audibly when visited by bees, who grab onto them and vibrate their flight muscles to shake loose the pollen in a process called buzz pollination.

children.description: Melastomes are a family of flowering plants known for their distinctive four-petaled flowers and prominent stamens. These plants typically have opposite leaves with curved veins that run parallel to the leaf edges, creating a unique ribbed pattern. Most species in this family are found in tropical regions, though a few hardy members like meadowbeauties have made their way to temperate areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Melastomes can be easily identified by their flowers with four petals and eight stamens that have distinctive curved or bent anthers. Their leaves also have a characteristic pattern of several prominent veins that curve from the base to the tip of the leaf.
children.funFact: The stamens of melastome flowers often have bright yellow, purple, or pink anthers that bend backward in a distinctive hook or elbow shape, making them look like tiny colorful question marks!

children.description: The myrtles, evening primroses, and allies are a diverse group of flowering plants that share similar flower structures and seed development patterns. Most members of this order have flowers with parts arranged in fours or eights, and their seeds develop in distinctive ways within specialized fruit structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants are characterized by having their flower parts (petals, sepals, and stamens) typically arranged in multiples of four, and many species have a unique floral tube structure where petals and stamens arise from the rim.
children.funFact: Evening primroses in this group are famous for opening their bright yellow flowers specifically at dusk, earning them the nickname 'evening stars' as they attract night-flying moths for pollination.

children.name: Sapindales
Sapindaceae
Acer
children.description: Maples are deciduous trees and shrubs known for their distinctive winged seeds that helicopter down in autumn and their often spectacular fall foliage. Most maples have palmately lobed leaves (shaped like a hand with fingers), though some species like box elder have compound leaves with separate leaflets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Maples are easily identified by their paired winged seeds called samaras and their opposite leaf arrangement (leaves grow directly across from each other on the stem). This opposite branching pattern sets them apart from most other trees, which have alternating leaves.
children.funFact: Sugar maples can live over 400 years and produce the sweetest sap of all maples - it takes about 40 gallons of sap to make just one gallon of pure maple syrup!

children.name: Aesculus
children.description: Buckeyes and horse-chestnuts are deciduous trees and shrubs known for their distinctive palmate leaves that spread out like fingers from a central point. They produce showy clusters of tubular flowers in spring, followed by large, glossy brown seeds enclosed in spiky or smooth capsules. These plants are popular ornamental species valued for their attractive foliage and striking flower displays.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The combination of palmate compound leaves (typically 5-7 leaflets arranged like a hand), upright flower clusters, and large glossy seeds makes this group easily recognizable. Their seeds are particularly distinctive, being large, round, and mahogany-colored with a lighter colored scar where they attached to the pod.
children.funFact: The Ohio buckeye earned its nickname "buckeye" because its large, glossy brown seed with a light-colored scar resembles the eye of a white-tailed deer, and Ohio is known as the "Buckeye State" because of the abundance of these trees there.

children.name: Koelreuteria
children.description: Koelreuteria is a small genus of deciduous trees in the soapberry family, known for their showy clusters of bright yellow flowers that bloom in summer. These trees are characterized by their compound leaves with serrated leaflets and distinctive papery, balloon-like seed pods that follow the flowers. The genus includes several species native to Asia, with one commonly planted as an ornamental tree in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Koelreuteria trees are easily recognized by their large, loose clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers and their inflated, papery seed capsules that look like small lanterns. The combination of pinnately compound leaves and these balloon-like fruits makes them quite distinctive among ornamental trees.
children.funFact: The golden rain tree gets its common name from the way its bright yellow petals fall like golden raindrops, carpeting the ground beneath the tree in summer.

children.name: Cardiospermum
children.description: Cardiospermum is a genus of climbing vines in the soapberry family known for their distinctive inflated seed pods that look like little balloons. These tropical and subtropical plants produce small white flowers and have compound leaves with toothed leaflets. The seeds inside the papery pods are typically black with white heart-shaped markings, giving them the common name 'heartseed.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: The inflated, balloon-like seed pods make Cardiospermum easily recognizable among climbing vines. Unlike many other members of the soapberry family, these plants are herbaceous annual or perennial vines rather than trees or shrubs.
children.funFact: The heart-shaped white marking on each black seed is actually a scar called a hilum, which shows where the seed was attached to the pod - this distinctive feature has made the seeds popular in folk medicine and jewelry making around the world.

children.description: The soapberry family is a diverse group of trees, shrubs, and vines that includes some of New England's most beloved trees like maples and horse-chestnuts. Most members of this family produce distinctive fruits and have compound leaves, though maples are notable exceptions with their simple, lobed leaves. Many species in this family contain natural soap-like compounds called saponins in their roots, bark, or fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have flowers with unequal petals and often produce distinctive winged or inflated fruits. The presence of saponins, which create a soapy lather when mixed with water, is a key chemical characteristic that unites this diverse group.
children.funFact: The family gets its name from the tropical soapberry trees whose fruits were traditionally used as natural soap, but it also includes sugar maples, which produce the sap we use to make maple syrup!

children.name: Anacardiaceae
Rhus
children.description: Sumacs are deciduous shrubs and small trees known for their compound leaves that turn brilliant red, orange, and yellow in fall. They produce clusters of small flowers in spring or summer, followed by dense, cone-shaped clusters of fuzzy red berries that persist through winter. These hardy plants often form colonies through underground roots and are commonly found along roadsides, forest edges, and disturbed areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sumacs can be distinguished from other shrubs by their distinctive compound leaves arranged alternately on branches and their characteristic dense, upright clusters of red berries. The combination of fuzzy red fruit clusters and brilliant fall color makes them easily recognizable in the landscape.
children.funFact: The tart red berries of sumacs can be steeped in cold water to make a refreshing pink lemonade-like drink that's rich in vitamin C and has been enjoyed by Indigenous peoples for centuries.

children.name: Toxicodendron
children.description: Toxicodendron is a genus of woody plants that includes the notorious poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac. All members of this group contain urushiol, a potent oil that causes allergic skin reactions in most people who come into contact with it. These plants are found throughout North America and play important ecological roles despite their reputation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Toxicodendron apart from other plants in the cashew family is their high concentration of urushiol oil in all plant parts - leaves, stems, roots, and even smoke from burning plants. They also typically have compound leaves arranged in groups of three (poison ivy) or more (poison sumac).
children.funFact: The urushiol oil that makes these plants so irritating to humans is actually their natural defense system, and it's so potent that even 500-year-old dried specimens in museums can still cause allergic reactions!

children.name: Cotinus
children.description: Smoketrees are distinctive deciduous shrubs or small trees known for their incredible fall color displays and unique flowering habit. Members of this genus produce clusters of tiny flowers that develop into feathery, smoke-like plumes of seeds that give the plants their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the sumac family, smoketrees produce distinctive puffy, cloud-like seed heads that persist through summer and into fall. Their leaves turn brilliant oranges, reds, and purples in autumn, often more vivid than most other native trees.
children.funFact: The 'smoke' that gives smoketrees their name comes from the elongated, fuzzy stalks of sterile flowers that create a hazy, ethereal appearance around the tree from late spring through summer.

children.description: The Cashew Family includes a diverse group of woody plants that produce distinctive clusters of small flowers and often have compound leaves. Many members of this family contain resinous saps or oils that can cause skin reactions in humans, while others produce edible fruits or nuts. You'll find these plants as shrubs, small trees, or climbing vines throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have small, five-petaled flowers arranged in dense clusters, and their fruits are often small drupes. Many species contain urushiol oil or other irritating compounds in their sap, bark, or leaves.
children.funFact: This family includes both some of our most problematic plants (like poison ivy) and some of our most beloved foods - cashews, pistachios, and mangoes are all distant relatives of New England's sumacs!

children.name: Rutaceae
Phellodendron
children.description: Corktrees are deciduous trees in the citrus family known for their distinctive thick, corky bark that develops deep furrows and ridges. These Asian natives produce small greenish flowers in clusters and develop small black berries, with male and female flowers typically found on separate trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The deeply furrowed, cork-like bark is the most distinctive feature, along with their compound leaves that have an odd number of leaflets and emit a citrusy scent when crushed.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, corktrees are not related to the cork oak that produces commercial cork - they're actually members of the citrus family and their bark was traditionally used in Chinese medicine.

children.name: Zanthoxylum
children.description: Prickly-ashes are small trees or shrubs in the citrus family that get their name from the sharp prickles found on their bark and stems. These aromatic plants produce small clusters of tiny flowers and have compound leaves that release a distinctive, spicy scent when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other members of the citrus family, prickly-ashes are covered in sharp thorns or prickles and can tolerate cold northern climates. Their leaves and bark have a unique numbing, tingling sensation when chewed.
children.funFact: Northern prickly ash is sometimes called 'toothache tree' because Native Americans and early settlers chewed its bark to numb tooth pain - the plant contains compounds that create a temporary numbing effect in the mouth.

children.name: Ptelea
children.description: Hoptrees are small deciduous trees or large shrubs in the citrus family, known for their distinctive three-leaflet compound leaves and clusters of small, fragrant flowers. They produce papery, circular winged fruits that hang in clusters and resemble hops used in brewing, giving them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hoptrees are easily distinguished by their three-part compound leaves and unique circular, flat-winged fruits that are unlike any other tree in New England.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'hoptree,' these plants are actually related to citrus trees and their leaves give off a citrusy smell when crushed.

children.name: Ruta
children.description: Rues are aromatic herbs and shrubs in the citrus family known for their strong, distinctive smell and bluish-green compound leaves. These Mediterranean plants have been cultivated for centuries for their medicinal properties and as ornamental garden plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rues are distinguished by their deeply divided, blue-green leaves that release a pungent odor when crushed, and their small yellow flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters.
children.funFact: Common rue was once called the 'herb of grace' and was believed to ward off plague and evil spirits in medieval times.

children.name: Citrus
children.description: Citrus is a genus of flowering trees and shrubs famous for producing edible fruits like oranges, lemons, and limes. These plants are characterized by their fragrant white or pink flowers, glossy green leaves, and juicy fruits with thick, oil-rich peels. Most citrus species are native to tropical and subtropical regions of Asia.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Citrus plants are easily recognized by their distinctive fruits with segmented flesh inside a thick, aromatic rind, and their compound leaves that often have winged leaf stalks called petioles.
children.funFact: The trifoliate orange found in New England is actually one of the most cold-hardy citrus relatives, able to survive temperatures as low as -20°F, though its small, bitter fruits are not typically eaten fresh.

children.name: Tetradium
children.description: Tetradium is a small genus of deciduous trees in the citrus family, native to Asia but occasionally planted as ornamentals in temperate regions. These trees are known for their compound leaves with multiple leaflets and clusters of small, fragrant white or cream-colored flowers that bloom in late summer. They produce small, reddish fruits that split open to reveal shiny black seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tetradium trees can be identified by their large compound leaves with 7-15 oval leaflets and their distinctive late-summer flowering time when most other trees have finished blooming. The flowers have a strong, somewhat medicinal fragrance and are arranged in large, flat-topped clusters.
children.funFact: Korean Euodia is sometimes called the 'bee-bee tree' because its late-summer flowers provide crucial nectar for honeybees when few other sources are available, making it extremely valuable for beekeepers.

children.name: Dictamnus
children.description: Dictamnus is a small genus of aromatic perennial herbs in the rue family, known for their distinctive citrus-like fragrance and showy flower spikes. These plants are characterized by their compound leaves and tall racemes of white or pink flowers that bloom in late spring to early summer. They are long-lived garden plants that prefer well-drained soils and can persist for decades once established.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dictamnus plants are unique among their relatives for producing volatile oils so abundantly that the vapors can actually be ignited on calm, warm evenings without harming the plant. The flowers have long, prominent stamens that extend well beyond the petals, giving them a distinctive spidery appearance.
children.funFact: White dittany is sometimes called 'burning bush' because on hot, still summer evenings, you can actually light a match near the flower spike and ignite the volatile lemon-scented oils the plant releases, creating a brief, harmless flash of flame.

children.name: Skimmia
children.description: Skimmia is a small genus of evergreen shrubs native to Asia, prized for their glossy, leathery leaves and clusters of small, fragrant flowers. These ornamental plants are popular in gardens for their attractive berries and ability to thrive in shade. Most species are dioecious, meaning individual plants are either male or female.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Skimmias can be distinguished from other shrubs by their thick, waxy leaves with prominent oil glands that release a citrus-like scent when crushed, and their dense terminal clusters of small four-petaled flowers.
children.funFact: Despite being members of the citrus family (Rutaceae), Skimmia berries are toxic to humans and pets, unlike their edible citrus cousins.

children.description: The citrus family is a diverse group of plants that includes familiar citrus fruits like oranges and lemons, as well as many aromatic trees and shrubs. Members of this family are united by their distinctive flowers with four or five petals and their leaves that contain oil glands, giving them a characteristic fragrant smell when crushed. In New England, you'll find native species like hoptrees and prickly-ashes, along with some cultivated ornamental plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Citrus family plants can be easily identified by their aromatic leaves that release a strong, often citrusy scent when crushed or bruised. Their flowers typically have the same number of petals as sepals, and many species have thorns or spines on their stems.
children.funFact: The oil glands in citrus family leaves are so potent that some species like gas plant (Dictamnus) can actually ignite their volatile oils on hot summer evenings, earning the nickname 'burning bush.'

children.name: Simaroubaceae
Ailanthus
children.description: Ailanthuses are fast-growing deciduous trees in the quassia family, known for their ability to thrive in disturbed urban environments and poor soils. These trees have large compound leaves with many leaflets and produce clusters of small flowers followed by winged seeds that spin like helicopter blades when they fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ailanthus trees can be distinguished from similar species like sumacs by their smooth-edged leaflets that have small notches near the base, and their distinctive musty odor when leaves or bark are crushed.
children.funFact: A single mature tree-of-heaven can produce over 300,000 seeds per year, helping explain how this originally Asian species has spread so successfully across North America since its introduction in the 1700s.

children.description: The Quassia Family consists of trees and shrubs known for their bitter-tasting compounds, which have been used medicinally and as natural insecticides for centuries. These plants typically have compound leaves arranged alternately on their branches and produce small, clustered flowers. Most members of this family are found in tropical regions around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their extremely bitter wood and bark, which contains unique compounds called quassinoids. Unlike many other tree families, their flowers are often unisexual and their fruits typically split into separate winged segments.
children.funFact: The Tree of Heaven (Ailanthus), New England's only representative of this family, can grow up to 6 feet in a single year and is sometimes called a 'ghetto palm' because it thrives in urban environments where other trees struggle.

children.name: Meliaceae
Toona
children.description: Toona is a genus of deciduous trees in the mahogany family, native to Asia but now cultivated in many parts of the world including New England. These fast-growing trees are known for their compound leaves with many leaflets and their fragrant, edible young shoots that are prized in Asian cuisine.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mahogany family members, Toona trees have pinnately compound leaves that can be quite large, and they produce small, fragrant white or pink flowers in large drooping clusters.
children.funFact: The young leaves and shoots of the Tun tree smell strongly of onions when crushed and are considered a delicacy in Chinese cooking, earning it the nickname 'Chinese mahogany' or 'fragrant spring tree.'

children.description: The mahogany family includes trees and shrubs known for their valuable timber and compound leaves. Members of this tropical and subtropical family typically have pinnately compound leaves arranged alternately on branches, and produce capsule or drupe fruits. Most species are prized for their durable, fine-grained wood that's been used in furniture-making for centuries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mahogany family trees can be distinguished by their compound leaves with leaflets arranged like a feather, and their often fragrant flowers that are typically small and clustered together. The woody fruits usually split open to release winged seeds.
children.funFact: The famous mahogany wood used in high-end furniture comes from trees in this family, and some species like the Chinese mahogany (our single New England representative) were historically so valuable that entire trade routes were established around transporting their timber.

children.description: The Sapindales order brings together an eclectic mix of trees and shrubs that might seem unrelated at first glance, but share similar flower structures and chemical compounds. This diverse group includes everything from the maple trees that give us syrup to poison ivy, citrus fruits, and tropical mahogany trees. While they vary greatly in appearance, most members have compound leaves and small, clustered flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have flowers with separate petals arranged around a central disk, and many produce distinctive fruits like samaras (winged seeds) in maples or drupes in cashews. They're also united by shared chemical compounds, particularly various oils and resins that often make them aromatic or even toxic.
children.funFact: This order includes both some of our most beloved plants (like maple syrup trees and orange trees) and some of our most avoided ones (like poison ivy and poison sumac) - sometimes even within the same family!

children.name: Malvales
Malvaceae
Malva
children.description: Mallows are a group of flowering plants known for their distinctive five-petaled flowers that often have a papery, delicate appearance. These plants typically have round or heart-shaped leaves and produce small, wheel-shaped fruits that break apart into segments often called 'cheeses' due to their appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mallows can be identified by their characteristic flowers with five petals that are often notched at the tips, and their distinctive fruits that split into wedge-shaped segments arranged in a circle around a central axis.
children.funFact: The fruits of mallows are commonly called 'cheeses' because their round, segmented shape resembles wheels of cheese, and children have traditionally enjoyed eating these mild-flavored, nutty-tasting seed pods as a wild snack.

children.name: Hibiscus
children.description: Hibiscuses are flowering plants known for their large, showy blooms that typically have five petals and a prominent central column of fused stamens. These plants belong to the mallow family and produce distinctive funnel or trumpet-shaped flowers that can be quite eye-catching in gardens and natural areas. Most hibiscus species prefer moist soils and sunny locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hibiscuses are easily recognized by their characteristic flower structure with a long, protruding column of stamens and pistils extending from the center of the bloom. Their flowers are typically much larger than other members of the mallow family, and the petals often have a delicate, papery texture.
children.funFact: The flowers of most hibiscus species last only one day, opening in the morning and closing by evening, but the plants produce so many buds that they can bloom continuously for months during the growing season.

children.name: Tilia
children.description: Tilia is a genus of deciduous trees commonly known as lindens, basswoods, or lime trees (though unrelated to citrus limes). These stately trees are beloved for their heart-shaped leaves, fragrant yellowish flowers that bloom in summer, and their importance to pollinators. All members of this genus produce distinctive small, round fruits that hang from wing-like bracts that help them helicopter to the ground when they fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tilia trees are easily recognized by their asymmetrical, serrated heart-shaped leaves and their unique flowering structure where clusters of small, intensely fragrant flowers hang beneath a papery, leaf-like bract. The fibrous inner bark is exceptionally strong and has been used historically for rope-making.
children.funFact: Basswood flowers produce some of the finest honey in North America, with a distinctive light color and delicate flavor that's highly prized by beekeepers.

children.name: Abelmoschus
children.description: Okras are tropical plants in the mallow family known for their distinctive seed pods and large, colorful hibiscus-like flowers. These fast-growing annuals produce edible leaves, flowers, and most famously, their green finger-shaped pods that become slimy when cooked. While native to Africa and Asia, some species have been cultivated in warmer parts of New England as garden vegetables.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Okras can be distinguished from other mallows by their deeply lobed leaves and their characteristic ribbed, elongated seed pods that split open when mature. Their flowers are typically large and showy, often yellow or white with dark centers.
children.funFact: The sliminess that okra is famous for comes from mucilage, a natural thickening agent that has been used for everything from thickening soups to making paper and even as a potential substitute for blood plasma in medical emergencies.

children.name: Abutilon
children.description: Indian mallows are a genus of flowering plants in the mallow family, characterized by their heart-shaped or rounded leaves and hibiscus-like flowers. These plants typically have soft, velvety stems and leaves, giving them a distinctive fuzzy texture. They produce small, wheel-shaped seed pods that split into segments when mature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Indian mallows can be distinguished from other mallows by their typically yellow or orange flowers (rather than pink or white) and their characteristic wheel-shaped fruit that resembles a tiny cheese wheel divided into sections.
children.funFact: Velvetleaf, our only New England species, was originally brought from Asia as a fiber crop in the 1700s but quickly escaped cultivation and is now considered one of the most troublesome agricultural weeds in North America.

children.name: Alcea
children.description: Hollyhocks are tall, impressive flowering plants in the mallow family known for their towering spikes of large, colorful flowers. These plants typically grow 4-8 feet tall and produce showy blooms in summer that attract bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Originally from Asia, hollyhocks have become beloved garden plants around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hollyhocks are distinguished from other mallows by their exceptionally tall growth habit and their flowers arranged in long, dense spikes along the stem. The flowers are typically much larger than most other mallow family members, often 3-4 inches across.
children.funFact: Hollyhocks were so popular in medieval times that they were often planted around castle walls and cottage gardens, earning them the nickname 'outhouse flowers' because they were commonly grown near privies to provide privacy screening.

children.name: Callirhoe
children.description: Poppymallows are a small genus of low-growing wildflowers in the mallow family, known for their cup-shaped blooms that range from deep magenta to wine-red in color. These prairie natives typically have deeply divided, palmate leaves and produce their distinctive flowers on trailing or sprawling stems. They're drought-tolerant plants that thrive in sandy or rocky soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Poppymallows can be distinguished from other mallows by their distinctive wine-cup shaped flowers that are typically much deeper red or magenta than most mallow relatives. Their deeply lobed, finger-like leaves and low, spreading growth habit also set them apart from the more upright mallows.
children.funFact: The winecup mallow gets its name from its deep wine-colored, cup-shaped flowers that only open in bright sunlight and close up on cloudy days or in the evening, like nature's own solar-powered cups.

children.name: Althaea
children.description: Marshmallows (Althaea) are a small genus of flowering plants in the mallow family, known for their soft, fuzzy leaves and delicate pink or white flowers. These herbaceous perennials typically grow in wet, marshy areas and have been valued for centuries for their medicinal properties. The plants produce mucilage, a thick, gummy substance that gives them their characteristic slimy texture when crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Marshmallows can be distinguished from other mallows by their densely hairy, velvety leaves that are often deeply lobed, and their preference for wet, saline soils near marshes and coastlines. Their flowers are typically smaller and paler than those of other mallow relatives.
children.funFact: The original marshmallow confection was actually made from the mucilaginous root of the marsh mallow plant (Althaea officinalis), which was boiled down and sweetened to create a soothing treat for sore throats - quite different from today's gelatin-based marshmallows!

children.name: Gossypium
children.description: Cottons are a small genus of flowering plants in the mallow family, best known for producing the fluffy white fibers we use to make cotton textiles. These warm-weather plants have distinctive yellow or white hibiscus-like flowers and develop seed pods called bolls that split open to reveal cotton fibers surrounding the seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cotton plants are distinguished from other mallows by their unique seed fibers that are long, white, and fluffy enough to be spun into thread. The seeds are also covered in both long spinnable fibers and short fuzz, unlike most related plants.
children.funFact: A single cotton plant can produce enough fiber to make about 7 t-shirts, and cotton fibers are nearly pure cellulose, making them some of the purest natural fibers in the plant kingdom.

children.name: Sida
children.description: Sidas are small flowering plants in the mallow family, characterized by their heart-shaped leaves and small yellow or orange flowers. These hardy plants are often found in disturbed soils, waste areas, and along roadsides throughout warmer regions. They produce distinctive wheel-shaped fruits that split into segments when mature.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sidas can be distinguished from other mallows by their typically smaller flowers and their unique fruits that break apart into individual wedge-shaped segments, each containing a single seed.
children.funFact: The prickly fanpetals gets its name from the small spines found on its stems and the fan-like arrangement of its fruit segments, which were traditionally used in some cultures for medicinal purposes.

children.name: Kosteletzkya
children.description: Kosteletzkya is a small genus of flowering plants in the mallow family that includes herbaceous perennials and shrubs adapted to wetland environments. These plants are characterized by their hibiscus-like flowers and ability to thrive in salty or brackish conditions where few other flowering plants can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mallows that prefer dry upland areas, Kosteletzkya species are specially adapted to coastal marshes and wetlands, with salt-tolerant roots and stems that can withstand regular flooding.
children.funFact: The saltmarsh mallow can filter salt from seawater through special glands in its leaves, making it one of the few flowering plants that actually thrives in salty conditions that would kill most other plants.

children.description: The Mallow and Hibiscus Family includes plants known for their distinctive five-petaled flowers and heart-shaped or lobed leaves. This diverse family ranges from small weedy mallows growing in sidewalk cracks to towering basswood trees and showy garden hibiscuses. Many members produce useful fibers, with cotton being the most famous example.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members typically have flowers with five petals and a distinctive column of fused stamens (male parts) surrounding the style. The leaves often have a soft, velvety texture and star-shaped hairs when viewed under magnification.
children.funFact: The marshmallow candy was originally made from the mucilaginous root of the marsh mallow plant (Althaea officinalis), a member of this family that grows in New England's salt marshes.

children.name: Cistaceae
Lechea
children.description: Pinweeds are a group of small, often overlooked wildflowers in the rock-rose family that typically grow in sandy, dry soils throughout New England. These delicate plants produce tiny flowers and have narrow, small leaves that help them conserve water in harsh growing conditions. Most pinweeds are low-growing perennials that form small colonies in open, sunny areas like beaches, pine barrens, and rocky outcrops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pinweeds can be distinguished from other small wildflowers by their extremely tiny flowers (often less than 1/8 inch across) that have three petals and their characteristic narrow, linear leaves. Unlike many other members of the rock-rose family, pinweeds have inconspicuous flowers that open only briefly in the morning.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny, barely noticeable flowers, pinweeds are actually related to the showy rock-roses found in gardens, and their name comes from their thin, needle-like leaves that resemble pine needles rather than typical wildflower foliage.

children.name: Crocanthemum
children.description: Frostweeds are small, low-growing wildflowers in the rock-rose family that produce delicate yellow flowers with papery petals. These hardy plants are adapted to dry, sandy soils and open areas like fields, prairies, and woodland edges. They get their common name from the fascinating ice formations that appear on their stems during the first hard frosts of autumn.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Frostweeds can be distinguished from other wildflowers by their distinctive yellow flowers that have crinkled, tissue-paper-like petals and their narrow, often fuzzy leaves. Unlike many yellow wildflowers, frostweeds produce two different types of flowers - showy ones in spring and small, inconspicuous self-pollinating ones later in the season.
children.funFact: On cold autumn mornings, frostweeds create magical ribbon-like ice sculptures when sap freezes and expands, bursting through the stem and forming delicate, curling "frost flowers" that can be several inches tall.

children.name: Hudsonia
children.description: Hudsonia is a small genus of low-growing, shrubby plants that specialize in surviving in some of New England's harshest environments. These tough little plants form dense mats or cushions and produce bright yellow flowers that create stunning displays in sandy, nutrient-poor soils where few other plants can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering shrubs, Hudsonia species have tiny, scale-like leaves that are densely packed along their stems, giving them a distinctive fuzzy or heath-like appearance. Their flowers are small but numerous, creating carpet-like blooms of golden yellow.
children.funFact: These plants are so well-adapted to extreme conditions that they can survive being buried by shifting sand dunes and will simply grow new shoots up through the sand to reach sunlight again.

children.description: The rock-rose family consists of small, hardy plants that thrive in sandy, rocky, or other harsh growing conditions. These tough little survivors produce delicate five-petaled flowers that often seem surprisingly beautiful given their rugged habitats. Most species in this family are low-growing herbs or small shrubs adapted to dry, nutrient-poor soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rock-rose family members have distinctive flowers with five petals that are often crinkled like tissue paper, and their leaves are typically small and narrow. Many species have two different types of flowers - showy ones that open in sunlight and smaller, closed ones that self-pollinate.
children.funFact: Some frostweeds get their name because on cold mornings, beautiful ribbon-like ice crystals form along their stems as sap freezes and expands through cracks in the plant tissue.

children.name: Thymelaeaceae
Dirca
children.description: Leatherwoods are small, deciduous shrubs known for their remarkably flexible branches and tough, fibrous bark that feels like leather. These woodland plants produce small yellow flowers in early spring before their leaves emerge, and they prefer moist, shaded environments in rich forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The bark is so tough and pliable that it's nearly impossible to break by hand, earning these plants their common name. Unlike most shrubs, leatherwood branches can be bent into complete circles without snapping.
children.funFact: Indigenous peoples traditionally used leatherwood's incredibly strong bark fibers to make ropes, baskets, and even bowstrings because of its exceptional flexibility and durability.

children.name: Daphne
children.description: Daphnes are small to medium-sized shrubs in the family Thymelaeaceae, known for their fragrant, tubular flowers and often evergreen leaves. These plants are found throughout temperate regions of Europe, Asia, and parts of Africa, with most species preferring well-drained soils in woodland or mountainous areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Daphnes are distinguished by their four-petaled flowers that lack true petals but have colorful, petal-like sepals, and their tough, leathery bark that was historically used to make paper in some cultures.
children.funFact: Despite their beautiful, sweet-scented flowers, all parts of Daphne plants are highly toxic to humans and animals, containing compounds that can cause severe skin irritation and serious illness if ingested.

children.description: The Stringbarks (Thymelaeaceae) are a family of shrubs and small trees known for their tough, fibrous bark that can be peeled off in long strips - hence the name 'stringbark.' These plants typically have simple leaves and small, often fragrant flowers that lack true petals but have colorful sepals that look like petals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets stringbarks apart is their unique four-parted flowers with no true petals, only petal-like sepals, and their characteristic tough, stringy bark that separates into long fibers when pulled.
children.funFact: The bark of leatherwood (Dirca) was traditionally used by Native Americans to make rope, baskets, and even fishing lines because of its incredible strength and flexibility when wet.

children.description: The Mallows, Rock Roses, and Allies are a diverse group of flowering plants that includes familiar garden flowers like hibiscus and hollyhock, as well as wild relatives found throughout New England. Most members of this group have showy, colorful flowers with prominent stamens and often heart-shaped or lobed leaves. They range from small herbaceous plants to shrubs and even trees in tropical regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Many plants in this order have flowers with numerous stamens that are often fused together into columns or bundles, creating a distinctive appearance. The flower petals are typically separate and often have a papery or delicate texture.
children.funFact: Cotton belongs to this group - those fluffy white fibers we use for clothing come from the seed pods of a plant closely related to the hibiscus in your garden!

children.name: Boraginales
Boraginaceae
Myosotis
children.description: Forget-me-nots are small, delicate wildflowers known for their tiny five-petaled blooms that are typically bright blue with yellow centers. These charming plants belong to the borage family and are found in various habitats from woodlands to wetlands throughout New England. Most species are low-growing annuals or perennials that form small clusters of flowers on slender stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Forget-me-nots can be distinguished from other small blue flowers by their distinctive five-petaled blooms with bright yellow centers and their characteristic coiled flower clusters that unfurl as new buds open. Their leaves are typically simple, alternate, and covered with soft hairs.
children.funFact: The name 'forget-me-not' comes from a medieval legend about a knight who fell into a river while picking these flowers for his beloved, shouting 'forget me not' as he was swept away by the current.

children.name: Symphytum
children.description: Comfreys are robust perennial herbs in the borage family known for their large, coarse leaves and clusters of bell-shaped flowers that typically hang downward. These plants are characterized by their hairy, somewhat rough texture and their ability to grow quite tall, often reaching 2-4 feet in height. All comfrey species contain compounds that have historically made them valuable as medicinal plants, though they require careful handling.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Comfreys can be distinguished from other borage family plants by their distinctively large, lance-shaped leaves and their drooping flower clusters that come in colors ranging from white and yellow to pink and purple. Unlike many of their relatives, comfreys tend to be much more robust and taller plants.
children.funFact: Common comfrey was once called 'knitbone' because people believed it could help heal broken bones and wounds, and it's still used today by some gardeners as a natural fertilizer due to its high potassium content.

children.name: Phacelia
children.description: Scorpionweeds are wildflowers in the borage family known for their distinctive coiled flower clusters that unfurl as they bloom, resembling a scorpion's tail. These annual herbs typically produce small, bell-shaped or funnel-shaped flowers in shades of blue, purple, pink, or white. They're often found in disturbed soils, fields, and woodland edges throughout temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic curled, one-sided flower clusters that gradually straighten as blooms open from bottom to top set scorpionweeds apart from other wildflowers. Their deeply lobed or divided leaves and typically hairy stems also help distinguish them from similar-looking plants.
children.funFact: Lacy phacelia is so beloved by bees and other pollinators that it's sometimes called 'bee's friend' and is deliberately planted by beekeepers to support their hives!

children.name: Hydrophyllum
children.description: Waterleaves are woodland wildflowers that get their name from the pale, water-mark-like patterns that often appear on their deeply lobed leaves. These native perennial herbs bloom in late spring with clusters of small, bell-shaped flowers that range from white to pale purple, and they prefer rich, moist soils in shaded forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Waterleaves can be identified by their distinctive palmate leaves (divided like fingers on a hand) with prominent water-stain markings, and their coiled flower clusters that unfurl as they bloom, similar to a fiddlehead fern.
children.funFact: The water-mark patterns on waterleaf foliage were once thought to predict rainfall, leading some folk traditions to use these plants as natural weather forecasters.

children.name: Echium
children.description: Viper's-buglosses are bristly wildflowers in the borage family known for their distinctive funnel-shaped flowers that bloom in shades of blue, purple, or pink. These European natives have rough, hairy stems and leaves, and their flowers are arranged in curved, scorpion-tail-like clusters that gradually unfurl as they bloom. Both species found in New England are considered non-native plants that have naturalized in fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the borage family, viper's-buglosses have very prominent stamens that stick out conspicuously from their funnel-shaped flowers, giving them a distinctive bristly appearance. Their extremely rough, almost sandpaper-like texture from dense bristly hairs also sets them apart from smoother borage relatives.
children.funFact: The name 'viper's-bugloss' comes from the belief that the plant's spotted stem resembled a snake's skin and its seed looked like a viper's head, leading medieval herbalists to think it could cure snakebites according to the 'doctrine of signatures.'

children.name: Mertensia
children.description: Bluebells are delicate wildflowers known for their distinctive trumpet-shaped blooms that often change color as they mature, typically starting pink and turning blue. These plants belong to the borage family and are found in diverse habitats from woodlands to coastal areas. They produce clusters of nodding flowers that are favorites among early spring pollinators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the borage family, Mertensia flowers are notably smooth and hairless, and they characteristically change from pink buds to blue flowers as they age. Their leaves are also unusually smooth compared to the typically rough, hairy leaves of most borage family plants.
children.funFact: Virginia bluebells are sometimes called 'lungwort' because early settlers believed the spotted appearance of some plants' leaves resembled diseased lungs, leading them to use it as a folk remedy for respiratory ailments.

children.name: Hackelia
children.description: Stickseeds are small wildflowers in the borage family that get their name from their distinctive burr-like seeds covered in tiny hooked barbs. These modest plants produce clusters of small white or blue flowers and are found in woodlands and disturbed areas throughout New England. The sticky seeds readily attach to clothing, fur, and feathers, making them excellent hitchhikers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stickseeds can be identified by their characteristic nutlets (seeds) that are armed with barbed prickles, unlike the smooth or merely bumpy seeds of related borage family members. Their flowers are typically smaller and less showy than those of other borages like forget-me-nots.
children.funFact: The hooked barbs on stickseed fruits are so effective at attachment that they inspired part of the design for Velcro, demonstrating how nature's solutions can inspire human innovations.

children.name: Pulmonaria
children.description: Lungworts are low-growing perennial herbs in the borage family known for their distinctive spotted leaves and clusters of small, tubular flowers. These woodland plants typically bloom in early spring, producing flowers that often change color as they age, starting as pink or red buds and maturing to blue or purple.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lungworts are easily recognized by their rough, hairy leaves that are often marked with light-colored spots or patches, giving them a mottled appearance that was once thought to resemble diseased lungs.
children.funFact: The name 'lungwort' comes from the medieval 'Doctrine of Signatures,' where people believed the spotted leaves resembled diseased lungs and therefore the plant could cure respiratory ailments.

children.name: Nemophila
children.description: Baby blue eyes and allies are delicate annual wildflowers known for their charming cup-shaped blooms that come in shades of blue, white, and purple. These low-growing plants typically have soft, hairy leaves and prefer cool, moist conditions, often blooming in spring and early summer. They're members of the borage family and are beloved by gardeners for their cottage garden appeal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other borage family members, Nemophila flowers have distinctly bowl or cup-shaped petals rather than small tubular blooms. Their flowers are also notably larger and more showy than most of their relatives, with some species featuring distinctive spots or markings.
children.funFact: The name 'Nemophila' comes from Greek words meaning 'grove-loving,' reflecting these plants' preference for shaded woodland edges and cool, protected spots.

children.name: Lithospermum
children.description: Stoneseeds, puccoons, and gromwells are a group of wildflowers in the borage family known for their distinctive hard, white seeds that look like tiny polished stones. These plants typically have small white or yellow flowers arranged in clusters and rough, hairy leaves that feel somewhat sandpaper-like to the touch.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The genus is easily identified by its extremely hard, smooth, white seeds that are much more stone-like than other borage family plants. Unlike their relatives with softer seeds, Lithospermum seeds are so hard they can persist in the soil for many years.
children.funFact: The seeds are so hard and stone-like that they were once ground up and used as a folk remedy, and the name 'Lithospermum' literally means 'stone seed' in Greek.

children.name: Cynoglossum
children.description: Hound's-tongues are members of the borage family known for their distinctive rough, tongue-shaped leaves that feel somewhat like sandpaper. These plants produce small, five-petaled flowers that are typically blue, purple, or pink, and develop into unique seed pods covered with hooked bristles that stick to clothing and animal fur.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other borage family members, hound's-tongues have particularly rough, hairy leaves and their seeds are covered with barbed hooks that make them extremely clingy. The seeds are also flattened and arranged in clusters of four, called nutlets.
children.funFact: The name 'hound's-tongue' comes from the shape and rough texture of the leaves, which were thought to resemble a dog's tongue, and historically the plant was used in folk medicine to treat dog bites.

children.name: Andersonglossum
children.description: Andersonglossum is a small genus of woodland wildflowers in the borage family, commonly known as wild comfreys. These perennial herbs produce clusters of small, bell-shaped flowers and have distinctive hairy leaves that were once used in folk medicine.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true comfrey (Symphytum), wild comfreys have much smaller flowers and different seed structures called nutlets that are smooth rather than wrinkled.
children.funFact: This genus was only recently recognized as separate from true comfrey in 2014, when DNA studies revealed that North American 'comfreys' were actually quite different from their European cousins.

children.name: Borago
children.description: Borages are herbaceous plants in the borage family known for their distinctive star-shaped, bright blue flowers and fuzzy, cucumber-scented leaves. These annual or perennial herbs have been cultivated for centuries both as culinary herbs and ornamental plants. The genus is characterized by its bristly, hairy stems and leaves that give the plants a rough texture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Borages are distinguished from other borage family members by their large, drooping clusters of vivid blue, five-petaled flowers and their particularly coarse, bristly hairs covering the entire plant. The leaves have a unique cucumber-like fragrance when crushed.
children.funFact: Borage flowers are edible and taste like cucumber, making them a popular garnish for summer drinks and salads, while the leaves were once believed to give courage to warriors before battle.

children.name: Brunnera
children.description: Brunnera is a small genus of spring-blooming perennial plants in the borage family, known for their heart-shaped leaves and delicate clusters of small blue flowers. These woodland plants are native to eastern Europe and western Asia, but have become popular garden plants that sometimes escape cultivation. They thrive in shady, moist conditions and are valued for their attractive foliage and early spring blooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brunnera can be distinguished from other borage family plants by its distinctive heart-shaped basal leaves and tiny forget-me-not-like blue flowers that bloom in loose, branching clusters. Unlike true forget-me-nots, Brunnera plants are much larger and have prominent heart-shaped leaves rather than narrow ones.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Siberian bugloss,' Brunnera macrophylla doesn't actually come from Siberia - it's native to the Caucasus Mountains and was named after Swiss botanist Samuel Brunner.

children.name: Plagiobothrys
children.description: Popcornflowers are small annual wildflowers in the borage family, named for their tiny white flowers that resemble kernels of popped corn. These delicate plants typically grow in moist or wet areas like shorelines, meadows, and seasonal pools. They produce clusters of small, five-petaled white flowers along curved, coiled stems that unfurl as the plant blooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Popcornflowers can be distinguished from other small white wildflowers by their characteristic coiled flower clusters that straighten out as they bloom, plus their rough, hairy leaves and stems. The tiny flowers have a distinctive yellow center and are much smaller than most other white wildflowers you'll encounter.
children.funFact: The curved, coiled flower stems of popcornflowers are called 'scorpioid cymes' because they resemble a scorpion's curled tail before they unfurl to reveal the flowers.

children.name: Buglossoides
children.description: Buglossoides is a genus of small annual herbs in the borage family, known for their rough, hairy stems and leaves. These plants produce tiny white or pale blue flowers and are often found growing as weeds in disturbed soils like farm fields and roadsides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other borage family plants by their small, inconspicuous flowers and their hard, smooth, whitish seeds that lack the typical ridges or bumps found in related genera.
children.funFact: The name 'gromwell' comes from an old French word meaning 'grain of the sun,' referring to the plant's small, pearl-like seeds that were once thought to have medicinal properties for treating kidney stones.

children.name: Ellisia
children.description: Aunt Lucies are delicate annual wildflowers in the borage family, known for their small white or pale blue flowers and deeply lobed leaves. These low-growing plants typically reach only 1-2 feet tall and prefer moist, shaded areas in woodlands and along stream banks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other members of the borage family, Aunt Lucies have extremely fragile stems that break easily when touched, and their flowers lack the typical rough, hairy texture found on most borage plants.
children.funFact: The common name 'Aunt Lucy' comes from the plant's tendency to 'faint' or wilt dramatically when picked, as if swooning like a delicate Victorian lady.

children.description: The borage family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes many beloved wildflowers and garden plants. Most members of this family are herbaceous plants with simple, often hairy leaves and small flowers that typically come in shades of blue, purple, pink, or white. These plants are found in a wide variety of habitats from woodlands to meadows to disturbed areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Borage family flowers are usually arranged in distinctive coiled clusters that unfurl as the buds open, resembling a scorpion's tail. The flowers typically have five petals fused into a tube or funnel shape, and many species have notably rough, bristly hairs on their stems and leaves.
children.funFact: Many borage family plants change color as their flowers age - forget-me-nots often start pink and turn blue, while Virginia bluebells begin as pink buds and open to sky-blue flowers, creating a beautiful two-toned display in spring woodlands.

children.description: Borages are an order of flowering plants that includes many beloved garden flowers and wildflowers known for their distinctive flower clusters. Most members of this group have small, tubular flowers arranged in coiled clusters that unfurl as the flowers bloom, creating a characteristic spiral or scorpion-tail appearance. The flowers are typically blue, purple, pink, or white, and many species have rough, hairy leaves and stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Borages are easily recognized by their flowers arranged in curved, coiled clusters called cymes that gradually unroll as new buds open. The flowers typically have five petals fused into a tube, and many species have distinctively rough, bristly hairs covering their stems and leaves.
children.funFact: The forget-me-not, one of New England's most cherished wildflowers and a member of this order, gets its name from medieval legend that says God forgot to name this tiny blue flower, so it called out 'Forget me not!' to remind Him.

children.name: Cornales
Cornaceae
Cornus
children.description: Dogwoods are a diverse group of woody plants that can be shrubs, small trees, or even tiny groundcover plants. They're known for their distinctive flowers (which are often actually colorful bracts surrounding tiny true flowers), opposite leaves with curved veins, and colorful berries that provide important food for wildlife. Most dogwoods also display beautiful fall colors and interesting bark patterns.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dogwoods can be identified by their opposite leaves with distinctive curved parallel veins that follow the leaf's shape, and their small clustered flowers often surrounded by showy white or pink bracts. Their berries are typically bright red, blue, or white and contain hard stone-like seeds.
children.funFact: The tiny Canadian bunchberry is actually a dogwood despite being only 6 inches tall, making it one of the smallest members of a genus that also includes 30-foot trees!

children.description: The dogwood family includes trees, shrubs, and herbaceous plants that typically have simple leaves arranged opposite each other on the stem. Most members produce small flowers clustered together, often surrounded by showy bracts that look like petals, followed by berry-like fruits that are important food sources for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dogwoods are easily recognized by their distinctive leaf venation pattern, where the veins curve toward the leaf tip and run roughly parallel to the leaf edges. Many species also have the characteristic four-petaled flowers or four large, colorful bracts that resemble flower petals.
children.funFact: The beautiful white 'petals' of flowering dogwood aren't actually petals at all - they're specialized leaves called bracts that surround the tiny true flowers in the center.

children.name: Hydrangeaceae
Hydrangea
children.description: Hydrangeas are a group of flowering shrubs and vines known for their spectacular clusters of showy flowers that bloom throughout summer and fall. These plants are beloved by gardeners and can be found growing both wild in forests and cultivated in gardens across New England. Most hydrangeas prefer partial shade and moist, well-drained soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hydrangeas are easily recognized by their large, rounded or cone-shaped flower clusters made up of many small individual flowers. Unlike many other flowering shrubs, their flowers often change color as they age or in response to soil chemistry.
children.funFact: The flower color of many hydrangeas can actually change based on soil pH - acidic soil produces blue flowers while alkaline soil creates pink ones, with the same plant capable of producing different colors in different locations!

children.name: Philadelphus
children.description: Mock oranges are deciduous shrubs known for their showy white flowers that bloom in late spring to early summer. These hardy plants produce clusters of four-petaled flowers and have opposite leaves with prominent veins. They get their name because their fragrant blooms (in scented species) smell similar to orange blossoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mock oranges can be distinguished from other flowering shrubs by their opposite leaves and four-petaled white flowers that bloom in dense clusters. Unlike true orange trees, they are cold-hardy shrubs that lose their leaves in winter.
children.funFact: Despite their name, mock oranges are not related to citrus trees at all - they belong to the hydrangea family and were simply named for their sweet orange-like fragrance.

children.name: Deutzia
children.description: Deutzia is a genus of deciduous flowering shrubs known for their abundant clusters of small, white or pink flowers that bloom in late spring to early summer. These shrubs have opposite leaves and produce tiny star-shaped flowers with five petals that create showy displays along their arching branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Deutzia can be distinguished from other flowering shrubs by their distinctive star-shaped flowers with deeply notched petals and their opposite leaf arrangement. The flowers also have a unique feature where the stamens have flattened, wing-like filaments.
children.funFact: Deutzia is named after Johan van der Deutz, an 18th-century Dutch patron of botany, and while most species are native to Asia, they've become popular ornamental shrubs worldwide due to their reliable spring flower displays.

children.name: Kirengeshoma
children.description: Kirengeshoma is a small genus of perennial woodland plants known for their distinctive yellow, bell-shaped flowers that hang gracefully from arching stems. These shade-loving plants have large, maple-like leaves and prefer moist, acidic soils in forest settings. They are prized by gardeners for their elegant late-summer blooms and attractive foliage.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the hydrangea family, Kirengeshoma has thick, waxy yellow petals that never fully open, giving the flowers their characteristic bell or lantern shape. The flowers hang downward in clusters, and the plant has a uniquely graceful, arching growth habit.
children.funFact: The name 'Kirengeshoma' comes from Japanese and means 'yellow autumn flower,' reflecting its native origins in the mountains of Japan and Korea where it blooms in late summer to early fall.

children.description: The hydrangea family is a group of flowering shrubs and small trees known for their showy, often clustered flowers and opposite leaves. These plants typically produce flowers with four or five petals and have simple leaves that grow in pairs across from each other on the stem. Most members of this family are popular ornamental plants prized for their beautiful blooms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their characteristic flower structure with numerous stamens and their tendency to produce flowers in dense, rounded or flat-topped clusters. Unlike many related plant families, hydrangeas often have sterile outer flowers with enlarged petals surrounding smaller fertile flowers in the center.
children.funFact: Many hydrangeas can change their flower color based on soil pH - acidic soils produce blue flowers while alkaline soils create pink ones!

children.name: Nyssaceae
Nyssa
children.description: Tupelos are deciduous trees known for their distinctive oval leaves and brilliant fall colors. They are part of the dogwood family and typically grow in wet or swampy areas, though they can adapt to drier soils. These trees produce small clusters of flowers in spring followed by dark blue berries that are important food sources for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tupelos can be distinguished from other trees by their simple, alternate leaves with smooth edges and their characteristic horizontal branching pattern. Their bark has a distinctive blocky, alligator-hide appearance on mature trees.
children.funFact: Black tupelo is one of the first trees to change color in fall, often turning brilliant red, orange, and purple as early as late August, earning it the nickname 'first sign of autumn.'

children.description: The tupelo family is a small group of deciduous trees known for their distinctive fruits and stunning fall colors. These trees typically grow in wet areas like swamps and floodplains, where they can tolerate standing water better than most other trees. They're characterized by their simple, alternate leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers that develop into berry-like fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tupelos are easily distinguished by their unique fruits - small, dark blue drupes that often appear in clusters - and their ability to thrive in waterlogged soils where few other trees can survive. Their distinctive horizontal branching pattern and brilliant orange to red fall foliage also help set them apart from other wetland trees.
children.funFact: Black tupelo trees can live for over 600 years and are considered some of the first trees to change color in fall, earning them the nickname 'first sign of autumn.'

children.description: The Cornales order includes some of New England's most beloved flowering trees and shrubs, from the showy white bracts of dogwoods to the puffy flower clusters of hydrangeas. These plants are all woody species that produce small, often inconspicuous flowers arranged in dense clusters, though many species make up for tiny blooms with colorful surrounding leaves or bracts. Most members of this group are deciduous and well-adapted to temperate climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flowering plant orders, Cornales members typically have their flower parts arranged in fours, and their leaves show distinctive curved veins that follow the leaf edges. Many species also produce stone fruits or berries with hard seeds inside.
children.funFact: The spectacular white 'petals' of flowering dogwood aren't actually petals at all—they're specialized leaves called bracts that surround the tree's tiny true flowers in the center!

children.name: Geraniales
Geraniaceae
Geranium
children.description: The Geranium genus includes true geraniums and cranesbills, a diverse group of herbaceous plants known for their distinctive five-petaled flowers and deeply divided, often palm-shaped leaves. These hardy plants range from delicate woodland wildflowers to robust garden perennials, with most species producing small but charming blooms in shades of pink, purple, blue, or white. They're found in a variety of habitats from forests to meadows to rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True geraniums are easily recognized by their unique seed pods that split explosively when ripe, flinging seeds away from the parent plant. The long, pointed seed pods resemble a crane's bill, which gives many species their common name of 'cranesbill.'
children.funFact: Don't confuse these with the common garden 'geraniums' sold at nurseries - those colorful potted plants are actually members of the Pelargonium genus and are native to South Africa!

children.name: Erodium
children.description: Stork's-bills are small flowering plants in the geranium family, known for their distinctive long, pointed seed capsules that resemble a stork's beak. These low-growing herbs produce small pink or purple flowers and have deeply divided, feathery leaves that often form rosettes close to the ground.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the true geraniums, stork's-bills have seed capsules with long, twisted tails that spiral dramatically when they dry out. Their flowers also typically have only 5 stamens instead of the 10 found in true geraniums.
children.funFact: When the seed capsule dries out, its spiral tail acts like a corkscrew that literally drills the seed into the ground, ensuring it gets planted at the perfect depth for germination.

children.description: The Geranium family includes herbaceous plants known for their distinctive five-petaled flowers and deeply divided, often palm-shaped leaves. These plants are found in gardens and wild spaces throughout New England, from woodland edges to disturbed soils along roadsides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their unique seed pods that split explosively when ripe, often launching seeds several feet away. The flowers typically have five petals arranged symmetrically, and the leaves are usually deeply lobed or divided.
children.funFact: The common names 'cranesbill' and 'stork's-bill' come from the long, pointed seed pods that resemble the bills of these birds - and when the pods split open, they curl back dramatically like a bird opening its beak!

children.description: Geraniales is a diverse order of flowering plants that includes the familiar garden geraniums, delicate bridal wreath shrubs, and their botanical relatives. These plants typically produce flowers with five petals arranged in a regular pattern, and many develop distinctive fruits that split open to release their seeds. Members of this group can be found as herbs, shrubs, or small trees in gardens and wild spaces throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Geraniales apart is their unique seed dispersal mechanisms - many species have fruits that explosively split open or develop long, beak-like extensions that help scatter seeds. Their flowers also typically have twice as many stamens as petals, creating a distinctive floral structure.
children.funFact: Wild geraniums have spring-loaded seed pods that can launch their seeds up to 30 feet away when ripe, earning them the nickname 'spotted geranium cannons' among some botanists!

children.name: Vitales
Vitaceae
Vitis
children.description: Grapevines are woody climbing plants that produce clusters of small, round berries and have distinctive lobed leaves. They use long, twisting tendrils to wrap around supports as they climb toward sunlight, often covering trees, fences, and other structures. Most species are native to North America, though the familiar wine grape originally came from Europe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grapevines can be identified by their heart-shaped or lobed leaves, coiling tendrils that emerge opposite the leaves, and distinctive bark that peels off in long strips on mature stems. Their small flowers grow in dense, elongated clusters that later develop into the familiar grape bunches.
children.funFact: Wild grapes were so abundant when European settlers arrived that they named Martha's Vineyard after the native grapevines covering the island, and many place names throughout New England still reference the wild 'fox grapes' that grew everywhere.

children.name: Parthenocissus
children.description: Virginia creepers are climbing vines known for their distinctive palmate leaves that turn brilliant red in fall. These woody vines use specialized tendrils with adhesive disks to climb up trees, walls, and other surfaces. All species in this genus are deciduous and produce small, dark blue berries that are important food sources for birds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Virginia creepers are distinguished from other climbing vines by their tendrils that end in small, sticky adhesive pads that allow them to cling directly to smooth surfaces like bark or stone. Their palmate leaves (typically 3-5 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand) also set them apart from most other native climbing plants.
children.funFact: The adhesive disks on Virginia creeper tendrils are so strong that they can support the weight of the entire vine, and they work so well that the plant can climb straight up glass windows and smooth concrete walls.

children.name: Ampelopsis
children.description: Porcelainberry is a genus of climbing woody vines in the grape family that are known for their vigorous growth and distinctive colorful berries. These fast-growing vines use tendrils to climb up trees, fences, and other structures, and can quickly cover large areas with their heart-shaped leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grapes, porcelainberry produces small berries that change from white to yellow, orange, blue, and purple all on the same cluster, creating a distinctive multicolored display. The berries are also smaller and less palatable than grapes, and the bark has a characteristic spotted appearance.
children.funFact: The colorful berries that give porcelainberry its name contain very little sugar compared to grapes, making them unappetizing to most animals - which actually helps the invasive species spread since the seeds pass through birds undigested.

children.description: The Grape Family is a group of climbing plants that use specialized tendrils to wrap around supports and pull themselves upward toward sunlight. Most members are woody vines with distinctive lobed or compound leaves and produce small clusters of berries. These vigorous climbers can be found scrambling up trees, fences, and buildings throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their coiling tendrils that emerge opposite the leaves, helping them climb. Unlike many other climbing plants, grape family vines have a unique way their tendrils branch and curl to grip surfaces.
children.funFact: Virginia Creeper can climb smooth walls without any support structures by producing tiny adhesive discs at the tips of its tendrils that stick like natural glue!

children.description: The Grapes and Allies order includes woody vines and climbing plants that use specialized structures called tendrils to grasp onto supports as they grow. Most members of this group produce small flowers arranged in clusters and develop fleshy berries or similar fruits. These plants are found worldwide in both temperate and tropical regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their climbing habit with leaf-opposed tendrils, and their flowers typically have parts in fours or fives with the petals often falling off early. The stems frequently show a distinctive pith pattern when cut in cross-section.
children.funFact: Wild grapes in New England were so abundant that Viking explorers around 1000 CE called the region 'Vinland' - though some of what they called grapes may have actually been other native berries!

children.name: Celastrales
Celastraceae
Euonymus
children.description: Spindles are a diverse group of shrubs and small trees known for their distinctive four-sided stems and colorful autumn displays. These woody plants produce small, inconspicuous flowers in spring or early summer, followed by bright pink, red, or orange fruits that split open to reveal colorful seeds. Many species are popular in landscaping for their reliable fall color and attractive berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spindles are easily recognized by their distinctive four-angled or winged stems and their unique fruits that split open like tiny lanterns to reveal brightly colored seeds. Their opposite leaves and small, four-petaled flowers also help distinguish them from other shrubs.
children.funFact: The winged euonymus is nicknamed 'burning bush' because its leaves turn such an intense, fiery red in fall that the entire shrub appears to be glowing like flames.

children.name: Celastrus
children.description: Bittersweets are woody climbing vines that twist and wrap around trees and shrubs to reach sunlight. They produce small greenish flowers in spring and are best known for their colorful berries that split open in fall to reveal bright red seeds inside orange capsules. These vigorous climbers can grow quite large and are often used in fall decorations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bittersweets can be identified by their alternate, oval leaves and their distinctive three-part fruit capsules that split open to expose bright red berries. Unlike many other climbing vines, they climb by twisting their entire stem around supports rather than using tendrils or aerial roots.
children.funFact: The invasive Asian bittersweet can climb so aggressively that it sometimes strangles and kills the trees it grows on, earning it the nickname 'tree strangler.'

children.name: Parnassia
children.description: Grass of Parnassus is a genus of delicate wildflowers that, despite their name, are not actually grasses at all. These plants produce distinctive white flowers with intricate veining and are typically found in wet, boggy areas like fens and marshes. They are small perennial herbs that bloom in late summer and fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These flowers are easily recognized by their five white petals with greenish veins and unique sterile stamens that look like tiny fringed scales alternating with the fertile stamens. The heart-shaped leaves and single flower per stem also help distinguish them from other bog plants.
children.funFact: The name 'grass of Parnassus' comes from the ancient Greek belief that these flowers grew on Mount Parnassus, the sacred mountain of Apollo and the Muses, even though they're not grasses and don't actually grow there!

children.description: The staff-vine family is a diverse group of plants that includes shrubs, small trees, and climbing vines. Most members of this family are woody plants with simple leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers that often have four or five petals. Many species in this family are known for their colorful fruits and seeds that provide important food sources for birds and other wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Staff-vine family members typically have flowers with their parts arranged in fours or fives, and many species produce distinctive capsule fruits that split open to reveal brightly colored seeds with colorful arils (seed coverings).
children.funFact: Despite its name, grass of Parnassus isn't actually a grass at all - it's a small flowering plant in the staff-vine family that was named after Mount Parnassus in Greece, where it was first described by ancient botanists.

children.description: Staff-vines and allies are a diverse group of flowering plants that includes both woody vines and shrubs. Most members of this order have simple leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers that often grow in clusters. They're commonly found in woodlands and forest edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants typically have flowers with parts in fours or fives, and many produce colorful berries or distinctive winged fruits. Their leaves are usually arranged alternately on the stem and have smooth or finely-toothed edges.
