children.funFact: American bittersweet, a member of this group, produces beautiful orange and red berries that were traditionally used in fall decorations, but the plant's aggressive vining habit can actually strangle trees by wrapping tightly around their trunks.

children.name: Aquifoliales
Aquifoliaceae
Ilex
children.description: Hollies are a diverse group of shrubs and trees best known for their glossy leaves and bright red berries that provide crucial winter food for birds. These woody plants can be found in various habitats from wetlands to upland forests, with some species keeping their leaves year-round while others drop them in fall. Most hollies have separate male and female plants, so you need both to get those famous berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hollies are unique among New England woody plants for their combination of simple, alternate leaves (often with spiny edges) and small, typically red berries that persist through winter. The flowers are small and inconspicuous, usually white or greenish, and the plants are almost always either all-male or all-female.
children.funFact: Only female holly plants produce berries, and they need a male plant nearby to pollinate them - so if your holly isn't making berries, it might be a bachelor!

children.description: The holly family consists of woody plants known for their distinctive berries and often spiny, evergreen leaves. Most members of this family are shrubs or small trees that produce small, inconspicuous flowers followed by colorful berries that persist through winter. These plants are found in both temperate and tropical regions worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Holly family members are distinguished by their simple, alternate leaves and small flowers with parts typically in fours or fives. The bright red, black, or yellow berries are another key identifying feature, along with the waxy, leathery texture of many species' leaves.
children.funFact: Holly berries are an important winter food source for birds, but they're toxic to humans and most mammals - the plants have evolved this strategy to ensure birds, rather than ground-dwelling animals, disperse their seeds!

children.description: Hollies and allies are a diverse group of flowering plants that includes the familiar holly trees and shrubs we see throughout New England. Most members of this group are woody plants with simple leaves and small, often inconspicuous flowers that develop into colorful berries. They're particularly well-adapted to temperate climates and play important ecological roles as food sources for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets hollies apart is their unique combination of alternate leaf arrangement, small flowers with parts typically in fours or fives, and their characteristic berry-like fruits called drupes. Many species are also dioecious, meaning individual plants are either male or female.
children.funFact: Only female holly plants produce the bright red berries we associate with winter decorations - you need both male and female plants nearby for the females to fruit!

children.name: Cucurbitales
Cucurbitaceae
Cucurbita
children.description: Gourds in the genus Cucurbita are the familiar squashes and pumpkins that have been cultivated by humans for thousands of years. These plants are trailing or climbing vines with large, broad leaves and produce the orange, yellow, and green fruits we associate with fall harvests and cooking.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the gourd family, Cucurbita species have distinctively thick, corky stems and large, unlobed seed cotyledons. Their fruits also have a characteristic hard rind when mature and contain flat, oval seeds.
children.funFact: All three New England Cucurbita species were originally domesticated by Indigenous peoples in the Americas over 8,000 years ago, making them some of humanity's oldest cultivated crops.

children.name: Cucumis
children.description: Cucumis is a genus of vining plants that includes some of our most familiar garden vegetables - melons and cucumbers. These plants are characterized by their trailing or climbing stems with tendrils, large leaves, and yellow flowers that develop into the fleshy fruits we enjoy eating. All members of this genus are annual plants that thrive in warm weather and produce separate male and female flowers on the same plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the cucumber family, Cucumis species have distinctively rough, sandpapery leaves and stems covered in small bristly hairs. Their fruits also have a unique cellular structure that makes them particularly juicy and refreshing compared to related gourds and squashes.
children.funFact: Cucumbers are actually about 96% water, making them one of the most hydrating foods you can eat - they're essentially nature's water bottles!

children.name: Echinocystis
children.description: Echinocystis is a genus of climbing vines in the cucumber family that produces distinctive spiny, balloon-like seed pods. These fast-growing annual vines use tendrils to climb over other plants and can quickly cover large areas during the growing season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the cucumber family, Echinocystis produces inflated, papery pods covered in soft spines rather than fleshy fruits. The vines also have deeply lobed leaves and clusters of small white flowers.
children.funFact: The spiny seed pods of prickly cucumber are filled with air and can float on water, allowing the seeds to disperse along waterways to new locations.

children.name: Sicyos
children.description: Bur cucumbers are climbing vines in the gourd family that produce small, spiky seed pods covered in bristles. These annual plants use tendrils to scramble over other vegetation and are found in moist areas like stream banks and woodland edges. They're related to cucumbers and squash but produce tiny, inedible fruits instead of large edible ones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the gourd family, bur cucumbers produce clusters of small, bristly seed pods rather than large fleshy fruits. Their seeds are also uniquely adapted with hooked bristles that easily catch onto fur and clothing.
children.funFact: The spiky seed pods are nature's velcro - they stick so tenaciously to anything that brushes against them that early settlers sometimes called them 'beggar's lice' for how persistently they clung to clothing.

children.name: Lagenaria
children.description: Lagenaria is a genus of climbing vines in the gourd family that produce large, hard-shelled fruits. These plants are known for their vigorous growth habit and distinctive bottle-shaped or rounded fruits that develop thick, woody shells when mature. The vines have large, heart-shaped leaves and produce white flowers that bloom at night.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lagenaria gourds are distinguished from other gourds by their extremely hard, waterproof shells and their white, night-blooming flowers. Unlike many other gourd genera, their mature fruits can be carved and crafted into durable containers, bowls, and musical instruments.
children.funFact: Archaeological evidence shows that Lagenaria gourds were among humanity's first water containers and storage vessels, used by civilizations around the world for over 10,000 years before pottery was invented.

children.name: Citrullus
children.description: Watermelons are a small genus of trailing vine plants in the gourd family that produce large, round to oval fruits with thick rinds and juicy flesh. These annual plants have deeply lobed leaves and yellow flowers, and they spread along the ground with long, branching stems. All species in this genus are native to Africa but are now cultivated worldwide in warm climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Watermelons can be distinguished from other gourds by their characteristic large, heavy fruits with smooth, often striped rinds and sweet, watery flesh containing flat, dark seeds. Unlike related melons, watermelons have deeply divided, almost feathery leaves rather than simple rounded ones.
children.funFact: Watermelons are actually about 92% water, making them one of the most hydrating fruits you can eat!

children.description: The gourd family includes familiar vining plants that produce some of our most beloved fruits and vegetables, including cucumbers, melons, squashes, pumpkins, and watermelons. These plants are characterized by their sprawling or climbing growth habit, large lobed leaves, and hollow stems that help them spread across the ground or climb up supports. Most members produce separate male and female flowers on the same plant, followed by fleshy fruits that can range from tiny ornamental gourds to massive pumpkins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their distinctive tendrils that coil and spiral to help the vines climb, and their typically yellow, funnel-shaped flowers. The fruits are technically berries with a hard rind and are unique in having seeds embedded in the fleshy interior rather than in a central core.
children.funFact: Despite being botanically classified as fruits, many gourd family members like cucumbers and squash are commonly treated as vegetables in cooking, while others like melons and watermelons are enjoyed as sweet fruits - making this one of the most culinarily diverse plant families!

children.name: Begoniaceae
Begonia
children.description: Begonias are flowering plants known for their colorful, asymmetrical leaves and showy flowers that come in separate male and female forms on the same plant. Most begonias are tropical plants commonly grown as houseplants or garden annuals, but a few hardy species can survive freezing temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Begonias have distinctively lopsided, heart-shaped leaves that are often different sizes on each side of the stem, and their flowers have an unusual arrangement with male flowers having many stamens and female flowers having winged seed pods.
children.funFact: The hardy begonia is the only member of this mostly tropical family that can survive New England winters, originally coming from China and spreading by underground rhizomes to form colonies.

children.description: Begonias and their allies are a family of flowering plants known for their colorful, often asymmetrical leaves and showy flowers. Most members of this family are tropical or subtropical plants that prefer warm, humid conditions and are popular as houseplants or garden ornamentals. They typically have succulent or semi-succulent stems and produce separate male and female flowers on the same plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Begonias are easily recognized by their distinctly asymmetrical, often heart-shaped leaves where one side is noticeably larger than the other. Their flowers are also unique, with male flowers having numerous stamens and female flowers having winged seed pods.
children.funFact: The asymmetrical leaves of begonias aren't just for show - this uneven shape helps the plant maximize light capture in the dappled shade of forest floors where many wild begonias naturally grow.

children.description: The Cucurbitales order brings together an interesting mix of plants that includes familiar garden vegetables like cucumbers, squash, and pumpkins alongside colorful begonia flowers. Despite their different appearances, these plants share similar flower structures and often have distinctive vine-like or succulent growth habits. Most members of this group have separate male and female flowers on the same plant.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have unisexual flowers (separate male and female flowers) and often develop fleshy fruits or seed capsules. Many species in this group are either climbing vines with tendrils or have thick, succulent stems and leaves.
children.funFact: The largest fruit in the world comes from this order - giant pumpkins can weigh over 2,000 pounds, while the smallest members include tiny begonia flowers that are barely visible to the naked eye!

children.name: Piperales
Aristolochiaceae
Asarum
children.description: Wild gingers are low-growing woodland plants with distinctive heart-shaped leaves and unusual flowers that bloom close to the ground. These shade-loving perennials spread by underground stems called rhizomes, forming colonies on the forest floor. Despite their name, they're not related to culinary ginger but get their common name from their spicy-scented roots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wild gingers produce unique cup-shaped or urn-shaped flowers that are often hidden beneath the leaves and have three petals that are typically brownish or purplish rather than brightly colored. Their heart-shaped leaves and ground-hugging growth habit make them easily recognizable among forest wildflowers.
children.funFact: Wild ginger flowers are pollinated by beetles and flies that are attracted to their musty, sometimes unpleasant smell - quite different from the sweet fragrances of most flowers!

children.name: Aristolochia
children.description: Aristolochia is a fascinating genus of flowering plants commonly known as pipevines and birthworts. These plants are characterized by their unique pipe-shaped or curved flowers that often have unusual colors and patterns. Most species in this group are climbing vines or low-growing herbs that prefer shaded woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical flowers, Aristolochia blooms lack petals and instead have a distinctive curved or S-shaped tube that often flares into a pouch or boot-like shape. The flowers frequently have mottled brown, purple, or greenish colors rather than bright petals.
children.funFact: Many pipevine flowers are designed as clever insect traps - they lure flies and other pollinators inside with their smell, then temporarily trap them with downward-pointing hairs until the insects pick up pollen and can escape to pollinate the next flower.

children.description: The birthwort family includes herbaceous plants with heart-shaped leaves and unusual flowers that often have a strong, sometimes unpleasant odor. These plants typically produce flowers with three petals or sepals that are often brownish or purplish in color, and many species grow close to the ground or as climbing vines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their distinctive heart-shaped leaves and their unusual flowers that lack true petals, instead having colorful sepals that often form tube or pouch-like structures.
children.funFact: Many plants in this family, especially the pipevines, act as 'trap flowers' that temporarily imprison insects to ensure pollination - the insects crawl into the flower but can't escape until the pollen is ready, then the flower releases them covered in pollen!

children.name: Saururaceae
Houttuynia
children.description: Houttuynia is a small genus of flowering plants in the lizard's-tail family, containing just one species that's found in New England. These are herbaceous perennial plants with distinctive heart-shaped leaves and small white flowers arranged in dense spikes. They spread by underground rhizomes and are known for their strong, distinctive smell when the leaves are crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Houttuynia is easily recognized by its unique combination of heart-shaped leaves with prominent veins, tiny white flowers clustered in cone-like spikes, and the plant's characteristic fishy or citrusy odor when bruised.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Chameleon Plant,' the colorful varieties with red, pink, and cream variegated leaves are actually cultivated forms - the wild species has plain green foliage and gets its common name from its ability to adapt to different growing conditions.

children.name: Saururus
children.description: Lizard's tails are unique wetland plants with distinctive white, spike-like flower clusters that lack petals and sepals. These perennial herbs grow in shallow water or wet soil, producing heart-shaped leaves and drooping flower spikes that curve downward like a lizard's tail.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, lizard's tail flowers have no petals or sepals - just tiny white stamens clustered on a distinctive drooping, curved spike. The heart-shaped leaves and wetland habitat also help distinguish them from other native plants.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting a connection to reptiles, lizard's tails are actually related to black pepper plants and belong to the same botanical family (Saururaceae) as some Asian medicinal herbs.

children.description: The lizard's tail family is a small group of wetland-loving plants known for their distinctive flower spikes that lack petals and sepals. These perennial herbs thrive in moist soils near ponds, streams, and swampy areas, producing heart-shaped leaves and unique bottlebrush-like flower clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, members of this family produce tiny flowers completely without petals or sepals, arranged in dense, elongated spikes. Their heart-shaped leaves and preference for wet habitats also help distinguish them from other plant families.
children.funFact: The family gets its name from the drooping, tail-like flower spikes of the lizard's tail plant, which can bend and curve like a reptile's tail as they mature.

children.description: Piperales is an ancient order of flowering plants that includes some unusual and aromatic species. These plants are known for their simple flowers that often lack petals and their distinctive chemical compounds that give many species strong scents or medicinal properties.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have flowers without petals that are arranged in dense spikes or clusters, and many produce oils and compounds that make them aromatic or give them medicinal uses.
children.funFact: This order includes wild ginger and Dutchman's pipe, both native to New England, as well as black pepper - one of the world's most valuable spices that comes from a tropical member of this same plant group.

children.name: Oxalidales
Oxalidaceae
Oxalis
children.description: Woodsorrels are small herbaceous plants easily recognized by their distinctive three-leaflet leaves that fold downward at night or when touched. They produce delicate five-petaled flowers in yellow, pink, purple, or white, followed by explosive seed pods that can shoot seeds several feet away when ripe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true clovers, woodsorrels have heart-shaped leaflets and their leaves have a distinctive sour, lemony taste due to oxalic acid. Their seed pods are also uniquely cylindrical and split explosively when mature.
children.funFact: Many woodsorrel leaves can perform rapid movement called nyctinasty, folding their leaflets downward within minutes when disturbed, then slowly reopening when left alone.

children.description: The Woodsorrel Family consists of small herbaceous plants known for their distinctive three-leaflet leaves that fold down at night or when touched. These plants produce delicate five-petaled flowers in colors ranging from white and pink to yellow, and have seed pods that explosively burst open when ripe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be easily identified by their clover-like leaves that demonstrate sleep movements, folding closed in response to darkness or physical contact. Unlike true clovers, woodsorrels have five-petaled flowers rather than the clustered pea-like flowers of the legume family.
children.funFact: Woodsorrel leaves have a pleasant sour taste due to oxalic acid content and have been used as a natural remedy for scurvy, earning some species the nickname 'sourgrass.'

children.description: The Oxalidales order includes plants known for their distinctive heart-shaped or clover-like leaves that often fold up at night or when touched. Most members in New England belong to the woodsorrel family, which are small herbaceous plants with delicate flowers and leaves that have a pleasant sour taste due to oxalic acid.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants are easily recognized by their three-leaflet compound leaves that fold along the midrib and their characteristic five-petaled flowers. The leaves often have a distinctive shamrock-like appearance and exhibit sleep movements, closing at dusk.
children.funFact: Woodsorrels were historically called 'sourgrass' and were eaten by Native Americans and early settlers as a tangy snack or brewed into a lemony tea, earning them the nickname 'wood lemon.'

children.name: Magnoliales
Magnoliaceae
Magnolia
children.description: Magnolias are a group of flowering trees and shrubs known for their large, showy blooms and distinctive cone-like fruits. These ancient plants produce flowers with thick, waxy petals that often appear before the leaves emerge in spring, creating stunning displays of white, pink, purple, or yellow blossoms. All magnolias have simple, oval-shaped leaves and develop unique aggregate fruits that split open to reveal bright red or orange seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Magnolias are easily recognized by their large, solitary flowers with numerous petals arranged in a spiral pattern, rather than the typical ring arrangement of most flowering plants. Their flower buds are also distinctively large and fuzzy, protected by stipules that fall away as the flower opens.
children.funFact: Magnolias are among Earth's most ancient flowering plants, having evolved over 100 million years ago when dinosaurs roamed the planet - they're so old that they evolved before bees existed, so they're actually pollinated by beetles!

children.name: Liriodendron
children.description: Tulip trees are tall, stately deciduous trees known for their distinctive tulip-shaped flowers and uniquely-shaped leaves. They are among the tallest hardwood trees in eastern North America and belong to the ancient magnolia family, representing a very old lineage of flowering trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tulip trees have unmistakable four-lobed leaves that look almost square with notched tops, unlike any other tree in New England. Their large, greenish-yellow flowers shaped like tulips bloom high in the canopy during late spring.
children.funFact: Tulip trees are sometimes called "living fossils" because their ancestors grew alongside dinosaurs over 100 million years ago, making them one of the most ancient types of flowering trees still alive today.

children.description: The magnolia family includes some of our most spectacular flowering trees, known for their large, showy blooms and distinctive cone-like fruits. These ancient trees are considered among the most primitive flowering plants on Earth, having existed for over 100 million years. Family members share similar flower structures with multiple petals and stamens arranged in spirals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, magnolia family members have flowers with parts arranged in spirals rather than rings, and their fruits are aggregate cones made up of many small individual fruits. Their large, simple leaves often have smooth edges and prominent veining.
children.funFact: Magnolia flowers evolved to be pollinated by beetles rather than bees, which is why they're built so sturdy - they need to withstand beetles crawling around inside them!

children.name: Annonaceae
Asimina
children.description: Pawpaws are small deciduous trees or large shrubs in the custard apple family, known for their tropical-like appearance despite growing in temperate climates. They produce large, oblong leaves and distinctive maroon flowers that bloom in early spring before the leaves emerge. These native North American plants are the only members of their tropical family that can survive freezing temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pawpaws stand out from other New England trees with their unusually large, drooping leaves (6-12 inches long) that have a tropical appearance and their unique six-petaled maroon flowers. Unlike most native trees, they produce large, banana-shaped fruits with creamy, custard-like flesh.
children.funFact: Pawpaws are the largest native fruit in North America and were a favorite food of both Native Americans and early European settlers - even George Washington and Thomas Jefferson enjoyed them!

children.description: The custard-apple family consists of tropical and subtropical trees and shrubs known for their large, often fragrant flowers and fleshy fruits. These plants typically have simple, alternate leaves and produce flowers with six petals arranged in two rows of three.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their primitive flower structure with numerous separate carpels and stamens, and their fruits often have a custard-like texture when ripe.
children.funFact: The pawpaw is the largest native fruit in North America and was a favorite food of both Native Americans and early European settlers, earning it the nickname 'poor man's banana' for its tropical flavor.

children.description: The Magnoliales are an ancient order of flowering plants that includes some of the most primitive blooms on Earth. These plants typically have large, showy flowers with many separate petals and stamens arranged in a spiral pattern, rather than the more organized flower parts seen in most modern flowering plants. Most members are trees or shrubs with simple, often large leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, Magnoliales have flower parts that are arranged spirally rather than in distinct whorls, and their petals and sepals often look very similar to each other. Their pollen grains also have a single groove (monosulcate), which is considered a primitive characteristic.
children.funFact: Magnolias are so ancient that they evolved before bees existed, so their flowers were originally designed to be pollinated by beetles - which is why magnolia flowers are particularly sturdy and fragrant.

children.name: Nymphaeales
Nymphaeaceae
Nuphar
children.description: Yellow pond-lilies are aquatic plants that float on the surface of quiet waters like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They're easily recognized by their bright yellow, cup-shaped flowers that rise above the water and their large, heart-shaped leaves that can be either floating or submerged.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike white water-lilies, yellow pond-lilies have distinctive yellow flowers with thick, waxy petals that never fully open, giving them a goblet-like appearance. Their leaves are also typically more oval or heart-shaped rather than perfectly round.
children.funFact: The thick, spongy underwater stems of yellow pond-lilies were traditionally used by Native Americans as a food source, often ground into flour or roasted like potatoes.

children.name: Nymphaea
children.description: Waterlilies are aquatic plants that grow rooted in muddy lake and pond bottoms, with their large, round leaves floating on the water's surface. They produce beautiful, fragrant flowers that sit on or just above the water, typically blooming from late spring through early fall. These perennial plants have thick, fleshy underwater stems called rhizomes that anchor them to the bottom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic flowering plants, waterlilies have distinctive circular or heart-shaped floating leaves with a deep notch cut from the edge to the center. Their flowers have numerous petals arranged in multiple layers and close up at night or on cloudy days.
children.funFact: Waterlily flowers are masters of temperature control - they can actually generate heat to warm themselves up to 35°F above the surrounding air temperature, which helps attract pollinators and protects the reproductive parts from cool weather.

children.description: The Waterlily Family includes aquatic plants that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These plants are easily recognized by their large, round floating leaves and showy flowers that sit on or just above the water surface. Most have thick, fleshy underground stems called rhizomes that anchor them to the muddy bottom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, waterlilies have distinctive circular or heart-shaped leaves that float flat on the water surface, and their flowers have many petals arranged in a spiral pattern. Their leaves have a waxy coating that repels water, and the flowers often open and close at specific times of day.
children.funFact: Waterlily flowers are considered among the most ancient flower types on Earth - some fossils of waterlily-like plants date back over 100 million years, meaning they may have bloomed while dinosaurs roamed the planet!

children.name: Cabombaceae
Brasenia
children.description: Brasenia is a genus containing just one living species - the watershield, an aquatic plant that floats on the surface of ponds and lakes. This ancient plant produces distinctive oval leaves that float on the water's surface and small, inconspicuous purple flowers that emerge above the water. The entire underwater portion of the plant is covered in a thick, jelly-like coating.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Watershield is easily recognized by its unique gelatinous coating that covers all submerged parts of the plant, making stems and leaf undersides feel incredibly slimy to the touch. Unlike water lilies, watershield leaves are attached to their stems at the center rather than having a slit extending to the center.
children.funFact: Brasenia is considered a 'living fossil' - it's the sole surviving member of an ancient plant family, with fossils showing virtually identical species existed over 100 million years ago during the time of dinosaurs.

children.name: Cabomba
children.description: Fanworts are aquatic plants with uniquely shaped leaves that live completely submerged in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They get their name from their delicate, fan-shaped underwater leaves that are finely divided into thread-like segments, creating a feathery appearance that sways gracefully in the current.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most aquatic plants, fanworts have two completely different types of leaves - the submerged fan-shaped leaves and small, oval floating leaves that appear at the water surface during flowering season.
children.funFact: Fanworts are considered living fossils, belonging to one of the most ancient lineages of flowering plants that evolved over 100 million years ago when dinosaurs still roamed the Earth.

children.description: The fanwort family is a small group of aquatic flowering plants that live completely submerged in freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams. These plants have delicate, finely divided underwater leaves that look like tiny fans or feathers, which help them capture nutrients and oxygen from the water. All members of this family produce small flowers that float on or just above the water surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most aquatic plants, fanwort family members have two completely different types of leaves - the submerged leaves are finely divided and feathery, while any floating leaves are simple and shield-shaped. Their flowers are also uniquely small and have parts arranged in threes.
children.funFact: Fanworts are considered "living fossils" - they represent one of the most ancient lineages of flowering plants, with fossils dating back over 100 million years to the age of dinosaurs.

children.description: Waterlilies, fanworts, and allies are aquatic flowering plants that live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These plants are specially adapted for life in water, with roots anchored in muddy bottoms and leaves that either float on the surface or grow underwater. They represent some of the most ancient flowering plant lineages on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, members of this group have very simple flower structures and lack the complex petal arrangements found in more evolved plant families. Their leaves are often circular or shield-shaped and have waxy surfaces that repel water.
children.funFact: Waterlilies are considered living fossils - they split off from other flowering plants over 130 million years ago, making them closer relatives to magnolias than to most other aquatic plants!

children.name: Santalales
Santalaceae
Comandra
children.description: Comandras are small, inconspicuous plants that are actually parasites, secretly tapping into the roots of nearby trees and shrubs to steal nutrients. These sneaky plants can photosynthesize on their own but supplement their diet by connecting to host plants through their root systems. They produce tiny clusters of white or greenish flowers and have narrow, oval leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most plants, comandras are root parasites that can partially survive by stealing nutrients from other plants while still maintaining their own green leaves for photosynthesis.
children.funFact: Bastard toadflax got its unusual name because early botanists thought it looked similar to true toadflax plants, but the 'bastard' part refers to it being an imposter that doesn't actually belong to that plant family.

children.name: Arceuthobium
children.description: Dwarf-mistletoes are tiny parasitic plants that live on the branches of coniferous trees, drawing water and nutrients directly from their host. Unlike the familiar mistletoe used in holiday decorations, these plants are extremely small and often go unnoticed, appearing as small bumps or swellings on tree branches. They produce sticky seeds that are explosively shot from the plant to infect nearby trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dwarf-mistletoes are much smaller than other mistletoes and specialize in parasitizing coniferous trees rather than deciduous ones. They create characteristic swollen areas called 'witches' brooms' on infected branches, distinguishing them from other parasitic plants.
children.funFact: Dwarf-mistletoes can explosively launch their seeds up to 50 feet at speeds of over 60 miles per hour, making them some of nature's most impressive plant projectiles!

children.name: Geocaulon
children.description: Geocaulon is a small genus of parasitic plants that tap into the roots of other plants to steal nutrients and water. These low-growing perennials have simple, alternate leaves and produce small, inconspicuous flowers followed by colorful berries. They belong to the sandalwood family and maintain a partially parasitic lifestyle while still conducting some photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most parasitic plants, Geocaulon species are only partially parasitic and retain their green leaves for photosynthesis. They can be distinguished from related genera by their specific leaf arrangement and the bright orange to red berries they produce.
children.funFact: Northern Comandra gets its nutrients by sending out underground root connections called haustoria that attach to nearby plants like a botanical vampire, allowing it to survive in poor soils where other plants struggle.

children.name: Pyrularia
children.description: Pyrularia is a small genus of parasitic shrubs that tap into the roots of other plants to steal nutrients and water. These unusual plants have their own leaves and can photosynthesize, but they supplement their nutrition by connecting to nearby host plants through specialized root structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most plants, Pyrularia species are root parasites that form underground connections with other plants while still maintaining their own green leaves and stems above ground.
children.funFact: Buffalo-nut gets its common name from its large, olive-shaped fruits that were once eaten by American bison and other wildlife.

children.name: Viscum
children.description: Viscum is a genus of parasitic plants commonly known as mistletoes that grow on the branches and trunks of trees. These evergreen plants tap into their host trees to obtain water and nutrients, while still performing some of their own photosynthesis with their green leaves. They form distinctive rounded, bushy clumps that remain visible year-round on deciduous trees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mistletoe genera, Viscum species have thick, leathery leaves and produce small, inconspicuous flowers followed by sticky white berries. They are true parasites that send specialized root-like structures called haustoria directly into their host tree's vascular system.
children.funFact: European mistletoe berries are so sticky that birds often wipe them off their beaks onto tree branches, inadvertently planting new mistletoe colonies - the plant's name even comes from the Anglo-Saxon words 'mistel' (dung) and 'tan' (twig)!

children.description: The sandalwood family is a fascinating group of parasitic and semi-parasitic plants that obtain nutrients by connecting to the roots or branches of other plants. These plants have adapted to steal water and minerals from their host plants, though some can still photosynthesize on their own. Members of this family range from small ground-hugging herbs to mistletoes that grow high in tree branches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most plants that are completely independent, sandalwood family members are parasitic or semi-parasitic, forming specialized connections called haustoria that tap into their host plants' vascular systems. Many have reduced leaves and inconspicuous flowers, reflecting their parasitic lifestyle.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, like dwarf-mistletoes, can actually shoot their seeds up to 50 feet away at speeds of up to 60 mph when their fruits explosively burst open!

children.description: Santalales is an order of flowering plants that includes the famous sandalwood trees, mistletoes, and their relatives. What unites these seemingly different plants is that they are all parasitic or semi-parasitic, meaning they obtain some or all of their nutrients by attaching to and feeding off other plants. This group represents one of nature's most successful experiments in plant parasitism.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants that are completely self-sufficient, members of Santalales have evolved specialized structures called haustoria that penetrate host plants to steal water, nutrients, or both. They range from partial parasites that still photosynthesize to complete parasites that have lost the ability to make their own food.
children.funFact: Mistletoe's famous role in holiday traditions comes from ancient beliefs about its mysterious ability to grow on tree branches without roots in soil - something we now know is due to its parasitic lifestyle!

children.name: Laurales
Lauraceae
Sassafras
children.description: Sassafras is a small genus of deciduous trees in the laurel family, known for their distinctive aromatic properties and variable leaf shapes. These trees are famous for their spicy, root beer-like scent that can be detected when leaves, bark, or roots are crushed or broken.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sassafras trees are unique among North American trees for having three different leaf shapes on the same tree: simple oval leaves, two-lobed mitten-shaped leaves, and three-lobed leaves that resemble a turkey's foot.
children.funFact: Sassafras root was once the main flavoring ingredient in root beer, and the tree was so valued by early European colonists that it became one of North America's first export crops to Europe.

children.name: Lindera
children.description: Spicebushes are aromatic shrubs in the laurel family known for their fragrant leaves, bark, and berries that smell spicy when crushed. These deciduous shrubs typically grow in woodland understories and produce small yellow flowers in early spring before their leaves emerge. All parts of the plant contain aromatic oils that give them their distinctive spicy scent.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Spicebushes can be identified by their strong spicy fragrance when any part is crushed or broken, and their bright red berries that appear on female plants in late summer. Unlike many other woodland shrubs, they produce clusters of tiny yellow flowers directly along their bare branches in very early spring.
children.funFact: Northern spicebush berries were once dried and ground as a substitute for allspice by early American colonists, earning it the nickname 'wild allspice.'

children.name: Persea
children.description: Persea is a genus of evergreen trees and shrubs in the laurel family, best known for producing the beloved avocado. These plants are characterized by their leathery leaves, small yellowish-green flowers, and large, nutrient-rich fruits with a single large seed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the laurel family, Persea species produce large, fleshy fruits that are technically berries. Their flowers lack petals and instead have six petal-like sepals that form the bloom.
children.funFact: The avocado is sometimes called an 'evolutionary anachronism' because it likely evolved to be dispersed by giant ground sloths and other megafauna that went extinct thousands of years ago!

children.description: The laurel family consists of aromatic trees and shrubs that produce fragrant oils in their leaves, bark, and wood. Most members of this ancient plant family are found in tropical regions, but a few hardy species have adapted to temperate climates like New England. These plants are known for their distinctive spicy or sweet scents when their leaves or twigs are crushed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Laurels can be identified by their aromatic properties and their small, inconspicuous flowers that typically have six petals and are arranged in clusters. Unlike many other flowering trees, they often have leaves with smooth edges and prominent veining.
children.funFact: Sassafras trees in this family were once so valuable that they helped finance early European exploration of North America - the aromatic root bark was worth more than its weight in gold for making medicines and root beer!

children.name: Calycanthaceae
Calycanthus
children.description: Sweetshrub is a small genus of aromatic deciduous shrubs known for their uniquely fragrant flowers and leaves. These native North American plants produce distinctive reddish-brown flowers with multiple petals that release a sweet, fruity scent when crushed. They typically grow in woodland understories and along stream banks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweetshrubs are easily recognized by their opposite, simple leaves and their unusual flowers that have numerous tepals (petal-like structures) arranged in multiple whorls, creating a layered appearance. The flowers lack true petals and sepals, instead having these specialized tepals that are all similar in appearance.
children.funFact: The sweet fragrance of sweetshrub flowers was so prized by early American colonists that they would dry the petals and use them as a natural potpourri, earning the plant the nickname 'allspice bush.'

children.description: The spicebush family is a small group of aromatic shrubs known for their fragrant bark, leaves, and flowers. These plants produce distinctive flowers with numerous petals and sepals that are often difficult to distinguish from each other, creating a unique layered appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have flowers with many similar-looking petals and sepals arranged in a spiral pattern, rather than the typical distinct separation found in most flowering plants. Their bark and crushed leaves release a sweet, spicy fragrance.
children.funFact: Despite being called the 'spicebush family,' it's not related to the common spicebush (Lindera benzoin) that also grows in New England - that's actually in the laurel family!

children.description: Laurales is an ancient order of flowering plants that includes aromatic trees and shrubs known for their fragrant leaves, bark, and flowers. These plants are characterized by their simple leaves and often produce oils that give them distinctive scents - from the spicy aroma of spicebush to the bay-like fragrance of sassafras.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order typically have flowers with parts in multiples of three and lack true petals, instead having colorful sepals. Their leaves often contain oil glands that release strong fragrances when crushed.
children.funFact: Sassafras was once the primary flavoring for root beer, and its leaves can have three different shapes - oval, mitten-shaped, or three-lobed - all on the same tree!

children.name: Proteales
Nelumbonaceae
Nelumbo
children.description: Lotuses are aquatic plants known for their spectacular large, round flowers that rise above the water surface on tall stems. These ancient plants have distinctive circular leaves that can grow over a foot wide and repel water, causing droplets to bead up and roll off. They grow from thick rhizomes buried in muddy pond and lake bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lotuses are easily distinguished from water lilies by their leaves and flowers that stand well above the water surface, rather than floating on it. Their unique seed pods have a distinctive flat-topped appearance with holes where seeds develop.
children.funFact: Lotus seeds can remain viable for over 1,000 years - some seeds found in ancient lake beds have successfully germinated after centuries of dormancy!

children.description: The lotus family consists of aquatic plants with large, distinctive circular leaves and showy flowers that rise above the water surface. These ancient plants are found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving waterways, where they grow from thick underground stems called rhizomes. The family contains only one genus, Nelumbo, with just two species worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lotus plants are easily recognized by their large, shield-shaped leaves with a waxy surface that causes water to bead up and roll off, and their prominent flowers with numerous petals arranged around a distinctive flat-topped seed pod.
children.funFact: Lotus seeds can remain viable for over 1,000 years - some ancient seeds found in dry lake beds have successfully sprouted after centuries of dormancy!

children.name: Platanaceae
Platanus
children.description: Planes are large deciduous trees known for their distinctive mottled bark that peels off in patches, creating a camouflage-like pattern of cream, gray, and brown colors. These fast-growing trees are commonly found along riverbanks and in floodplains, where they can tolerate periodic flooding and wet soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Planes can be easily identified by their exfoliating bark that sheds in irregular patches and their large, broad leaves with prominent veins that resemble maple leaves but are arranged alternately on branches rather than opposite each other.
children.funFact: The American sycamore can live for several hundred years and is one of the most massive trees in eastern North America, with some specimens reaching over 100 feet tall and 14 feet in diameter.

children.description: The plane family is a small group of deciduous trees known for their distinctive mottled bark that flakes off in irregular patches, revealing lighter colors underneath. These trees are characterized by their ball-shaped flower clusters and spiky, round seed balls that hang from branches on long stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plane trees are easily recognized by their unique exfoliating bark that creates a camouflage-like pattern of brown, gray, and cream patches. Their spherical seed heads, typically hanging in clusters of 1-3 balls, are unlike any other tree family.
children.funFact: London planetrees, a hybrid between American sycamore and Oriental plane, were specifically developed for urban environments because they can tolerate air pollution and compacted soil better than most trees.

children.description: Proteales is a diverse order of flowering plants that includes some surprisingly different-looking species like sacred lotuses, sycamore trees, and their relatives. Despite their varied appearances, these plants share similar flower structures and genetic characteristics that reveal their evolutionary relationship. Most members of this group are trees or shrubs, though they can be found in many different habitats from wetlands to dry uplands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Proteales typically have flowers with parts arranged in multiples of three or six, and many produce distinctive fruits or seed structures. Unlike many other flowering plant orders, they often have very ancient evolutionary origins and unique pollination strategies.
children.funFact: The sacred lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) in this order has seeds that can remain viable for over 1,000 years - some of the longest-living seeds known to science!

children.name: Buxales
Buxaceae
Pachysandra
children.description: Pachysandra is a small genus of low-growing, evergreen plants that form dense carpets of glossy green foliage. These hardy perennials are popular groundcovers that thrive in shaded areas where many other plants struggle to grow. They spread slowly by underground stems called rhizomes, creating thick mats that help prevent soil erosion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pachysandra plants are easily recognized by their thick, leathery leaves arranged in whorls at the stem tips and their small, inconspicuous white flower spikes that appear in early spring. Unlike many groundcovers, they maintain their rich green color year-round even in deep shade.
children.funFact: The name 'Pachysandra' comes from Greek words meaning 'thick' and 'male,' referring to the plant's thick stamens in its tiny flowers.

children.name: Buxus
children.description: Boxes are a genus of slow-growing, evergreen shrubs and small trees known for their dense, compact growth habit and small, leathery leaves. These woody plants are prized for their ability to tolerate heavy pruning and maintain their shape, making them popular choices for formal gardens and topiary work. All members of this genus produce tiny, inconspicuous flowers and have opposite leaves that remain green year-round.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Boxes are distinguished from other evergreen shrubs by their extremely small, oval leaves that are thick and waxy, and their ability to produce new growth from old wood when pruned. Their flowers lack petals and are clustered in small groups along the stems.
children.funFact: Boxwood has been used for centuries to create intricate topiary sculptures because it can regrow from cuts made into decades-old wood, allowing gardeners to maintain complex shapes for generations.

children.description: The boxwood family is a small group of woody plants known for their small, simple leaves and tiny, inconspicuous flowers. These evergreen or semi-evergreen shrubs and small trees are popular in gardens and landscaping because of their dense, compact growth and ability to be pruned into neat shapes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have flowers that lack petals and are typically arranged in small clusters, with male and female flowers often found together on the same plant. Their leaves are usually opposite or alternate, leathery, and remain green throughout much of the year.
children.funFact: Pachysandra, a common ground cover in New England gardens, spreads by underground stems and can form dense carpets that help prevent soil erosion in shady areas where grass won't grow.

children.description: The Buxales order is a small group of woody plants that includes boxwoods and pachysandras, characterized by their simple leaves and inconspicuous flowers. These plants are mostly shrubs or small trees that produce tiny, often greenish flowers without petals. They're commonly found in temperate regions and are popular in landscaping for their evergreen foliage and ability to tolerate pruning.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many flowering plants, members of Buxales have very small, simple flowers that lack petals and are often wind-pollinated rather than insect-pollinated. Their leaves are typically small, leathery, and arranged alternately or opposite on the stems.
children.funFact: Boxwood has been prized for centuries in topiary art because its dense, small leaves and slow growth rate make it perfect for creating intricate sculpted shapes that hold their form for years.

children.name: Crossosomatales
Staphyleaceae
Staphylea
children.description: Bladdernuts are small deciduous trees or shrubs known for their distinctive inflated seed pods that look like little paper lanterns. All members of this genus produce compound leaves with multiple leaflets and small, white or greenish flowers that bloom in drooping clusters during spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The inflated, papery seed capsules that give bladdernuts their name are unique among New England woody plants. These balloon-like pods contain hard, rattling seeds and persist on branches well into winter.
children.funFact: The seeds inside bladdernut pods make a distinctive rattling sound when shaken, earning them the folk name 'rattle pods' and making them popular for natural crafts and children's toys.

children.description: The bladdernut family is a small group of shrubs and small trees known for their distinctive inflated seed pods that look like little balloons or bladders. These woody plants produce clusters of white or greenish flowers in spring, followed by papery, three-lobed capsules that contain hard seeds that rattle when shaken.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The inflated, balloon-like seed capsules are the most distinctive feature of this family, setting them apart from other woody plants. The combination of opposite compound leaves and these characteristic papery pods makes identification relatively straightforward.
children.funFact: The dried seed pods of bladdernuts were traditionally used as children's toys and rattles because the hard seeds create a distinctive rattling sound when the papery capsule is shaken.

children.description: Crossosomatales is a small but diverse order of flowering plants that includes shrubs and small trees found in various habitats around the world. The group gets its common name from the rockflowers of western North America, though it also contains the bladdernut family found in New England's forests. These plants typically have simple leaves and small, often fragrant flowers that develop into distinctive fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are united by specific flower structures and genetic relationships rather than obvious visual similarities. The bladdernut family, which represents this order in New England, is easily recognized by its inflated, papery seed capsules that look like small balloons.
children.funFact: The inflated seed capsules of bladdernuts make a rattling sound when shaken, earning them folk names like 'rattle bush' in some regions.

children.name: Ceratophyllales
Ceratophyllaceae
Ceratophyllum
children.description: Hornworts are submerged aquatic plants that live entirely underwater in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They have finely divided, feathery leaves arranged in whorls around their stems, creating a distinctive bottle-brush appearance. These plants are completely rootless, instead anchoring themselves to the bottom with modified leaves or floating freely in the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, hornworts lack true roots entirely and have leaves that are forked multiple times into thread-like segments. Their small flowers are hidden among the leaves and are either male or female on the same plant.
children.funFact: Hornworts are living water purifiers - they absorb nutrients directly from the water through their leaves, helping to reduce algae growth and keep aquatic ecosystems healthy.

children.description: Coontails are a small family of aquatic plants that live completely submerged in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These rootless plants float freely in the water column or may anchor themselves loosely to the bottom with modified stems. They have distinctive whorled leaves that branch out in circles around their stems, creating a bushy, tail-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most aquatic plants, coontails have no true roots at any stage of their life cycle and remain completely submerged, never producing floating or emergent leaves. Their leaves are arranged in dense whorls and are deeply divided into narrow, forked segments that give them a feathery texture.
children.funFact: Coontails are sometimes called 'hornworts' because their fruits have long, curved spines that resemble tiny horns, though they're not related to the hornworts that are bryophytes.

children.description: Coontails are a unique order of aquatic flowering plants that live completely submerged in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These plants have no roots and instead float freely in the water column or anchor themselves loosely to the bottom with modified stems. They get their name from their distinctive whorled, finely-divided leaves that resemble the bushy tail of a raccoon.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, coontails are completely rootless and have leaves arranged in dense whorls around the stem with fork-like divisions. They are also unique among flowering plants for being wind-pollinated while living entirely underwater.
children.funFact: Coontails can reproduce entirely without seeds - they spread by fragmentation, where broken pieces of the plant can grow into new individuals, making them remarkably resilient colonizers of aquatic habitats.

children.name: Poales
Cyperaceae
Carex
children.description: True sedges (Carex) are grass-like plants that form one of the largest and most diverse plant genera in New England, with an impressive 176 species found throughout the region. These perennial herbs typically grow in wet or moist environments like marshes, bogs, pond edges, and woodland streams, though some species thrive in drier upland areas. They're characterized by their three-sided stems, narrow leaves, and distinctive flower clusters that develop into small, seed-bearing structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike grasses which have round, hollow stems, true sedges have solid, triangular stems that you can feel by rolling them between your fingers. Their flowers are also quite different - sedges produce tiny, inconspicuous flowers in spikes or clusters, with seeds enclosed in small sac-like structures called perigynia.
children.funFact: Sedges are so diverse that botanists often joke 'sedges have edges' to help people remember their triangular stems, and some species like Pennsylvania sedge are actually excellent alternatives to traditional grass lawns in shady areas!

children.name: Cyperus
children.description: Flatsedges are a diverse group of grass-like plants that belong to the sedge family and thrive in wet or moist environments throughout New England. These plants are characterized by their triangular stems, clustered flower heads, and ability to grow in everything from marshes and pond edges to disturbed soils and agricultural fields. Many species produce small, nutlike seeds and have extensive underground root systems that help them spread and colonize new areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, flatsedges have solid, triangular stems (remember: 'sedges have edges') and their flowers are arranged in distinctive umbrella-like clusters or dense heads. Their leaves are typically arranged in three ranks around the stem, and their flower clusters often have leaf-like bracts at the base.
children.funFact: Yellow nutsedge was actually cultivated as a food crop by ancient Egyptians over 4,000 years ago - its small tubers are edible and nutty-flavored, earning it the nickname 'earth almond,' though today it's more commonly known as a persistent garden weed.

children.name: Eleocharis
children.description: Spikerushes are grass-like wetland plants in the sedge family that get their name from their distinctive flower clusters that look like tiny spikes at the tip of slender stems. These hardy plants thrive in wet soils, from shallow pond edges to marshy areas, where they often form dense colonies. All spikerushes share the characteristic of having simple, unbranched stems topped with a single compact spike of small flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, spikerushes have solid (not hollow) stems that are typically triangular or round in cross-section. Their single terminal spike and lack of leaves along the stem make them easy to distinguish from other sedges and rushes.
children.funFact: Some spikerushes like Needle Spikerush are popular in aquascaping and aquarium design because they can grow both underwater and on land, creating beautiful carpet-like effects in planted tanks.

children.name: Scirpus
children.description: Scirpus bulrushes are tall, grass-like plants that thrive in wet places like marshes, swamps, and the edges of ponds and streams. These hardy perennials have triangular or round stems topped with clusters of small, brownish flowers that later produce tiny seeds. They're important wetland plants that help filter water and provide food and shelter for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other sedges, Scirpus bulrushes typically have softer, more leafy stems and their flower clusters are often drooping or nodding rather than upright and rigid.
children.funFact: The northeastern bulrush (Scirpus ancistrochaetus) is so rare that it's federally endangered and found in only a handful of locations, making it one of New England's most elusive wetland plants.

children.name: Rhynchospora
children.description: Beaksedges are wetland plants in the sedge family that get their name from their distinctive seed heads, which end in a pointed beak-like structure. These grass-like plants typically grow in wet, acidic soils like bogs, marshes, and pond edges throughout New England. They produce small clusters of brownish or whitish flowers that develop into the characteristic beaked fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sedges, beaksedges have fruits topped with a prominent beak or tubercle that gives them their common name. Their flower clusters are also typically more compact and rounded compared to the elongated spikes of many other sedge genera.
children.funFact: The beaked fruits of these plants can float on water, helping them disperse their seeds to new wetland habitats during floods or high water periods.

children.name: Schoenoplectus
children.description: Schoenoplectus bulrushes are tall, grass-like wetland plants that thrive in marshes, pond edges, and shallow water throughout New England. These sturdy sedges produce clusters of small, brownish flower spikes and have thick, often triangular stems that can grow several feet tall. They're essential components of wetland ecosystems, providing habitat for wildlife and helping to filter water naturally.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, Schoenoplectus bulrushes have solid, often three-sided stems and produce distinctive clusters of small, scaly flowers called spikelets. Their stems are typically much thicker and more robust than other sedges, and they often grow directly from underwater rhizomes.
children.funFact: Native Americans traditionally used bulrush stems to weave baskets, mats, and even canoes, while the starchy roots were harvested as an important food source - earning them the nickname 'marsh potato.'

children.name: Eriophorum
children.description: Cottongrasses are distinctive wetland plants that aren't actually grasses at all, but rather members of the sedge family. They're easily recognized by their fluffy, cotton-like seed heads that appear white and wispy, especially when they catch the light in bogs and wet meadows. These hardy plants thrive in acidic, nutrient-poor soils where few other plants can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, cottongrasses have triangular stems and produce those characteristic puffy white seed heads that look like cotton balls on stalks. Their flowers are arranged in clusters called spikelets, and they lack the flat leaf blades typical of grasses.
children.funFact: The fluffy 'cotton' of cottongrass seed heads was once collected and used to stuff pillows and mattresses by early settlers, and some Indigenous peoples traditionally used the soft fibers for wound dressing and tinder for starting fires.

children.name: Trichophorum
children.description: Deergrasses are small, grass-like sedges that form dense tufts or clumps in wet, acidic habitats like bogs, fens, and marshy areas. These hardy plants produce clusters of tiny brown flowers that lack the showy petals we might expect, instead focusing their energy on wind dispersal of seeds. All four New England species prefer cool, northern climates and can often be found growing alongside sphagnum moss and other bog plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, deergrasses have solid, triangular stems and their flowers are arranged in small, compact clusters called spikelets. They're distinguished from other sedges by their particularly dense, cushion-like growth pattern and their preference for very acidic, nutrient-poor soils.
children.funFact: Cotton Deergrass gets its name from the fluffy white bristles that surround its seeds, creating cotton-like tufts that help the seeds float on water and catch the wind for dispersal across wetland habitats.

children.name: Scleria
children.description: Nutrushes are sedges that produce distinctive hard, bead-like fruits that give them their common name. These grasslike plants typically grow in wetlands, sandy areas, and open woodlands throughout New England. Unlike true grasses, nutrushes have solid stems and their leaves are arranged in three rows around the stem.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nutrushes can be identified by their characteristic hard, white or grayish nutlike fruits that sit in cup-shaped bases. They differ from other sedges by having these prominent, bony fruits and often having bristly or rough-textured leaves.
children.funFact: The hard fruits of nutrushes were historically used by some Native American groups as beads for jewelry and decoration, earning them the nickname 'bead sedges.'

children.name: Bolboschoenus
children.description: Clubrushes are sturdy wetland grasses that thrive in salty or brackish water environments like salt marshes, coastal areas, and tidal rivers. These robust plants have thick, triangular stems and produce distinctive brown, club-shaped flower clusters that give them their common name. All members of this genus are specially adapted to handle saltwater conditions that would kill most other plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sedges, clubrushes have particularly thick, sturdy stems and can tolerate high salt concentrations in soil and water. Their flower clusters are notably dense and rounded, resembling small clubs or maces.
children.funFact: Clubrushes can filter salt from seawater through their roots and actually excrete excess salt through special glands on their leaves, making them natural desalination plants!

children.name: Schoenoplectiella
children.description: Schoenoplectiella is a genus of small to medium-sized bulrushes that thrive in wetland environments throughout New England. These grass-like plants are members of the sedge family and are characterized by their clumping growth habit and distinctive flower clusters that appear as small, brownish spikelets at the tips of their stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger cousins in the genus Schoenoplectus, Schoenoplectiella species are generally smaller and more delicate, with thinner stems and fewer flowers per cluster. They can be distinguished from other sedges by their terminal flower clusters and three-sided stems that are solid rather than hollow.
children.funFact: Despite their modest appearance, these bulrushes are ecological powerhouses that help filter water pollutants and provide important nesting materials for wetland birds like red-winged blackbirds.

children.name: Dulichium
children.description: Dulichium is a small genus of sedges that includes just a few species worldwide, with only one found in New England. These distinctive wetland plants are easily recognized by their unusual three-ranked leaf arrangement, where leaves spiral around the stem in three vertical rows rather than the typical two-ranked pattern of most sedges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sedges which typically have leaves arranged in two rows, Dulichium species have their leaves arranged in three distinct vertical ranks around the stem, giving them a very distinctive appearance that's hard to mistake.
children.funFact: The name 'Three-way Sedge' comes from the plant's unique leaf arrangement in three ranks, which creates a triangular cross-section when viewed from above - a rare feature among North American sedges.

children.name: Bulbostylis
children.description: Bulbostylis is a genus of small, grass-like plants in the sedge family that typically grow in dense tufts or clumps. These delicate plants produce tiny flowers arranged in small clusters and are characterized by their hair-like, thread-thin leaves that give them a wispy appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other sedges, Bulbostylis species have extremely fine, capillary leaves that are much thinner than typical sedge foliage, and their flower clusters are very small and compact compared to the larger, more prominent flower heads of most sedges.
children.funFact: The name 'Bulbostylis' comes from the Greek words for 'bulb' and 'style,' referring to the swollen base of the flower's female parts, though the plants themselves don't actually grow from bulbs.

children.name: Cladium
children.description: Sawgrasses are tall, sturdy sedges that grow in wetland areas like marshes, bogs, and pond edges. They get their name from their long, narrow leaves that have tiny sharp teeth along the edges, making them feel rough like a saw blade. These perennial plants form dense clumps and can grow several feet tall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other sedges, sawgrasses have distinctly saw-toothed leaf margins that can actually cut skin if handled carelessly. They also produce round, brown seed heads rather than the typical triangular or flattened seed clusters of many sedges.
children.funFact: The smooth saw-grass was traditionally used by Native Americans to weave baskets and mats, with the tough, serrated leaves providing both durability and a natural grip texture.

children.name: Fimbristylis
children.description: Fringe Rush is a genus of small, grass-like plants in the sedge family that grow in wet, sandy areas. These plants have thin, wiry stems topped with clusters of tiny brown flowers, and despite their common name, they're actually sedges rather than true rushes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fringe Rush can be identified by its distinctive flower clusters that have a fringed or feathery appearance, and its three-sided stems that are characteristic of sedges.
children.funFact: The name 'Fimbristylis' comes from Latin words meaning 'fringed style,' referring to the feathery appearance of the flower's reproductive parts.

children.name: Fuirena
children.description: Umbrella-sedges are small wetland plants in the sedge family that get their name from their distinctive flowering heads, which spread out like tiny umbrellas at the top of triangular stems. These grasslike plants typically grow in wet, sandy soils around ponds, marshes, and other freshwater areas. Like other sedges, they have solid, three-sided stems rather than the hollow, round stems of true grasses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other sedges, umbrella-sedges have their flowers arranged in distinctive umbrella-shaped clusters at the stem tips, making them easy to identify. Their flower heads also have prominent bristly scales that give them a fuzzy, textured appearance.
children.funFact: The Dwarf Umbrella-sedge is considered rare in New England and is listed as a species of conservation concern in several states due to habitat loss from wetland development.

children.name: Ficinia
children.description: Star grasses are sedge-like plants that belong to the family Cyperaceae, despite their common name suggesting they're grasses. These coastal plants are adapted to harsh saltwater environments and sandy soils, forming dense clumps or mats. They have distinctive triangular stems and small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Star grasses can be distinguished from true grasses by their solid, triangular stems (rather than hollow, round stems) and their fruit structure called an achene. Unlike many sedges, they're particularly well-adapted to salt spray and coastal conditions.
children.funFact: The Knobby Clubrush gets its name from the distinctive swollen, knob-like nodes along its stems, which help it store water and nutrients in harsh coastal environments.

children.description: Sedges are grass-like plants that thrive in wet places like marshes, bogs, and pond edges, though some grow in drier habitats too. They have solid, often triangular stems and their flowers are arranged in small clusters called spikelets that lack showy petals. With 272 species in New England, sedges form one of our region's most diverse plant families.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses which have hollow, round stems, sedges typically have solid, triangular stems that you can feel when you roll them between your fingers. The old saying 'sedges have edges' helps distinguish them from the round stems of grasses and rushes.
children.funFact: Cotton grass (Eriophorum) creates some of nature's most beautiful displays when its fluffy white seed heads wave in the breeze across New England bogs, looking like patches of cotton balls scattered across the landscape.

children.name: Poaceae
Dichanthelium
children.description: Rosette grasses are a diverse group of native grasses that get their name from their distinctive growth pattern - they form low, circular clusters of leaves (rosettes) at ground level, especially during their early growth phases. These grasses are commonly found in woodlands, fields, and disturbed areas throughout New England, where they play important roles in local ecosystems. Many species have charming common names like 'witchgrass' and 'panic grass,' reflecting their historical significance to early settlers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other grasses that grow in simple upright clumps, rosette grasses have a unique two-stage growth pattern where they first form flat, ground-hugging rosettes before sending up flowering stems. Their leaves are typically broader than many other native grasses, and they often have a distinctive branching pattern in their seed heads.
children.funFact: Many rosette grasses are ecological shape-shifters - they can look completely different in spring (as low rosettes) versus summer (as tall, branching grass plants), which historically made them very challenging for botanists to identify and classify!

children.name: Poa
children.description: Meadow-grasses are a large genus of cool-season grasses that form the backbone of many New England lawns, meadows, and natural grasslands. These perennial grasses are known for their ability to create dense, soft turf and their tolerance of cooler temperatures. They typically have narrow, flat leaves and produce delicate, branched flower clusters called panicles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Poa grasses can be identified by their boat-shaped leaf tips and the distinctive membranous ligule (a small flap) where the leaf blade meets the stem. Their flower clusters are typically open and pyramid-shaped, quite different from the spike-like arrangements of many other grass genera.
children.funFact: Kentucky bluegrass (Poa pratensis) isn't actually native to Kentucky or even North America – it was brought over by European settlers and became so successful that it's now the foundation of countless American lawns and sports fields.

children.name: Bromus
children.description: Bromes are annual or perennial grasses that belong to the genus Bromus, found in a wide variety of habitats from woodlands to prairies to disturbed areas. These grasses typically have drooping or nodding seed heads (panicles) with distinctive flattened spikelets that contain multiple small flowers. Many species are important for wildlife food and some are used for forage, though several non-native species have become problematic weeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bromes can be identified by their characteristic drooping seed heads and flattened, often large spikelets that typically hang from slender branches. Unlike many other grasses, their spikelets are usually compressed from the sides and often have prominent awns (bristle-like extensions) on their seeds.
children.funFact: Cheatgrass, one of the most notorious brome species, gets its name because it 'cheats' ranchers by growing quickly in spring but becoming dry and nutritionally worthless by summer, leaving livestock without proper forage.

children.name: Elymus
children.description: Wild ryes and wheatgrasses are tall, graceful grasses that form an important part of New England's meadows, prairies, and woodland edges. These perennial grasses are characterized by their distinctive spike-like flower clusters and their ability to thrive in diverse habitats from wetlands to dry slopes. Many species in this genus are valuable for wildlife habitat and soil stabilization.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Elymus can be identified by their dense, elongated flower spikes where individual spikelets are arranged directly along the central stem without stalks. Unlike many other grasses, their spikelets typically contain multiple florets and have prominent bristle-like awns extending from the seeds.
children.funFact: Quack grass, despite being considered a troublesome weed by gardeners, gets its name not from the sound a duck makes, but from the Old English word 'cwice' meaning 'living' or 'vigorous' - a reference to its incredibly persistent spreading habit through underground rhizomes.

children.name: Glyceria
children.description: Sweet grasses are a group of wetland grasses that love to grow in moist to wet environments like marshes, pond edges, and stream banks. These grasses are characterized by their sweet-tasting seeds (hence the name) and their preference for consistently damp soil. All members of this genus produce clusters of small, delicate flowers that develop into nutritious seeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sweet grasses can be distinguished from other wetland grasses by their typically broad, flat leaf blades and their loose, open flower clusters. Many species have a distinctive floating or semi-aquatic growth habit, with some able to grow partially submerged in shallow water.
