children.funFact: The seeds of sweet grasses were traditionally harvested by Native American tribes as a nutritious food source, and some species like fowl mannagrass are still important food for waterfowl and other wetland wildlife today.

children.name: Eragrostis
children.description: Lovegrasses are a diverse genus of delicate grasses known for their open, airy flower clusters that dance gracefully in the wind. These grasses typically have fine, narrow leaves and produce clouds of tiny seeds that give them their distinctive feathery appearance. Most species are annual grasses that thrive in sandy or disturbed soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lovegrasses can be identified by their characteristic open, branching seed heads with numerous tiny florets, and their tendency to form distinctive tufted clumps. Their seed heads often have a purple or reddish tinge that sets them apart from other common grasses.
children.funFact: Despite their romantic name, lovegrasses got their moniker not from matters of the heart, but from their seeds' tendency to cling lovingly to clothing and fur, making them excellent hitchhikers for spreading to new locations.

children.name: Panicum
children.description: Panicgrasses are a diverse group of annual and perennial grasses that produce their seeds in branched, open clusters called panicles. These adaptable grasses can be found in a wide variety of habitats, from wetlands and prairies to disturbed areas like roadsides and fields. Many species are important for wildlife as they provide food for birds and serve as host plants for butterfly caterpillars.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Panicgrasses are characterized by their distinctive branched flower clusters (panicles) and small, round to oval seeds that lack the long bristles found on many other grass genera. Their leaf sheaths are typically smooth and the ligule (small flap where leaf meets stem) is usually hairy rather than membranous.
children.funFact: Switchgrass, one of New England's native panicgrasses, can grow up to 8 feet tall and is being researched as a renewable biofuel source because of its ability to produce large amounts of biomass on marginal land.

children.name: Agrostis
children.description: Bent grasses are a group of fine-textured grasses that form the backbone of many New England lawns, golf courses, and natural meadows. These adaptable grasses are known for their ability to create dense, carpet-like growth and their tolerance of cool, moist conditions typical of our region.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bent grasses can be identified by their very narrow, flat leaf blades and delicate, open flower clusters that appear almost cloud-like when in bloom. Unlike many other grasses, they often spread by underground stems or surface runners, allowing them to fill in gaps and create uniform stands.
children.funFact: Colonial bent grass was one of the first grasses intentionally brought to North America by European settlers in the 1600s, packed in their ships specifically to create the familiar lawns and pastures of home.

children.name: Festuca
children.description: Fescues are a diverse group of grasses that range from tiny annual species to robust perennial turf grasses. They're characterized by their narrow leaves and distinctive flower clusters called panicles, which often have a delicate, branching appearance. These adaptable grasses can be found in many habitats, from lawns and pastures to rocky slopes and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Fescues can be distinguished from other grasses by their rolled or folded leaf blades and their panicles with branches that typically bear flowers only near their tips. Many species also have bristle-like awns extending from their seeds.
children.funFact: Red fescue has become so popular for lawns and golf courses that it's now one of the most widely planted grasses in the world, yet it originally grew wild in the meadows and coastal areas of New England.

children.name: Setaria
children.description: Foxtails and bristlegrasses are annual grasses known for their distinctive fuzzy, cylindrical flower heads that resemble a fox's tail or bottle brush. These common grasses produce dense clusters of tiny flowers surrounded by bristles, giving them their characteristic appearance. They're typically found in disturbed soils, gardens, fields, and roadsides throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grasses, Setaria species have dense, spike-like flower heads with prominent bristles that extend beyond the actual flowers. These bristles are typically yellow, green, or purplish and give the seed heads their distinctive fuzzy, tail-like appearance.
children.funFact: Several species in this genus, including foxtail millet (Setaria italica), were among the first grasses domesticated by humans over 9,000 years ago and are still important food crops in parts of Asia and Africa today.

children.name: Sporobolus
children.description: Sporobolus is a genus of hardy grasses that includes both the familiar cordgrasses of salt marshes and the drought-tolerant dropseeds of prairies and sandy areas. These grasses are known for their ability to thrive in challenging environments, from salty coastal wetlands to dry, nutrient-poor soils. They produce small, often inconspicuous flowers and have narrow, pointed leaves that help them conserve water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Sporobolus have tiny seeds that often fall freely from the seed head when ripe, which is where the "dropseed" name comes from. Their flower clusters are typically narrow and dense, and the individual flowers lack the prominent bristles found in many other grass genera.
children.funFact: Saltmarsh Cordgrass is so effective at filtering salt from seawater that it actually excretes salt crystals through special glands on its leaves, which you can sometimes see sparkling in the sunlight!

children.name: Calamagrostis
children.description: Reedgrasses are tall, hardy perennial grasses that form the backbone of many New England wetlands, prairies, and coastal areas. These grasses are characterized by their feathery, plume-like seed heads and their ability to spread through underground stems called rhizomes, often forming large colonies that help stabilize soil and prevent erosion.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Reedgrasses can be distinguished from other grasses by their distinctive fluffy, often purplish or silvery flower clusters and their typically tall stature. They also have a characteristic tuft of silky hairs (called a callus) at the base of each seed that helps with wind dispersal.
children.funFact: American marram grass is so effective at binding sand dunes that it's been intentionally planted along coastlines worldwide to prevent beach erosion, earning it the nickname 'dune builder.'

children.name: Aristida
children.description: Threeawns and wiregrasses are a group of native grasses known for their distinctive seed heads that bear three long, needle-like projections called awns. These hardy grasses typically grow in dry, sandy, or disturbed soils and are often among the first plants to colonize bare ground. Most species have narrow, wiry leaves and produce small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in loose, open clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The three prominent awns (bristle-like appendages) extending from each seed make this group unmistakable among grasses. These awns are typically much longer than the seed itself and often have a twisted or bent appearance.
children.funFact: The barbed awns of threeawn grasses can actually drill seeds into the ground by twisting as they absorb and release moisture, helping the plant spread into new areas without any help from animals or wind.

children.name: Muhlenbergia
children.description: Muhly grasses are a diverse group of native grasses that range from tiny, delicate species to robust clump-forming plants. They're found in various habitats from woodlands to wetlands, and are characterized by their small, often inconspicuous flower clusters and narrow grass blades. Many muhly species are important for wildlife, providing seeds for birds and nesting material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Muhly grasses are distinguished from other grasses by their typically small, open flower clusters (panicles) with tiny spikelets that often have a delicate, airy appearance. Their seed heads are usually much less dense and showy than other common grass genera.
children.funFact: The genus is named after Gotthilf Heinrich Ernst Muhlenberg, an 18th-century German-American botanist who was also a Lutheran minister and is considered one of the founding fathers of American botany.

children.name: Anthoxanthum
children.description: Sweetgrasses are a small group of fragrant grasses that release a sweet, hay-like scent when crushed or dried. These perennial grasses typically grow in cool, moist environments and are known for their distinctive aroma that comes from natural compounds called coumarins. They form clumps or tufts and produce small, delicate flower clusters in spring and early summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other grasses, sweetgrasses have only two stamens per flower instead of the usual three. Their sweet, vanilla-like fragrance when dried or crushed is also unique among New England grasses.
children.funFact: Sweet vernal grass was one of the first European grasses introduced to North America and is responsible for much of the characteristic sweet smell of new-mown hay in fields and meadows.

children.name: Echinochloa
children.description: Barnyard grasses are a group of annual grasses that typically grow in wet, disturbed areas like farm fields, ditches, and pond edges. These robust grasses have broad, flat leaves and produce distinctive seed heads with branching clusters of small, bristly flowers that can range from green to purple.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasses, barnyard grasses lack ligules (the small flap where the leaf meets the stem) and have seed heads with short, stiff bristles or awns that give them a rough, bristly appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being considered weeds by many farmers, barnyard grasses like Jungle Rice have been cultivated as food crops for thousands of years in parts of Asia and Africa, with their nutritious seeds ground into flour or cooked like rice.

children.name: Lolium
children.description: Ryegrasses are a group of cool-season grasses that are incredibly important for lawns, pastures, and hay fields throughout New England. These hardy perennial and annual grasses form dense, fine-textured turf and are prized for their ability to germinate quickly and tolerate heavy foot traffic. They're among the most widely planted grasses in temperate regions worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ryegrasses can be identified by their distinctive seed heads that have spikelets arranged alternately along a zigzag stem, creating a flattened appearance. Unlike many other grasses, their leaf blades have a characteristic glossy underside and prominent parallel veins.
children.funFact: Perennial ryegrass is so tough and quick to establish that it's used on professional sports fields, including Wimbledon's tennis courts and many major league soccer stadiums around the world.

children.name: Digitaria
children.description: Digitaria is a genus of annual grasses commonly known as crabgrasses and cottontops. These low-growing grasses spread outward in a sprawling pattern and are characterized by their finger-like seed heads that branch out from a central point. They're often considered weedy plants that thrive in disturbed soils and open areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Digitaria can be identified by their distinctive seed heads that resemble spread fingers or a bird's foot, with multiple narrow spikes radiating from the tip of the stem. Unlike many other grasses, they tend to grow in a prostrate, mat-forming habit rather than standing upright.
children.funFact: Despite being considered lawn weeds by many homeowners, crabgrasses are actually nutritious plants - their seeds were historically harvested as food by Native Americans and are still eaten in some parts of the world today.

children.name: Leymus
children.description: Leymus is a genus of hardy perennial grasses commonly known as lyme grasses or wildrye grasses. These robust grasses are specially adapted to challenging coastal and northern environments, with strong root systems that help stabilize sandy soils and dunes. All members of this genus share the ability to thrive in harsh conditions where many other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Leymus grasses can be distinguished from other grass genera by their thick, blue-green to gray-green leaf blades and their distinctive spike-like flower clusters. They also have creeping underground stems (rhizomes) that help them spread and form colonies.
children.funFact: These grasses are nature's sand engineers - their extensive root systems can extend up to 10 feet deep and help prevent coastal erosion by binding sand dunes together.

children.name: Cenchrus
children.description: Sandburs and fountain grasses are tough, adaptable grasses that produce distinctive seed heads with spiky, bristly structures. These grasses are well-suited to sandy soils and disturbed areas, making them common in coastal regions, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their spiny burs or bristly plumes that surround their seeds, which readily stick to clothing and animal fur for dispersal.
children.funFact: The spiny burs of sandburs are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired the invention of Velcro after Swiss engineer George de Mestral studied how they stuck to his dog's fur during walks.

children.name: Phyllostachys
children.description: Phyllostachys is a genus of running bamboos that have become established in New England, despite being native to Asia. These are tall, woody grasses that spread by underground stems called rhizomes, forming dense groves over time. All members of this genus are characterized by their jointed, hollow stems and distinctive groove that runs along one side of each stem segment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike clumping bamboos, Phyllostachys species are aggressive spreaders that send out runners underground. They can be identified by the distinctive groove or channel that runs along one side of each internode (stem segment between joints).
children.funFact: Some Phyllostachys bamboos can grow up to 3 feet in a single day during peak growing season, making them among the fastest-growing plants on Earth.

children.name: Phleum
children.description: Timothies are a small genus of perennial grasses known for their distinctive cylindrical flower spikes that look like fuzzy bottlebrushes. These cool-season grasses grow in dense clumps and are found in meadows, fields, and mountainous areas throughout New England. They're important both as wildlife food sources and as cultivated forage crops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Timothies can be identified by their compact, spike-like flower heads that are much denser and more cylindrical than most other grass species. The flower spikes feel soft to the touch and have a characteristic bottlebrush appearance that sets them apart from the looser, more open flower clusters of related grasses.
children.funFact: Timothy grass was named after Timothy Hanson, an 18th-century American farmer who promoted its cultivation, and it became so valuable as hay that it was sometimes called 'timothy gold' by colonial farmers.

children.name: Phalaris
children.description: Canarygrasses are tall, robust grasses that thrive in wet or marshy areas throughout New England. These perennial grasses are known for their dense, cylindrical flower clusters and their ability to form large colonies through underground stems called rhizomes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasses, canarygrasses have distinctive shiny, flattened seed heads that are densely packed and often have a whitish or pale green appearance. Their leaves are typically broader than most wetland grasses and have a distinctive ribbed texture.
children.funFact: Reed canary grass was once widely planted for erosion control and livestock feed, but it has become so successful at spreading that it's now considered an invasive species in many wetland areas.

children.name: Danthonia
children.description: Oatgrasses are small, hardy perennial grasses that form dense tufts or clumps in dry, nutrient-poor soils. These grasses get their name from their distinctive seed heads that somewhat resemble oat grains, though they're much smaller and more delicate. They're particularly well-adapted to sandy, acidic soils where many other plants struggle to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oatgrasses can be identified by their characteristic flattened, twisted awns (bristle-like appendages) that extend from their seeds, giving the seed heads a distinctive feathery appearance. Unlike many other grasses, they tend to grow in tight bunches rather than spreading by underground stems.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'poverty oatgrass,' these hardy plants actually help improve soil quality over time by adding organic matter and helping prevent erosion in challenging growing conditions.

children.name: Anatherum
children.description: New World Bluestems are native grasses that form an important part of North America's grassland ecosystems. These perennial grasses are characterized by their distinctive seed heads and their ability to thrive in poor, sandy soils where other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grass genera, New World Bluestems have distinctive fuzzy, bottlebrush-like seed heads that turn reddish-bronze in fall. Their stems often have a bluish tint at the base, giving them their common name.
children.funFact: Broomsedge bluestem was historically used to make brooms and brushes by early American settlers, which is how it got its common name.

children.name: Miscanthus
children.description: Silvergrasses are tall, clump-forming perennial grasses known for their graceful, feathery seed heads that shimmer silver or tan in autumn sunlight. These ornamental grasses can grow 6-12 feet tall and produce distinctive plume-like flower clusters that persist through winter, creating beautiful texture in the landscape.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many native grasses, silvergrasses form large, dense clumps with arching leaves that have a prominent white midrib. Their showy, persistent seed plumes are much more ornamental than most other tall grasses in New England.
children.funFact: Chinese silver grass can produce over 20,000 seeds per plant, and while beautiful in gardens, it has become invasive in many areas because it spreads so effectively by both seeds and underground rhizomes.

children.name: Alopecurus
children.description: Foxtail grasses are a small group of cool-season grasses known for their distinctive cylindrical flower spikes that resemble a fox's bushy tail. These perennial grasses typically grow in moist meadows, fields, and along waterways throughout New England. They're important forage grasses that provide food for wildlife and livestock.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grasses, foxtail grasses have dense, soft, cylindrical flower heads that are unmistakably fuzzy and tail-like in appearance. Their flower spikes are typically much more compact and uniform than those of other common grass genera.
children.funFact: Meadow foxtail is one of the earliest grasses to flower in spring, often blooming before most other grasses have even started growing actively.

children.name: Cinna
children.description: Cinna is a small genus of tall, graceful grasses commonly known as woodreeds that thrive in moist, shaded woodland environments. These perennial grasses are characterized by their drooping flower clusters and preference for cool, damp soils found in forests and woodland edges throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Woodreeds can be distinguished from other forest grasses by their distinctive drooping or nodding flower panicles and their unusually large, flat seed heads that flutter in the breeze.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'reeds,' woodreeds are true grasses that have adapted to forest life, making them some of the few grass species that actually prefer shade over full sunlight.

children.name: Zizania
children.description: Wild rice (Zizania) is a genus of tall, aquatic grasses that grow in shallow waters of lakes, rivers, and wetlands. These native plants can reach impressive heights of 6-10 feet above the water surface and produce distinctive seed heads containing nutritious grains. Unlike cultivated rice, wild rice species are naturally occurring in North America and have been an important food source for indigenous peoples for thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wild rice can be distinguished from other aquatic grasses by its exceptionally tall stature and unique flowering structure, with separate male and female flowers on the same plant - males hanging below and females standing upright above.
children.funFact: Despite its name, wild rice isn't actually rice at all - it's more closely related to oats and belongs to a completely different genus than Asian rice (Oryza)!

children.name: Leersia
children.description: Leersia is a genus of wetland grasses that thrive in soggy soils and shallow water throughout New England. These perennial grasses are commonly found along pond edges, in marshes, and in wet meadows where their spreading root systems help stabilize muddy shorelines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasses, Leersia species have distinctive flattened, ribbon-like leaves with very sharp, saw-toothed edges that can easily cut skin. Their small flowers lack the typical chaffy scales (glumes) found in most grass flowers.
children.funFact: Rice cutgrass earned its common name because its razor-sharp leaf edges can slice through skin like paper cuts, making it one of the few grasses that hikers actively try to avoid brushing against.

children.name: Hordeum
children.description: Barleys are grasses in the genus Hordeum that produce distinctive seed heads with long, bristly awns (hair-like projections). These hardy grasses can thrive in various conditions from cultivated fields to wild meadows and roadsides. They are annual or perennial plants that belong to the same family as wheat, oats, and other cereal grains.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barley species are distinguished by their characteristic three-flowered spikelets arranged along the stem, with prominent bristle-like awns that give the seed heads a fuzzy, bottlebrush appearance. The awns are typically much longer than in related grasses like wheat.
children.funFact: Common Barley is one of humanity's oldest cultivated crops, with archaeological evidence showing it was grown over 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent, and today it's still a key ingredient in beer and whiskey production.

children.name: Paspalum
children.description: Paspalum is a genus of warm-season grasses that typically grow in open, sunny areas like fields, roadsides, and disturbed soils. These grasses produce their seeds on distinctive finger-like spikes that branch out from the main stem, creating a characteristic hand-like appearance. They are perennial grasses that spread by both seeds and underground stems called rhizomes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Paspalum grasses can be identified by their unique seed heads that consist of multiple narrow, finger-like branches (racemes) arranged along the stem. Unlike many other grasses, their tiny seeds are arranged in neat rows along one side of each branch, giving the seed heads a very orderly appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Paspalum' comes from the Greek word 'paspalos,' which was used by ancient botanists to describe a type of millet, reflecting the grain-like seeds these grasses produce.

children.name: Coleataenia
children.commonName: beaked panicgrasses, redtop panicgrasses, cutthroatgrasses, and allies
children.description: Coleataenia is a genus of native perennial grasses that includes the redtop panicgrasses and their close relatives. These grasses are characterized by their open, branching flower clusters called panicles and their ability to grow in a variety of habitats from wet meadows to dry fields. They are important components of New England's grassland ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other panicgrasses by their relatively large seeds and distinctive leaf sheaths that often have a reddish tinge. Their panicles are typically more open and spreading compared to the denser flower clusters of many related grasses.
children.funFact: The name 'cutthroatgrass' comes from the sharp edges of some species' leaves, which can actually give you a paper-cut-like injury if you run your finger along them carelessly!

children.name: Sorghum
children.description: Sorghum is a genus of tall, sturdy grasses that includes both cultivated crops and wild species. These plants are characterized by their robust stems, broad leaves, and distinctive seed heads that cluster together in dense, branching formations. Most sorghums are warm-season grasses that thrive in hot, dry conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sorghum grasses can be identified by their thick, solid stems (unlike the hollow stems of many other grasses) and their large, dense flower clusters that often have a reddish or purplish tint. The seeds are typically round and come in various colors from white to deep red or purple.
children.funFact: Johnson grass, one of the two New England sorghums, is considered one of the world's most invasive weeds and can grow up to 8 feet tall, but it's actually named after Colonel William Johnson who accidentally introduced it to Alabama in the 1840s as a potential forage crop.

children.name: Aira
children.description: Hair Grass (Aira) is a genus of small, delicate annual grasses known for their fine, thread-like appearance. These diminutive grasses typically grow in dense tufts and produce tiny, shimmering flower clusters that catch the light beautifully. They're often found in sandy soils, disturbed areas, and open grasslands throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hair grasses are distinguished from other small grasses by their extremely fine leaves and stems, plus their characteristic loose, open flower clusters (panicles) that appear almost cloud-like. Their seeds are also notably tiny and lack the bristles or awns found on many related grass species.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, hair grasses are remarkably hardy pioneers that can quickly colonize bare, sandy soil where few other plants can establish themselves.

children.name: Piptatheropsis
children.description: Piptatheropsis is a small genus of native perennial grasses commonly known as ricegrasses. These cool-season grasses are characterized by their delicate, open flower clusters and small, rice-like seeds that give them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ricegrasses can be distinguished from other grasses by their distinctive twisted, bent awns (bristle-like extensions) on their seeds and their loose, branching seed heads that often have a delicate, airy appearance.
children.funFact: The genus name Piptatheropsis comes from Greek words meaning 'falling grain-like,' referring to how the mature seeds readily drop from the plant to disperse and start new colonies.

children.name: Avena
children.description: Oats are annual grasses in the genus Avena that produce distinctive drooping flower clusters called panicles. These grasses have flat, narrow leaves and seeds that are typically enclosed in papery husks called hulls. The genus includes both wild species and the cultivated oat that has been an important food crop for thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Oats can be distinguished from other grasses by their loose, open flower clusters that hang downward and their relatively large seeds that dangle from delicate branches. Unlike wheat or barley, oat seeds typically remain tightly attached to their hulls even after ripening.
children.funFact: Wild oats have a remarkable adaptation called a hygroscopic awn - a twisted, bristle-like structure that literally screws the seed into the ground by coiling and uncoiling with changes in humidity.

children.name: Sphenopholis
children.description: Sphenopholis is a small genus of delicate native grasses commonly known as wedgescales or wedgegrasses. These slender perennial grasses are characterized by their distinctive seed heads with wedge-shaped scales that give the genus its common name. They typically grow in woodlands, prairies, and open areas throughout eastern North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wedgescales can be identified by their unique glumes (outer scales of the flower) that are distinctly unequal in size and shape, with the upper glume being much broader and more wedge-shaped than the lower one. This creates the characteristic wedge appearance that separates them from other native grass genera.
children.funFact: The genus name Sphenopholis literally means 'wedge scale' in Greek, directly referencing the distinctive wedge-shaped flower parts that make these grasses instantly recognizable to botanists.

children.name: Bouteloua
children.description: Gramas are hardy prairie grasses known for their distinctive seed heads that often curve to one side like tiny flags or brushes. These drought-tolerant grasses are typically found in open, sunny areas and are important components of grassland ecosystems. They're warm-season grasses that do most of their growing during the hot summer months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gramas can be identified by their characteristic flowering spikes that hang to one side of the stem, creating an asymmetrical appearance that's quite different from other grass families. The seed heads often look like small combs or brushes arranged along the stem.
children.funFact: Blue Grama grass is so tough and drought-resistant that it can survive on as little as 10 inches of rainfall per year, making it a champion of survival in some of North America's harshest grasslands.

children.name: Zoysia
children.description: Zoysia grasses are warm-season perennial grasses known for their dense, carpet-like growth and exceptional durability. These Asian natives spread through underground stems called rhizomes and above-ground runners called stolons, creating thick, resilient turf that can handle heavy foot traffic.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike cool-season grasses common in New England, Zoysia grasses go dormant and turn brown in winter, then green up late in spring. They have distinctive stiff, narrow leaves and form much denser mats than most other lawn grasses.
children.funFact: Zoysia grass is so tough that it was originally used on golf courses and athletic fields because it could withstand intense use while requiring less water and fertilizer than traditional lawn grasses.

children.name: Koeleria
children.description: Junegrasses are delicate perennial grasses that form small tufts or clumps in open, often sandy or rocky habitats. These grasses are characterized by their narrow, soft leaves and distinctive flower clusters that appear as dense, spike-like panicles in early summer. They're typically found in prairies, meadows, and disturbed areas where they can tolerate dry conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Junegrasses can be identified by their compact, cylindrical flower heads that are denser and more spike-like than most other native grasses. Their seed heads have a silvery or pale appearance and the individual flowers are quite small with prominent, often twisted bristles called awns.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting they bloom in June, junegrasses actually flower from late spring through mid-summer, and their seeds were traditionally collected by Native American tribes as a food source.

children.name: Phragmites
children.description: Phragmites is a genus of tall, perennial grasses that form dense colonies in wetland areas. These robust plants are characterized by their thick, bamboo-like stems and large, feathery seed heads that sway in the wind. They spread primarily through underground rhizomes, creating extensive stands along shorelines, marshes, and ditches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Phragmites stands out from other wetland grasses by its impressive height (often 6-15 feet tall), distinctive purplish-brown plume-like flower heads, and its ability to form nearly impenetrable monocultures. The stems are notably sturdy and hollow, more robust than most other marsh grasses.
children.funFact: Common reed has been used by humans for thousands of years to make everything from musical instruments and arrows to thatching material for roofs, and a single plant can live for over 100 years while spreading to cover several acres.

children.name: Dactylis
children.description: Dactylis is a small genus of perennial grasses commonly known as cocks-foot or orchard grasses. These are tall, clumping grasses that form dense tufts and are widely cultivated as forage crops for livestock. They're characterized by their distinctive flattened flower clusters that branch out like fingers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The flower heads have a unique clustered appearance where the spikelets are densely packed on one side of short branches, creating an irregular, lumpy look that's quite different from the more uniform seed heads of other common grasses.
children.funFact: Orchard grass got its common name because it was traditionally planted in orchards, where it could thrive in the partial shade between fruit trees while providing valuable hay for farm animals.

children.name: Schizachyrium
children.description: Little bluestems and allies are native bunch grasses that form clumps rather than spreading by runners. These warm-season grasses are known for their distinctive blue-green stems that often take on reddish or purplish tints, especially in fall and winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasses, Schizachyrium species have flattened, compressed stems and their seed heads consist of finger-like spikes that emerge from a single point, creating a distinctive branched appearance.
children.funFact: Little bluestem was once so abundant across the American prairies that it was called the 'prairie king' and could grow tall enough to hide a horse and rider.

children.name: Microstegium
children.description: Microstegium is a genus of small annual grasses known for their delicate, bamboo-like appearance and ability to spread rapidly in forest understories. These grasses are characterized by their thin, lance-shaped leaves and slender stems that often grow in dense mats across the forest floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Microstegium grasses can be distinguished from other small grasses by their asymmetrical leaf bases where the blade meets the stem, and their preference for shaded woodland environments rather than open sunny areas.
children.funFact: Japanese stiltgrass was accidentally introduced to the United States around 1919 when it was used as packing material for porcelain shipped from Asia, and it has since become one of the most problematic invasive grasses in eastern forests.

children.name: Andropogon
children.description: Bluestems are tall prairie grasses known for their distinctive blue-green stems and feathery seed heads. These warm-season grasses are important components of grassland ecosystems and were historically dominant across much of North America's Great Plains.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bluestems can be identified by their flattened, blue-tinged stems and their fluffy, often purplish seed heads that appear in late summer. Unlike cool-season grasses, they do most of their growing during the hottest parts of summer.
children.funFact: Big bluestem was once so abundant across the American prairie that it earned the nickname 'king of grasses' and could grow tall enough to hide a person on horseback.

children.name: Holcus
children.description: Holcus is a small genus of perennial grasses native to Europe and western Asia. These soft, tufted grasses are characterized by their velvety, grayish-green appearance and their ability to thrive in poor, acidic soils where other grasses struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Holcus grasses can be identified by their distinctively soft, fuzzy leaves and stems that feel almost woolly to the touch. Their seed heads are dense, pale clusters that appear silvery-white or pinkish when mature.
children.funFact: Despite its common name 'Yorkshire fog,' this grass has nothing to do with weather - the term 'fog' comes from an old English word meaning 'long grass left standing in fields after hay harvest.'

children.name: Sorghastrum
children.description: Indiangrasses are tall, graceful perennial grasses that form distinctive clumps in prairies and open areas. They are warm-season grasses, meaning they do most of their growing during the hottest months of summer when many other plants slow down.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These grasses are easily recognized by their distinctive bronze to golden-colored seed heads that appear in late summer and fall, creating feathery plumes that catch the light beautifully.
children.funFact: Indiangrass can grow up to 8 feet tall and has roots that extend down 12 feet or more, making it incredibly drought-tolerant and an important plant for preventing soil erosion.

children.name: Distichlis
children.description: Distichlis is a small genus of perennial grasses that are specially adapted to live in salty environments like salt marshes, coastal areas, and alkaline soils. These tough grasses have extensive underground root systems that help them spread and survive in harsh conditions where most other plants cannot grow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasses, Distichlis species are highly salt-tolerant and have separate male and female plants (dioecious). Their leaves are often rolled or folded, and they have a distinctive two-ranked leaf arrangement.
children.funFact: Saltgrass can actually remove salt from soil through its roots and excrete it through special glands on its leaves, making the surrounding area more hospitable for other plants over time.

children.name: Oryzopsis
children.description: Oryzopsis is a small genus of native perennial grasses commonly known as mountain ricegrasses. These hardy grasses are adapted to cooler climates and often grow in woodland areas or mountain slopes, producing small rice-like seeds that give them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mountain ricegrasses can be distinguished from other grasses by their distinctive plump, rice-like seeds and their preference for shaded or partially shaded forest environments rather than open grasslands.
children.funFact: The name 'Oryzopsis' literally means 'rice-like' in Greek, referring to the resemblance of their seeds to grains of rice.

children.name: Chasmanthium
children.description: Chasmanthium is a small genus of ornamental grasses native to North America. These perennials are known for their distinctive flattened seed heads that dangle gracefully from arching stems, creating an attractive drooping effect that persists well into winter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasses with round or oval seed heads, Chasmanthium produces uniquely flattened, drooping clusters of seeds that look almost like dangling ornaments. The seed heads are compressed from side to side, giving them a distinctive flat, oval appearance.
children.funFact: The flattened seed heads of river oats are so ornamental that they're prized by florists for dried flower arrangements and can remain attractive on the plant for months after the growing season ends.

children.name: Tridens
children.description: Tridens is a small genus of perennial grasses native to North America. These grasses are characterized by their distinctive three-toothed flower structures, which give the genus its name meaning 'three teeth.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tridens grasses can be identified by their unique seed heads where each floret has three prominent teeth or awns at the tip, distinguishing them from other native grass genera.
children.funFact: The genus name Tridens literally means 'three teeth' in Latin, directly referring to the three-pronged appearance of their seed structures.

children.name: Avenella
children.description: Avenella is a small genus of perennial grasses that includes the distinctive wavy hair-grass. These grasses are characterized by their delicate, fine-textured appearance and their ability to thrive in acidic, nutrient-poor soils where many other plants struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Avenella grasses are distinguished from related oat grasses by their particularly fine, hair-like leaves and their preference for very acidic conditions. The wavy, curled appearance of their leaf blades gives them their common name and helps separate them from similar-looking grasses.
children.funFact: Wavy hair-grass is so tolerant of acidic conditions that it can grow in soils with pH levels as low as 3.5, making it one of the few grasses that can colonize extremely acidic sites like abandoned mines or areas affected by acid rain.

children.name: Eleusine
children.description: Eleusine is a small genus of annual grasses that are found in warm regions around the world. These grasses are characterized by their distinctive flattened flower clusters that spread out like fingers from the top of the stem, giving them a very recognizable appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasses, Eleusine species have their seed heads arranged in distinctive finger-like spikes that radiate from a central point at the stem tip, rather than forming feathery or cylindrical clusters.
children.funFact: Goose Grass gets its name because geese and other waterfowl eagerly eat its nutritious seeds, and the plant often grows in areas where these birds gather.

children.name: Triticum
children.description: Wheats are annual grasses that have been cultivated by humans for thousands of years as one of our most important food crops. These plants produce dense clusters of seeds (grains) arranged in characteristic spike-like flower heads that contain the wheat we use to make bread, pasta, and countless other foods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wheat can be distinguished from other grasses by its distinctive rectangular seeds that remain tightly attached to tough, papery husks called glumes, and its dense, compact flower spikes that don't branch like many other cereal grasses.
children.funFact: Modern bread wheat is actually a hybrid of three different ancient grass species, making it hexaploid with six sets of chromosomes - twice as many chromosome sets as humans have!

children.name: Tripsacum
children.description: Tripsacum is a genus of tall, robust grasses native to the Americas. These perennial grasses are closely related to corn and teosinte, sharing similar genetic characteristics that make them important in agricultural research.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tripsacum grasses have distinctive seed heads with separate male and female flowers arranged in rows, and their sturdy stems can grow much taller than typical prairie grasses, often reaching 6-8 feet in height.
children.funFact: Eastern gamagrass is sometimes called "corn's wild cousin" because it can actually hybridize with corn, making it valuable for developing new crop varieties with improved drought tolerance.

children.name: Zea
children.description: Corns and teosintes are large annual grasses in the genus Zea, best known for including maize (corn). These plants are characterized by their tall, sturdy stems and broad leaves, with distinctive separate male and female flower clusters on the same plant. While wild teosintes are native to Central America, domesticated corn is now grown worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grasses, Zea species have dramatically separated male flowers (tassels at the top) and female flowers (silk-covered ears along the stem). The seeds are also much larger than typical grass seeds and are arranged in tight rows on a thick central cob.
children.funFact: Corn looks so different from its wild ancestor teosinte that scientists debated for decades whether they were even related - teosinte has tiny triangular seeds and looks more like a typical wild grass than the massive ears of corn we know today.

children.name: Patis
children.description: Patis is a small genus of native grasses that includes just one species found in New England's mountainous regions. These perennial grasses are specially adapted to grow in rocky, high-elevation habitats where many other plants struggle to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Black-fruit mountain-ricegrass can be identified by its distinctive dark-colored seeds and its preference for growing in rocky crevices and steep slopes at higher elevations.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'mountain-ricegrass,' this plant is not actually related to true rice but gets its name from its small, grain-like seeds that were historically used as food by Indigenous peoples.

children.name: Brachyelytrum
children.description: Shorthusks are a small genus of woodland grasses that grow in shaded forest environments. They are characterized by their short, bristle-like seed coverings (called husks) that give them their common name. These delicate grasses typically form small clumps and prefer moist, rich soils under the forest canopy.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasses that thrive in open, sunny areas, shorthusks are specifically adapted to low-light forest conditions. Their seed husks are notably shorter and more bristly compared to other woodland grasses, and their leaves are typically broader than those of sun-loving grass species.
children.funFact: Northern Shorthusk is one of the few grasses that can successfully reproduce and thrive in deep forest shade, making it a unique member of the grass family that has carved out a specialized ecological niche.

children.name: Greeneochloa
children.description: Greeneochloa is a small genus of perennial grasses that are closely related to reedgrasses. These grasses typically grow in wetland habitats and have narrow, elongated flower clusters called panicles. In New England, this genus is represented by only one species, Nuttall's Reedgrass.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Greeneochloa differs from other reedgrasses by having more compact, contracted flower clusters and distinctive seed characteristics. The panicles are notably narrow and dense compared to the more open, spreading clusters of most related grasses.
children.funFact: This genus was named relatively recently in botanical history and contains only a few species worldwide, making it one of the smaller grass genera in North America.

children.name: Milium
children.description: Milium is a small genus of cool-season grasses known for their delicate, open flower clusters and shade tolerance. These perennial grasses typically grow in woodland environments and produce small, shiny seeds that are an important food source for birds and small mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasses that prefer sunny locations, Milium species are specially adapted to thrive in shaded forest understories. They can be identified by their loose, airy panicles of tiny flowers and their ability to grow well under tree canopies where other grasses struggle.
children.funFact: Wood Millet can photosynthesize efficiently in light levels as low as 1% of full sunlight, making it one of the most shade-tolerant grasses in North American forests.

children.name: Piptochaetium
children.description: Needlegrasses are a genus of perennial grasses known for their distinctive seed heads with long, needle-like projections called awns. These grasses typically grow in clumps and produce seeds with sharp, twisted awns that help them disperse and drill into the soil for germination.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other grasses, needlegrasses have seeds with prominent, twisted awns that can be several inches long, giving them their characteristic needle-like appearance.
children.funFact: The twisted awns of needlegrass seeds actually move like tiny screws when they get wet and dry, literally drilling the seeds into the ground for better germination success.

children.name: Arrhenatherum
children.description: Arrhenatherum is a small genus of tall perennial grasses in the oat family. These grasses are characterized by their impressive height, often reaching 3-5 feet tall, and their loose, open flower clusters that sway gracefully in the wind.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arrhenatherum can be distinguished from other oat grasses by its distinctive swollen, bulb-like stem bases and its tall stature. The spikelets also have a characteristic bent awn (bristle-like appendage) that helps identify the genus.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'oat grass,' Arrhenatherum elatius is not related to cultivated oats and was originally introduced from Europe as a forage grass for livestock.

children.name: Briza
children.description: Rattlesnake grasses are delicate ornamental grasses known for their distinctive seed heads that dangle and shake in the slightest breeze. These European natives have heart-shaped or oval seed clusters that hang from thin, flexible stems, creating a graceful nodding appearance. They are cool-season grasses that prefer moist, fertile soils and partial shade.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The hanging, heart-shaped seed heads that tremble and rattle in the wind are unique among New England grasses, giving them their common name of 'quaking grass.'
children.funFact: The seed heads make a gentle rattling sound when shaken, which historically led people to believe they could ward off snakes - hence the name 'rattlesnake grass.'

children.name: Schizachne
children.description: Schizachne is a small genus of native grasses found in cool, northern regions. These perennial grasses are characterized by their delicate, open flower clusters and preference for shady woodland environments. In New England, this genus is represented by just one species, the purple oat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other grasses, Schizachne species have distinctive drooping flower clusters with relatively large, loose spikelets that give them an almost oat-like appearance. Their preference for forest understory habitats also sets them apart from most other native grasses.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'purple oat,' Schizachne purpurascens is not related to true oats at all - it just happens to have similar-looking drooping seed heads that reminded early botanists of oat plants.

children.name: Secale
children.description: Secale is a small genus of annual grasses in the wheat family that includes rye and its wild relatives. These hardy grasses are characterized by their tall stems, narrow leaves, and distinctive spike-like flower clusters that produce the familiar rye grain.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rye can be distinguished from wheat and barley by its longer, more slender seed spikes and its exceptional ability to grow in poor soils and harsh climates where other cereal grains struggle.
children.funFact: Rye is so cold-hardy that it can survive winters that would kill wheat, making it historically crucial for survival in northern European countries where it became known as 'the grain of the poor' due to its reliability in difficult growing conditions.

children.name: Kellochloa
children.description: Kellochloa is a small genus of grasses that includes just a few species worldwide. These are annual grasses that typically grow in disturbed soils and open areas. In New England, this genus is represented by a single species known as warty panic grass.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kellochloa grasses are distinguished from other panic grasses by their distinctive warty or bumpy seed surfaces, which give them their common name. They also have characteristic branching patterns in their flower clusters.
children.funFact: The warty panic grass was only recently recognized as belonging to its own genus Kellochloa, having previously been classified with other panic grasses in the genus Panicum.

children.name: Deschampsia
children.description: Hair grass is a genus of delicate perennial grasses known for their fine, hair-like leaves and airy, feathery flower clusters. These cool-season grasses typically form dense tufts or clumps and prefer moist, acidic soils in cooler climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hair grasses are distinguished from other grasses by their extremely fine, thread-like leaves and their distinctive open, cloud-like seed heads that shimmer and sway gracefully in the breeze.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Deschampsia' honors French botanist Louis Auguste Deschamps, who collected plants during Captain Nicolas Baudin's expedition to Australia in the early 1800s.

children.name: Torreyochloa
children.description: Torreyochloa is a small genus of aquatic grasses that grow in shallow water and wetland areas. These perennial grasses are adapted to life in and around water, with hollow stems and narrow leaves that help them thrive in marshy conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other wetland grasses, Torreyochloa species have distinctively compressed flower clusters and specialized floating abilities that allow them to colonize deeper water areas than most grasses can tolerate.
children.funFact: This genus was named after American botanist John Torrey, and despite being native to North America, it's so rare that pale false mannagrass is considered endangered or critically imperiled in most states where it occurs.

children.name: Triplasis
children.description: Triplasis is a small genus of native grasses that includes just a few species found in sandy, coastal areas of North America. These grasses are specially adapted to grow in harsh, nutrient-poor sandy soils where many other plants cannot survive. They play an important role in stabilizing sand dunes and coastal environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Triplasis grasses have distinctive three-awned spikelets (the awn is a bristle-like appendage on the seed) and produce small, purplish flower clusters. They are much smaller and more delicate than most other coastal grasses, typically growing only 1-3 feet tall.
children.funFact: Purple Sandgrass gets its name from its beautiful purple-tinged flower heads that appear in late summer, creating subtle splashes of color across otherwise barren sandy landscapes.

children.name: Pseudosasa
children.description: Arrow Bamboos are a genus of running bamboos native to East Asia, particularly Japan and Korea. These are medium-sized bamboos that spread by underground stems called rhizomes, forming dense colonies over time. They are characterized by their straight, hollow stems and relatively broad leaves compared to many other bamboo species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arrow Bamboos can be distinguished from other bamboo genera by their combination of running growth habit, relatively few branches per node on the stem, and distinctively broad, lance-shaped leaves that are typically 6-12 inches long.
children.funFact: The name 'Arrow Bamboo' comes from the traditional use of their straight, strong stems to make arrows in Japan, where they were prized by samurai for their consistency and durability.

children.name: Amphicarpum
children.description: Amphicarpum is a small genus of grasses known for their unique reproductive strategy of producing two different types of seeds. These grasses are found in sandy, acidic soils and wetland edges throughout eastern North America. The genus gets its name from the Greek words meaning 'both' and 'fruit,' referring to this distinctive dual seed production.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most grasses that produce only one type of seed, Amphicarpum species create both above-ground seeds that can disperse in the wind and below-ground seeds that remain buried in the soil.
children.funFact: Peanutgrass produces its underground seeds on special stems that actually grow down into the soil, similar to how peanuts develop their pods below ground.

children.name: Chloris
children.description: Windmill grasses are warm-season grasses named for their distinctive flower clusters that radiate outward like the spokes of a windmill. These grasses typically have multiple finger-like seed heads arranged in a whorl at the top of the stem, creating their characteristic windmill appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other grasses, windmill grasses have their seed spikes arranged in a distinctive circular pattern at the stem tip, resembling windmill blades. The spikes radiate outward from a central point rather than being arranged along the stem.
children.funFact: Tumble windmillgrass gets its name because the entire plant can break off at the base when mature and tumble across the landscape like a tumbleweed, dispersing its seeds as it rolls.

children.name: Thinopyrum
children.description: Thinopyrum is a genus of perennial grasses that are closely related to wheat and other cereal grains. These hardy grasses are known for their ability to grow in challenging environments like sandy soils and coastal areas. They form dense clumps or colonies through underground rhizomes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thinopyrum grasses can be distinguished from related wheat grasses by their thick, rigid stems and their ability to spread aggressively through underground runners. Their seed heads are typically more compact and dense than those of similar grass species.
children.funFact: Some Thinopyrum species have been used by plant breeders to develop salt-tolerant wheat varieties by crossing them with domestic wheat crops.

children.name: Coix
children.description: Coix is a small genus of tropical grasses known for their distinctive hard, bead-like seeds that have been used for thousands of years in jewelry and decoration. These tall annual grasses produce unique seed structures that look like polished beads or tears, which is how they got their common name Job's Tears.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other grasses, Coix species produce their seeds enclosed in a hard, glossy, bead-like covering called a utricle that becomes extremely durable when dried. This gives the seeds their characteristic smooth, rounded appearance that sets them apart from typical grass seeds.
children.funFact: Job's Tears seeds are so durable and naturally perforated that they've been used as beads in jewelry and rosaries for over 4,000 years, and are still harvested today for craft purposes around the world.

children.name: Cynodon
children.description: Bermuda grasses are a small genus of warm-season perennial grasses known for their exceptional drought tolerance and ability to spread rapidly through both underground rhizomes and above-ground stolons. These tough, low-growing grasses form dense mats and are famous for their use in lawns, golf courses, and athletic fields in warmer climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bermuda grasses can be identified by their distinctive finger-like seed heads that radiate from a central point, typically in groups of 3-7 spikes. Unlike many other grasses, they spread aggressively through both underground and surface runners, creating thick, interwoven mats.
children.funFact: Despite its name, Bermuda grass likely originated in Africa and has become so successful worldwide that it's considered both a valuable turf grass and a persistent weed, earning the nickname 'devil's grass' in some regions.

children.name: Apera
children.description: Apera is a small genus of annual grasses native to Europe and Asia, with only one species found in New England. These delicate grasses are characterized by their fine, silky appearance and loose, open flower clusters that give them an airy, graceful look.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Apera grasses can be distinguished from other bent grasses by their very fine, thread-like leaves and their distinctively loose, spreading flower panicles that often have a silvery or purplish tint.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'silky-bent,' Dense Silky-bent actually has a very open, sparse appearance - its name refers to the silky texture of its delicate flower clusters rather than any dense growth habit.

children.name: Puccinellia
children.description: Salt grass is a genus of hardy grasses that specialize in growing in salty, alkaline soils where most other plants can't survive. These tough grasses are commonly found in salt marshes, along coastlines, and in other areas with high salt content in the soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Salt grasses are distinguished from other grasses by their exceptional salt tolerance and their ability to thrive in alkaline conditions that would kill most vegetation. They typically have dense, low-growing forms that help them withstand harsh coastal conditions.
children.funFact: Salt grasses have special salt glands that allow them to excrete excess salt through their leaves, making them natural desalinators that can literally taste salty to the touch!

children.name: Bambusa
children.description: Bambusa is a genus of large, woody bamboos known for their thick, sturdy stems called culms and their ability to grow extremely quickly. These bamboos typically form dense clumps rather than spreading widely, and they're characterized by their segmented stems with distinct nodes and internodes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bamboo genera, Bambusa species are clumping bamboos that grow in tight clusters rather than running bamboos that spread aggressively through underground rhizomes. They also tend to have thicker, more robust culms compared to many temperate bamboo species.
children.funFact: Some Bambusa species can grow up to 4 feet in a single day, making them among the fastest-growing plants on Earth!

children.name: Arthraxon
children.description: Arthraxon is a genus of small, delicate grasses that typically form low-growing mats or carpets across the ground. These grasses are characterized by their short stature and spreading growth habit, often creating dense patches in suitable habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arthraxon grasses are distinguished from other grass genera by their very small size, heart-shaped leaf bases that clasp the stem, and their tendency to root at the nodes where stems touch the ground.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'small carpetgrass,' Arthraxon hispidus is actually an invasive species from Asia that can quickly spread to form thick mats that crowd out native plants.

children.name: Corynephorus
children.description: Corynephorus is a small genus of delicate grasses known for their distinctive club-shaped awns (bristle-like appendages) on their seeds. These grasses are typically found in sandy, well-drained soils and are adapted to harsh, nutrient-poor environments where few other plants can thrive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The genus is easily recognized by its characteristic awns that are swollen at the tip like tiny clubs, giving them their common name 'hairgrass.' The plants form small tufts with narrow, often grayish leaves.
children.funFact: Gray Hairgrass is considered quite rare in New England, having likely been introduced from Europe and found mainly in coastal sandy areas where it helps stabilize dunes.

children.name: Diplachne
children.description: Diplachne is a genus of grasses commonly known as sprangletops, characterized by their tall, upright growth and distinctive flowering heads. These grasses typically have narrow leaves and produce clusters of small flowers arranged in branching, open panicles that give them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sprangletops can be distinguished from other grasses by their loose, spreading flower clusters and their preference for wet, marshy habitats where they often form dense stands.
children.funFact: The name 'sprangletop' comes from the way their delicate flower clusters appear to sparkle or 'sprangle' in the sunlight, creating a shimmering effect across wetland meadows.

children.description: Grasses are one of the most successful and widespread plant families on Earth, characterized by their narrow leaves with parallel veins and hollow, jointed stems called culms. They produce tiny flowers arranged in dense clusters called spikelets, which lack showy petals but are perfectly adapted for wind pollination. This diverse family includes everything from your backyard lawn to towering bamboos, and even our most important food crops like wheat, corn, and rice.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grasses can be distinguished from other plants by their unique combination of narrow leaves that wrap around hollow, segmented stems at nodes, and their distinctive flower clusters (spikelets) that contain small, inconspicuous flowers protected by specialized bracts called glumes.
children.funFact: Grasses literally shaped human civilization - nearly 70% of the world's food calories come from just three grass species: wheat, rice, and corn!

children.name: Juncaceae
Juncus
children.description: Rushes are grass-like plants that thrive in wet places like marshes, pond edges, and ditches throughout New England. They have narrow, cylindrical or flattened leaves and produce small, inconspicuous brown or green flowers clustered together. These hardy plants are perfectly adapted to life in soggy soils where many other plants can't survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike sedges which have triangular stems, rushes have round stems that are often hollow. Their flowers are also much smaller and less showy than those of grasses, appearing as tiny brown capsules arranged in dense clusters.
children.funFact: Some rush species like Soft Rush were traditionally used by Native Americans and early settlers to weave baskets and mats, and the pith from inside the stems was used as wicks for candles and oil lamps.

children.name: Luzula
children.description: Woodrushes are grass-like plants that belong to the rush family, thriving in cooler climates and often found in woodlands, meadows, and alpine areas. Unlike true grasses, they have small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in clusters and produce tiny seeds with distinctive white, thread-like appendages. These hardy perennials are well-adapted to acidic soils and can tolerate shade better than many similar-looking plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Woodrushes can be distinguished from true grasses by their three-petaled flowers and from other rushes by their flat, hairy leaves with distinct parallel veins. Their seeds have characteristic white, cottony tufts that help with wind dispersal.
children.funFact: The name 'woodrush' comes from their preference for woodland habitats, and their seeds' fluffy white appendages were once used as makeshift cotton for stuffing pillows and mattresses in some rural areas.

children.name: Oreojuncus
children.description: Oreojuncus is a small genus of rush plants that are specially adapted to life in cold, mountainous environments. These hardy perennial plants grow in dense cushions or mats, helping them survive harsh alpine conditions with strong winds and extreme temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other rushes, Oreojuncus species have distinctively three-parted (trifid) leaves and form tight, cushion-like growth patterns rather than growing as individual upright stems.
children.funFact: Highland rush can survive in some of the most extreme environments in New England, growing on exposed mountain summits where temperatures can drop well below freezing even in summer.

children.description: Rushes and allies are grass-like plants that typically grow in wet or marshy areas throughout New England. These hardy perennials have narrow, often cylindrical leaves and produce small, inconspicuous flowers clustered together in dense groups. Unlike true grasses, they have six-petaled flowers and round or triangular stems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rush family plants can be distinguished from grasses by their six tiny petals (grass flowers lack petals) and their solid, often round stems rather than the hollow, flat stems of most grasses. Many rushes also have a distinctive "pith" or spongy interior when you break open their stems.
children.funFact: Some rush species were historically used to make rush lights - a primitive form of candle where the pith was soaked in fat and burned for illumination in colonial homes.

children.name: Typhaceae
Sparganium
children.description: Bur-reeds are aquatic plants that grow in shallow waters of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They get their name from their distinctive round, spiky seed heads that look like medieval weapons called burs or maces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, bur-reeds have separate spherical clusters of male and female flowers on the same plant, with the prickly female flower heads developing into the characteristic spiky seed balls.
children.funFact: Bur-reed seeds can remain viable for decades in pond sediments, allowing them to sprout and colonize new areas when water levels change or sediments are disturbed.

children.name: Typha
children.description: Cattails are tall wetland plants instantly recognizable by their distinctive brown, sausage-shaped flower spikes that sit atop long, straight stems. These aquatic perennials have long, narrow leaves that grow directly from the base and can reach heights of 6-10 feet. They form dense colonies in marshes, pond edges, and other wet areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wetland grasses and sedges, cattails produce the characteristic dense, cylindrical brown seed heads (called catkins) that look like corn dogs on a stick. Their leaves are also much wider and flatter than most other marsh plants.
children.funFact: A single cattail seed head contains over 100,000 tiny seeds, each equipped with fluffy white hairs that help them float on the wind for miles to colonize new wetlands.

children.description: The Typhaceae family includes wetland plants that are masters of aquatic living, with long, narrow leaves and distinctive flower clusters. These plants are commonly found growing in marshes, pond edges, and wet ditches throughout New England, where their roots help stabilize shorelines and their dense growth provides important habitat for wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are easily recognized by their unique flower arrangements - cattails have their famous brown, sausage-like spikes, while bur-reeds produce round, spiky ball-shaped flower clusters. Unlike most flowering plants, their tiny flowers lack petals and are packed densely together in these specialized structures.
children.funFact: A single cattail seed head can contain over 200,000 seeds, each equipped with fluffy white hairs that help them float on the wind for miles before settling in a new wetland home.

children.name: Xyridaceae
Xyris
children.description: Yellow-eyed grasses are small wetland plants that produce cheerful yellow flowers on tall, slender stems rising above grass-like leaves. Despite their common name, they're not true grasses but belong to their own plant family, typically growing in bogs, wet sandy areas, and acidic soils throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants are easily recognized by their distinctive bright yellow flowers that bloom one at a time from brown, cone-like flower heads, combined with their narrow, iris-like leaves that grow in tufts at the base of the plant.
children.funFact: Each yellow-eyed grass flower opens for just one day, typically in the morning, and by afternoon the petals have already fallen off, making timing crucial for flower photographers!

children.description: Yellow-eyed grasses are small wetland plants that look like grasses but aren't actually grasses at all. They grow in acidic, nutrient-poor soils like bogs, pond edges, and wet sandy areas. Despite their grass-like appearance with narrow leaves, they produce distinctive small yellow flowers that bloom from compact, cone-like heads.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, yellow-eyed grasses have three-petaled yellow flowers that emerge from dense, scaly flower heads. Their leaves are also flatter and more twisted than typical grass blades.
children.funFact: Yellow-eyed grasses are considered living indicators of healthy wetland ecosystems - they only thrive in very clean, acidic water with low nutrients, so finding them often means you've discovered a pristine bog or marsh.

children.name: Eriocaulaceae
Eriocaulon
children.description: Pipeworts are small aquatic or semi-aquatic plants that produce distinctive white, button-like flower heads on long, slender stems. These plants typically grow in shallow water or wet sandy soils, forming dense colonies in bogs, pond edges, and other wetland habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pipeworts are easily recognized by their tiny white flowers packed into dense, round heads that look like small buttons or pinheads sitting atop thin, leafless stems. Their narrow, grass-like leaves grow in a basal rosette directly from the base of the plant.
children.funFact: The name 'pipewort' comes from the hollow stems that were historically used as pipe cleaners and lamp wicks by early settlers.

children.description: Pipeworts are small aquatic or wetland plants that form distinctive button-like flower heads on slender stalks. These unique plants typically grow in shallow water, wet sand, or boggy areas, sending up their characteristic cylindrical flower clusters above grass-like leaves. They're specialized for life in nutrient-poor, acidic wetland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The compact, dense flower heads that look like tiny white or gray buttons on thin stems are unmistakable. Unlike grasses or sedges that might share their habitat, pipeworts have their tiny flowers packed tightly into these rounded, pipe-cleaner-like clusters.
children.funFact: Despite their simple appearance, pipewort flower heads are actually complex structures containing hundreds of tiny individual flowers, each no bigger than a pinhead!

children.description: This diverse order includes some of our most common and important plants - from the grasses in your lawn to the cattails in wetlands. These plants are mostly herbaceous (non-woody) and typically have narrow, blade-like leaves with parallel veins. Many members of this group are wind-pollinated and produce small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in dense clusters or spikes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants that have broad leaves with branching vein patterns, members of Poales typically have narrow leaves with parallel veins running from base to tip. Their flowers are usually small and lack showy petals, instead relying on wind rather than insects for pollination.
children.funFact: Grasses from this order feed more people worldwide than any other plant family - including rice, wheat, corn, oats, and barley that form the foundation of human agriculture.

children.name: Asparagales
Orchidaceae
Platanthera
children.description: Bog orchids are a diverse group of native orchids that typically grow in wet, boggy areas and moist woodlands throughout New England. These elegant wildflowers are known for their distinctive spurred flowers that come in shades of white, green, purple, and orange, often arranged in tall, showy spikes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other orchid groups, bog orchids have a prominent spur extending from the back of each flower, which serves as a nectar repository for pollinators. Their flowers are typically small to medium-sized and arranged in dense, elongated clusters rather than appearing as single large blooms.
children.funFact: Many bog orchids are pollinated by specific moths and butterflies that have tongues long enough to reach the nectar stored deep within the flower's spur, creating specialized partnerships between plant and pollinator.

children.name: Spiranthes
children.description: Ladies'-tresses are delicate native orchids that produce small white, cream, or yellow flowers arranged in distinctive spiral patterns around tall, slender stems. These graceful wildflowers typically bloom from late summer through fall, growing in a variety of habitats from wetlands and meadows to dry woodlands and roadside ditches.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The characteristic twisted or spiraling arrangement of tiny tubular flowers around the stem makes ladies'-tresses easily recognizable among New England's orchids. Their flowers are much smaller and more numerous than most other native orchids, creating dense, spiraled flower spikes.
children.funFact: The name 'ladies'-tresses' comes from the flowers' resemblance to braided or twisted hair, and some species can actually change the direction of their spiral from year to year on the same plant!

children.name: Cypripedium
children.description: Hardy slipper orchids are a group of wild orchids famous for their distinctive pouch-shaped flowers that resemble tiny slippers or moccasins. These native New England wildflowers grow slowly in woodland habitats and can live for decades, producing their showy blooms in late spring and early summer. Unlike many orchids that grow in tropical climates, these species are adapted to survive harsh New England winters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The inflated, slipper-like lip petal (called a labellum) sets them apart from all other orchids, creating a trap that forces visiting insects to crawl past the reproductive parts. Most also have distinctively pleated or ribbed leaves that emerge directly from the ground.
children.funFact: Lady's slipper orchids can take up to 16 years to bloom for the first time, making them some of the slowest-maturing wildflowers in New England forests.

children.name: Goodyera
children.description: Rattlesnake plantains are small, ground-dwelling orchids known for their distinctive leaves that feature white or silver veining patterns reminiscent of snakeskin. These woodland orchids grow close to the forest floor and produce delicate spikes of small white flowers during summer months. Despite their name, they are not related to plantains at all, but are true members of the orchid family.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orchids, rattlesnake plantains are easily recognized by their basal rosette of evergreen leaves with prominent white or silver netted veining patterns. They also tend to grow in colonies through underground rhizomes, creating patches of these distinctive patterned leaves on the forest floor.
children.funFact: The intricate white veining on their leaves is actually caused by air spaces between leaf cells that reflect light, creating the striking snake-like patterns that give these orchids their common name.

children.name: Neottia
