children.description: Neottia is a genus of small, delicate orchids commonly known as twayblades. These woodland orchids are characterized by having just two broad leaves at the base of their stem and tiny, inconspicuous flowers arranged in a slender spike.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Twayblades are easily recognized by their signature pair of opposite leaves positioned partway up the stem, which gives them their common name. Their flowers are much smaller and less showy than most other orchids, often appearing greenish or yellowish-brown.
children.funFact: Despite being orchids, twayblades are often overlooked by hikers because their flowers are so small and subdued in color that they blend perfectly into the forest floor.

children.name: Corallorhiza
children.description: Coralroots are unusual orchids that have given up the typical plant lifestyle of making their own food through photosynthesis. Instead, they live as parasites, getting all their nutrients from fungi in the soil, which is why they appear as leafless, often colorless stems rising directly from the ground. These mysterious orchids emerge from underground coral-like root masses that give them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orchids and other plants, coralroots completely lack green leaves and cannot photosynthesize. They appear as simple, unbranched stems with small flowers arranged along the top portion.
children.funFact: Because they don't need sunlight to survive, coralroots can grow in the deep shade of dense forests where most other flowering plants cannot thrive.

children.name: Malaxis
children.description: Adder's mouth orchids are small, delicate wildflowers that belong to the orchid family. These tiny plants typically grow 4-8 inches tall and produce clusters of minute greenish or white flowers that are easy to overlook. They prefer moist, shaded habitats like boggy areas, wet woods, and moss-covered logs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike showier orchids, adder's mouth species have extremely small flowers (often less than 1/8 inch across) arranged in slender spikes. Their flowers lack the prominent lip petal typical of most orchids, instead having a simple, tongue-like projection.
children.funFact: These orchids get their common name from their single leaf (in some species) that resembles a snake's tongue, and their tiny flowers were thought to look like a serpent's open mouth.

children.name: Galearis
children.description: Galearis is a small genus of terrestrial orchids that grow from underground bulbs and produce distinctive hooded flowers. These orchids are found in cooler climates and typically bloom in spring or early summer, with flowers arranged in compact clusters above broad leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Galearis are characterized by their helmet-like or hooded upper petals that form a distinctive shape over the flower's reproductive parts. Unlike many other orchids, they have relatively few, broad leaves that are often arranged near the base of the plant.
children.funFact: The name Galearis comes from the Latin word 'galea' meaning helmet, referring to the distinctive hooded shape of the flowers that resembles a medieval knight's helmet.

children.name: Isotria
children.description: Whorled Pogonias are rare and distinctive orchids that grow in forest environments. They are characterized by their leaves arranged in a circular pattern (whorl) around the stem, creating a unique umbrella-like appearance. Both species in this genus are uncommon woodland orchids that can be difficult to spot in their natural habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orchids, Whorled Pogonias have their leaves arranged in a single whorl around the stem rather than alternately along it. This distinctive leaf arrangement, combined with their woodland habitat, sets them apart from other New England orchids.
children.funFact: The Small Whorled Pogonia is so rare that it's listed as federally threatened, and some populations can remain dormant underground for years before emerging again.

children.name: Liparis
children.description: Widelip orchids are a small genus of delicate terrestrial orchids known for their distinctive wide, translucent lip petals that give them their common name. These small orchids typically grow in wet, boggy areas and have just two broad leaves at the base of their flowering stems. They produce small clusters of greenish or purplish flowers that bloom in summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other orchids, widelip orchids have very broad, flat lip petals that are often translucent or waxy in appearance, and their flowers lack the prominent column structure typical of showier orchid species.
children.funFact: The fen orchid is considered one of New England's rarest orchids and is listed as endangered or threatened in several states due to habitat loss from wetland development.

children.name: Epipactis
children.description: Helleborines are terrestrial orchids with broad, ribbed leaves and tall spikes of greenish or purplish flowers. These hardy orchids often grow in shaded woodlands and can form colonies through underground rhizomes. They are part of the orchid family but look quite different from the showy tropical orchids most people know.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other orchids, helleborines have wide, prominently veined leaves that look almost like those of lily-of-the-valley, and their flowers are relatively small and arranged in a loose spike rather than being large and showy.
children.funFact: The broad-leaved helleborine is actually native to Europe and Asia but has become so well-established in North American forests that many people assume it's a native wildflower.

children.name: Pogonia
children.description: Pogonia is a small genus of terrestrial orchids known for their delicate, fragrant pink flowers. These orchids typically grow in boggy, acidic wetlands and produce a single flower atop a slender stem with just one or two leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other orchids, Pogonia species have a distinctive bearded lip petal covered in yellow bristles or hairs, which gives them their common name of 'bearded orchids.'
children.funFact: The Rose Pogonia's sweet fragrance is strongest in the morning and is designed to attract small bees and flies as pollinators in its wetland habitat.

children.name: Calopogon
children.description: Grasspinks are a small genus of terrestrial orchids that grow from underground tubers in acidic, boggy habitats. These delicate wildflowers are known for their distinctive pink to magenta blooms that appear on slender stems rising from grass-like leaves. They typically bloom in early summer and can form small colonies in suitable wetland conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orchids, grasspinks have their lip (labellum) positioned at the top of the flower rather than the bottom, and their column is topped with a brush-like tuft of yellow hairs. The flowers also appear to be 'upside-down' compared to typical orchid orientation.
children.funFact: Grasspink flowers use deceptive pollination - they offer no nectar reward but trick bees into visiting by mimicking other flowers that do provide nectar, with the bee getting dusted with pollen as it searches unsuccessfully for a meal.

children.name: Arethusa
children.description: Dragon's mouths are a small genus of terrestrial orchids known for their dramatic, solitary flowers that emerge from boggy wetlands in late spring and early summer. These plants grow from underground bulbs and produce a single leaf that appears after the flower blooms, making them unique among New England's native orchids.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bog orchids, dragon's mouths produce their showy pink-purple flower before the leaf emerges, and the flower has a distinctive fringed lip that resembles an open mouth with teeth.
children.funFact: The dragon's mouth orchid was named after Arethusa, a Greek nymph who was transformed into a spring to escape unwanted attention, fitting since these orchids emerge from wet, spring-fed bogs.

children.name: Triphora
children.description: Noddingcaps are tiny, delicate orchids that get their name from their drooping flower buds that nod downward like little caps. These small terrestrial orchids are among the most inconspicuous members of the orchid family, often growing only 2-8 inches tall in shady forest floors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orchids, Noddingcaps have their flowers pointing downward and often remain partially closed, making them easily overlooked. They also lack green leaves during flowering, instead having small scale-like structures along their stem.
children.funFact: Noddingcaps are saprophytic orchids that get their nutrients from decaying organic matter in the soil through a partnership with fungi, allowing them to survive without photosynthesis during their flowering period.

children.name: Tipularia
children.description: Crane-fly orchids are a small genus of terrestrial orchids that get their name from their delicate, spider-like flowers that resemble crane flies in flight. These woodland orchids are unusual because they produce a single leaf in fall that persists through winter, then dies back before the flowering stem emerges in summer. They grow from underground corms and prefer shaded forest floors with rich, well-drained soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most orchids, crane-fly orchids have a distinctive seasonal cycle where the leaf and flower appear at completely different times of year. Their flowers lack spurs and have a characteristic greenish-purple coloration that sets them apart from other native orchids.
children.funFact: The single leaf of a crane-fly orchid is purple underneath, which may help it absorb more light during the dim winter months when the forest canopy is bare.

children.name: Dactylorhiza
children.description: Marsh orchids are a group of terrestrial orchids that typically grow in wet meadows, bogs, and other moist habitats. These orchids are known for their distinctive hand-shaped underground tubers and colorful flower spikes that bloom in summer. Most species in this genus prefer cool, northern climates and alkaline soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Marsh orchids can be distinguished from other orchids by their deeply divided, finger-like leaves and their preference for consistently moist, open habitats rather than forests. Their flowers are arranged in dense, cylindrical spikes and often have spotted or streaked petals.
children.funFact: The genus name Dactylorhiza literally means 'finger root' in Greek, referring to the distinctive hand-shaped underground tubers that these orchids use to store energy.

children.description: Orchids are a diverse family of flowering plants known for their complex, often showy flowers with three petals and three sepals. The most distinctive feature is that one petal, called the lip or labellum, is usually enlarged and different in shape or color from the other petals. All orchids have their reproductive parts fused together into a single structure called a column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Orchids are unique among flowering plants for having their pollen grains clumped together into waxy masses called pollinia, rather than loose individual grains. Their flowers are also bilaterally symmetric and have specialized relationships with specific pollinators.
children.funFact: Many New England orchids, like coralroots and some bog orchids, don't rely on photosynthesis for all their energy—instead they partner with fungi in the soil to obtain nutrients, which is why some species can bloom in deep forest shade or even lack green leaves entirely.

children.name: Asparagaceae
Scilla
children.description: Squills are small bulbous plants that produce delicate, star-shaped flowers in early spring, often blooming through snow. These hardy perennials belong to the lily family and are characterized by their narrow, strap-like leaves and clusters of small blue, white, or pink flowers on short stems. Most species found in New England are actually native to Europe and Asia but have naturalized in our region.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Squills can be distinguished from other early spring bulbs by their typically blue flowers (though some are white or pink) arranged in loose clusters or spikes, and their solid, non-hollow leaves that emerge directly from the ground. Unlike crocuses, squills have six petals and prominent stamens, and unlike grape hyacinths, their flowers are star-shaped rather than urn-shaped.
children.funFact: Despite their common name "Siberian squill," Scilla siberica doesn't actually come from Siberia – it's native to southwestern Russia and the Caucasus region, and the misleading name has stuck since the 1700s.

children.name: Hosta
children.description: Hostas are popular shade-loving perennial plants known for their large, distinctive leaves and tall spikes of bell-shaped flowers. These herbaceous plants form clumps of broad, often heart-shaped leaves that come in various shades of green, blue-green, or variegated patterns with white or yellow edges. They bloom in summer with fragrant white, lavender, or purple flowers that attract hummingbirds and bees.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hostas are easily recognized by their prominent leaf veins, clumping growth habit, and the way their leaves emerge directly from the ground in a rosette pattern. Unlike many other shade plants, hostas produce showy flower spikes that rise well above the foliage.
children.funFact: Originally from East Asia, hostas were so prized by Japanese nobility that for centuries they were forbidden to be taken out of the country, earning them the nickname 'forbidden plants.'

children.name: Maianthemum
children.description: Mayflowers and false Solomon's seals are delicate woodland plants that carpet the forest floor with their broad, oval leaves and clusters of small white flowers. These low-growing perennials are part of the lily family and thrive in the cool, moist conditions of New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They typically bloom in late spring and early summer, producing small berries later in the season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true Solomon's seal which has flowers hanging underneath the stem, these plants have their tiny white flowers arranged in upright clusters or spikes at the end of the stem. Their leaves are also typically broader and more heart-shaped than those of related woodland plants.
children.funFact: Canada mayflower is sometimes called 'two-leaved Solomon's seal' because it usually has just two leaves, making it easy to distinguish from its relatives that have multiple leaves arranged along the stem.

children.name: Muscari
children.description: Grape hyacinths are small, spring-blooming bulbs that produce dense clusters of tiny, bell-shaped flowers arranged in spike-like formations. These charming plants get their name from their resemblance to tiny bunches of grapes, with flowers typically appearing in shades of blue, purple, or white. They're popular garden plants that naturalize easily and often return year after year.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true hyacinths, grape hyacinths have much smaller individual flowers that are tightly packed into compact, oval-shaped clusters. Their flowers are also more rounded and bell-like rather than the star-shaped blooms of many other spring bulbs.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, grape hyacinths aren't actually related to true hyacinths at all - they belong to the asparagus family and are more closely related to asparagus plants than to the hyacinths they're named after!

children.name: Polygonatum
children.description: Solomon's seals are graceful woodland plants with arching stems that bear oval leaves arranged alternately along their length. They produce small, bell-shaped white or greenish flowers that dangle beneath the stem, followed by dark blue or black berries in late summer.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the false Solomon's seals, true Solomon's seals have flowers that hang individually or in small clusters directly beneath the stem rather than in terminal clusters at the tip.
children.funFact: The name 'Solomon's seal' comes from the circular scars left on the underground rhizome when each year's stem dies back, which were thought to resemble the legendary seal of King Solomon.

children.name: Yucca
children.description: Yuccas are distinctive plants with sword-like leaves arranged in rosettes and tall spikes of white, bell-shaped flowers. These hardy perennials are known for their tough, fibrous leaves that often have sharp points and sometimes curly threads along the edges. Despite their southwestern appearance, several species have naturalized in New England gardens and coastal areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plants with similar spiky leaves, yuccas produce their flowers on dramatic tall stalks that can reach several feet high, with clusters of creamy white blooms. Their leaves are much thicker and more rigid than ornamental grasses, and they maintain their structure year-round.
children.funFact: Yuccas have one of nature's most exclusive pollination partnerships - they can only be pollinated by tiny yucca moths, and in return, the moths' caterpillars feed exclusively on yucca seeds!

children.name: Ornithogalum
children.description: Star-of-Bethlehem plants are bulbous perennials that produce clusters of distinctive white, star-shaped flowers in spring. These members of the lily family grow from underground bulbs and have narrow, grass-like leaves with a characteristic white stripe running down the center. They're originally from Europe and western Asia but have naturalized in many parts of New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The six-petaled white flowers with green stripes on the outside of each petal are unmistakable, along with the narrow leaves marked by a prominent white midrib stripe. Unlike many other spring bulbs, star-of-Bethlehem flowers open only in bright sunlight and close on cloudy days.
children.funFact: The flowers are nicknamed 'sleepyheads' because they close up tight on cloudy days and at night, only opening wide when the sun is shining brightly.

children.name: Asparagus
children.description: Asparagus is a genus of perennial plants known for their distinctive feathery foliage and edible shoots. These plants produce small, scale-like leaves and develop intricate branching stems that create a delicate, fern-like appearance. Many species in this genus are valued both as food crops and ornamental plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Asparagus plants are unique among vegetables for their modified stems called cladodes that perform photosynthesis instead of true leaves. Their characteristic spear-like shoots emerge directly from underground crowns and can grow several inches in a single day.
children.funFact: Wild asparagus can live for over 100 years, with some established crowns continuing to produce edible shoots for decades once they reach maturity at around 3 years old.

children.name: Hyacinthoides
children.description: Bluebells are spring-blooming bulbous plants that produce graceful, drooping bell-shaped flowers in shades of blue, purple, or occasionally white. These perennial herbs emerge from underground bulbs and develop narrow, strap-like leaves along with tall flower spikes that create stunning woodland displays in late spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other spring bulbs, bluebells have distinctively curved or drooping flower spikes with multiple tubular, bell-shaped blooms hanging from one side of the stem. Their flowers have six petals that are fused at the base, creating the characteristic bell shape that gives them their common name.
children.funFact: The Spanish Bluebell is actually an introduced species from the Iberian Peninsula that can hybridize with the native English Bluebell, creating conservation concerns in Europe where the pure native populations are threatened by this genetic mixing.

children.name: Camassia
children.description: Camas are beautiful spring-blooming wildflowers in the lily family that produce tall spikes of star-shaped blue or purple flowers. These plants grow from deep bulbs and have long, narrow leaves that emerge in early spring before the impressive flower stalks appear. They thrive in moist meadows, prairies, and woodland edges.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Camas can be distinguished from other lily family members by their dense, elongated clusters of six-petaled flowers arranged along tall, unbranched stems. Unlike many lilies, their flowers are typically blue to purple rather than white or yellow.
children.funFact: Indigenous peoples of North America have harvested camas bulbs as an important food source for thousands of years, pit-roasting them to convert starches into sweet, nutritious meals - but they had to be very careful not to confuse them with the deadly poisonous death camas!

children.name: Convallaria
children.description: Lilies of the valley are small woodland plants known for their distinctive bell-shaped white flowers that dangle from arching stems. These perennial herbs spread through underground rhizomes and produce broad, oval leaves that emerge directly from the ground. They're beloved for their sweet fragrance and are often associated with shaded forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true lilies, lilies of the valley have flowers that hang downward like tiny bells rather than facing upward or outward. Their leaves emerge in pairs directly from the base of the plant rather than along a tall stem.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance and sweet scent, all parts of lily of the valley plants contain toxic compounds called cardiac glycosides that can be dangerous if ingested by humans or animals.

children.name: Puschkinia
children.description: Striped squills are small bulbous flowering plants that belong to the asparagus family. These early spring bloomers produce delicate white or pale blue flowers with distinctive dark blue stripes running down each petal, creating their characteristic striped appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other spring bulbs, striped squills have unique flowers with dark blue stripes on white or pale blue petals, and their stamens are fused together to form a distinctive corona or crown structure.
children.funFact: Striped squills are named after the Russian botanist Apollo Apollosovich Mussin-Pushkin and naturally grow in the mountains of the Middle East, making them surprisingly hardy for such delicate-looking flowers.

children.name: Hyacinthus
children.description: Hyacinths are a small genus of bulbous flowering plants known for their dense, fragrant flower spikes that emerge in spring. These perennial plants grow from underground bulbs and produce thick, strap-shaped leaves along with their characteristic cone-shaped clusters of small, bell-shaped flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hyacinths are distinguished from other bulb flowers by their tightly packed, cylindrical flower spikes and their intensely sweet fragrance that can be detected from a considerable distance.
children.funFact: The common garden hyacinth we see today is actually native to the eastern Mediterranean region and was so prized by the Ottoman Empire that bulb exports were once banned to maintain their exclusivity.

children.name: Liriope
children.description: Liliturfs are small, clump-forming perennial plants that look like ornamental grass but are actually related to lilies. They produce dense tufts of narrow, arching leaves that stay green year-round, making them popular landscaping plants. In late summer, they send up spikes of small purple or white flowers followed by dark berries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, liliturfs have broader, more substantial leaves and produce colorful flower spikes and berries. Their evergreen foliage and lily-like flowers help distinguish them from similar-looking ornamental grasses.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'lilyturf,' these plants aren't actually turf grasses at all - they're members of the asparagus family and are more closely related to hostas than to lawn grass!

children.name: Triteleia
children.description: Triplet lilies are bulbous perennial plants that produce clusters of funnel-shaped flowers in shades of blue, purple, or white. These wildflowers grow from underground corms (swollen stem bases) and typically bloom in late spring to early summer. They belong to the asparagus family and are native to western North America, with only one species found in New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true lilies, triplet lilies have their flowers arranged in loose, umbrella-like clusters called umbels at the top of leafless stems. Their narrow, grass-like leaves emerge from the base of the plant and often wither by the time the flowers bloom.
children.funFact: The name 'triplet lily' comes from the fact that their flower parts are typically arranged in sets of three - three petals, three sepals, and six stamens arranged in two groups of three.

children.name: Barnardia
children.description: Barnardia is a small genus of bulbous perennial plants in the asparagus family that produce clusters of small, bell-shaped flowers. These plants grow from underground bulbs and send up narrow, grass-like leaves along with tall flowering stems in late summer or fall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barnardia differs from related bulb plants by its distinctive timing of blooming in autumn rather than spring, and its flowers are arranged in dense, elongated clusters rather than loose sprays.
children.funFact: Despite being called Japanese jacinth, Barnardia japonica was only recently separated from the genus Scilla and given its own genus name in honor of botanist Edward Barnard.

children.description: The agave and allies family includes a diverse group of plants that range from desert-dwelling yuccas to woodland favorites like Solomon's seal and lily of the valley. Despite their varied appearances, these plants share similar flower structures with six petals (or petal-like parts) and typically grow from bulbs, rhizomes, or thick rootstocks. Many produce clusters of small, often fragrant flowers that are beloved by gardeners and pollinators alike.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their six-part flowers and parallel-veined leaves, though they've been reclassified from the traditional lily family based on genetic studies. Unlike true lilies, many have their ovaries positioned above the flower parts and often grow in different arrangements.
children.funFact: This family includes both the tough, spiky yucca plants that can survive in harsh deserts and the delicate, sweet-scented lily of the valley that thrives in cool, shaded woodlands—showing remarkable adaptability across completely different environments.

children.name: Amaryllidaceae
Allium
children.description: Onions (Allium) are a diverse genus of plants that includes familiar kitchen staples like garlic, chives, and onions, as well as many wild relatives. All members of this group are bulbous plants that produce the characteristic sharp, pungent smell and taste we associate with onions and garlic when their tissues are crushed or cut. They typically have narrow, strap-like leaves and produce clusters of small flowers on tall stalks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Allium apart from other bulbous plants is their distinctive sulfur compounds that create their signature smell and flavor when cell walls are broken. They also have a unique flower structure with six petals arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels.
children.funFact: The strong smell that makes you cry when cutting onions is actually a chemical defense mechanism - wild Allium species evolved these sulfur compounds to protect their nutritious bulbs from being eaten by animals and insects.

children.name: Narcissus
children.description: Daffodils are beloved spring-blooming bulb flowers that belong to the amaryllis family. All members of this genus share the distinctive trumpet or cup-shaped corona (center) surrounded by six petals, creating their iconic flower shape. They grow from underground bulbs and typically bloom in early spring with white, yellow, or combinations of both colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets daffodils apart from other spring bulbs is their unique corona structure - the trumpet or cup-like center that extends from the middle of the flower. Unlike tulips or crocuses, daffodils also contain toxic alkaloids that make them deer and rodent resistant.
children.funFact: Daffodils are named after Narcissus from Greek mythology, who fell in love with his own reflection - which is why these flowers often appear to be looking down at their reflection in spring puddles!

children.name: Galanthus
children.description: Snowdrops are small, bulbous perennial flowers that bloom in late winter or early spring, often pushing through snow. These delicate plants produce distinctive white, bell-shaped flowers that hang downward from slender green stems, with each flower featuring white petals marked by green spots or stripes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snowdrops are easily recognized by their pure white, drooping flowers with characteristic green markings, and their ability to bloom in cold weather when most other plants are still dormant. Unlike other early spring bulbs, snowdrops have narrow, strap-like leaves and flowers that hang singly from each stem.
children.funFact: Snowdrops contain a compound called galantamine, which is now used in modern medicine to help treat Alzheimer's disease and was traditionally used in folk remedies.

children.name: Leucojum
children.description: Snowflakes are delicate spring-blooming bulb plants that produce drooping, bell-shaped white flowers with distinctive green spots on the petals. These charming woodland plants emerge early in the year, often pushing through the last snow, and are beloved for their graceful appearance in shade gardens and naturalized areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the snowdrops (Galanthus), snowflakes have all six petals the same length and are marked with green or yellow spots, giving them a more symmetrical, bell-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their common name suggesting winter blooms, Summer Snowflakes actually flower in late spring, while Spring Snowflakes bloom in early spring - both much later than actual snowfall!

children.name: Lycoris
children.description: Hurricane lilies are bulbous flowering plants that earned their name for their dramatic timing - they send up leafless flower stalks in late summer or early fall, often after storms or heavy rains. These striking flowers appear on naked stems before any leaves emerge, creating an almost magical appearance in the landscape. The leaves develop later in fall or spring, then die back before the flowers appear again.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hurricane lilies are easily recognized by their unusual growth pattern where showy flowers appear on bare stems completely separate from their leaves in time. Their flowers have six curved, narrow petals that often curl backward and long, prominent stamens that extend well beyond the petals.
children.funFact: Hurricane lilies are sometimes called "naked ladies" because their flowers appear without any leaves - the foliage and flowers are never present at the same time, leading to their mysterious sudden appearance in gardens.

children.name: Ipheion
children.description: Ipheion is a small genus of bulbous perennial plants native to South America that produce delicate, star-shaped flowers. These low-growing plants emerge from underground bulbs and are known for their grass-like leaves and sweet-scented blooms that appear in spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ipheion flowers have six pointed petals arranged in a perfect star shape, and the leaves emit a distinctive onion-like scent when crushed, despite not being true onions.
children.funFact: Though native to Argentina and Uruguay, spring starflower has naturalized so well in some parts of New England that many people assume it's a native wildflower.

children.name: Tulbaghia
children.description: Wild Garlics are a genus of flowering plants native to southern Africa that are known for their distinctive garlic-like scent when crushed. These perennial plants produce clusters of small, tubular flowers and grow from underground bulbs, making them popular ornamental plants in gardens.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true garlic, Wild Garlics have star-shaped flowers that bloom in rounded clusters above grass-like leaves, and they're grown primarily for their ornamental value rather than culinary use.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'garlic,' these plants are more closely related to lilies than to true garlic, but they still produce that familiar pungent aroma that helps repel deer and other garden pests.

children.description: The amaryllis family includes bulbous plants that produce distinctive flowers with six petals arranged in a star or trumpet shape. Most members grow from underground bulbs and have long, narrow leaves that emerge directly from the ground. This diverse family ranges from the familiar kitchen onion to showy spring flowers like daffodils and snowdrops.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bulbous plants, amaryllis family members have flowers that emerge from a papery sheath called a spathe. Their bulbs are true bulbs (made of layered scales) rather than corms or tubers, and they typically have six stamens.
children.funFact: Many plants in this family contain powerful chemical compounds - onions make you cry, garlic fights bacteria, and daffodils are poisonous enough that rodents won't eat their bulbs!

children.name: Iridaceae
Iris
children.description: Irises are perennial flowering plants known for their distinctive three-petaled flowers that often display vibrant blues, purples, yellows, and whites. These plants typically grow from underground rhizomes or bulbs and produce long, sword-like leaves that grow in fan-shaped clusters. Most irises thrive in moist environments, though some species have adapted to drier conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Iris flowers have a unique structure with three upright petals called 'standards' and three drooping petals called 'falls,' often with intricate patterns and markings. The flower's design creates a distinctive landing platform that guides pollinators directly to the nectar.
children.funFact: The iris gets its name from the Greek goddess of the rainbow, and the flower has been used as a symbol of royalty for over 1,400 years - it's the inspiration for the fleur-de-lis.

children.name: Crocus
children.description: Crocuses are small, cheerful bulb flowers that emerge in early spring, often pushing through snow to bloom. They produce cup-shaped flowers in purple, white, yellow, or striped patterns, with six petals and bright orange stamens. These hardy perennials grow from underground corms and typically reach just 3-6 inches tall.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other early spring bulbs, crocuses have grass-like leaves with distinctive white stripes down the center and flowers that emerge directly from the ground without tall stems. Their three prominent stamens and thread-like stigmas are also characteristic features.
children.funFact: Crocus flowers are natural weather predictors - they close their petals tightly when bad weather approaches and only open fully in sunshine and warmth.

children.name: Sisyrinchium
children.description: Blue-eyed grasses are small, delicate wildflowers that belong to the iris family, despite their grass-like name and appearance. These charming plants produce tiny six-petaled flowers that are typically blue or purple with bright yellow centers, though some species may have white or pale blue blooms. They grow in tufts of narrow, flat leaves that do indeed resemble grass blades.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, blue-eyed grasses have flat, sword-like leaves and distinctive iris-family flowers with six petals arranged in a perfect star pattern. Their stems are also characteristically flattened rather than round, helping to separate them from both grasses and other small wildflowers.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'grasses,' these plants are actually more closely related to irises and crocuses than to any true grass species.

children.description: The iris family includes beautiful flowering plants known for their distinctive three-petaled flowers and sword-like leaves. These plants grow from underground bulbs, corms, or rhizomes and produce showy blooms in a wide range of colors including purple, blue, yellow, and white.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have flowers with three petals and three sepals that often look similar, creating a six-part flower arrangement. Their leaves are typically long, narrow, and arranged in a fan-like pattern.
children.funFact: Many iris family plants, including crocuses, are among the earliest spring bloomers and can even push through snow to flower, with some species like autumn crocus actually blooming in fall while their leaves don't appear until the following spring.

children.name: Asphodelaceae
Hemerocallis
children.description: Daylilies are popular flowering plants known for their large, showy blooms that typically last just one day, hence their common name. These hardy perennials grow from thick, fleshy roots and produce long, arching leaves that emerge directly from the ground in fountain-like clumps.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true lilies, daylilies have flowers that open in the morning and close by evening, with new buds opening on successive days. Their leaves are also narrower and more grass-like compared to the broader leaves of true lilies.
children.funFact: Despite their name, daylilies aren't actually lilies at all - they're more closely related to agave plants and were historically used as food in Asia, where both the flowers and young shoots are edible.

children.description: The Aloe family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes familiar garden favorites like daylilies, as well as succulent plants like aloes and asphodels. Most members of this family have long, narrow leaves that grow from the base of the plant and produce colorful flowers arranged on tall stalks. These plants are found worldwide and range from desert succulents to moisture-loving perennials.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have six-petaled flowers and leaves with parallel veins, distinguishing them from plants with net-veined leaves. Unlike true lilies, many species in this family have thick, fleshy roots or stems for storing water.
children.funFact: Despite being called "daylilies," these plants aren't actually true lilies at all - each individual flower blooms for just one day, which is how they got their common name!

children.name: Hypoxidaceae
Hypoxis
children.description: Stargrasses are small wildflowers that produce bright yellow, star-shaped blooms close to the ground. These perennial plants grow from underground bulbs and have narrow, grass-like leaves that often appear hairy or fuzzy.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, stargrasses produce showy six-petaled flowers and belong to the amaryllis family. Their star-shaped yellow blooms and hairy, grass-like leaves make them easy to identify.
children.funFact: Despite their name, stargrasses aren't actually grasses at all - they're more closely related to daffodils and amaryllis than to lawn grass.

children.description: Stargrasses and allies are a small family of herbaceous flowering plants that grow from underground bulbs or corms. They produce grass-like leaves and bright yellow, star-shaped flowers that typically have six petals. These plants are found in grasslands, meadows, and open woodlands.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, stargrasses produce showy yellow flowers with six petals arranged in a star pattern. Their leaves are also broader than typical grass blades and arise directly from the underground storage organ.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, stargrasses aren't actually grasses at all - they're more closely related to lilies and amaryllis!

children.description: Asparagales is a large and diverse order of flowering plants that includes some of our most beloved garden flowers and economically important crops. These plants are typically herbaceous with specialized underground storage organs like bulbs, rhizomes, or thick roots, and most have long, narrow leaves arranged in a spiral or two rows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other monocots, many Asparagales have six stamens and often produce colorful, showy flowers arranged in clusters or spikes. They're distinguished from lilies by their inferior ovaries (ovary positioned below the flower parts) and unique seed chemistry.
children.funFact: This order includes both the world's most complex flowers (orchids with over 25,000 species) and some of our most essential kitchen staples like onions, garlic, and asparagus!

children.name: Alismatales
children.commonName: Aroids, Water Plantains, Seagrass, and allies

children.name: Potamogetonaceae
Potamogeton
children.description: Pondweeds are aquatic plants that live completely or mostly submerged in freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. These perennial plants have adapted to underwater life with flexible stems and leaves that can handle water currents and changing water levels. Most species produce small, inconspicuous flowers that emerge above the water surface on spikes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, pondweeds have distinctive stipules (small leaf-like structures) at the base of their leaves and produce their flowers on spikes that rise above the water surface. Their leaves can be completely submerged, floating on the surface, or both, depending on the species.
children.funFact: Some pondweed species can reproduce without flowering through winter buds called turions that sink to the bottom of the water body and sprout into new plants the following spring.

children.name: Stuckenia
children.description: Stuckenia is a genus of aquatic plants commonly known as pondweeds that live completely submerged in freshwater environments. These plants have adapted to underwater life with thin, thread-like leaves and specialized flowering structures that can reach the water's surface to reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other pondweeds, Stuckenia species have very narrow, linear leaves that are typically less than 2mm wide and lack the broader leaf blades found in many related genera.
children.funFact: Fennel-leaf Pondweed can survive in both fresh and slightly brackish water, making it one of the most salt-tolerant pondweeds in New England.

children.name: Zannichellia
children.description: Zannichellia is a genus of delicate aquatic plants commonly known as horned pondweeds. These submerged freshwater plants have thin, grass-like leaves and tiny flowers that bloom underwater, making them well-adapted to life in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many aquatic plants, Zannichellia produces distinctive curved, horn-like fruits that give it its common name. The plants are completely submerged and have thread-like leaves arranged in clusters along the stem.
children.funFact: Horned pondweed can reproduce both by seeds and by breaking apart into fragments, allowing it to quickly colonize new aquatic habitats even when conditions aren't perfect for flowering.

children.description: The pondweed family consists of aquatic plants that live completely submerged in freshwater lakes, ponds, rivers, and streams. These plants have adapted to underwater life with thin, flexible leaves and specialized flowers that can pollinate while submerged or at the water's surface. All members of this family are perennial herbs with creeping underground stems called rhizomes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other aquatic plants, pondweeds have tiny, inconspicuous flowers arranged in dense spikes and produce small, hard fruits. Their leaves are typically alternate and often have a distinctive sheath where they attach to the stem.
children.funFact: Some pondweeds can reproduce without pollination through a process called apomixis, essentially cloning themselves to create genetically identical offspring.

children.name: Araceae
Arisaema
children.description: Arisaema species are fascinating woodland plants known for their distinctive flower structure that resembles a preacher standing in a pulpit or a hooded cobra. These perennial herbs grow from underground corms and produce their characteristic spathe (the hood-like covering) that surrounds a central spike called a spadix where the tiny flowers actually grow. They're members of the arum family and typically prefer shaded, moist forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Arisaema apart from other arums is their unique hooded spathe that curves over the flower spike, creating that distinctive 'pulpit' appearance. Unlike many of their tropical relatives, these species are adapted to temperate climates and can survive New England winters.
children.funFact: Many jack-in-the-pulpit plants can actually change sex from year to year - young or stressed plants tend to be male, while older, more robust plants become female and produce bright red berries.

children.name: Lemna
children.description: Duckweeds are tiny floating aquatic plants that form some of the smallest flowers in the plant kingdom. These miniature plants consist of simple leaf-like structures called fronds that float on the water's surface, often covering ponds and slow-moving waters with bright green carpets.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, duckweeds have extremely reduced structures with no obvious stems or leaves - just small, flat, oval fronds that may have simple roots dangling beneath.
children.funFact: Despite being among the world's smallest flowering plants, duckweeds are also some of the fastest-growing, able to double their population in just 2-3 days under ideal conditions.

children.name: Wolffia
children.description: Watermeals are the world's smallest flowering plants, appearing as tiny green specks floating on the surface of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These minuscule plants lack roots, stems, and leaves, consisting of just a simple oval or round body called a thallus that's often smaller than a grain of rice. They reproduce mainly by budding, creating dense floating mats that can cover entire water surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other duckweeds, watermeals have no roots at all and are significantly smaller, often measuring less than 1.5 millimeters across. They also lack the distinct leaf-like structures found in their relatives, appearing instead as simple, rootless green dots.
children.funFact: A single Wolffia plant weighs about as much as two grains of salt and is so small that a dozen could fit comfortably on the head of a pin!

children.name: Pinellia
children.description: Pinellia is a genus of small perennial plants in the arum family that produce distinctive three-part leaves and unusual hooded flowers. These Asian natives have adapted well to New England's climate and are often found in shaded, moist areas where they form small colonies through underground tubers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other arum family members, Pinellia species have characteristic trifoliate leaves (divided into three leaflets) and produce small plantlets along their flower stalks that can drop off and grow into new plants.
children.funFact: Pinellia plants can reproduce without seeds by growing tiny bulbils (baby plants) right on their flower stalks, which eventually fall off and take root to create exact clones of the parent plant.

children.name: Symplocarpus
children.description: Skunk cabbages are unusual wildflowers that emerge very early in spring, often pushing through snow and ice in wet, marshy areas. They're famous for their ability to generate heat, which helps them melt through frozen ground, and their distinctive skunk-like odor when crushed or damaged. These hardy plants have large, cabbage-like leaves and produce their flowers inside a protective hood-like structure called a spathe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other early spring flowers, skunk cabbages can actually produce their own heat through a process called thermogenesis, warming the air around them by up to 35°F above ambient temperature. Their flowers are also unique in being enclosed within a mottled purple and green hood that emerges before the leaves.
children.funFact: Skunk cabbage flowers can maintain their internal temperature at around 72°F even when surrounded by snow, making them one of the few plants that are literally warm-blooded like animals!

children.name: Peltandra
children.description: Arrow Arums are aquatic plants that grow in shallow water and wetlands, easily recognized by their distinctive arrow-shaped leaves that give the genus its common name. These perennial plants produce small flowers clustered on a spike-like structure called a spadix, which is partially enclosed by a leaf-like bract called a spathe.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arrow Arums can be distinguished from other wetland plants by their bold, arrow-shaped leaves and their characteristic arum family flower structure with a spadix and spathe. Unlike many other aroids, Arrow Arums are native to North America and well-adapted to temperate wetland conditions.
children.funFact: Arrow Arums were an important food source for Native American tribes, who would process the starchy roots to remove toxic compounds and create a nutritious flour-like substance.

children.name: Calla
children.description: Marsh callas are aquatic plants in the arum family that thrive in wetland environments like bogs, swamps, and shallow water edges. They are characterized by their distinctive heart-shaped leaves and small white spathe (a modified leaf) that surrounds their tiny clustered flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the arum family, marsh callas have a relatively small, flat white spathe rather than a large, showy one, and their flowers lack petals entirely. Their creeping rhizomes and ability to grow partially submerged in water also set them apart from their terrestrial relatives.
children.funFact: Marsh calla berries turn bright red when ripe and float on water, allowing them to disperse to new wetland locations by hitchhiking on water currents and waterfowl.

children.name: Spirodela
children.description: Greater duckweeds are tiny floating aquatic plants that form some of the smallest flowering plants in the world. They consist of small, flat, oval-shaped fronds (leaf-like structures) that float on the surface of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Unlike many aquatic plants, they have multiple roots dangling beneath each frond.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Greater duckweeds are distinguished from other duckweeds by having multiple roots per frond (usually 3-12) rather than just one root. They are also typically larger than other duckweed species, with fronds reaching up to half an inch across.
children.funFact: Despite being among the world's smallest flowering plants, greater duckweeds can reproduce so rapidly through budding that they can double their population in just 2-3 days under ideal conditions.

children.name: Orontium
children.description: Orontium is a genus containing just one species - the Golden Club, a unique aquatic plant found in wetlands and shallow waters. These plants are members of the arum family and produce distinctive bright yellow, club-shaped flower spikes that emerge from the water on long stalks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other members of the arum family, Golden Club flowers lack the typical leafy spathe (hood) that surrounds the flower spike, leaving the bright yellow spadix completely exposed.
children.funFact: Golden Club is sometimes called 'Never-wet' because its waxy leaves repel water so effectively that they appear completely dry even when submerged.

children.name: Pistia
children.description: Pistia is a genus containing just one species - the Water Lettuce, a free-floating aquatic plant that forms rosettes of soft, velvety leaves on the water's surface. These tropical plants reproduce rapidly through runners called stolons, creating dense mats that can quickly cover ponds and slow-moving waterways. They're popular in water gardens but can become invasive in warm climates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Water Lettuce is easily recognized by its pale green, wedge-shaped leaves with prominent parallel veins and a distinctive velvety texture that repels water. Unlike other floating plants, its leaves form tight rosettes that sit above the water surface like floating heads of lettuce.
children.funFact: Water Lettuce leaves are covered in tiny hairs that trap air bubbles, making them so water-repellent that they stay completely dry even when submerged - water simply rolls right off!

children.name: Arum
children.description: Arum lilies are distinctive flowering plants known for their unusual flower structure and arrow-shaped leaves. They produce a large, hood-like bract called a spathe that surrounds a central spike (spadix) containing tiny flowers, creating what looks like a single dramatic bloom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true lilies, arums have their tiny flowers clustered on a central spike and surrounded by a single large, showy bract. Their leaves are typically arrow or heart-shaped rather than long and narrow.
children.funFact: Arum flowers can actually generate heat and emit strong odors to attract flies and beetles for pollination, sometimes warming up to 15°F above the surrounding air temperature.

children.name: Caladium
children.description: Caladium is a genus of tropical plants known for their stunning heart-shaped leaves with vibrant patterns and colors. These plants are prized as ornamental houseplants and garden specimens for their colorful foliage rather than their flowers. They belong to the arum family and are native to South and Central America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caladiums are distinguished by their large, papery-thin, heart-shaped leaves that display brilliant combinations of red, pink, white, and green in striking patterns. Unlike many other aroids, they're grown primarily for their spectacular leaf coloration rather than their inconspicuous flowers.
children.funFact: Caladiums are sometimes called 'angel wings' or 'elephant ears' because of their distinctive leaf shape, and they go completely dormant in winter, dying back to underground tubers that can be stored and replanted the following year.

children.name: Lysichiton
children.description: Skunk cabbages in the genus Lysichiton are distinctive wetland plants known for their large, broad leaves and unusual flowering structure. They produce a bright yellow, hood-like spathe that surrounds a thick spike of tiny flowers, followed by enormous cabbage-like leaves that can grow several feet long. These plants thrive in wet, boggy areas and are among the first to emerge in early spring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other skunk cabbages, Lysichiton species have bright yellow spathes and lack the mottled purple coloring found in eastern skunk cabbage. Their leaves are also much larger and more paddle-shaped than their eastern relatives.
children.funFact: Western skunk cabbage can generate its own heat through cellular respiration, allowing it to melt through snow and bloom in late winter when temperatures are still near freezing.

children.name: Landoltia
children.description: Landoltia is a genus of tiny floating aquatic plants commonly known as dotted duckweed. These miniature plants consist of small, oval-shaped leaf-like structures called fronds that float on the water surface, often forming dense green mats in ponds, marshes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Landoltia can be distinguished from other duckweed genera by its distinctive red or purple spots on the underside of the fronds, which give it the common name 'dotted duckweed.'
children.funFact: Despite being one of the world's smallest flowering plants, dotted duckweed is among the fastest-growing plants on Earth and can double its population in just 2-3 days under ideal conditions.

children.name: Colocasia
children.description: Elephant ears are tropical plants in the arum family known for their enormous, heart-shaped leaves that can grow several feet wide. These plants grow from underground tubers and produce the classic hood-like flower structure called a spathe that's typical of their plant family. While most species are native to Southeast Asia, some have become established in warmer parts of North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Elephant ears are distinguished from other arum family plants by their exceptionally large, broad leaves and their tendency to form dense colonies from spreading tubers. Their leaves are typically much larger and more rounded than related plants like skunk cabbage or jack-in-the-pulpit.
children.funFact: The most common species, taro, has been cultivated as a food crop for over 7,000 years and its starchy tubers feed millions of people worldwide, though the leaves and raw tubers contain calcium oxalate crystals that must be cooked out to make them safe to eat.

children.name: Zantedeschia
children.description: Calla lilies are elegant flowering plants native to southern Africa, known for their distinctive trumpet-shaped blooms and arrow-shaped leaves. These perennial plants grow from underground rhizomes and produce a single large, colorful bract (called a spathe) that surrounds a central spike of tiny flowers. While not true lilies, they've become popular ornamental plants worldwide for their striking appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Calla lilies are easily recognized by their unique funnel or trumpet-shaped flower bracts that come in various colors including white, yellow, pink, and purple. Unlike many other flowering plants, what appears to be the main flower is actually a modified leaf called a spathe, with the real flowers being tiny and clustered on the central spike.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, calla lilies aren't actually lilies at all - they're more closely related to plants like skunk cabbage and jack-in-the-pulpit, all belonging to the arum family!

children.description: The Arum Family is a diverse group of flowering plants that includes everything from tiny floating duckweeds to large tropical elephant ears. Most members share a distinctive flower structure called a spadix - a fleshy spike covered in tiny flowers - often surrounded by a showy leaf-like bract called a spathe. Many species thrive in wet environments like marshes, ponds, and forest floors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The spadix and spathe flower arrangement is the family's signature feature, seen clearly in jack-in-the-pulpits and skunk cabbages. Many species also produce calcium oxalate crystals in their tissues, making them irritating or toxic if eaten raw.
children.funFact: Duckweeds in this family are among the world's smallest flowering plants, with some species like watermeal being barely visible to the naked eye, yet they're closely related to giant elephant ears with leaves several feet across.

children.name: Alismataceae
Sagittaria
children.description: Arrowheads are aquatic plants that get their name from their distinctive arrow-shaped leaves, though leaf shapes can vary from narrow and grass-like to broad and heart-shaped. These wetland specialists grow in shallow water, marshes, and muddy shores throughout New England, with their roots anchored underwater and leaves either floating on the surface or standing above it. Most species produce small white flowers on tall stalks that emerge above the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Arrowheads are easily recognized by their three-petaled white flowers and their tendency to grow with at least part of the plant submerged in water. Unlike many other aquatic plants, they often have distinctly arrow-shaped leaves with pointed lobes extending backward from the base.
children.funFact: Many arrowhead species produce starchy tubers underground that were traditionally harvested by Native Americans as 'duck potatoes' - an important food source that tastes similar to regular potatoes when cooked.

children.name: Alisma
children.description: Water-plantains are aquatic plants that grow in shallow water or muddy shores of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They produce distinctive three-petaled white or pale pink flowers arranged in branching clusters above the water, and their leaves can be either broad and oval-shaped or narrow and grass-like depending on the species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, water-plantains have flowers with exactly three rounded petals and prominent yellow centers, and their leaves show clear parallel or curved veins running from base to tip.
children.funFact: Water-plantains can produce two completely different leaf shapes on the same plant - broad oval leaves when growing above water and narrow ribbon-like leaves when submerged.

children.description: The Water-Plantain family consists of aquatic and semi-aquatic flowering plants that thrive in wetlands, pond edges, and shallow water throughout New England. These plants are perfectly adapted to life in and around water, with many species able to grow both submerged and above the water surface. All members of this family produce small white or pink flowers arranged in branched clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Water-plantain family plants have distinctive parallel-veined leaves that often emerge directly from the base of the plant, and their flowers always have three petals and three sepals. Unlike many other aquatic plants, they produce true flowers above water rather than relying on underwater pollination.
children.funFact: Many arrowheads in this family can produce three different types of leaves on the same plant: thin ribbon-like leaves underwater, oval floating leaves on the surface, and the characteristic arrow-shaped leaves above water!

children.name: Hydrocharitaceae
Elodea
children.description: Waterweeds are submerged aquatic plants that live entirely underwater in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They have long, flexible stems with small oval leaves arranged in whorls of three around the stem, creating a distinctive layered appearance. These plants are completely adapted to underwater life, obtaining nutrients directly from the water through their leaves.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many aquatic plants that have leaves floating on the surface, waterweeds remain completely submerged with all their leaves underwater. Their leaves are arranged in distinctive whorls of three, which helps distinguish them from other submerged plants that may have opposite or alternate leaf arrangements.
children.funFact: Waterweeds are either all male or all female plants, and interestingly, some species like Canadian Waterweed have only female plants in North America - they reproduce entirely through fragmentation, with broken stem pieces growing into new plants.

children.name: Najas
children.description: Naiads are delicate aquatic plants that live completely submerged in freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams. These slender plants have narrow, opposite leaves arranged in whorls around their stems and produce tiny flowers underwater. They're important food sources for waterfowl and provide shelter for small fish and aquatic invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other aquatic plants, naiads have small spiny teeth along their leaf margins and sheaths that wrap around the stem where leaves attach. Their flowers are among the smallest of any flowering plant and lack petals entirely.
children.funFact: Naiads are named after the water nymphs of Greek mythology, and they're so well-adapted to underwater life that their pollen is actually dispersed through the water rather than by wind or insects.

children.name: Vallisneria
children.description: Tapegrasses are aquatic plants that live completely submerged in freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers. They have long, ribbon-like leaves that grow in clusters from the base of the plant and can reach several feet in length, creating underwater meadows.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other aquatic plants, tapegrasses have distinctively long, narrow leaves that are typically less than an inch wide but can grow up to 6 feet long, resembling green ribbons or tape floating in the water.
children.funFact: Female tapegrass flowers rise to the water's surface on long spiral stems, while male flowers break free and float to the surface to pollinate them - one of nature's most romantic underwater courtship displays.

children.name: Hydrocharis
children.description: Hydrocharis is a genus of aquatic flowering plants commonly known as frog-bits. These free-floating water plants have heart-shaped or rounded leaves that sit on the water surface, resembling tiny water lilies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true water lilies, frog-bits are much smaller with leaves typically only 1-2 inches across, and they float freely rather than being rooted to the bottom with long stems.
children.funFact: The name 'frog-bit' comes from the old belief that frogs would nibble on these floating leaves, though they actually prefer them as resting platforms rather than food.

children.name: Hydrilla
children.description: Hydrilla is a genus containing just one species of submerged aquatic plant that grows entirely underwater in freshwater environments. These plants have small, narrow leaves arranged in whorls around their stems and can form dense underwater meadows in lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hydrilla can be distinguished from other aquatic plants by its leaves being arranged in whorls of 3-10 around the stem, with tiny teeth along the leaf edges that feel rough to the touch.
children.funFact: Hydrilla is sometimes called 'Florida elodea' and is notorious for being one of the world's most aggressive aquatic invasive species, capable of growing up to an inch per day under ideal conditions.

children.description: The tape-grass family consists of aquatic plants that live completely or partially submerged in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These plants have adapted to underwater life with thin, ribbon-like or oval leaves that can photosynthesize beneath the surface. Most species in this family are perennial plants that spread through underground runners or fragments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other aquatic plant families, tape-grass family members have flowers that either bloom underwater or rise to the surface on long stalks. Their leaves are typically arranged in whorls around the stem or grow in rosettes from the base of the plant.
children.funFact: Some species like Vallisneria have remarkable pollination strategies where male flowers break free and float to the surface to reach female flowers, creating tiny 'flower boats' drifting across the water.

children.name: Juncaginaceae
Triglochin
children.description: Arrowgrasses are slender, grass-like plants that grow in wet, salty environments like salt marshes and alkaline wetlands. Despite their name and appearance, they're not true grasses but belong to their own plant family. These hardy plants have narrow, fleshy leaves and produce small spikes of tiny flowers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, arrowgrasses have their flowers arranged in dense, narrow spikes and produce distinctive three-chambered seed pods. Their leaves are typically thick and succulent-like, helping them survive in salty conditions.
children.funFact: Arrowgrasses get their name from their sharp-pointed seed pods that were traditionally used as arrowheads by some Indigenous peoples.

children.description: The Arrowgrass family is a small group of grasslike plants that thrive in wet, salty environments like salt marshes and alkaline wetlands. These perennial herbs grow from underground rhizomes and produce narrow, linear leaves that emerge directly from the base of the plant. They're specially adapted to tolerate high salt concentrations that would kill most other plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true grasses, arrowgrasses produce small, inconspicuous flowers arranged in dense spikes, and their fruits split into several one-seeded segments when ripe. Their leaves are thick and succulent-like, helping them store water and cope with salty conditions.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, arrowgrasses aren't actually grasses at all - they're more closely related to water plantains and pondweeds, and some species can be toxic to livestock if eaten in large quantities.

children.name: Tofieldiaceae
Triantha
children.description: Sticky false asphodels are small perennial wildflowers that grow in wet, acidic habitats like bogs and marshes. These plants produce clusters of small white or cream-colored flowers on tall stems and have narrow, grass-like leaves that grow from the base. They are related to lilies and get their common name from their resemblance to true asphodels.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These plants have sticky stems that can trap small insects, making them carnivorous plants. The sticky hairs on their flower stalks help them supplement their nutrition by digesting trapped prey.
children.funFact: Triantha glutinosa was only recently discovered to be carnivorous in 2021, making it one of the newest additions to the list of known carnivorous plants!

children.description: The tofieldia family is a small group of herbaceous perennial plants that grow in wet, boggy habitats. These plants produce small, white or greenish flowers arranged in dense spikes or clusters atop slender stems, and they typically have grass-like leaves that grow in tufts from the base.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their sticky flower stalks and three-chambered seed capsules that split open when ripe. Unlike many related lily-family plants, they have very small, inconspicuous flowers and prefer consistently wet soils.
children.funFact: Some members of this family, including our local sticky false asphodels, are carnivorous plants that trap tiny insects on their sticky flower stems to supplement their nutrition in nutrient-poor bog soils.

children.name: Zosteraceae
Zostera
children.description: Eelgrasses are truly aquatic flowering plants that live completely submerged in shallow saltwater and brackish environments. Unlike typical marine algae, these are actual flowering plants that have adapted to life underwater, forming extensive underwater meadows along coastlines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eelgrasses are distinguished from other marine plants by their long, ribbon-like leaves and their ability to produce flowers and seeds while completely submerged in saltwater.
children.funFact: Eelgrass is one of the few flowering plants that can pollinate underwater, releasing clouds of pollen that drift through the water to reach other plants.

children.description: Seagrasses in the family Zosteraceae are true flowering plants that have adapted to live completely underwater in marine environments. Unlike seaweeds which are algae, these are actual grasses with roots, stems, and leaves that can photosynthesize while submerged in saltwater. They form underwater meadows that provide critical habitat for marine life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other marine plants, Zosteraceae members are true angiosperms (flowering plants) with long, ribbon-like leaves and extensive root systems that anchor them in sandy or muddy sea floors. They can reproduce both through underwater pollination and by spreading through underground rhizomes.
children.funFact: Seagrasses are one of the only groups of flowering plants that can complete their entire life cycle underwater, including pollination - their pollen is carried by water currents instead of wind or insects.

children.name: Butomaceae
Butomus
children.description: Flowering-rushes are aquatic plants that grow in shallow water along pond and lake edges. Despite their name, they are not true rushes but belong to their own plant family and produce showy pink flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true rushes which have small, inconspicuous flowers, flowering-rushes have large, attractive pink flowers with six petals arranged in terminal umbels. They also have distinctive triangular stems and long, narrow leaves that emerge from the base of the plant.
children.funFact: The single species in this genus is considered both beautiful and problematic - while prized as an ornamental water garden plant, it's also classified as an invasive species in many parts of North America where it can form dense stands that crowd out native vegetation.

children.description: The flowering-rush family is a small group of aquatic plants that live in shallow water or wet areas. These plants have long, narrow leaves that grow in clusters and produce showy pink flowers on tall stems that rise above the water surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true rushes, these plants produce large, colorful flowers with 6 petals arranged in two circles. Their flowers are much more ornate than the small, inconspicuous flowers of grass-like plants they might be confused with.
children.funFact: Despite its name, flowering-rush is not actually related to true rushes - it's more closely related to water plantains and gets its name simply because of its rush-like appearance.

children.name: Scheuchzeriaceae
Scheuchzeria
children.description: Pod-grasses are a unique group of wetland plants that grow in acidic bogs and marshes. Despite their name, they're not true grasses but rather distinctive aquatic plants with narrow, rush-like leaves and small greenish flowers. These specialized plants are perfectly adapted to life in nutrient-poor, waterlogged soils.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pod-grasses can be identified by their distinctive inflated seed pods that split open along one side, and their alternate arrangement of narrow leaves along the stem, unlike true rushes which have different leaf patterns.
children.funFact: Rannoch-rush is considered a glacial relict species, meaning it's a survivor from the ice age that now exists only in scattered, isolated populations in the coldest bogs of northern regions.

children.description: The Pod-grass family is a small group of aquatic plants that live in wetlands like bogs and marshes. These plants have narrow, grass-like leaves and produce small flowers followed by distinctive inflated pods that give them their name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pod-grasses are easily recognized by their unique fruit structure - small, balloon-like pods that split open to release seeds, which is quite different from the solid fruits of most other marsh plants.
children.funFact: Despite their common name, pod-grasses aren't actually grasses at all - they're more closely related to water lilies and other aquatic flowering plants!

children.name: Ruppiaceae
Ruppia
children.description: Widgeonweeds are delicate aquatic plants that live completely underwater in salty or brackish water environments. These slender plants have thin, grass-like leaves and produce tiny flowers that bloom beneath the water's surface. They're specially adapted to life in coastal waters where salt levels can vary with the tides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most aquatic plants, widgeonweeds can tolerate a wide range of salt levels and actually bloom underwater rather than sending flowers to the surface. Their thread-like leaves and ability to thrive in both salt and brackish water sets them apart from freshwater aquatic grasses.
children.funFact: Widgeonweeds got their name because they're a favorite food of widgeon ducks and other waterfowl - the seeds and tender shoots provide important nutrition for migrating birds along coastal flyways.

children.description: The widgeonweed family consists of delicate aquatic plants that live entirely underwater in saltwater and brackish environments. These slender plants have thin, grass-like leaves and produce tiny flowers that bloom beneath the water's surface, making them well-adapted to marine life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most aquatic plants that prefer freshwater, widgeonweeds are specially adapted to thrive in salty conditions, with flowers that pollinate underwater rather than above the surface.
children.funFact: Widgeonweeds got their name because waterfowl, especially widgeon ducks, love to eat their nutritious seeds and shoots, making these plants an important food source in coastal ecosystems.

children.description: This diverse order consists mostly of aquatic and semi-aquatic flowering plants that have adapted to life in or near water. Members include familiar wetland plants like arums and water plantains, as well as fully submerged species like pondweeds and seagrasses. Despite their varied appearances, these plants share ancient evolutionary roots and similar reproductive strategies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most flowering plants, many members of this group have simplified flowers without typical petals, and their pollen is often adapted for water dispersal rather than wind or insect pollination. Their leaves frequently show adaptations for aquatic life, such as air-filled tissues for buoyancy or ribbon-like shapes that move with water currents.
children.funFact: Seagrasses in this group are among the few flowering plants that have returned to live completely in saltwater oceans, where they form underwater meadows that provide crucial habitat for marine life.

children.name: Liliales
Liliaceae
Lilium
children.description: True lilies are stunning wildflowers known for their large, showy blooms with six petals that curve backward and prominent stamens that extend outward. These perennial plants grow from scaly bulbs and produce tall stems with lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls or spirals. Most species bloom in summer and can be found in meadows, woodlands, and wet areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other plants commonly called 'lilies,' true lilies have distinctive recurved petals that curve backward, creating a turban-like shape, and their flowers always have exactly six stamens with large, often colorful anthers.
children.funFact: The tiger lily can reproduce without pollination by forming small black bulbils along its stem that drop to the ground and grow into new plants, making it one of the few lilies that can clone itself!

children.name: Erythronium
