children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their ability to tolerate very dry conditions and their preference for rocky substrates. They have distinctive leaf arrangements and spore capsules that help distinguish them from other moss families.
children.funFact: These hardy mosses can survive extreme dehydration by curling up their leaves when dry, then quickly returning to life when moisture returns - like tiny resurrection plants!

children.name: Saelaniaceae
Saelania
children.description: Saelania is a small genus of mosses that contains only one species found in New England - the Blue Dew-moss. These are hardy, cushion-forming mosses that grow in dense, compact mats on rocks and soil in harsh environments. They are well-adapted to survive in challenging conditions like high altitudes and exposed locations.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Blue Dew-moss gets its name from its distinctive blue-green to grayish coloration, which helps distinguish it from other small cushion mosses. The plants form tight, rounded cushions with short, densely packed shoots.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'Blue Dew-moss,' this hardy little plant is actually quite drought-tolerant and can survive in some of the most exposed, windswept locations where few other mosses can grow.

children.description: Saelaniaceae is a small family of mosses that includes only one genus, Saelania. These are tiny, cushion-forming mosses that grow in harsh, exposed environments like rock crevices and cliff faces. They are adapted to survive in extremely dry conditions and can tolerate long periods without water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their very small size, dense cushion-like growth form, and specialized leaves that curl tightly when dry to conserve moisture. They have a unique cell structure that helps them survive in rocky, nutrient-poor habitats.
children.funFact: Saelania mosses can survive being completely dried out for months and will quickly revive and turn green again within hours of receiving moisture, making them true resurrection plants.

children.description: Grimmiales are small, cushion-forming mosses that specialize in surviving in some of nature's toughest spots. These hardy little plants are masters of dry, rocky habitats where few other mosses can thrive, often growing directly on bare rock surfaces, concrete, or in sandy soil.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their ability to curl their leaves tightly when dry to conserve moisture, and they typically form dense, compact cushions or mats. Their leaves often have thick cell walls and specialized structures that help them survive extreme dehydration.
children.funFact: Some Grimmiales mosses can survive losing up to 95% of their water content and appear completely dead, only to spring back to life within minutes of getting wet again.

children.name: Orthotrichales
Orthotrichaceae
Ulota
children.description: Ulota is a genus of small mosses commonly known as pincushion mosses due to their distinctive cushion-like growth form. These mosses typically grow on tree bark, rocks, or other surfaces, forming compact, rounded clumps that resemble tiny green pincushions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ulota mosses are characterized by their leaves that curl and crisp when dry, then unfurl when wet. They also have distinctive capsules (spore-bearing structures) that are often ribbed or furrowed when dry.
children.funFact: Pincushion mosses can survive extreme dehydration by curling their leaves tightly when dry, then quickly spring back to life when moisture returns - sometimes in just minutes!

children.name: Orthotrichum
children.description: Bristle mosses are small, cushion-forming mosses that typically grow on tree bark, rocks, and other hard surfaces. They get their name from the distinctive bristle-like structures (called peristome teeth) that surround the opening of their spore capsules, which help control spore release.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other mosses, bristle mosses have specialized double rows of teeth around their capsule openings that move in response to humidity changes. Their capsules are also typically immersed in or barely emerging from the surrounding leaves when mature.
children.funFact: The bristle-like teeth of these mosses act like tiny humidity sensors, opening and closing to release spores only when conditions are just right for dispersal and germination.

children.name: Lewinskya
children.description: Lewinskya is a genus of small, cushion-forming mosses commonly known as bristle mosses. These mosses typically grow on tree bark, rocks, and other surfaces, forming dense, rounded patches that can withstand dry conditions better than many other moss species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bristle mosses are distinguished by their distinctive spore capsules that have prominent bristle-like structures (called peristome teeth) around the opening, which help control spore release.
children.funFact: These mosses can survive extreme dehydration by curling up their leaves tightly, then quickly spring back to life when moisture returns - a process that can happen repeatedly without harming the plant.

children.name: Nyholmiella
children.description: Nyholmiella is a small genus of mosses that includes some of the tiniest bristle mosses found in nature. These diminutive plants form small cushions or mats on rocks, bark, and soil, and are characterized by their distinctive bristle-like structures that help with spore dispersal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Nyholmiella mosses are distinguished by their extremely small size and blunt, rounded leaf tips that give them a softer appearance compared to other bristle mosses with sharp-pointed leaves.
children.funFact: Despite being among the smallest mosses in New England, Nyholmiella species are remarkably hardy and can survive in harsh conditions by entering a state of dormancy during dry periods, then quickly resuming growth when moisture returns.

children.name: Drummondia
children.description: Drummondia is a genus containing just one species of moss found in New England - the Train Track Moss. This distinctive moss forms flat, creeping mats that spread along surfaces, creating carpet-like patches in its preferred habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Train Track Moss gets its name from its tendency to grow along railroad tracks and other disturbed, sunny locations - unusual for most mosses which prefer shaded, moist environments.
children.funFact: This hardy moss is one of the few mosses that actually thrives in direct sunlight and can tolerate the heat and dryness found along railway corridors.

children.name: Plenogemma
children.description: Plenogemma is a small genus of mosses known for their distinctive cushion-like growth form. These tiny plants create dense, rounded mats that resemble miniature pincushions on rocks, soil, and other surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely compact, cushion-forming growth habit and small, tightly overlapping leaves that give them a distinctive frizzled appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, these moss cushions can be surprisingly long-lived, with some individual colonies persisting for decades in the same spot.

children.description: The Orthotrichaceae family consists of small, cushion-forming mosses that typically grow on tree bark, rocks, and other hard surfaces. These mosses are characterized by their upright growth pattern and distinctive spore capsules that often have specialized structures for spore release. Most species in this family are quite tolerant of dry conditions and can be found in both urban and natural environments throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their capsules, which are often ribbed or grooved and typically have a ring of teeth around the opening that help control spore dispersal. Many species also have specialized hairs on their leaves that help them retain moisture.
children.funFact: Many Orthotrichaceae mosses can survive extreme dehydration by curling up their leaves tightly when dry, then quickly returning to active growth when moisture returns - earning some species the nickname 'resurrection mosses.'

children.description: Orthotrichales is an order of small mosses that typically grow as compact cushions or tufts on tree bark, rocks, and occasionally soil. These mosses are characterized by their distinctive spore capsules that often have prominent vertical ridges and specialized structures called peristome teeth that help with spore dispersal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order can be identified by their unique capsule structure with vertical pleats or ridges, and their peristome teeth are often arranged in a distinctive pattern that differs from other moss groups.
children.funFact: Many Orthotrichales mosses are excellent air quality indicators - they're particularly sensitive to air pollution, so finding healthy populations of these mosses often signals clean air in the area.

children.name: Pottiales
Pottiaceae
Syntrichia
children.description: Syntrichia is a genus of small cushion-forming mosses that are remarkably tough and drought-resistant. These mosses are commonly found growing on rocks, soil, and tree bark, where they form dense, rounded patches that can survive extremely dry conditions by curling up their leaves to conserve moisture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Syntrichia mosses are distinguished by their thick, fleshy leaves that have distinctive hair-like tips called awns, and their ability to tightly curl their leaves when dry, giving them a twisted, screw-like appearance.
children.funFact: These mosses are so drought-tolerant that they can lose up to 95% of their water content and appear completely dead, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet again.

children.name: Weissia
children.description: Weissia is a genus of small, cushion-forming mosses that grow in dense tufts or patches. These tiny mosses are commonly found on bare soil, disturbed ground, and rocky surfaces where they form green carpets. They are part of the beardless moss family and play an important role as pioneer species in colonizing new habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Weissia mosses can be distinguished from other small soil mosses by their distinctive spore capsules that have small mouth openings (peristomes) or may lack them entirely. Their leaves are typically narrow and pointed, often with a prominent midrib.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'beardless mosses,' some Weissia species actually do have tiny tooth-like structures around their capsule openings, but these are much smaller and less conspicuous than the elaborate 'beards' found in related moss families.

children.name: Geheebia
children.description: Geheebia is a small genus of beard mosses that form dense, cushion-like mats on rocks and tree bark. These tiny mosses are characterized by their thread-like stems and small, overlapping leaves that give them a distinctive texture. They thrive in humid environments and can often be found growing in shaded areas throughout New England's forests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Geheebia mosses can be distinguished from other beard mosses by their particularly dense growth pattern and the way their leaves are arranged in tight spirals around the stem, creating a rope-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'beard moss,' these plants can actually change color dramatically when wet versus dry, with the Rusty Beard-moss living up to its name by displaying rusty reddish-brown hues when moisture levels change.

children.name: Streblotrichum
children.description: Streblotrichum is a small genus of mosses known for their distinctive twisted and curled leaves that give them a characteristic beard-like appearance. These tiny mosses typically grow in small cushions or patches on soil, rocks, or disturbed ground in various habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The twisted, spirally-curled leaves that resemble tiny corkscrews or bird claws set Streblotrichum apart from other moss genera, along with their distinctive capsule shape and peristome structure.
children.funFact: The name 'Streblotrichum' literally means 'twisted hair' in Greek, perfectly describing the characteristic curly appearance of their leaves that earned them the common name 'bird's-claw beard-moss.'

children.name: Tortula
children.description: Tortula is a genus of small mosses that are well-adapted to dry conditions and urban environments. These hardy mosses form dense, cushion-like patches and can survive in places where other mosses struggle, including on walls, rocks, and concrete surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tortula mosses have distinctive twisted, corkscrew-shaped leaves when dry, which is where their common name 'screw-moss' comes from. Their leaves untwist and spread out when wet, helping them capture moisture efficiently.
children.funFact: Wall Screw-moss can survive being completely dried out for months, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet - making it one of nature's most resilient urban colonizers.

children.name: Tortella
children.description: Tortella is a genus of small mosses known for their distinctive twisted appearance. These mosses typically grow in dense, cushion-like mats and are characterized by their spirally twisted leaves that become more pronounced when the moss dries out.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Tortella can be identified by their leaves that twist and curl in a distinctive spiral pattern, especially when dry. This twisting behavior is more pronounced than in most other moss genera.
children.funFact: The name 'Tortella' comes from the Latin word meaning 'little twisted thing,' perfectly describing how these mosses curl their leaves into tight spirals to conserve moisture during dry periods.

children.name: Barbula
children.description: Barbula is a genus of small mosses known for their distinctive twisted leaf tips that curl when dry, giving them a characteristic corkscrew appearance. These mosses are typically found growing on soil, rocks, and disturbed ground in a variety of habitats. They are part of the larger family of mosses called Pottiaceae, which are known for their ability to tolerate dry conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barbula mosses are easily recognized by their leaves that twist and curl in a spiral pattern when they dry out, resembling tiny corkscrews. The spore capsules are often cylindrical and held upright on slender stalks.
children.funFact: The name 'Barbula' comes from the Latin word for 'little beard,' referring to the hair-like structures (called peristome teeth) that surround the opening of the spore capsule and help disperse the tiny spores.

children.name: Acaulon
children.description: Acaulon is a genus of tiny mosses that are among the smallest you'll find in New England. These diminutive plants form small, inconspicuous patches on soil and are so small they're easily overlooked without close inspection. They belong to a group of mosses that have very short or nearly absent stems, giving them their characteristically low-growing appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Acaulon mosses are distinguished by their extremely small size and their habit of growing directly on bare soil rather than on rocks or trees. Unlike many other mosses, they rarely produce the tall stalks (sporophytes) that hold spore capsules, instead reproducing mainly through tiny spores released directly from capsules that sit close to the ground.
children.funFact: Despite being one of the smallest mosses in New England, Acaulon plays an important ecological role as a pioneer species, being among the first plants to colonize disturbed or bare soil.

children.name: Ephemerum
children.description: Ephemerum is a genus of tiny, ephemeral mosses that live up to their name by having extremely short lifecycles. These microscopic mosses are among the smallest in the world, often completing their entire life cycle in just a few weeks or months before disappearing until conditions are right again.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mosses, Ephemerum species lack the typical leafy shoots (gametophores) that we associate with mosses, instead producing only small, bud-like structures. They also reproduce primarily through spores rather than the vegetative reproduction common in many other moss groups.
children.funFact: Ephemerum mosses are so small that an entire plant, including its spore capsule, can be smaller than the head of a pin and may only be visible with a magnifying glass.

children.name: Gymnostomum
children.description: Gymnostomum is a genus of small mosses that typically grow in harsh, mineral-rich environments like limestone cliffs and concrete structures. These tiny plants form dense, cushion-like patches and are known for their ability to tolerate high levels of minerals and alkaline conditions that would be toxic to most other mosses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctive capsules (spore-containing structures) that lack a ring of teeth around the opening, which is unusual among mosses and gives the genus its name meaning 'naked mouth.'
children.funFact: Verdigris Tufa-moss gets its name from its blue-green coloration that resembles verdigris, the patina that forms on weathered copper, making it one of the most uniquely colored mosses in New England.

children.name: Hyophila
children.description: Hyophila is a small genus of mosses that typically grow in dense, cushion-like patches on soil, rocks, and disturbed ground. These tiny mosses are part of the pottiaceae family and are known for their ability to colonize bare or recently disturbed areas where other plants struggle to establish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hyophila mosses can be identified by their small size, dense growth pattern, and distinctive leaf shape with rolled margins that help them conserve moisture in dry conditions.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny and easily overlooked, Hyophila mosses are pioneer species that help stabilize soil and create conditions for other plants to grow, making them important ecosystem engineers in disturbed habitats.

children.description: The Pottiaceae family consists of small but hardy mosses that are masters of surviving in dry, challenging environments. These tough little plants often form cushions or mats on soil, rocks, and disturbed ground, and many can quickly revive after periods of drought. You'll commonly find them growing on bare earth, walls, rooftops, and other exposed locations where many other mosses can't survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pottiaceae mosses are distinguished by their typically twisted, spiraled leaves that often have thick midribs and specialized cells that help retain moisture. Many species in this family also have distinctive spore capsules with twisted teeth that help disperse spores.
children.funFact: Some Pottiaceae mosses can lose up to 98% of their water content and appear completely dead, only to spring back to life within minutes of getting wet again - earning them the nickname 'resurrection mosses.'

children.description: Pottiales is an order of small mosses that are commonly found growing in disturbed habitats like soil, rocks, and concrete surfaces. These hardy little plants are often among the first to colonize bare ground and can tolerate dry conditions better than many other mosses. They typically form small cushions or mats of tiny, densely packed shoots.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pottiales mosses are characterized by their small size, simple leaves that often have thickened borders, and spore capsules that usually have a twisted, corkscrew-like structure called a peristome. Many species in this order have leaves with specialized water-conducting cells that help them survive in drier environments.
children.funFact: Some Pottiales mosses can survive being completely dried out for months and then spring back to life when water returns, earning them the nickname 'resurrection mosses.'

children.name: Splachnales
Splachnaceae
Tetraplodon
children.description: Cruet-mosses are small but distinctive mosses that get their name from their unique spore capsules, which are shaped like tiny cruets or bottles with narrow necks. These specialized mosses have adapted to grow in nutrient-rich environments, particularly where animal droppings or decaying organic matter provide extra nitrogen. They're found in both woodland and alpine environments across New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The bottle-shaped spore capsules with constricted necks clearly distinguish cruet-mosses from other moss groups. Their preference for nitrogen-rich substrates, especially animal waste, also sets them apart from most other mosses.
children.funFact: Cruet-mosses are nature's recyclers - they specialize in growing on animal droppings and help break down waste materials while creating their own little green gardens in these unlikely spots.

children.name: Splachnum
children.description: Splachnum is a unique genus of mosses that have evolved a fascinating partnership with the animal kingdom. These small mosses are specialists that grow exclusively on animal dung, where they play an important role in nutrient cycling by helping decompose organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Splachnum apart from other mosses is their highly specialized habitat requirement and their distinctive spore capsules, which are often enlarged and colorful to attract insects that help disperse their spores.
children.funFact: These clever mosses actually mimic flowers by producing brightly colored, sometimes umbrella-shaped capsules that attract flies and other insects, tricking them into carrying moss spores to new dung piles!

children.name: Tayloria
children.description: Poo mosses are a small genus of specialized mosses that have evolved a unique survival strategy. These tiny plants grow exclusively on animal dung, particularly from herbivorous mammals like deer, moose, and cattle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mosses that grow on soil, rocks, or wood, poo mosses are obligate coprophiles, meaning they can only complete their life cycle on fresh animal droppings.
children.funFact: Poo mosses have evolved to take advantage of the nitrogen-rich environment of dung, and their spores are often dispersed by the very animals whose waste they depend on for survival.

children.description: Dung mosses are a specialized family of mosses that have evolved to grow exclusively on animal droppings and decaying organic matter. These small but remarkable plants have developed unique adaptations to thrive in nutrient-rich environments that most other mosses cannot tolerate. They play an important ecological role by helping decompose waste materials in forest and field ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mosses, dung mosses have enlarged, often colorful capsules (spore containers) that are specifically designed to attract flies and other insects. These capsules frequently have distinctive umbrella-like or swollen shapes that make them easily recognizable.
children.funFact: Dung mosses actually rely on flies to help spread their spores - the insects are attracted to the mosses' bright colors and fruity scents, mistaking them for something edible, and accidentally carry spores to new dung piles on their bodies.

children.name: Meesiaceae
Paludella
children.description: Paludella is a genus containing just one species of moss found in wetland environments. This moss forms distinctive tufted cushions in fens, bogs, and other calcium-rich wetlands throughout cooler regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Paludella squarrosa is easily recognized by its characteristic backwards-curved (squarrose) leaves that give it a distinctly tufted, almost porcupine-like appearance when viewed up close.
children.funFact: Despite being the only species in its genus, Tufted Fen-moss plays an important role as an indicator species - its presence often signals high-quality, mineral-rich wetland habitats that support diverse plant communities.

children.name: Leptobryum
children.description: Leptobryum is a small genus of mosses known for their delicate, thread-like appearance and distinctive pear-shaped spore capsules. These tiny mosses typically grow in disturbed soils, forming small patches or scattered individual plants rather than dense mats like many other moss species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Leptobryum mosses are recognized by their characteristically swollen, pear-shaped capsules that hang from slender, often reddish stalks. The leaves are small and narrow, giving the plants their thread-like appearance that distinguishes them from bulkier moss genera.
children.funFact: Golden Thread-moss is considered a pioneer species that often appears on freshly disturbed soil, making it one of the first mosses to colonize areas like construction sites or bare patches in gardens.

children.name: Meesia
children.description: Meesia is a small genus of mosses known for their distinctive humped or swollen capsules that contain spores. These mosses are typically found in wet, alkaline habitats like fens and boggy areas. They are relatively uncommon and specialized mosses that prefer calcium-rich environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Meesia mosses are easily recognized by their characteristic swollen, pear-shaped spore capsules that appear humped or bulging compared to other mosses. The capsules are typically held upright on relatively short stalks.
children.funFact: The common name 'humpmoss' comes from the distinctively swollen, hump-backed appearance of their spore capsules, which look quite different from the more cylindrical capsules of most other mosses.

children.description: Meesiaceae is a small family of mosses that typically grow in wet, nutrient-poor environments like bogs, fens, and other wetlands. These mosses are known for their distinctive curved capsules (spore-containing structures) that often droop or nod downward when mature. Most members of this family are found in cooler northern regions and are well-adapted to waterlogged, acidic conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The curved or drooping capsules set Meesiaceae apart from many other moss families, along with their preference for extremely wet habitats. Their leaves are often arranged in a distinctive pattern and have specialized cells that help them thrive in waterlogged conditions.
children.funFact: Some Meesiaceae mosses can actually float on water and continue photosynthesis even when partially submerged, making them true aquatic plants that blur the line between terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

children.description: Splachnales is an order of mosses that includes some of nature's most specialized recyclers. These mosses have evolved unique adaptations to thrive in nutrient-rich environments, particularly around decomposing organic matter like animal dung and decaying plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive spore capsules that often have specialized structures for spore dispersal, and many species have adapted to grow specifically on dung or other organic substrates rich in nitrogen.
children.funFact: Dung mosses in this group have evolved colorful, umbrella-like structures on their spore capsules that attract flies, which then help disperse the moss spores - making these mosses some of the few that actively recruit animals for reproduction!

children.name: Bartramiales
Bartramiaceae
Philonotis
children.description: Philonotis is a genus of small mosses that typically grow in wet, alkaline environments like springs, seeps, and stream banks. These mosses form distinctive cushion-like or mat-forming colonies and are often found where mineral-rich water flows over rocks or soil. They play an important role in wetland ecosystems by helping to stabilize soil and create microhabitats for other small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Philonotis mosses can be distinguished from other wetland mosses by their tendency to grow in perfectly spherical, apple-shaped capsules (spore containers) and their preference for calcareous or mineral-rich water sources rather than acidic bogs.
children.funFact: The common name "apple-moss" comes from the round, apple-like shape of their spore capsules, which often have a distinctive reddish color when mature.

children.name: Bartramia
children.description: Bartramia is a genus of mosses known for their distinctive apple-shaped capsules that give them their common name of apple-moss. These mosses form small, cushion-like clumps and are found growing on soil, rocks, and decaying wood in various habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Bartramia mosses is their round, apple-shaped spore capsules that sit atop curved stalks, making them easily recognizable among other moss species.
children.funFact: The spore capsules of apple-moss are ribbed and grooved like tiny apples, and when mature, they open by splitting along these grooves to release their spores.

children.name: Plagiopus
children.description: Plagiopus is a small genus of mosses that includes just one species found in New England. These are distinctive mosses that grow in small, dense cushions or mats, typically found on rocks and soil in mountainous areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Plagiopus mosses are recognized by their unique leaf arrangement and the way their capsules (spore-bearing structures) are positioned at an angle rather than upright.
children.funFact: The name 'Plagiopus' literally means 'oblique foot,' referring to the angled position of the moss's spore capsules.

children.name: Conostomum
children.description: Conostomum is a small genus of mosses known for their distinctive cone-shaped spore capsules that give them their common name of helmet-moss. These mosses are typically found in rocky, mountainous areas and are adapted to harsh alpine conditions. They form small, cushion-like patches on rocks and soil in high-elevation environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Conostomum is its uniquely shaped spore capsule that resembles a pointed helmet or cone, which is quite different from the more cylindrical capsules of most other mosses.
children.funFact: Helmet-moss is considered one of the hardiest mosses in New England, capable of surviving extreme temperature fluctuations and intense UV radiation at high elevations where few other plants can thrive.

children.description: Bartramiaceae is a family of mosses that typically form dense, cushion-like mats or tufts in moist environments. These mosses are commonly found growing on soil, rocks, and wet surfaces like stream banks, where they create soft, spongy carpets that help retain moisture in their habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their spherical spore capsules that are often ribbed or grooved, and their leaves typically have a distinctive apple-green color when fresh and moist.
children.funFact: Some Bartramiaceae mosses can absorb and hold up to 20 times their dry weight in water, making them natural sponges that help prevent soil erosion along waterways.

children.description: Bartramiales is a small order of mosses that includes just one family found in New England. These mosses are characterized by their distinctive spherical spore capsules that sit atop long, thin stalks called setae. They typically grow in cushion-like clumps or mats in various habitats from soil to rock surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are easily recognized by their round, ball-shaped spore capsules that look like tiny green marbles on sticks. The capsules have a unique ribbed or pleated surface texture that helps distinguish them from other moss groups.
children.funFact: The spore capsules of Bartramiales mosses are perfectly spherical and can actually roll around when they fall, helping to disperse spores over greater distances than many other moss types.

children.name: Aulacomniales
Aulacomniaceae
Aulacomnium
children.description: Aulacomnium mosses are small, cushion-forming mosses that thrive in wet, acidic environments like bogs, fens, and moist woodlands. These hardy mosses are characterized by their distinctive grooved or ribbed leaves that help channel water, making them well-adapted to life in constantly moist conditions. They form compact, often colorful patches ranging from bright green to reddish-brown.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Aulacomnium apart from other mosses is their deeply grooved or furrowed leaves that create distinct ridges running lengthwise. Many species in this genus also produce unique reproductive structures called gemmae - small bud-like clusters that can break off to form new plants.
children.funFact: Ribbed bog moss can survive being completely frozen and thawed repeatedly, making it one of the most cold-hardy mosses in New England's harsh winter climate.

children.description: The Aulacomniaceae are a family of mosses known for their distinctive growth patterns and specialized reproductive structures. These mosses typically form cushions or turfs and are characterized by their ability to produce both sexual spores and specialized vegetative propagules called gemmae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique gemma cups or modified leaf tips that produce small, multicellular propagules for asexual reproduction. They also have distinctive peristome teeth (structures around the spore capsule opening) that help identify them from other moss families.
children.funFact: Some Aulacomniaceae mosses can reproduce without sex by dropping tiny plantlets called gemmae from specialized cups, allowing them to quickly colonize new areas even when conditions aren't right for sexual reproduction.

children.description: Aulacomniales is a small order of mosses that includes just one family found in New England. These are typically medium-sized mosses that grow in dense cushions or mats, often found in wet or moist environments like stream banks, wet rocks, and boggy areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mosses are distinguished by their distinctive leaf structure and the way their spore capsules are positioned, often curved or bent rather than straight upright.
children.funFact: Despite being a small group with only 4 species in New England, these mosses are incredibly hardy and can survive being submerged underwater for extended periods during floods.

children.name: Hedwigiales
Hedwigiaceae
Hedwigia
children.description: Hoarmosses are small, cushion-forming mosses that grow directly on rock surfaces, particularly granite and other hard stones. These hardy little plants create dense, grayish-green mats that can withstand extreme drying and freezing conditions. They're commonly found on exposed rocky outcrops, stone walls, and boulders throughout New England's forests and mountains.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hoarmosses are easily recognized by their distinctive hair-pointed leaves that give them a silvery or hoary appearance, especially when dry. Unlike many other rock-dwelling mosses, they lack a central stem (costa) in their leaves and have specialized leaf cells that help them survive on bare rock.
children.funFact: Hoarmosses can survive being completely dried out for months, appearing almost dead, but will quickly turn green and resume photosynthesis within minutes of getting wet again.

children.description: The Hoarmoss Family consists of small, cushion-forming mosses that grow directly on rock surfaces, particularly on exposed cliffs and boulders. These hardy mosses are well-adapted to dry conditions and can often be found in sunny, exposed locations where few other mosses can survive. They form compact, grayish-green mats that can cover large areas of bare rock.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hoarmosses are unique among mosses for their ability to thrive on bare rock in full sunlight and dry conditions. Their leaves often have a distinctive grayish appearance due to specialized hair-like extensions that help reflect light and conserve moisture.
children.funFact: Hoarmosses get their common name from their gray, frost-like appearance - 'hoar' is an old English word meaning gray or grayish-white, like hoarfrost.

children.description: Hedwigiales is a small order of mosses that includes species commonly known as hoarmosses. These mosses are characterized by their unique reproductive structures and often grow as cushions or mats on rocks and tree bark. They represent an ancient lineage of mosses with distinctive features that set them apart from other moss groups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hedwigiales mosses have specialized spore-bearing structures called capsules that lack a lid (operculum) and instead split open irregularly to release spores. Their leaves often have thick, waxy coatings that give them a distinctive appearance and help them retain moisture.
children.funFact: The name 'hoarmoss' comes from their frosted or whitish appearance, which resembles hoarfrost on a cold morning, caused by the waxy coating on their leaves that reflects light.

children.name: Funariales
Funariaceae
Physcomitrium
children.description: Goblet mosses are small, delicate mosses that get their name from their distinctive urn-shaped spore capsules that look like tiny goblets or cups. These mosses are annual plants, meaning they complete their entire life cycle in one year, which is unusual among mosses that typically live for multiple years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The goblet-shaped spore capsules with wide mouths and the annual growth habit set these mosses apart from most other moss species, which tend to have cylindrical capsules and perennial growth.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny plants often less than an inch tall, goblet mosses can produce thousands of spores from each capsule, helping them quickly colonize disturbed soil after events like floods or construction.

children.name: Funaria
children.description: Funaria is a genus of small mosses that are among the most common and widely distributed mosses in the world. These mosses typically grow in disturbed soils and are often found in areas that have been burned or otherwise cleared, earning them the common name of bonfire mosses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Funaria mosses are recognized by their distinctive curved, pear-shaped spore capsules that hang from twisted stalks, and their bright green, rosette-forming leaves that often have a silvery appearance when dry.
children.funFact: Bonfire moss gets its name from its tendency to be one of the first plants to colonize burned areas, where it helps stabilize the soil and begin the process of ecological recovery.

children.description: Funariaceae is a family of small mosses that are often among the first to appear in disturbed soils, gardens, and other human-modified landscapes. These hardy little plants are excellent colonizers, quickly establishing themselves in areas where other mosses might struggle to take hold. They're characterized by their relatively simple structure and their ability to complete their life cycle rapidly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family typically have distinctive capsules (spore-containing structures) that are often pear-shaped or bulbous, and many species have capsules that bend or curve as they mature. Their leaves are usually soft and somewhat translucent compared to many other moss families.
children.funFact: Funaria, one of the genera in this family, is commonly called "cord moss" because its spore capsules hang from curved stalks that look like tiny cords, and it's one of the most frequently studied mosses in biology classes worldwide.

children.description: Funariales is a small order of mosses that includes some of the most common and recognizable moss species found in disturbed habitats. These mosses are often pioneers, quickly colonizing bare soil, roadsides, gardens, and other human-modified environments where other plants struggle to establish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their relatively large, pear-shaped capsules (spore containers) that often have a distinctive neck region. The capsules typically have a well-developed peristome with teeth that help control spore release.
children.funFact: The common cord-moss in this order is often one of the first mosses that botanists learn to identify because it's so widespread in urban and suburban areas, thriving in sidewalk cracks and disturbed soil.

children.name: Diphysciales
Diphysciaceae
Diphyscium
children.description: Diphyscium is a unique genus of moss with only one species found in New England - the aptly named Powder Gun Moss. These small mosses are distinguished by their unusual spore-dispersal mechanism, where spores are shot out in puffs like powder from a tiny cannon. They typically grow on acidic soil in shaded forest areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mosses, Diphyscium has a distinctive spore capsule that opens with a special lid and shoots spores out forcefully rather than simply releasing them passively.
children.funFact: The Powder Gun Moss earned its common name because when ripe, its spore capsules actually make tiny 'popping' sounds as they explosively release clouds of spores into the air.

children.description: Diphysciaceae is a small family of mosses that includes just one genus found in New England. These are tiny, inconspicuous mosses that grow on soil, rocks, and decaying wood in shaded areas. They have a unique spore-bearing structure that sets them apart from other moss families.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive capsules (spore containers) that are held upright and have a peculiar opening mechanism with multiple slits rather than a simple lid like most mosses.
children.funFact: Despite being mosses, Diphysciaceae species are so small and rare that they're often overlooked even by experienced botanists, making them some of the most mysterious plants in New England's forests.

children.description: Diphysciales is a small order of mosses that includes just one family found in New England. These are tiny, often overlooked mosses that grow in specialized habitats and have unique spore-producing structures. They represent one of the more uncommon groups of mosses you might encounter while exploring.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their distinctive capsules (spore-producing structures) that have unusual opening mechanisms and specific cellular arrangements that set them apart from other moss groups.
children.funFact: This entire order is represented by just a single species in all of New England, making any encounter with a Diphysciales moss a truly special botanical discovery.

children.name: Buxbaumiales
Buxbaumiaceae
Buxbaumia
children.description: Buxbaumia is a unique genus of mosses that produces some of the most unusual-looking spore capsules in the plant kingdom. These tiny mosses have greatly reduced leafy parts and are known for their distinctive, asymmetrical capsules that sit atop slender stalks, giving them their common name 'bug-on-a-stick.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike typical mosses, Buxbaumia species have extremely small, scale-like leaves that are barely visible, and their large, flattened spore capsules are strongly asymmetrical with a distinctive tilted appearance.
children.funFact: The spore capsules of Buxbaumia can be up to 100 times larger than the tiny plant body that produces them, making them look like alien creatures perched on sticks in the forest.

children.description: The Buxbaumiaceae are a small family of unusual mosses known for their bizarre, asymmetrical appearance. These tiny mosses have extremely reduced leafy stems and produce distinctive, flattened capsules (spore containers) that look almost alien compared to typical mosses.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mosses, Buxbaumiaceae have highly asymmetrical, flattened capsules that are tilted at an angle rather than standing upright. Their leafy shoots are so reduced they're barely visible, making the odd-shaped capsules the most noticeable feature.
children.funFact: These mosses are sometimes called 'bug-on-a-stick' because their strange, lopsided capsules perched on thin stalks look like tiny insects when viewed from a distance.

children.description: Buxbaumiales is a small order of mosses known for their highly unusual and distinctive sporophytes (spore-producing structures). These mosses produce some of the most bizarre-looking capsules in the entire moss world, often appearing flattened, asymmetrical, or boot-shaped rather than the typical cylindrical form of most moss capsules.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are instantly recognizable by their extremely flattened, asymmetrical spore capsules that look nothing like typical moss capsules. The capsules often appear tilted or lopsided and have a unique internal structure with specialized spore-dispersal mechanisms.
children.funFact: The capsules of Buxbaumiales mosses are so unusual that early botanists sometimes mistook them for fungi or lichens rather than recognizing them as moss reproductive structures!

children.name: Encalyptales
Encalyptaceae
Encalypta
children.description: Encalypta is a genus of small mosses known for their distinctive hood-like structures that cover their spore capsules. These mosses typically grow in small cushions or tufts on soil, rocks, or disturbed ground. They are part of the larger group of mosses that reproduce by releasing spores from capsules held above the plant on thin stalks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Encalypta apart from other mosses is the large, bell-shaped or cylindrical hood (called a calyptra) that completely covers the spore capsule, often extending well below it. This protective covering is much more prominent and longer-lasting than the small caps found on most other moss genera.
children.funFact: The name 'Extinguisher Moss' comes from the hood's resemblance to the cone-shaped caps once used to snuff out candle flames - when the spore capsule is mature, it looks just like a tiny candle extinguisher!

children.description: Encalyptaceae is a small family of mosses known for their distinctive protective caps that cover their spore capsules. These mosses are typically found growing on soil, rocks, or disturbed ground in various habitats. The family contains only one genus, Encalypta, with species distributed across temperate regions of the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The most distinctive feature of Encalyptaceae mosses is their large, hood-like calyptra (cap) that completely covers the spore capsule, often extending well below it. This protective covering is much more prominent and extensive than in most other moss families.
children.funFact: The name 'Encalypta' comes from Greek words meaning 'veiled' or 'covered,' referring to the characteristic hood that makes these mosses look like they're wearing tiny caps or bonnets.

children.description: Encalyptales is a small order of mosses known for their distinctive reproductive structures. These mosses are characterized by having a special cap-like covering called a calyptra that protects their spore capsules, which splits open in a unique way when the spores are ready to be released.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order have capsules that open by splitting lengthwise into segments, rather than having a removable lid like most other mosses. The calyptra (protective cap) is particularly large and prominent, often covering most of the capsule.
children.funFact: The name 'Encalyptales' comes from Greek words meaning 'covered' or 'veiled,' referring to the distinctive hood-like calyptra that covers their spore capsules like a tiny cap.

children.name: Sphagnales
Sphagnaceae
Sphagnum
children.description: Sphagnum mosses are the spongy, water-loving mosses that dominate bogs and wetlands throughout New England. These remarkable plants can absorb and hold up to 20 times their weight in water, creating the acidic, waterlogged conditions that define bog ecosystems. They grow in dense carpets that slowly build up over centuries to form peat deposits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mosses, Sphagnum species have specialized hollow cells that act like tiny water tanks, giving them their incredible water-absorbing ability. They also lack roots and instead absorb water and nutrients directly through their leaves.
children.funFact: Sphagnum moss was used as natural bandages during World War I because of its absorbent properties and natural antiseptic compounds that help prevent infection.

children.description: The peat moss family consists of soft, spongy mosses that form thick carpets in wetlands, bogs, and other moist environments. These mosses have a unique ability to absorb and hold enormous amounts of water - up to 20 times their dry weight - making them feel like natural sponges when you squeeze them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mosses, peat mosses have specialized hollow cells that can rapidly absorb water, and they lack true roots, instead anchoring themselves with simple structures called rhizoids.
children.funFact: Peat moss is so effective at preserving organic matter that ancient peat bogs have yielded perfectly preserved human remains thousands of years old, including clothing and even stomach contents!

children.description: Peat mosses are specialized bog mosses that form the spongy, acidic carpets found in wetlands throughout New England. These remarkable plants can absorb and hold up to 20 times their weight in water, creating the waterlogged conditions that preserve organic matter and form peat deposits over thousands of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mosses, peat mosses have unique hollow cells that act like tiny water tanks, and they actively acidify their environment by releasing hydrogen ions. They also lack the root-like structures (rhizoids) that most other mosses use for attachment.
children.funFact: Peat mosses are so effective at preserving organic matter that bog bodies thousands of years old have been found perfectly preserved in peat deposits, complete with skin, hair, and clothing intact.

children.name: Polytrichales
Polytrichaceae
Polytrichum
children.description: Haircap mosses are among the largest and most recognizable mosses you'll encounter in New England forests and fields. These sturdy mosses form dense, upright colonies that can grow several inches tall, with narrow, pointed leaves arranged in neat spirals around their stems. They're called 'haircap' mosses because their spore capsules are topped with a fuzzy, hair-like covering.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mosses, haircap mosses have a well-developed water-conducting system similar to higher plants, allowing them to grow much taller than typical mosses. Their leaves also have special ridges on top that help them conserve water during dry periods.
children.funFact: Common haircap moss can live for decades and some colonies are estimated to be over 100 years old, making them among the longest-lived mosses in North America.

children.name: Atrichum
children.description: Smoothcap mosses are a group of medium to large mosses that get their name from their relatively smooth spore capsules, which lack the fuzzy hairs found on many other moss species. These mosses typically form dense patches or cushions in woodlands and are known for their distinctive wavy or undulating leaves that often have a slightly glossy appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives in the haircap moss family, smoothcap mosses have capsules that are smooth or only lightly hairy rather than densely fuzzy. Their leaves are also characteristically wavy or crimped, especially when dry, giving them a distinctive wrinkled texture.
children.funFact: The wavy, undulating leaves of smoothcap mosses aren't just for show - this crimped structure helps the moss conserve moisture by creating tiny pockets that trap humid air close to the leaf surface.

children.name: Pogonatum
children.description: Pogonatum is a genus of mosses commonly known as haircap mosses, characterized by their distinctive tall, upright growth and hair-like structures. These mosses form dense, cushion-like patches in forests and other habitats throughout New England. They are part of the larger haircap moss family and play important roles in forest ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pogonatum mosses can be distinguished from other haircap mosses by their relatively short stature and broad, flattened leaves that often have toothed margins. Their spore capsules are typically cylindrical and held upright on sturdy stalks.
children.funFact: The name 'Pogonatum' comes from Greek words meaning 'bearded' or 'hairy,' referring to the fuzzy cap that covers their spore capsules before they mature and release spores.

children.name: Polytrichastrum
children.description: Polytrichastrum is a genus of robust, upright mosses known for their distinctive hair-like structures and relatively large size compared to other mosses. These mosses form dense, cushion-like patches and are well-adapted to harsh, cold environments like alpine regions and northern latitudes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other haircap mosses by their specific leaf arrangement and the structure of their reproductive parts, particularly the shape and ridging of their spore capsules.
children.funFact: Polytrichastrum mosses can survive being frozen solid for months at a time, then quickly resume photosynthesis and growth when temperatures warm up in spring.

children.description: The Haircap Moss Family includes some of the tallest and most robust mosses you'll encounter in New England's forests and woodlands. These mosses are characterized by their relatively large size, upright growth habit, and distinctive hair-like caps that cover their spore capsules. They typically form dense, cushion-like patches on soil, decaying logs, and forest floors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other moss families, haircap mosses have uniquely structured leaves with parallel plates of cells (called lamellae) running along the leaf surface, giving them a distinctive ribbed appearance. Their spore capsules are also notably large and often have prominent hairy caps called calyptrae.
children.funFact: Some haircap mosses can grow over 16 inches tall, making them giants in the moss world and earning them the nickname 'tree mosses' for their impressive stature.

children.description: Aloe-mosses are a distinctive group of mosses known for their unusually large size and robust appearance compared to other moss species. They typically grow in dense, upright clusters and have thick, sturdy stems that can reach several inches in height. These mosses are commonly found in acidic soils, particularly in forests, bogs, and disturbed areas throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most mosses, aloe-mosses have leaves with special water-conducting cells called lamellae that run along the leaf surface, giving them a ridged appearance similar to tiny aloe plants. They also produce large, cube-shaped spore capsules that are easily visible to the naked eye.
children.funFact: Some aloe-mosses can live for decades and were historically used by Indigenous peoples and early settlers as natural sponges and bedding material due to their exceptional water-absorbing abilities.

children.name: Tetraphidales
Tetraphidaceae
Tetraphis
children.description: Tetraphis mosses are a small genus of mosses known for their distinctive four-toothed spore capsules. These mosses are found in cool, moist environments and have a unique reproductive strategy that sets them apart from other moss groups.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The name 'Tetraphis' comes from their characteristic four peristome teeth (rather than the 16 or more teeth found in most other mosses) that surround the opening of their spore capsules. They also produce specialized cup-shaped structures filled with tiny reproductive bodies called gemmae.
children.funFact: Tetraphis mosses can reproduce both sexually through spores and asexually through tiny green pellets called gemmae that develop in cup-shaped structures on the plant tips, allowing them to spread even when conditions aren't right for sexual reproduction.

children.name: Tetrodontium
children.description: Tetrodontium mosses are tiny, specialized mosses that form small cushions or patches on rock surfaces. These diminutive plants are among the smallest mosses you'll encounter, with individual shoots measuring just a few millimeters tall. They belong to a small genus with only a handful of species worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These mosses are characterized by their extremely small size and their spore capsules that have four teeth (hence 'tetrodontium' meaning 'four teeth'). They typically grow directly on bare rock or thin soil over rock, unlike many other mosses that prefer richer substrates.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Tetrodontium mosses are incredibly hardy and can survive in harsh alpine and subalpine environments where few other plants can establish themselves.

children.description: The Tetraphidaceae family includes small, distinctive mosses found growing on decaying wood, soil, and rocks in forests. These mosses are characterized by their unique spore capsules that have four teeth (hence 'tetra') around the opening, which is unusual since most mosses have 16 or more teeth. They form small cushions or mats in shaded, moist woodland environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets these mosses apart is their capsules having exactly four large, triangular teeth around the rim, while most other moss families have 16 or more smaller teeth. This four-toothed arrangement makes them easily recognizable when fruiting.
children.funFact: Tetraphis moss has a clever two-stage reproduction system - it produces tiny cup-shaped structures filled with special reproductive bodies called gemmae that can grow into new plants, in addition to its regular spore capsules.

children.description: Tetraphidales is a small but distinctive order of mosses that includes just two genera found in New England: Tetraphis and Tetrodontium. These mosses are characterized by their unique spore capsules that have exactly four teeth (called peristome teeth) around the opening, which is unusual since most mosses have 16 or more teeth. They are typically small, cushion-forming mosses that grow on decaying wood, soil, or rock surfaces in forest environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature of this group is their capsules with precisely four triangular peristome teeth, while most other mosses have 16, 32, or no teeth at all. They also produce distinctive cup-shaped structures called gemmae cups that contain small reproductive bodies.
children.funFact: Tetraphis mosses can reproduce without spores by growing tiny green "gems" called gemmae in special cup-shaped containers on their stems, which splash out during rainstorms to start new moss colonies nearby.

children.name: Andreaeales
Andreaeaceae
Andreaea
children.description: Andreaea is a genus of small, dark-colored mosses that specialize in growing on bare rock surfaces, especially granite and other acidic rocks. These hardy little mosses form dense, blackish or dark brown cushions that can survive in some of the harshest conditions where most other plants cannot grow.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mosses, Andreaea species release their spores through four vertical slits that open in their capsules, rather than through a removable cap. They also have a unique brownish-black coloration that helps distinguish them from other rock-dwelling mosses.
children.funFact: These mosses are so tough they can survive being completely dried out for months, then quickly spring back to life when moisture returns.

children.description: The Andreaeaceae family consists of small, dark-colored mosses that are specially adapted to grow on rocks and in harsh mountain environments. These tough little plants form dense, cushion-like mats that can withstand extreme weather conditions including freezing temperatures and strong winds. They're among the hardiest mosses you'll find, thriving where few other plants can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mosses, members of this family have a unique way of releasing their spores - their capsules split open along four vertical lines rather than having a removable cap. They also tend to be much darker in color, often appearing almost black or deep reddish-brown.
children.funFact: These remarkable mosses can survive being completely dried out for months and then spring back to life with just a little moisture, earning them the nickname 'resurrection mosses.'

children.description: Andreaeales is a small order of mosses that includes some of the most ancient and primitive moss species on Earth. These tiny, dark-colored mosses are specially adapted to grow on bare rock surfaces in harsh environments like mountain peaks and arctic regions. They form small, cushion-like patches that can survive extreme cold, drought, and intense UV radiation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other mosses, members of Andreaeales have spore capsules that split open along four vertical lines rather than having a removable lid. They also lack the central water-conducting strand found in most other moss groups.
children.funFact: These ancient mosses can remain dormant for months or even years during dry periods, then quickly spring back to life within minutes of getting wet - earning them the nickname 'resurrection mosses.'

children.name: Zygnematales
Desmidiaceae
Cosmarium
children.description: Cosmarium is a diverse genus of single-celled green algae known as desmids that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These microscopic organisms have distinctive two-part cells that are often symmetrical and beautifully decorated with intricate patterns, ridges, or bumps on their cell walls. They're an important part of freshwater ecosystems, serving as food for small aquatic animals and contributing to oxygen production.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cosmarium species are distinguished by their characteristic constriction in the middle that divides each cell into two mirror-image halves called semicells. Unlike some other desmid genera, Cosmarium cells typically have a relatively shallow constriction and often feature elaborate surface ornamentation that varies dramatically between species.
children.funFact: With 34 species found in New England alone, Cosmarium is one of the most species-rich desmid genera, and scientists often describe the intricate patterns on their cell walls as resembling tiny works of art visible only under a microscope.

children.name: Staurastrum
children.description: Staurastrum is a genus of microscopic green algae known for their stunning geometric shapes and intricate cell walls. These single-celled organisms are characterized by their radial symmetry, typically appearing star-like or cross-shaped when viewed from above, with elaborate spines, projections, or ornate patterns decorating their surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other desmid algae, Staurastrum species have cells that are typically broader than they are long and display pronounced radial symmetry with multiple arms or projections extending outward from a central body. Their cell walls are often heavily ornamented with spines, granules, or complex sculptural patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Staurastrum cells are considered some of nature's most beautiful microscopic art forms, with their intricate geometric patterns and symmetrical designs rivaling any human-made crystal or snowflake.

children.name: Micrasterias
children.description: Micrasterias is a genus of single-celled freshwater algae known for their stunning, symmetrical star-like shapes. These microscopic organisms are actually made up of two mirror-image halves connected at the center, creating intricate geometric patterns that look like living snowflakes. They're commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Micrasterias apart from other desmid algae is their deeply divided, ornate cell walls with elaborate lobes and projections that radiate outward like spokes on a wheel. Each species has its own unique pattern of indentations and extensions, making them look like microscopic works of art.
children.funFact: Despite being only about the width of a human hair, Micrasterias cells are considered some of the most beautiful organisms visible under a microscope, with their perfectly symmetrical patterns inspiring both scientists and artists for over 150 years.

children.name: Euastrum
children.description: Euastrum is a genus of single-celled green algae known for their stunning geometric beauty and perfect bilateral symmetry. These microscopic organisms are shaped like intricate stars or snowflakes, with each cell consisting of two mirror-image halves joined at the center. They live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and bog pools throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Euastrum species are distinguished from other desmids by their distinctively flattened, star-like or shield-like shapes with elaborate projections and ornate surface patterns. Each species has its own unique outline and decorative features, making them look like living works of art under the microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being only about the width of a human hair, Euastrum cells are considered some of the most beautiful organisms on Earth, with their perfectly symmetrical patterns rivaling the complexity of cathedral rose windows.

children.name: Staurodesmus
children.description: Staurodesmus is a genus of microscopic green algae that are part of the desmid family, single-celled organisms that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and wetlands. These tiny algae are characterized by their distinctive cell shapes, which are often deeply constricted in the middle, giving them a symmetrical, almost artistic appearance. Each cell is divided into two mirror-image halves connected by a narrow bridge called an isthmus.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Staurodesmus are distinguished from other desmids by their typically angular or star-shaped cell outlines when viewed from the end, and many species have prominent spines or projections extending from their cell walls. Unlike some related desmids, they tend to have relatively simple, geometric forms rather than highly ornate decorative patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these microscopic algae are like living jewels - their perfectly symmetrical forms and intricate geometric shapes have made them favorites among microscopists and even inspired decorative art patterns in Victorian times.

children.name: Desmidium
children.description: Desmidium is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive chain-like colonies of cells joined end-to-end. These microscopic organisms are commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they often create visible green masses in the water. Each cell in the chain has a unique twisted or spiral shape that gives the entire colony a characteristic corkscrew appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other chain-forming algae, Desmidium cells are joined by their flattened ends and twist along the length of the colony, creating a helical spiral pattern. The cells also have a distinctive constriction in the middle that divides each cell into two symmetrical halves.
children.funFact: When Desmidium colonies break apart during reproduction, the individual cell fragments can swim using tiny whip-like structures before settling down to form new spiral chains.

children.name: Xanthidium
children.description: Xanthidium is a genus of microscopic freshwater algae known for their distinctive geometric cell walls covered in spines and ornate decorations. These single-celled organisms are part of a group called desmids, which are green algae that live in clean, acidic waters like bogs and ponds. Each Xanthidium cell is symmetrical and often looks like a tiny decorated box or geometric jewel when viewed under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Xanthidium species are distinguished from other desmids by their heavily ornamented cell walls that feature prominent spines, ridges, and intricate surface patterns. Unlike smoother desmids, their cell walls look almost armor-like with elaborate sculptural details.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Xanthidium cells are considered some of the most beautiful microorganisms on Earth, with their intricate patterns and spines creating what microscopists often describe as 'living crystal palaces.'

children.name: Pleurotaenium
children.description: Pleurotaenium is a genus of single-celled green algae that are among the largest and most elegant members of the desmid family. These microscopic organisms have distinctively elongated, cylindrical cells that often appear ribbon-like or rod-shaped when viewed under a microscope. They live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other desmids that have a clear constriction dividing them into two symmetrical halves, Pleurotaenium cells are only slightly constricted in the middle, giving them a more uniform cylindrical appearance. Their cell walls are smooth and often decorated with subtle ridges or bands.
children.funFact: Some Pleurotaenium species can reach lengths of over 1,000 micrometers (1 millimeter), making them giants in the microscopic world and visible to the naked eye as tiny green threads in the water.

children.name: Hyalotheca
children.description: Hyalotheca is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive filamentous chains of cells. These microscopic algae are found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they often form slimy masses or floating mats on the water surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hyalotheca are characterized by their rectangular cells that are joined end-to-end in long, unbranched chains, with each cell containing distinctive star-shaped chloroplasts. The chains are typically surrounded by a thick, gelatinous sheath that gives them their characteristically slimy texture.
children.funFact: The name 'Hyalotheca' literally means 'glass case' in Greek, referring to the transparent, glassy appearance of the protective sheaths that surround these algae.

children.name: Triploceras
children.description: Triploceras is a genus of small, delicate hornworts found in moist, shaded environments throughout New England. These primitive plants lack true roots and instead anchor themselves with hair-like structures called rhizoids, growing as small, flattened green patches on soil, rocks, or decaying wood.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Triploceras can be identified by their characteristic three-lobed spore capsules that split open in a distinctive pattern when mature. Unlike mosses, they have a simpler structure with no true leaves, just flattened, ribbon-like plant bodies.
children.funFact: Despite being among the most ancient land plants on Earth, Triploceras species are still thriving today in the same types of environments their ancestors colonized hundreds of millions of years ago.

children.name: Spondylosium
children.description: Spondylosium is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms beautiful, ribbon-like colonies made up of individual cells joined end-to-end. These microscopic organisms are part of the desmid family and can be found in clean ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Each cell in the colony has a distinctive constricted middle section that gives them an hourglass-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other desmids that live as single cells, Spondylosium species form long, twisted filamentous colonies where cells remain connected after division. The cells are notably flattened and have a characteristic spiral twist to their colony formation.
children.funFact: Spondylosium colonies can twist and rotate as they move through the water, creating a graceful corkscrew motion that helps them navigate their aquatic environment.

children.name: Actinotaenium
children.description: Actinotaenium is a genus of tiny, single-celled green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and wetlands. These microscopic organisms have distinctive barrel-shaped or cylindrical cells that are typically wider in the middle and narrower at the ends, giving them a unique appearance under the microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Actinotaenium cells are solitary rather than forming chains or colonies, and they have a characteristic constricted shape that makes them easily recognizable. Their cell walls often show distinctive patterns or textures when viewed closely.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae play an important role in freshwater ecosystems by producing oxygen through photosynthesis and serving as food for microscopic animals.

children.name: Bambusina
children.description: Bambusina is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive filamentous chains of cells. These microscopic algae are found in clean, slow-moving or still waters like ponds, streams, and wetlands throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bambusina can be identified by its unique cell arrangement where cylindrical cells are connected end-to-end in unbranched chains, often with slight constrictions between cells that give it a bamboo-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite its name suggesting a connection to bamboo plants, Bambusina is actually a type of green algae that gets its name from the segmented, bamboo-like appearance of its cell chains under a microscope.

children.name: Tetmemorus
children.description: Tetmemorus is a genus of single-celled algae called desmids that live in freshwater environments like ponds and slow-moving streams. These microscopic organisms have distinctive flask-shaped or cylindrical cells that are deeply constricted in the middle, creating two symmetrical halves. They are part of the green algae group and play an important role in freshwater ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tetmemorus can be distinguished from other desmids by its elongated, cylindrical shape with rounded ends and a prominent central constriction that divides the cell into two mirror-image semicells. The cell wall often has a smooth surface, unlike many other desmids that have spines or ornate patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being only visible under a microscope, Tetmemorus cells can actually move by secreting mucilage through tiny pores in their cell walls, allowing them to glide slowly through the water.

children.name: Teilingia
children.description: Teilingia is a small genus of microscopic amoebas that live in soil and freshwater environments. These single-celled organisms are characterized by their ability to form protective cysts and their distinctive granular appearance under the microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Teilingia can be distinguished from other soil amoebas by its characteristic granulated cytoplasm and the specific way it forms its protective cyst stage.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Teilingia granulata plays an important role in soil ecosystems by helping to break down organic matter and cycling nutrients.

children.name: Cosmocladium
children.description: Cosmocladium is a genus of microscopic green algae that forms beautiful, delicate colonies in freshwater environments. These tiny organisms are characterized by their distinctive branching, tree-like colonial structure where individual cells are connected in a geometric pattern.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other colonial green algae, Cosmocladium forms highly organized, regularly branching colonies with cells arranged in a specific geometric pattern that resembles a miniature tree or coral.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Cosmocladium colonies can create intricate branching patterns that look like tiny underwater forests when viewed under a microscope.

children.name: Onychonema
children.description: Onychonema is a genus of microscopic green algae that forms thread-like filaments in freshwater environments. These tiny algae are part of the charophyte group, which are among the closest relatives to land plants in the tree of life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: This genus is characterized by its unbranched filamentous structure and distinctive cell wall features that help distinguish it from other thread-like green algae.
children.funFact: Despite being simple-looking algae, Onychonema belongs to a group that shares important cellular features with land plants, representing a key link in understanding how plants made the evolutionary leap from water to land.

children.name: Haplotaenium
children.description: Haplotaenium is a genus of tiny desmid green algae that live in freshwater environments. These microscopic organisms are single-celled and have a distinctive constricted shape that makes them look like they're pinched in the middle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their small size and relatively simple cell structure compared to other desmids, with smooth cell walls that lack the elaborate ornamentation found in many related algae.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae play an important role in freshwater ecosystems by producing oxygen through photosynthesis and serving as food for microscopic animals.

children.name: Sphaerozosma
children.description: Sphaerozosma is a genus of microscopic green algae that forms delicate, thread-like chains of cells. These tiny organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and wetlands throughout New England. Each cell in the chain is connected to its neighbors, creating beautiful filamentous structures that can only be seen under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sphaerozosma cells are characterized by their distinctive semicircular or crescent shape when viewed from the side, and they remain connected in unbranched chains. Unlike many other filamentous algae, the cell walls have special connecting structures that hold the chain together.
