children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Sphaerozosma chains can break apart and reform, allowing individual cells to 'walk' along surfaces by extending and contracting their connections like tiny living springs.

children.description: Desmidiaceae are single-celled green algae known for their stunning geometric beauty and perfect symmetry. These microscopic organisms are divided into two identical halves (called semicells) that mirror each other exactly, creating intricate patterns that look like living jewels under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other green algae, desmids have a distinctive constriction in the middle where the two symmetrical halves meet, and their cell walls are often decorated with elaborate pores, spines, or ornamental patterns.
children.funFact: Desmids are sometimes called the 'snowflakes of the microscopic world' because each species has its own unique and perfectly symmetrical design, with some resembling stars, crescents, or elaborate geometric medallions.

children.name: Closteriaceae
Closterium
children.description: Closterium is a genus of single-celled green algae that are easily recognized by their distinctive crescent or banana-shaped cells. These microscopic organisms are commonly found in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Each cell is typically elongated and curved, with pointed ends that often contain visible crystal-like structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Closterium species have their characteristic curved, moon-shaped cells that are usually much longer than they are wide. The cells are also notable for having small, moving granules at each pointed end that help distinguish them from similar-looking algae.
children.funFact: Closterium cells can actually 'walk' across surfaces by secreting mucilage from their pointed ends, allowing them to glide through their watery habitat in search of better conditions.

children.name: Spinoclosterium
children.description: Spinoclosterium is a genus of single-celled green algae that belongs to the desmid family. These microscopic organisms are characterized by their distinctive elongated, cylindrical shape and are typically found in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their smooth, spindle-shaped cells that lack the deep constriction in the middle that many other desmids possess. They also have pointed ends and a relatively simple, symmetrical cell structure.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Spinoclosterium cells can reproduce both sexually and asexually, allowing them to quickly colonize suitable freshwater habitats.

children.description: Closteriaceae is a family of single-celled green algae that are easily recognized by their distinctive crescent or banana-shaped cells. These microscopic organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Each cell is beautifully symmetrical and often appears to glow green under a microscope due to its chloroplasts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other green algae, members of Closteriaceae have their characteristic curved, elongated shape that resembles a crescent moon or banana. They also have distinctive vacuoles at each end of the cell that often contain moving crystals.
children.funFact: The tiny crystals inside Closterium cells are constantly dancing and jiggling around - scientists think this movement might help the algae sense gravity and orient themselves properly in the water!

children.name: Mesotaeniaceae
Netrium
children.description: Netrium is a genus of single-celled green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These microscopic organisms have elongated, cylindrical cells that are often slightly curved or twisted, giving them a distinctive sausage-like appearance. They belong to a group called desmids, which are known for their beautiful geometric shapes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many of their desmid relatives that have cells divided into two symmetrical halves, Netrium species have unsegmented cells without a clear constriction in the middle. Their smooth, elongated shape and lack of obvious ornamentation help distinguish them from other desmid genera.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Netrium cells can be surprisingly large for single-celled organisms, with some species reaching lengths of over 200 micrometers - that's about twice the width of a human hair!

children.name: Spirotaenia
children.description: Spirotaenia is a genus of microscopic green algae that consists of single cells with a distinctive elongated, cylindrical shape. These tiny organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and wet soils, where they photosynthesize like plants to make their own food. Each cell contains spiral-shaped chloroplasts that wind around the inside of the cell wall, giving them their characteristic appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Spirotaenia cells are notably long and narrow, often resembling tiny green threads or rods. The spiral arrangement of their chloroplasts is particularly distinctive and helps identify them under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being single-celled organisms, Spirotaenia can reproduce both by simply splitting in half and by a more complex process where two cells join together to exchange genetic material before forming new individuals.

children.name: Planotaenium
children.description: Planotaenium is a genus of desmid algae, which are single-celled green algae known for their beautiful geometric shapes. These microscopic organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and wetlands throughout New England. Each cell is symmetrical and divided into two identical halves called semicells.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Planotaenium cells are characterized by their flattened, ribbon-like shape when viewed from the side, and they have a distinctive constriction in the middle where the two halves meet. Unlike some other desmids, they lack elaborate spines or projections.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Planotaenium and other desmids are so geometrically perfect that Victorian-era microscopists used them as living art subjects, creating intricate arrangements to showcase nature's mathematical beauty.

children.name: Cylindrocystis
children.description: Cylindrocystis is a genus of single-celled green algae that are cylindrical or barrel-shaped, as their name suggests. These microscopic organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, streams, and wetlands throughout New England. They are part of the conjugating green algae group, which means they reproduce by joining together and exchanging genetic material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Cylindrocystis cells are distinctly cylindrical with rounded ends and contain large, star-shaped chloroplasts. They also lack the spiral chloroplast arrangements seen in related algae like Spirogyra.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae can sometimes form dense populations that give pond water a greenish tint, contributing to the natural productivity of aquatic ecosystems.

children.name: Mesotaenium
children.description: Mesotaenium is a genus of tiny freshwater green algae that live as single cells. These microscopic organisms are found in quiet waters like ponds, ditches, and wet soil, where they help form the base of aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Mesotaenium cells are cylindrical or barrel-shaped and always exist as solitary individuals rather than forming colonies or chains.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these single-celled algae can reproduce by simply splitting in half, creating two identical daughter cells.

children.name: Roya
children.description: Roya is a genus of parasitic fungi that specifically targets and infects rust fungi, earning them the nickname "hyperparasites." These tiny fungi act as natural biological control agents by attacking other fungal pathogens that can harm plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fungi that feed on plants or decompose organic matter, Roya species are specialized to parasitize other fungi, particularly rust fungi that cause plant diseases.
children.funFact: Roya fungi are like nature's pest control specialists - they're fungi that hunt other fungi, helping to keep plant-damaging rust diseases in check.

children.description: Mesotaeniaceae is a family of microscopic freshwater algae that are closely related to the more familiar desmids. These single-celled green algae are typically elongated or cylindrical in shape and can be found floating in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Unlike many other algae, members of this family reproduce both sexually and asexually, creating beautiful geometric patterns when they come together.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true desmids, Mesotaeniaceae algae lack the distinctive constriction or 'waist' in the middle of their cells. Their cell walls are smooth and unsegmented, giving them a simpler, more streamlined appearance than their ornately patterned desmid relatives.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can actually twist and spiral as they move through the water, using tiny projections to propel themselves in corkscrew-like motions that are visible under a microscope.

children.name: Gonatozygaceae
Gonatozygon
children.description: Gonatozygon is a genus of microscopic freshwater algae that belong to the desmid family. These single-celled organisms are characterized by their elongated, cylindrical shape and are commonly found in acidic waters like bogs and ponds throughout New England. They reproduce through a unique process called conjugation, where two cells join together to form a specialized reproductive structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other desmids that have a clear constriction dividing them into two symmetrical halves, Gonatozygon cells are unconstricted and maintain their cylindrical form. They also have distinctive end walls that can be smooth or decorated with various projections or spines.
children.funFact: When two Gonatozygon cells conjugate to reproduce, they form a distinctive zigzag-shaped structure called a zygospore, which is where the genus gets its name - 'gonato' meaning angle and 'zygon' meaning yoke or joining.

children.description: Gonatozygaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that live as single cells or in simple chains. These microscopic organisms are characterized by their distinctive cell shapes and reproductive structures, and they play important roles in aquatic ecosystems as primary producers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have unique cell wall structures and specialized reproductive cells called zygospores that help distinguish them from other green algae families.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these algae can be found in a variety of freshwater habitats from pristine mountain lakes to temporary puddles, showing remarkable adaptability to different water conditions.

children.name: Peniaceae
Penium
children.description: Penium is a genus of microscopic green algae that live as single cells in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and wetlands. These tiny organisms have distinctive elongated, cylindrical shapes and are part of a larger group called desmids, which are known for their symmetrical beauty.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other desmids that have obvious constrictions dividing them into two halves, Penium species appear as smooth, uninterrupted cylinders. Their cell walls often display delicate spiral or linear patterns that can only be seen under high magnification.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Penium cells can be quite large for single-celled organisms, sometimes reaching lengths of up to 200 micrometers - about twice the width of a human hair!

children.description: Peniaceae is a small family of microscopic green algae that are part of the desmid group. These single-celled organisms are characterized by their elongated, cylindrical shape and smooth cell walls without the constricted middle that many other desmids have. They live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other desmids which have a clear constriction dividing the cell into two symmetrical halves, members of Peniaceae have smooth, uninterrupted cylindrical cells. Their cell walls lack the ornate patterns and decorations found in many related desmid families.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae can form long chains by remaining attached after cell division, creating microscopic green filaments in the water.

children.description: Desmids are microscopic freshwater green algae known for their stunning geometric shapes and intricate patterns. These single-celled organisms are often called the 'jewels of the pond' because of their beautiful, symmetrical forms that look like tiny works of art under a microscope. They live in clean, acidic waters like bogs, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Desmids are unique among green algae for their distinctive two-part cell structure, with each half being a mirror image of the other, connected by a narrow bridge called an isthmus. Unlike other algae, they reproduce through a fascinating process where two cells come together and exchange genetic material.
children.funFact: Some desmids can actually move on their own by secreting mucilage through tiny pores in their cell walls, allowing them to glide gracefully through the water like microscopic dancers.

children.name: Charales
Characeae
Chara
children.description: Muskgrass (Chara) is a genus of large, complex green algae that grows underwater in freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams. These plant-like organisms have branching stems with whorls of smaller branches that give them a distinctive bushy appearance, often resembling submerged pine trees or bottle brushes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other freshwater algae, Chara species deposit calcium carbonate on their surfaces, making them feel rough and brittle to the touch, which is why they're called 'stoneworts.' They also produce a distinctive musty odor when crushed or disturbed.
children.funFact: Despite being algae, muskgrass plays such an important ecological role in freshwater ecosystems that it's often called a 'keystone species' - it provides shelter for fish and invertebrates, helps clarify water by reducing sediment, and can form underwater meadows covering acres of lake bottom.

children.name: Nitella
children.description: Nitella is a genus of aquatic plants commonly called stoneworts that live submerged in freshwater lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams. These delicate, green plants have a distinctive whorl-like branching pattern where clusters of thin, thread-like branches radiate out from nodes along the main stem, giving them an almost feathery appearance underwater.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other stoneworts in the genus Chara, Nitella species lack the protective cortical cells that wrap around their main stems, giving them a smoother, more translucent appearance. They also tend to be more delicate and flexible than their Chara relatives.
children.funFact: Despite being called stoneworts, Nitella species don't actually become encrusted with calcium carbonate like many of their Chara cousins, which is why they maintain their soft, delicate texture throughout their lives.

children.description: Stoneworts are unique freshwater algae that look remarkably like underwater plants, with branching stems and whorled leaves arranged in regular patterns. Despite their plant-like appearance, they're actually complex algae that form dense underwater meadows in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. These ancient organisms are considered living fossils, representing one of the oldest lineages of complex algae on Earth.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true aquatic plants, stoneworts lack flowers, seeds, and true roots, instead anchoring themselves with thread-like structures called rhizoids. They're easily recognized by their distinctive whorled branching pattern and often gritty texture from calcium carbonate deposits.
children.funFact: Stoneworts are so ancient that they're thought to be among the closest living relatives to the first land plants that colonized Earth over 400 million years ago.

children.description: Charales are an ancient order of freshwater green algae that look remarkably like underwater plants, with branched stems and whorled leaves. These complex algae are among the most plant-like of all algae, often forming dense underwater meadows in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. They're considered to be among the closest living relatives to land plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other algae, stoneworts have a complex structure with distinct nodes and internodes, much like the stems of higher plants. They also produce unique reproductive structures called oogonia and antheridia, and many species become encrusted with calcium carbonate, giving them their 'stonewort' nickname.
children.funFact: Some stoneworts are so heavily encrusted with calcium carbonate that they feel gritty or crunchy to the touch and can actually help clarify murky water by precipitating excess minerals.

children.name: Chaetosphaeridiales
Chaetosphaeridiaceae
Chaetosphaeridium
children.description: Chaetosphaeridium is a genus of tiny freshwater green algae that lives as single cells or in small colonies. These microscopic organisms are found in ponds, lakes, and other freshwater environments where they attach to surfaces or float freely in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their spherical cells surrounded by distinctive bristle-like projections called setae that extend outward from the cell surface.
children.funFact: Despite being simple single-celled algae, Chaetosphaeridium species are considered close relatives to the ancestors of all land plants, making them important for understanding how plants first evolved from aquatic environments.

children.description: Chaetosphaeridiaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that represents one of the earliest branching groups in the charophyte lineage, which gave rise to land plants. These microscopic algae are typically single-celled and live in aquatic environments, where they play important roles in freshwater ecosystems. They are considered living representatives of ancient algal forms that help scientists understand how plants first transitioned from water to land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their simple cellular structure and specific arrangement of flagella (whip-like structures used for movement). They lack the complex multicellular organization seen in more advanced charophyte algae.
children.funFact: Despite being simple single-celled organisms, Chaetosphaeridiaceae algae are actually more closely related to land plants than they are to other green algae, making them living windows into plant evolutionary history.

children.description: Chaetosphaeridiales is a small order of freshwater green algae that represents one of the most ancient lineages of plant-like organisms. These microscopic algae are found in freshwater environments like ponds and streams, where they live as single cells or form simple colonies. They are considered important evolutionary stepping stones between simpler algae and more complex land plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order have distinctive bristle-like projections called setae that extend from their cell walls, giving them a fuzzy appearance under the microscope. They also possess unique cell wall components and reproductive structures that set them apart from other green algae groups.
children.funFact: These tiny algae are evolutionary celebrities - they belong to one of the earliest branches of the green plant family tree and help scientists understand how plants first made the transition from water to land millions of years ago.

children.name: Coleochaetales
Coleochaetaceae
Coleochaete
children.description: Coleochaete is a genus of small, freshwater green algae that forms flat, disk-like colonies on rocks, wood, and other underwater surfaces. These microscopic organisms are considered to be among the closest relatives to land plants, representing an important evolutionary bridge between aquatic algae and terrestrial vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other green algae, Coleochaete species form distinctive flat, circular colonies with branching filaments that radiate outward from a central point. They also produce unique protective structures called sheaths around their reproductive cells.
children.funFact: Despite being tiny aquatic algae, Coleochaete species share key features with land plants including similar cell division patterns and protective structures around their eggs, making them living representatives of what early plant ancestors might have looked like over 400 million years ago.

children.description: Coleochaetaceae is a family of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive disk-shaped or cushion-like colonies on submerged surfaces like rocks, logs, and aquatic plants. These microscopic algae are considered among the closest relatives to land plants, representing an important evolutionary link between aquatic and terrestrial plant life. They reproduce through a unique combination of sexual and asexual methods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other green algae, members of this family produce specialized protective structures called sheaths around their reproductive cells, and their branching filaments radiate outward from a central point to form flat, circular colonies.
children.funFact: These tiny algae are evolutionary celebrities - they're thought to be one of the closest living relatives to the first plants that colonized land over 400 million years ago!

children.description: Coleochaetales are microscopic green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds and streams. These tiny organisms are particularly special because they represent one of the closest relatives to land plants, giving us clues about how plants first made the transition from water to land millions of years ago.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, members of this group have branching filaments and can form flat, disk-like colonies. They also produce specialized protective sheaths around their reproductive structures.
children.funFact: These humble algae share more genetic similarities with trees and flowers than they do with most other algae, making them living bridges in understanding plant evolution.

children.name: Klebsormidiales
Elakatotrichaceae
Elakatothrix
children.description: Elakatothrix is a genus of microscopic green algae that forms distinctive gelatinous colonies in freshwater environments. These tiny organisms are single-celled but live together in a jelly-like matrix that they produce, creating visible clumps or films in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Elakatothrix cells are embedded within a thick, gelatinous substance that gives their colonies a characteristic slimy, mucilaginous appearance. The cells are typically oval-shaped and arranged in a specific pattern within their jelly matrix.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic individually, Elakatothrix colonies can grow large enough to be seen floating as green, jelly-like masses on the water's surface, sometimes mistaken for frog spawn by casual observers.

children.description: Elakatotrichaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that consists of tiny, single-celled organisms. These microscopic algae are characterized by their elongated, needle-like or spindle-shaped cells that often have pointed ends. They live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive elongated cell shape and the way their cells divide, creating characteristic patterns. Unlike many other green algae, they typically remain as individual cells rather than forming colonies or filaments.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae play an important role in freshwater ecosystems by producing oxygen through photosynthesis and serving as food for microscopic animals.

children.description: Klebsormidiales is an order of simple green algae that form thread-like chains of cells. These microscopic organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, streams, and wet soil, where they photosynthesize to produce their own food. They represent some of the earliest branching groups in green algae evolution.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, members of Klebsormidiales have a very simple body structure with cells arranged in unbranched filaments. Their cell walls lack the complex layering found in more advanced green algae groups.
children.funFact: These tiny algae are considered evolutionary bridges between single-celled green algae and the more complex multicellular forms that eventually gave rise to land plants.

children.name: Sphaeropleales
Scenedesmaceae
Coelastrum
children.description: Coelastrum is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms beautiful, hollow spherical colonies made up of individual cells arranged in geometric patterns. These microscopic organisms are commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Each colony looks like a tiny, intricate sphere with cells connected at specific points, creating openings or windows between them.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae, Coelastrum colonies are distinctly hollow and spherical, with cells arranged in a single layer around the surface. The cells are connected by processes that create characteristic geometric patterns and gaps, giving the colonies a net-like or lattice appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Coelastrum' literally means 'hollow star' in Greek, referring to the star-like patterns created by the connected cells in their spherical colonies.

children.name: Desmodesmus
children.description: Desmodesmus is a genus of microscopic green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams throughout New England. These tiny organisms are typically found forming small colonies of 4-8 cells arranged in flat, rectangular groups that look like miniature green tiles under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae that exist as single cells, Desmodesmus species are easily recognized by their characteristic flat, plate-like colonies with cells arranged in neat rows. Many species also have small spines or projections on their outer cells that help distinguish them from similar algae.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Desmodesmus algae are incredibly important primary producers that help form the base of aquatic food webs, converting sunlight and carbon dioxide into food that supports everything from tiny water fleas to fish.

children.name: Scenedesmus
children.description: Scenedesmus is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive colonies of 2-8 cells arranged in flat, often curved rows. These microscopic organisms are commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they play an important role in aquatic food webs as primary producers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae that exist as single cells or irregular clusters, Scenedesmus species are easily recognized by their orderly colonial arrangement, with cells lined up side by side like tiny green beads on a string.
children.funFact: Scenedesmus colonies can rapidly multiply through a process called autospore formation, where each parent cell divides to create a perfect miniature replica of the entire colony inside itself before releasing it into the water.

children.name: Tetradesmus
children.description: Tetradesmus is a genus of small freshwater green algae that typically form colonies of four cells arranged in a flat, square pattern. These microscopic organisms are common in ponds, lakes, and other freshwater habitats throughout New England, where they play an important role in aquatic food webs as primary producers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Tetradesmus species characteristically arrange themselves in groups of exactly four cells that lie in the same plane, creating their distinctive flat, four-celled appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Tetradesmus algae can sometimes form blooms dense enough to give pond water a greenish tint, and they're often used in laboratory research to study algal growth and water quality.

children.name: Comasiella
children.description: Comasiella is a small genus of marine gastropod mollusks, commonly known as sea slugs or nudibranchs. These soft-bodied creatures are part of the diverse world of shell-less marine snails that crawl along the ocean floor and underwater surfaces. Members of this genus are typically small, delicate animals that breathe through specialized gills and feed on various marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Comasiella species are distinguished by their elongated, somewhat flattened body shape and specific arrangement of cerata (finger-like projections) along their backs. They have a characteristic curved or arched appearance, which is reflected in the species name 'arcuata' meaning curved or bow-shaped.
children.funFact: Despite being shell-less and seemingly defenseless, Comasiella sea slugs can incorporate stinging cells from their prey into their own tissues, essentially borrowing weapons from other creatures for protection.

children.name: Dimorphococcus
children.description: Dimorphococcus is a genus of green algae that lives in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These microscopic organisms are single-celled and get their name from their distinctive two different cell shapes that occur during their life cycle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Dimorphococcus apart from other green algae is its unique ability to exist in two very different cell forms - one crescent-shaped and another more rounded form.
children.funFact: Despite being only visible under a microscope, Dimorphococcus lunatus plays an important role in freshwater ecosystems by producing oxygen through photosynthesis and serving as food for tiny aquatic animals.

children.name: Westella
children.description: Westella is a genus of microscopic freshwater green algae that forms distinctive ball-like clusters of cells. These tiny aquatic organisms are part of the chlorophyte group and play an important role in freshwater ecosystems as primary producers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Westella is characterized by its unique colonial structure where individual cells are arranged in spherical clusters, giving them a grape-like or berry-like appearance under the microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Westella colonies can sometimes give pond water a slightly greenish tint when they bloom in large numbers during favorable conditions.

children.name: Tetrastrum
children.description: Tetrastrum is a genus of microscopic freshwater green algae that forms distinctive four-celled colonies. These tiny organisms live in ponds, lakes, and other freshwater habitats throughout New England, where they play an important role in aquatic ecosystems as primary producers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Tetrastrum apart from other green algae is its characteristic arrangement of exactly four cells that remain connected after cell division, forming a flat, cross-like or square pattern when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Tetrastrum colonies can sometimes contribute to the greenish tint you might notice in pond water during warmer months.

children.name: Verrucodesmus
children.description: Verrucodesmus is a genus of small millipedes that belong to the polydesmidan order, characterized by their segmented bodies and numerous pairs of legs. These tiny arthropods are soil-dwelling creatures that play an important role in decomposing organic matter in forest ecosystems. They are part of the diverse world of millipedes that help break down leaf litter and other plant material.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their warty or bumpy body surface texture, which gives them their name (verruco- means warty). They have distinctive body segments with lateral projections that help differentiate them from other millipede genera.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they have a thousand legs, Verrucodesmus millipedes actually have far fewer legs - typically around 30-90 pairs depending on their age and number of body segments.

children.name: Hariotina
children.description: Hariotina is a genus of marine bryozoans, which are tiny colonial animals that live together to form delicate, lace-like structures on the ocean floor. These filter-feeding creatures build calcium carbonate skeletons and are often mistaken for seaweed or coral by beachcombers who find their dried remains washed ashore.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hariotina create distinctive net-like or mesh-like colonial structures with a characteristic reticulated (grid-like) pattern, which gives the single New England species its name 'reticulata.'
children.funFact: Despite looking like a single organism, each Hariotina colony is actually made up of hundreds of tiny individual animals called zooids, each living in its own small chamber and working together to filter plankton from the water.

children.description: Scenedesmaceae is a family of freshwater green algae that form distinctive colonies or clusters of cells. These microscopic organisms are commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they play important roles as primary producers in aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their cells being arranged in flat, geometric colonies that often form distinctive shapes like stars, crosses, or neat rows. Unlike many other green algae that live as single cells, Scenedesmaceae species maintain these organized colonial arrangements throughout their life cycle.
children.funFact: Some Scenedesmaceae species can rapidly change their colony formation in response to chemical signals from predators, creating spiny projections or larger clusters that make them harder for tiny animals to eat.

children.name: Hydrodictyaceae
Pediastrum
children.description: Pediastrum is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms beautiful, flat colonies resembling tiny geometric wheels or stars. These microscopic organisms live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they float freely in the water as part of the phytoplankton community.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae, Pediastrum species arrange their cells in precise, flat geometric patterns with cells often connected by small projections or arranged in regular polygonal shapes.
children.funFact: Each Pediastrum colony starts from a single parent cell that divides to create the entire geometric arrangement, with the outer cells often developing horn-like projections that give the colony its distinctive star-shaped appearance.

children.name: Pseudopediastrum
children.description: Pseudopediastrum is a genus of microscopic green algae that form beautiful star-shaped or wheel-like colonies made up of individual cells arranged in flat, geometric patterns. These tiny aquatic organisms live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Each colony looks like a miniature work of art when viewed under a microscope, with cells connected to form intricate radial designs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other colonial green algae, Pseudopediastrum forms distinctly flat, disc-like colonies with cells arranged in precise geometric patterns rather than spherical or irregular clusters. The cells are often connected by narrow bridges or projections that give the colonies their characteristic star or wheel appearance.
children.funFact: These algae were originally classified in the genus Pediastrum for over 150 years before DNA studies revealed they were different enough to deserve their own separate genus in 2011.

children.name: Monactinus
children.description: Monactinus is a genus of microscopic green algae that live as single cells in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These tiny organisms are characterized by their distinctive star-like or radial shape, with projections extending outward from a central cell body. They are part of the larger group of green algae that help form the base of aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Monactinus apart from other green algae is their unique radiating cell structure, where multiple spine-like projections extend from the center of the cell in a symmetrical pattern. This gives them a distinctive star or wheel-like appearance when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these microscopic algae play a crucial role in freshwater ecosystems by producing oxygen through photosynthesis and serving as food for tiny aquatic animals.

children.name: Sorastrum
children.description: Sorastrum is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms beautiful, star-shaped colonies visible under a microscope. These tiny organisms consist of multiple cells arranged in a hollow, spherical pattern, with each cell extending spines or projections outward from the colony's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae, Sorastrum colonies have a distinctive radiating pattern where cells are connected at their bases but extend outward like spokes of a wheel. The cells typically have long, thin projections or spines that give the colony its characteristic star-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Sorastrum colonies can spin and rotate as they move through the water, creating a mesmerizing dance that early microscopists described as resembling tiny green stars tumbling through space.

children.name: Tetraedron
children.description: Tetraedron is a genus of microscopic freshwater green algae that are single-celled organisms found in ponds, lakes, and streams throughout New England. These tiny algae have distinctive geometric shapes, often appearing triangular or pyramid-like when viewed under a microscope. They play an important role in aquatic ecosystems as primary producers, converting sunlight into energy through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Tetraedron apart from other green algae is their characteristic angular, geometric cell shapes with pointed projections or spines. Unlike many other single-celled algae that are round or oval, Tetraedron cells have a distinctly angular, crystalline appearance.
children.funFact: The name 'Tetraedron' comes from the Greek words meaning 'four-faced,' referring to their geometric shapes that can resemble tiny green pyramids or crystals floating in the water.

children.name: Stauridium
children.description: Stauridium is a genus of single-celled marine organisms that belong to a group called dinoflagellates. These microscopic creatures have a distinctive cross-shaped or star-like appearance when viewed under a microscope, which is reflected in their name derived from the Greek word for 'cross.'
children.distinguishingFeatures: Stauridium can be identified by its characteristic four-armed or cruciform cell shape, which sets it apart from other dinoflagellates that typically have more rounded or elongated forms.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Stauridium plays an important role in marine food webs as both a producer through photosynthesis and as food for larger plankton and small marine animals.

children.name: Lacunastrum
children.description: Lacunastrum is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms delicate, lace-like colonies in quiet waters. These microscopic organisms create beautiful geometric patterns as their cells divide and remain connected, forming flat, perforated sheets that look almost like tiny doilies floating in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other colonial green algae, Lacunastrum forms distinctive flat colonies with regular gaps or holes (lacunae) between the cells, giving it a characteristic net-like or perforated appearance.
children.funFact: The name Lacunastrum literally means 'star with gaps,' referring to the star-like arrangement of cells around the holes in their delicate colonies.

children.name: Hydrodictyon
children.description: Water nets are fascinating freshwater green algae that form large, hollow, net-like colonies visible to the naked eye. These colonial organisms create beautiful geometric patterns that resemble fishing nets or lace floating in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most microscopic algae, water nets form distinctive large colonies with a characteristic net or mesh structure made up of cylindrical cells arranged in geometric patterns.
children.funFact: A single water net colony can grow to be several feet across, making it one of the largest structures created by single-celled organisms!

children.description: The Hydrodictyaceae are a fascinating family of freshwater green algae that form distinctive geometric colonies. These microscopic organisms arrange themselves in beautiful patterns like flat discs, hollow nets, or spiky spheres, creating some of nature's most perfectly symmetrical designs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other green algae that live as single cells, members of this family create organized colonies with cells arranged in precise geometric patterns. Each colony maintains its shape as it grows, with new cells filling in the pattern rather than breaking apart.
children.funFact: Water nets (Hydrodictyon) create hollow cylindrical nets that can grow over a foot long, earning them the nickname 'mermaid's stockings' - you might spot these delicate green mesh bags floating in quiet ponds and lakes.

children.name: Selenastraceae
Ankistrodesmus
children.description: Ankistrodesmus is a genus of tiny, single-celled green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These microscopic organisms are shaped like slender needles or crescents and often twist together in small bundles or colonies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their distinctive curved, needle-like or spindle-shaped cells that are typically pointed at both ends. Unlike many other green algae, Ankistrodesmus cells often arrange themselves in characteristic twisted or spiral patterns.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Ankistrodesmus algae are important primary producers that help form the base of freshwater food webs, providing food for tiny zooplankton and other aquatic creatures.

children.name: Kirchneriella
children.description: Kirchneriella is a genus of tiny freshwater green algae that live as single cells or in small colonies. These microscopic organisms are commonly found floating in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they help form the base of aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kirchneriella cells have a distinctive crescent or kidney shape and are often arranged in groups of 4, 8, or 16 cells held together by a thin mucilage envelope. Unlike many other green algae, they lack a rigid cell wall structure.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Kirchneriella can multiply so rapidly under the right conditions that they contribute to algal blooms that turn entire ponds green!

children.name: Monoraphidium
children.description: Monoraphidium is a genus of tiny, single-celled green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These microscopic organisms are characterized by their distinctive curved, crescent-shaped cells that often twist in a spiral pattern. They are important primary producers in aquatic ecosystems, using photosynthesis to convert sunlight into energy.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Monoraphidium are easily recognized by their elongated, curved or twisted cell shape that resembles a tiny crescent moon or banana. Unlike many other green algae, they remain as solitary cells rather than forming colonies or chains.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these tiny algae can reproduce so rapidly under favorable conditions that they can double their population in just a few hours, sometimes creating visible green blooms in water bodies.

children.name: Selenastrum
children.description: Selenastrum is a genus of tiny freshwater green algae that forms distinctive crescent or moon-shaped colonies. These microscopic organisms live in ponds, lakes, and other quiet freshwater environments where they float as part of the plankton community.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Selenastrum apart from other green algae is its characteristic curved, crescent-shaped colonial arrangement of cells, which gives it its name meaning 'moon star.'
children.funFact: The crescent shape of Selenastrum colonies helps them stay suspended in water by creating more surface area relative to their volume, making them better floaters in the plankton community.

children.name: Messastrum
children.description: Messastrum is a genus of microscopic green algae that forms distinctive star-shaped colonies in freshwater environments. These tiny organisms group together in geometric arrangements, creating beautiful crystalline patterns visible only under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae, Messastrum species arrange their cells in precise star or cross-shaped formations, with cells connected at specific angles to create their characteristic geometric appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Messastrum colonies create some of nature's most perfect geometric patterns, resembling tiny glass stars floating in pond water.

children.description: Selenastraceae is a family of microscopic green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams throughout New England. These single-celled organisms are characterized by their distinctive elongated, crescent-shaped, or needle-like cell forms that often appear curved or twisted. They play important roles in aquatic ecosystems as primary producers, converting sunlight into energy through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their unique cell shapes - ranging from slender crescents to long, thin needles - and their tendency to form loose colonies or exist as solitary cells. Unlike many other green algae, they typically lack rigid cell walls and have a more flexible cellular structure.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can rapidly change their swimming direction by flexing their crescent-shaped bodies, allowing them to navigate toward optimal light conditions in the water column.

children.name: Radiococcaceae
Palmodictyon
children.description: Palmodictyon is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive net-like or reticulated colonies. These microscopic organisms create beautiful geometric patterns as their cells arrange themselves in interconnected networks, often resembling tiny green fishnet stockings floating in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae that form simple sheets or spheres, Palmodictyon creates complex three-dimensional net structures with regular openings between the interconnected cells.
children.funFact: The name Palmodictyon literally means 'palm net,' referring to the hand-like branching pattern of their intricate colonial networks.

children.name: Planktosphaeria
children.description: Planktosphaeria is a genus of microscopic marine organisms that float freely in ocean waters as part of the plankton community. These single-celled creatures are characterized by their spherical shape and gelatinous appearance, making them look like tiny transparent bubbles drifting through the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Planktosphaeria apart is their distinctive gelatinous, sphere-like structure that gives them their name, which literally means 'floating sphere.' Unlike many other planktonic organisms, they maintain a perfectly rounded shape rather than having irregular or elongated forms.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, Planktosphaeria gelatinosa can be found floating in New England's coastal waters, where they drift with ocean currents like microscopic jellyfish made of living gel.

children.name: Coenochloris
children.description: Coenochloris is a genus of microscopic green algae that forms colonial clusters of cells held together in a gelatinous matrix. These tiny aquatic organisms are part of the diverse world of single-celled life that helps form the base of many food webs in freshwater environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae that exist as individual cells, Coenochloris species live in organized colonies where multiple cells are embedded together in a shared jelly-like substance.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, colonies of Coenochloris can contain dozens of individual cells all working together as a coordinated unit.

children.description: Radiococcaceae is a family of microscopic green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These tiny organisms are single-celled or form small colonies, and they get their energy through photosynthesis like plants do. They're an important part of the aquatic food web, serving as food for small animals and helping produce oxygen in water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their spherical or oval-shaped cells that often have distinctive cell walls with unique patterns or textures. Unlike some other green algae, they typically don't form long filaments or large, complex colonies.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these microscopic algae can sometimes turn entire ponds green when they bloom in large numbers during warm weather.

children.name: Neochloridaceae
Golenkinia
children.description: Golenkinia is a genus of microscopic green algae that lives in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These tiny organisms are single-celled and have a distinctive star-like appearance with long, thin spines radiating outward from a central cell body.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other green algae, Golenkinia cells are easily recognized by their characteristic radiating spines that give them a spiky, star-shaped appearance when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being only about 10-20 micrometers in diameter, Golenkinia's long spines can extend several times the length of the cell body, making it look like a tiny underwater sea urchin!

children.name: Chlorotetraedron
children.description: Chlorotetraedron is a genus of tiny green algae that lives in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These microscopic organisms are single-celled and get their energy through photosynthesis, just like plants do.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What makes Chlorotetraedron special is its distinctive four-sided, tetrahedral shape that looks like a tiny green pyramid when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these little algae play an important role in aquatic food webs as primary producers, forming the base of the food chain for many freshwater creatures.

children.description: Neochloridaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that live as single cells floating in ponds, lakes, and other aquatic environments. These microscopic organisms are characterized by their unique cell shapes and distinctive spines or projections that extend from their cell walls, giving them an almost star-like appearance under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their elaborate cell wall ornamentations, including spines, bristles, or geometric projections that make them easily recognizable among other green algae. Unlike many related algae, they maintain their distinctive sculptured cell walls throughout their life cycle.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, some Neochloridaceae algae have such intricate and beautiful geometric patterns on their cell walls that they look like microscopic works of art, with some species resembling tiny glass sculptures or crystalline stars.

children.name: Characiaceae
Actidesmium
children.description: Actidesmium is a small genus of slime molds that belongs to the plasmodial slime mold group. These fascinating organisms spend part of their life cycle as a mobile, blob-like plasmodium that engulfs bacteria and organic matter, then transform into stationary fruiting bodies that release spores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Actidesmium forms distinctive fruiting bodies with branched, coral-like structures called plasmodiocarps that follow the branching pattern of the original plasmodium. Unlike many other slime molds that form simple stalked sporangia, these create intricate branching networks.
children.funFact: Despite being called a 'mold,' Actidesmium is more closely related to amoebas than to fungi, and can actually crawl around like a giant single-celled organism during its feeding stage.

children.description: Characiaceae is a family of freshwater green algae that are typically microscopic and single-celled. These tiny algae are commonly found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they play an important role in aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their distinctive cell walls and unique method of reproduction through specialized spores called zoospores that can swim using whip-like flagella.
children.funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, these microscopic algae are crucial food sources for many small aquatic animals and help produce oxygen in freshwater ecosystems.

children.name: Sphaeropleaceae
Radiofilum
children.description: Radiofilum is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms delicate, thread-like filaments in ponds, streams, and other aquatic habitats. These microscopic algae are made up of cylindrical cells arranged end-to-end in unbranched chains, creating thin green strands that can sometimes be seen floating in the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Radiofilum can be distinguished from other filamentous green algae by its unique cell structure, where each cell contains a distinctive star-shaped or radiating chloroplast that gives the genus its name.
children.funFact: The name 'Radiofilum' literally means 'radiating thread,' referring to the star-like arrangement of the chloroplasts within each cell that radiate outward from the center like spokes on a wheel.

children.description: Sphaeropleaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that form long, unbranched filaments made up of cylindrical cells arranged end-to-end. These algae are found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams where they often form floating mats or attach to underwater surfaces. They reproduce through unique spores and are an important part of aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their distinctive reproductive structures called aplanospores, which are non-motile spores that develop within specialized cells. Unlike many other filamentous green algae, they have a unique cell wall composition and arrangement.
children.funFact: The single New England species in this family can form such dense floating mats in nutrient-rich waters that they were once mistaken for pond scum, but they're actually quite different from the blue-green algae that typically create true scums.

children.name: Cylindrocapsaceae
Cylindrocapsa
children.description: Cylindrocapsa is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive cylindrical colonies enclosed in transparent mucilage sheaths. These microscopic organisms consist of chains of cells arranged end-to-end within their protective gelatinous tubes, creating structures that look like tiny green sausages under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other colonial green algae, Cylindrocapsa forms strictly linear, unbranched chains of cells within well-defined cylindrical sheaths. The cells divide only in one plane, maintaining the characteristic tube-like colony structure.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, Cylindrocapsa colonies can sometimes be seen with the naked eye as tiny green threads floating in pond water, especially when they form dense populations in nutrient-rich conditions.

children.description: Cylindrocapsaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that forms simple, unbranched filaments made up of cylindrical cells arranged end-to-end. These microscopic aquatic organisms live in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They are single-celled algae that connect together to form thread-like chains visible to the naked eye.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other filamentous green algae, members of this family have distinctively cylindrical cells with thick, gelatinous walls that give the filaments a somewhat rigid, tube-like appearance.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic organisms, these algae can form long enough filaments that they sometimes create visible green masses floating in quiet waters during warm weather.

children.description: Sphaeropleales is a diverse order of green algae that includes both single-celled and colonial species found in freshwater environments throughout New England. These microscopic organisms are important primary producers in ponds, lakes, and streams, forming the base of many aquatic food webs. Many species in this group are known for their distinctive geometric arrangements, forming beautiful colonies that can be seen under a microscope.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their unique cell wall composition and reproductive structures that set them apart from other green algae. They typically reproduce through specialized spores called autospores that are released when the parent cell wall breaks open.
children.funFact: Some species in this order, like those in the family Hydrodictyaceae, form intricate net-like colonies that look like tiny underwater fishing nets, earning them the common name 'water nets.'

children.name: Chlamydomonadales
Volvocaceae
Volvox
children.description: Volvox are fascinating colonial green algae that form hollow, spherical colonies made up of hundreds to thousands of individual cells. These microscopic organisms swim through freshwater ponds and lakes by coordinating the beating of tiny whip-like structures called flagella on their surface cells. Each colony acts like a single organism, with cells working together to move toward light for photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike single-celled algae, Volvox forms large, visible spherical colonies that can be seen with the naked eye as tiny green dots in water. The colonies have a clear division of labor, with most cells handling movement and photosynthesis while specialized cells are responsible for reproduction.
children.funFact: Volvox colonies can contain their own "daughter colonies" developing inside the hollow sphere, which are eventually released to start new generations - like biological Russian nesting dolls!

children.name: Pandorina
children.description: Pandorina is a genus of colonial green algae that forms beautiful hollow spheres made up of 8-32 individual cells. These microscopic colonies swim through freshwater ponds and lakes using tiny whip-like structures called flagella, creating a coordinated swimming motion that looks like a tiny green ball rolling through the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike single-celled algae, Pandorina forms distinct spherical colonies where cells are arranged in a specific pattern and work together as a unit. The colonies are also smaller and more tightly packed than those of related colonial algae like Volvox.
children.funFact: Pandorina colonies exhibit a primitive form of teamwork - the cells on one side of the sphere have slightly longer flagella and beat more strongly, giving the colony a defined front and back as it swims.

children.name: Eudorina
children.description: Eudorina is a genus of colonial green algae that forms beautiful spherical colonies made up of 16-64 individual cells arranged in a hollow ball. These microscopic organisms swim through freshwater using coordinated beating of tiny whip-like structures called flagella. Each colony acts as a single organism, with the individual cells working together to move and eventually reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike simpler colonial algae like Volvox, Eudorina colonies are smaller and have a more loose arrangement of cells. The cells in Eudorina colonies are also more similar in size to each other, without the specialized reproductive cells that larger colonial algae possess.
children.funFact: Eudorina colonies can actually 'turn themselves inside out' during reproduction, flipping their entire spherical structure to release new daughter colonies from within!

children.description: Volvocaceae is a family of colonial green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds and lakes. These microscopic organisms form beautiful spherical colonies made up of many individual cells that work together, with some cells specializing in reproduction while others focus on movement and feeding.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike single-celled algae, Volvocaceae species form distinct multicellular colonies with organized structure and division of labor between cells. Their colonies are typically hollow spheres that can spin and roll through the water using coordinated flagella.
children.funFact: Volvox colonies can contain over 50,000 individual cells and represent one of the simplest examples of multicellular life, making them important for understanding how complex organisms evolved from single-celled ancestors.

children.name: Palmellopsidaceae
Asterococcus
children.description: Asterococcus is a genus of single-celled green algae that lives symbiotically inside other organisms, particularly lichens. These microscopic algae are photosynthetic, meaning they can make their own food using sunlight, and they share this energy with their host organisms in exchange for protection and nutrients.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike free-living algae, Asterococcus species are obligate symbionts that cannot survive on their own and must live within host organisms. They have thick cell walls and often form distinctive star-shaped colonies when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: The name 'Asterococcus' literally means 'star berry,' referring to the star-like arrangement of cells that these algae often form within their lichen hosts.

children.name: Chlamydocapsa
children.description: Chlamydocapsa is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive colonies enclosed in thick, gelatinous sheaths. These microscopic organisms live in quiet waters like ponds and slow-moving streams, where they create small, mucilaginous masses that can sometimes be seen floating near the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other colonial green algae, Chlamydocapsa cells are surrounded by particularly thick, layered mucilaginous envelopes that give the colonies their characteristic jelly-like appearance and protection.
children.funFact: The name 'Chlamydocapsa' literally means 'cloaked box,' referring to the protective gelatinous envelope that surrounds each cell like a transparent coat of armor.

children.description: Palmellopsidaceae is a small family of green algae that form distinctive colonies embedded in mucilaginous (jelly-like) sheaths. These microscopic algae are typically found in freshwater environments where they create small, gelatinous masses that can sometimes be seen with the naked eye.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their cells being surrounded by thick, gelatinous envelopes that give their colonies a distinctly slimy, mucilaginous appearance. Unlike many other green algae, they form well-organized colonial structures rather than existing as individual cells.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic organisms, colonies of Palmellopsidaceae can sometimes form visible gelatinous blobs in ponds and streams that feel slippery to the touch!

children.name: Haematococcaceae
Stephanosphaera
children.description: Stephanosphaera is a unique genus of green algae that forms distinctive hollow spherical colonies made up of individual cells arranged in a crown-like pattern. These microscopic organisms live in freshwater environments and are part of the diverse world of colonial algae that bridge the gap between single-celled and multicellular life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae, Stephanosphaera cells are arranged in a single ring or crown around the equator of a hollow sphere, giving it a very distinctive geometric appearance when viewed under a microscope.
children.funFact: Stephanosphaera colonies can break apart and reform, and individual cells can even escape their colony to live independently before potentially forming new colonies later.

children.name: Chlorogonium
children.description: Chlorogonium is a genus of single-celled green algae that are characterized by their elongated, spindle-shaped cells and ability to swim using two whip-like flagella. These microscopic organisms contain chloroplasts that give them their green color and allow them to make their own food through photosynthesis. They are commonly found in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, Chlorogonium cells have a distinctly elongated, torpedo-like shape rather than being round or oval. They also retain their ability to swim throughout their life cycle, unlike some related algae that lose their flagella as they mature.
children.funFact: Chlorogonium can perform a neat trick called phototaxis - they can actually swim toward or away from light sources depending on the light intensity, helping them find the perfect spot for photosynthesis.

children.description: Haematococcaceae is a family of single-celled green algae that are masters of transformation. These microscopic organisms can dramatically change their appearance and color depending on environmental conditions, often shifting from green to bright red or orange when stressed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other green algae, members of this family are known for their ability to produce large amounts of red pigments called carotenoids, which can completely mask their green chlorophyll and give them vivid red coloration.
children.funFact: Some species in this family are the source of astaxanthin, a powerful red antioxidant that's responsible for the pink color in flamingos and salmon when they eat these algae!

children.name: Chlorococcaceae
Oophila
children.description: Oophila is a unique genus of green algae that has formed an extraordinary partnership with spotted salamanders. These tiny algae actually live inside salamander eggs, creating one of nature's most remarkable symbiotic relationships between a plant and an animal.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other green algae that live freely in water or soil, Oophila species are the only algae known to live inside vertebrate eggs and tissues.
children.funFact: Salamander eggs containing Oophila algae develop faster and have higher survival rates because the algae provide oxygen to the developing embryos while feeding on the eggs' waste products.

children.description: Chlorococcaceae is a family of single-celled green algae that live in aquatic environments. These microscopic organisms are typically spherical or oval-shaped and contain chloroplasts that help them photosynthesize, turning sunlight into energy just like plants do.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their simple, non-motile cells that reproduce through the formation of multiple daughter cells within the parent cell wall. Unlike many other green algae, they don't have flagella for swimming.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like Oophila, have the remarkable ability to live inside the eggs of amphibians like salamanders, forming a beneficial partnership where the algae provides oxygen to the developing embryo.

children.name: Goniaceae
Gonium
children.description: Gonium is a genus of colonial green algae that forms flat, plate-like colonies of cells arranged in a distinctive geometric pattern. Each colony consists of 4 to 32 individual cells that are connected together and work as a coordinated unit, swimming through freshwater environments using tiny whip-like structures called flagella.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike single-celled green algae, Gonium forms flat, disc-shaped colonies where cells are arranged in a precise geometric pattern, typically as a hollow square or rectangular formation.
children.funFact: Gonium colonies swim in a coordinated fashion, with all the flagella beating in unison to propel the entire flat colony through the water like a tiny living frisbee.

children.description: Goniaceae is a family of microscopic green algae that live in freshwater environments like ponds and lakes. These tiny organisms are colonial, meaning individual cells stick together to form flat, plate-like structures that look like miniature green pancakes floating in the water. Each colony is made up of 4, 8, 16, or 32 identical cells arranged in a precise geometric pattern.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae that form spherical or chain-like colonies, Goniaceae members create distinctive flat, plate-shaped colonies where all cells lie in the same plane. Each cell in the colony has two flagella (whip-like structures) that beat in coordination to help the entire colony swim through the water.
children.funFact: The genus name 'Gonium' comes from the Greek word meaning 'angle' or 'corner,' referring to the geometric arrangement of cells that creates distinct angles and patterns within each tiny floating colony.

children.name: Chlamydomonadaceae
Chlamydomonas
children.description: Chlamydomonas is a genus of single-celled green algae that swim through water using two whip-like structures called flagella. These microscopic organisms are found in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and even snow, where they photosynthesize like plants to make their own food. Each cell has a distinctive cup-shaped chloroplast that gives it a bright green color.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other single-celled algae, Chlamydomonas cells are highly mobile swimmers with two prominent flagella that beat in a coordinated pattern. They also have a distinctive eyespot that helps them detect and move toward light sources.
children.funFact: The watermelon snow species can turn entire snowfields pink or red in alpine and polar regions, creating a striking natural phenomenon that early explorers thought was caused by minerals or atmospheric conditions.

children.description: Chlamydomonadaceae is a family of single-celled green algae that are commonly found in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams. These microscopic organisms are characterized by their ability to swim using two whip-like structures called flagella, and they contain chloroplasts that allow them to photosynthesize like plants.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are distinguished by their oval or egg-shaped cells with two equal-length flagella at the front end, and they typically have a prominent eyespot that helps them detect light.
children.funFact: Some species in this family can switch between being plant-like (photosynthetic) and animal-like (consuming other organisms) depending on environmental conditions, making them fascinating examples of life's versatility.

children.name: Tetrabaenaceae
Tetrabaena
children.description: Tetrabaena is a genus of colonial green algae that forms small, spherical colonies made up of exactly four cells. These microscopic freshwater organisms are photosynthetic, meaning they make their own food using sunlight, and represent an important step in the evolution from single-celled to multicellular life.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their single-celled relatives, Tetrabaena cells are permanently joined together in groups of four within a gelatinous sphere. This sets them apart from both solitary green algae and larger colonial forms like Volvox that contain hundreds of cells.
children.funFact: Tetrabaena colonies are so small that dozens could fit on the period at the end of this sentence, yet they represent one of the simplest examples of true multicellular cooperation in nature.

children.description: Tetrabaenaceae is a small family of freshwater green algae that forms simple colonies of exactly four cells arranged in a flat, square pattern. These microscopic organisms live in ponds, lakes, and other quiet freshwater environments throughout New England. Each cell in the colony is surrounded by a gelatinous sheath and can swim using tiny whip-like structures called flagella.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other colonial green algae that form spherical or irregular clusters, members of Tetrabaenaceae always arrange themselves in a precise four-cell square formation. This consistent geometric pattern makes them easily recognizable under a microscope.
children.funFact: Despite being microscopic, these algae are perfectly organized architects - they maintain their tidy four-cell square arrangement throughout their entire life cycle, never adding or losing cells from their geometric colony.

children.description: Chlamydomonadales are an order of green algae that includes both single-celled swimmers and colonial forms that live together in organized groups. These tiny organisms are found in freshwater environments like ponds, lakes, and streams throughout New England. Many have whip-like tails called flagella that help them move through the water toward light sources.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other algae, members of this order typically have two flagella for swimming and often possess a distinctive red eyespot that helps them detect light. They can exist as solitary cells or form beautiful spherical colonies of hundreds or thousands of individuals working together.
children.funFact: The famous Volvox colonies in this order demonstrate a simple form of multicellular cooperation, where some cells specialize in reproduction while others focus on swimming - an early example of cellular teamwork in the tree of life!

children.name: Chaetophorales
Chaetophoraceae
Chaetophora
children.description: Chaetophora is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms distinctive branched, gelatinous colonies in ponds, streams, and other aquatic environments. These colonial algae create soft, jelly-like masses that can range from small lumps to larger cushion-shaped formations attached to rocks, logs, or other underwater surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chaetophora colonies are characterized by their branching filaments embedded in a thick, gelatinous matrix, giving them a unique cushion-like or brain-like appearance that distinguishes them from other colonial algae.
children.funFact: Some Chaetophora colonies can grow large enough to resemble underwater brains or sponges, and they often feel surprisingly firm and rubbery when touched despite being made mostly of water and microscopic algae cells.

children.name: Draparnaldia
children.description: Draparnaldia is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms delicate, branched filaments resembling tiny underwater ferns. These algae create beautiful, feathery colonies that attach to rocks, logs, and other surfaces in cool, clean streams and ponds throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike simpler unbranched algae, Draparnaldia has a distinctive branching pattern with a main axis and smaller side branches that give it a feathery appearance. The branches are made up of different sized cells, with larger cells forming the main stem and smaller cells creating the delicate side branches.
children.funFact: Draparnaldia is often called 'water silk' because its soft, silky texture feels remarkably smooth when you run it through your fingers underwater.

children.name: Stigeoclonium
children.description: Stigeoclonium is a genus of freshwater green algae that forms branching, thread-like structures in streams, ponds, and other aquatic environments. These microscopic algae create delicate, feathery colonies that can often be seen as green, silky masses attached to rocks, plants, or other underwater surfaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other filamentous green algae, Stigeoclonium species have distinctively branched filaments that taper toward their tips, giving them a tree-like or feathery appearance under magnification.
children.funFact: Stigeoclonium algae are excellent indicators of water quality - they typically thrive in clean, well-oxygenated water, so finding them in a stream is often a good sign of healthy aquatic conditions.

children.description: Chaetophoraceae is a family of freshwater green algae that forms branching, filamentous structures in streams, ponds, and other aquatic environments. These algae create distinctive tree-like or feathery colonies that can be seen attached to rocks, wood, or other underwater surfaces. They are important primary producers in freshwater ecosystems, converting sunlight into energy through photosynthesis.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family are characterized by their highly branched filamentous growth pattern, with main axes that give rise to progressively smaller side branches. Unlike simpler unbranched filamentous algae, they form complex, often gelatinous colonies with a distinctive branching architecture.
